[[notes: This dedication is to Johann Adolf (1575-1616), Duke of Holstein-Gottorp. He was the Prince-Bishop of Lübeck, a semi-independent ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire. His titles reflect his extensive territorial claims and influence. The claim as 'Heir of Norway' refers to the historical lineage of his house, which had a claim to the Norwegian throne. 'Stormarn' and 'Dithmarschen' are historical regions in what is now northern Germany, within the larger duchy of Holstein.]]

Indeed, the art of medicine owes very much to our age, MOST EXCELLENT PRINCE, yet in this very era, the [[notes: Paracelsus (1493/94-1541) was a Swiss physician, alchemist, and philosopher whose radical medical system challenged traditional Galenic medicine. His followers, the 'Paracelsians', advocated for chemical remedies and a more mystical approach to healing, which was highly controversial and often viewed by traditionalists as a dangerous departure from established medical science.]] has severely afflicted it. Just as, indeed, in the fable of [[notes: Glaucus was a Greek sea-god, originally a mortal fisherman who transformed into a marine deity after eating a magical herb. The myth often describes him as having a fish-like lower body, sometimes mangled or disfigured, symbolizing a transformation that is not entirely positive. The author uses this imagery to vividly describe the fragmentation and corruption of medicine.]] the sea-god, in a shipwreck, some parts were bruised, some broken, some completely torn off and carried away by the waves, while against this, seaweed, shells, and whatever other marine debris clung to his mangled corpse: so too, the knowledge of our body acquired through greed, and indeed the entire method of healing, established from [[notes: 'Indicantibus et indicata' refers to medical signs (symptoms, indications) and the things indicated by them (diagnoses, treatments). It's a technical term in classical medicine referring to the systematic process of diagnosis and therapy based on observable signs. The author implies that this systematic and rational approach has been perverted or torn away.]] – completely torn away from the Art itself, the doctrine of diseases and health, as well as genuine [[notes: 'Pharmaceutice' refers to pharmacy, the preparation and dispensing of medicines according to scientific principles. The author laments its corruption.]] have been so broken, so bruised, that nothing of their original color remains; On the contrary, magic, divinatory astrology, [[notes: This Greek term, 'χειροποκινὴ' (cheiropokinē), is likely a variant or misspelling of a word related to manual deception or artificiality. Given the context of magic and charlatanism, it can be interpreted as 'sleight of hand' or 'charlatanic handiwork'—skills used for trickery rather than genuine art.]] charlatanic handiwork, [[notes: 'Ἐνθυσασμοὶ' (enthusiasmoi) is a Greek word meaning 'inspirations' or 'divine frenzies'. In a negative context, as here, it refers to deluded or false spiritual ecstasies, fanaticism, and ungrounded pronouncements, often associated with claims of supernatural insight or prophecy.]] deluded inspirations, a fictitious way of speaking and writing, and a certain new religion with the foulest slander and the most vain display of secrets, have occupied its innermost recesses.

<meta>This page continues the formal dedication to Johann Adolf, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp (1575–1616). The author uses classical metaphors to describe how traditional, Galenic medicine has been "disfigured" by modern mystical and alchemical practices.</meta>

## To the Most Reverend, Most Illustrious, and Most Serene Prince
# ->JOHN<-
### Elected Bishop of Lübeck,
### Heir of Norway,
### Duke of Holstein, Stormarn, and Dithmarschen,
### Count of Oldenburg and Delmenhorst.

<image-desc>An ornate decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

The medical art truly owes much to our century, **MOST EXCELLENT PRINCE**, yet in this very season, the school of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), was a radical physician who rejected traditional Greek medicine in favor of "chemical" and mystical cures.</note> has violently afflicted it. Just as, surely, the story goes that the sea-god Glaucus <note>The author is likely referencing a famous passage in Plato’s *Republic*, where the soul is compared to the sea-god Glaucus: his original form is unrecognizable because his limbs have been broken by waves and covered in seaweed and shells.</note> in a shipwreck had some parts bruised, some broken, some entirely severed and swept away by the waves, while seaweed, shells, and whatever other sea-rubbish there is clung to his mangled body: so too that knowledge of our body acquired through <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: ἀνατομὴν (anatomēn); the practice of dissection to understand the internal structure of the body, which was the foundation of traditional medical learning.</note>, and indeed the entire method of healing established upon symptoms and indications, has been completely torn away from the Art. The doctrine of diseases and health, as well as true pharmacology, have been so broken and so bruised that nothing of their original character remains. In their place, Magic, divining astrology, <term>alchemy</term> <note>original: χρυσοποιητικὴ (chrysopoiētikē); literally the "gold-making art."</note>, <term>divine inspirations</term> <note>original: ἐνθουσιασμοὶ (enthousiasmoi); the belief in being possessed or enlightened by a divine spirit rather than relying on rational study.</note>, a deceitful way of speaking and writing, and a certain "new religion" coupled with the most foul slander and the vainest display of "secrets," [occupy] its innermost depths...

<sig>(:) 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: occu-</meta>

<summary>In this dedication, the author laments the "disfiguration" of traditional medicine, comparing its current state under the influence of Paracelsus to the mangled body of the sea-god Glaucus. He argues that rational science and anatomy have been replaced by mysticism, alchemy, and "secret" displays of vanity.</summary>

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to John, Elect Bishop of Lübeck. The author transitions from describing the "disfigurement" of medicine to identifying the causes of its decline: the greed of Paracelsus's followers and the desperate credulity of the public.</meta>

...they occupied. And indeed, this evil has spread to such an extent that in many places the old and true **Art of Healing** <term>medendi Ars</term> <note>The traditional medical system based on Galen and Hippocrates, which prioritized balance in the body's humors.</note> has survived as nothing more than that "image of Glaucus" <note>Referring to the previous page's metaphor of the sea-god Glaucus, whose body became so encrusted with weeds and shells that he no longer looked human. The author argues medicine has become unrecognizable.</note>; even as the best and most learned men labor in vain for its restoration.

I believe the cause of such a pitiable shipwreck has been, beyond other things, not so much the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus, who advocated for chemical medicines (iatrochemistry) over traditional herbal and humoral treatments.</note> themselves as the too-easy credulity of the common people, who expect a cure for every single disease and gape at any lure of gold. For indeed, you may see the followers of Paracelsus led by the greatest desire for profit; and when that hope fails them, they attempt nothing new but instead promise the same old things under "changed sails" <note>original: *mutatis velis*. A nautical metaphor for changing tactics or disguising one's true intentions to deceive.</note>. 

Truly, I believe that if the people had denied the sect their expected profit, the whole movement would have perished long ago; just as we see it failing everywhere now, losing the tyranny it had once seized. For although an innate madness holds all the sick—even those decrepit with age—to expect a cure for absolutely every disease, they listen with a most willing ear to the Paracelsians who promise such great things, and they do not easily tolerate anyone who opposes that hope. 

Furthermore, not only the greedy, but also the wasteful and the ambitious are captured by the lust for amassing wealth; and thus the **art of making gold** <note>Alchemy, specifically the search for the Philosopher's Stone to transmute base metals into gold.</note> boasted by the Paracelsians flatters all these people more than words can say. Nevertheless, through infinite losses...

<summary>The author blames the rise of Paracelsian medicine on the public's desperate desire for universal cures and the alchemical promise of creating gold, which allowed "deceptive" practitioners to profit.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, medical ethics, alchemy, credulity, history of medicine, Glaucus metaphor, gold-making</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication to John, Elect Bishop of Lübeck. The previous page ended with the observation that people were beginning to turn away from the "tyranny" of the Paracelsian sect as their promises of universal cures failed to materialize.</meta>

<sig>(:) 3</sig>

...those who, having been more correctly instructed, offer their ears far less easily to the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the controversial physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who rejected traditional medicine in favor of chemical remedies.</note> than before; certainly, they now comply with the desires of those men with a less ready hand. If everyone continues to act in this way, it will soon be all over for that sect, and those who find it convenient may go and attend its funeral. 

It would not have been necessary, however, to arrive at this repentance only after such great labors, and to buy this wisdom at such enormous expense; if only, setting aside their passions, it had pleased them even slightly to take counsel with **reason** before all else. To do this before you attempt any great work is, after all, a law of **prudence** <term>prudentia</term> <note>In this context, *prudentia* refers to practical wisdom and the ability to judge the truth of a claim based on evidence and logic.</note> born within us. 

Indeed, it is plain for all to see that the Paracelsians themselves—as many as there are—just like Paracelsus himself, are both afflicted by various diseases and often perish from premature death. They likewise mourn both the illnesses and the deaths of their own kin. Who, therefore, would not immediately conclude from this that the things they tell of the "miracles" of their art and the "stupendous virtues" of their remedies are the rotten lies of **charlatans** <term>agyrtæ</term> <note>original: *agyrtarum*. A Greek-derived term for itinerant quacks or street performers who sold fraudulent medicines.</note>? 

For this reason, one must beware of their promises as one would the vain displays of lying men; certainly, one should not "play finger-flashing in the dark" <note>original: *micandum in tenebris*. A Roman proverb referring to a game of chance (*morra*) played in the dark; it implies dealing with someone so untrustworthy that you cannot even see their hands to ensure they aren't cheating.</note> with such people. Furthermore, who could tolerate someone promising skill in an art when he has never experienced its use, has not learned its principles through demonstrations, and has not received knowledge of it from heaven? But—

...would have performed. My duty in my <term>professorial office <note>The author refers to his formal role as a university teacher, which carries a responsibility to guide and protect his students.</note></term> has more than once reminded me to benefit the studies of <term>beginners <note>original Latin: 'tyronum'. These are young students or newcomers to the medical and philosophical arts.</note></term> in this area as well; however, it is only now that my many other occupations have finally permitted me to attend to it. At the same time, it seemed that I would be doing something worthwhile if I were to strip away that **mask**—by which it commonly wins a reputation for antiquity—from <term>Paracelsian medicine <note>A system of medicine based on the theories of Paracelsus (1493–1541), which often favored chemical and mineral remedies over traditional herbal ones.</note></term> and all its doctrine, and indeed from **chemistry**. This is the claim that it already began in **Egypt** in a former age, with <term>Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many ancient alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note></term> as its author.

For I see that until now, no one has attempted this; on the contrary, it is confirmed everywhere as if by a consensus of the "better" and more learned men. Furthermore, I have noticed that today, among most people, the fame of **Egyptian** and **Hermetic** wisdom is held in higher esteem than it ever deserved. This situation is also joined by no small cost to both the truth and to accepted doctrine; for from this, both malice and ignorance take a pretext for innovating and disturbing everything. Therefore, since the opportunity arose, I decided to point out this error publicly, and at least in some way to preserve the original security of our discipline, both medical and philosophical.

But whether the outcome will answer to my efforts, others may judge more correctly. You indeed, **MOST NOBLE PRINCE**, as you are free <note>The text on this page ends with the syllable "va-" and the catchword is "cuus," completing the word 'vacuus' (meaning free, empty, or at leisure).</note> from the cares of the state during your leisure...

<summary>The author explains his motivation for writing this critique: to fulfill his academic duty by debunking the false historical claims that link Paracelsian chemistry to ancient Egyptian or Hermetic wisdom. He argues that this false antiquity is being used as a dangerous pretext to overturn established medical and philosophical truths.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dedication from the previous page, where the author was discussing the failures of alchemical "gold-making." Here, Hermann Conring addresses his patron directly, appealing to the patron's expertise in mathematics and chemistry to validate his critique of Paracelsian medicine.</meta>

...I ask you again and again that you might be willing to take upon yourself the task of judging these works. For you possess such excellent skill in all arts—especially the mathematical sciences—that you have made the art of logical demonstration second nature to yourself. Equipped with this skill, a person is at last a truly capable judge of any sound teaching. You have also made such great progress in chemical experiments <note>original: "Chemicis exercitiis"</note> that it will be quite easy for you to decide whether the arguments I have set forth at length against the followers of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), was a Swiss physician and alchemist. His followers, the "Paracelsics," often combined mysticism with chemistry, a practice Conring frequently criticized.</note>—concerning the preparation of remedies and the proper use of medicines so prepared—are consistent with the truth or not. 

Indeed, if you approve of my view, it will gain great authority, and I may perhaps be able to safely disregard the petty chatter of those who disagree. But if you do not, I know that because of your great spirit and truly noble character, you will not reject my efforts, but will grant pardon to one who so confidently appeals to the fairness of your judgment. For my part, I pray to God that He may long preserve Your Highness <note>original: "Celsitud. Tuam"</note> for the benefit of the state. 

From the Julia Academy <note>The Academia Julia, or the University of Helmstedt, was a major Protestant university in the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, active from 1576 to 1810.</note> at Helmstedt, August 1, 1648 <note>original: "CIƆ. IƆ. C. XLIIX. Kalendis Sextilibus"</note>.

->To Your Highness,<-
->*your most devoted client,*<-
->**H. CONRING**<-

<meta>This page begins the main text of Hermann Conring’s treatise. It follows the dedication to his patron, transitioning from a personal appeal to a historical and critical investigation of medical sects. Conring is introducing his primary argument: that the "new" chemical medicine of the followers of Paracelsus is wrongly claiming the prestige of the "ancient" Egyptian Hermetic tradition.</meta>

HERMANN CONRING’S
<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: pro-</meta>

# ON THE ANCIENT EGYPTIAN AND THE NEW
## PARACELSIAN HERMETIC MEDICINE.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->*The sect of Paracelsus adopts the name of "Hermetics"; it must be investigated by what right they do so.*<-

Today, the fame of the "Hermetic" <term>Hermetic (from Hermes Trismegistus)</term> sect of physicians is celebrated and known even to the common people. For as many as follow in the footsteps of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often in opposition to traditional Galenic medicine.</note>—whether they are ashamed of their master, or they seek to win approval for a doctrine suspected of being a "new-fangled" invention by cloaking it in antiquity, or finally, because they have actually convinced themselves that the core beliefs of their school truly come from the author Hermes—they certainly prefer to be called "Hermetics" rather than "Paracelsians." 

Whether they do this rightfully or wrongly will soon be made clear. However, they are not using an unwise strategy. For indeed, one would hardly say that most of what Paracelsus wrote belongs to a sane man. Nor will it seem reasonable to anyone that medicine first burst forth from the head of Paracelsus alone—just as the goddess Pallas Athena <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom, who was said to have been born fully grown and armored from the forehead of Zeus (Jove).</note> was born from the brain of Jove in the Greek myths—and that all the mortals who preceded him were mere "mushrooms" or "blockheads" <note>original: "fungos fuisse aut stipites" — a Latin idiom used to describe people who are dull-witted or useless.</note>; yet this is something Paracelsus was not ashamed to boast. 

The name of Hermes (or Mercury), however, has truly been venerable since ancient times. This is true not only among the Egyptians, but by the clear consensus of many nations—especially the Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans—he was counted among the order of the gods. Consequently, it adds much to the recommendation of any matter, however new, to claim it proceeds from such a great author—

<summary>Hermann Conring begins his critique by noting that followers of Paracelsus prefer the title "Hermetic" to gain historical legitimacy. He contrasts the perceived madness of Paracelsus's original claims with the ancient, divine prestige associated with Hermes Trismegistus.</summary>
<keywords>Hermann Conring, Paracelsus, Hermes Trismegistus, Hermetic Medicine, Ancient Egypt, Medical Sects, Mercury</keywords>

...be considered progress. ## CHAPTER II.

### *That neither the Greeks, nor the Phoenicians, nor the Egyptians formerly attributed the invention of any medical art to Hermes.*

Therefore, I now place beyond controversy that this Hermes is the one whom the Romans once called Mercury, the Phoenicians Taautus, the Egyptians Thoth <note>original: θωὺθ</note>, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks Hermes <note>original: ἑρμὴν</note> (to use almost the very words of Philo of Byblos <note>A Phoenician historian (c. 64–141 AD) who wrote a history of Phoenicia, claiming to translate the works of the ancient priest Sanchuniathon.</note>). For although others may feel differently about this matter, I prefer today to believe it even without argument; both because whatever might be more consistent with the truth contributes nothing to my purpose, and because all of this is so uncertain that it is better to leave these things undecided than to lean one's opinion toward either side. Indeed, our purpose is sufficiently served if we determine whether he who was once considered Hermes <note>original: ἑρμῆς</note> or Mercury by common consent among the Greeks, Romans, Phoenicians, and especially the Egyptians, [contributed] anything to the medical art...

We believe it is clearly evident that nothing pertaining to medicine was received or brought from the Phoenicians by Taautus <note>Also known as Thoth or Hermes; the author uses the Phoenician name Taautus here</note>, but rather it came from the nephews of his uncle Sydycus—or perhaps specifically from one, Asclepius <note>The Greek god of healing, here integrated into a Phoenician genealogy</note>. Indeed, to that Sydycus, besides seven sons called the Cabiri or Corybantes <note>Deities or priests of ancient mystery cults, often associated with metalworking and protection</note>, an eighth son, Asclepius, was born of one of the seven Titanide sisters whom Saturn had fathered by Astarte (or Ashtoreth). To these sisters, Taautus communicated the sacred rites. All these things are recorded in those legendary records. Therefore, not even according to the Phoenician myths did Taautus or Hermes contribute anything to the art of medicine. Truly, this could not have escaped the notice of Sanchuniathon <note>A semi-mythical Phoenician author whose works were said to have been translated into Greek by Philo of Byblos</note>, since Philo praised him in this manner:

<margin>Eusebius, Book 1, Chapter 9</margin>
> *Sanchuniathon, a man of great learning, having devoted his efforts to the study of many matters and desiring intensely to know the history of all nations from the very first constitution of the universe, applied a certain special diligence in investigating the affairs of Taautus. He did so because he understood well enough that Taautus was the foremost of all under the sun to discover letters and begin the writing of books.*

Furthermore, that same Philo testified that Sanchuniathon had examined all the secret scrolls of the Ammoneans <note>Likely referring to the Egyptian priests or the inhabitants of the Oasis of Siwa, known for the temple of Ammon</note>. Who would believe that any of Taautus's deeds could have remained hidden from someone searching with such diligence into the sacred records of the Phoenicians?

Let us, therefore, proceed finally to the Egyptians. Indeed, it is believed today that the school of medicine which Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), who championed "spagyric" or chemical medicine</note> revived originated from the Egyptian Hermes. For this reason, even now that she has been raised to immortality, she takes great joy in the healing of men; and if anyone seeks help in their dreams, she manifests her divine presence and shows a ready ability to do good for those in need. Many who were even despaired of by physicians because of the difficulty of their disease receive health from her; and many who were completely blind <note>original: "oculis prorsus captos"</note> or mutilated in another part of the body, if they flee to the help of this Goddess, are restored to the integrity of their former vigor. For Galen <note>A Greek physician whose views dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, in *book 6 of On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, writes thus regarding Pamphilus the Botanist: <note>original Greek: "Βοτάνης μέμνηται, ὡς αὐτός φησιν, ἀετοῦ· περὶ ἧς ὁμολογεῖ μηδένα τῶν Ἑλλήνων εἰρηκέναι μηδὲν, ἀλλὰ ἔν τινι τῶν εἰς Ἑρμῆν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον ἀναφερομένων βιβλίων ἐγγράφθαι, περιέχοντι τὰς λϛ τῶν ὡροσκόπων βοτάνας."</note> *He mentions a plant, as he himself says, the Eagle-plant; concerning which he confesses that none of the Greeks have said anything, but that it stands recorded in a certain book among those attributed to the Egyptian Hermes, containing the thirty-six plants of the horoscopes.* <note>The "36 plants of the horoscopes" refers to an astrological medical system where specific plants were governed by the 36 "decans" or segments of the zodiac.</note> Clement himself also, in the sixth book of his *Stromata* <note>The title means "Miscellanies."</note>, where he recounted the ceremonies solemnized by Egyptian priests in a certain procession, adds these details, as indeed Gentianus Hervet <note>A 16th-century French scholar and translator.</note> has translated them: *“There are therefore forty-two books of Mercury which are highly necessary. The remaining six are studied by the <term>pastophori</term> <note>original: "οἱ παστοφόροι"; a class of Egyptian priests who carried the sacred shrines or images in processions.</note>, as they pertain to medicine—namely, on the construction of the body, on diseases, on instruments, on medicines, on the eyes, and finally on women.”* 

Therefore, at that time, there were displayed among the sacred rites of the Egyptians these books of Hermes: one on the subject of anatomy, one on what I interpret to be internal diseases, one on perhaps surgical instruments, one on medicines (in which perhaps a vast collection of remedies was handed down), one on diseases of the eyes, and finally one on the afflictions of women. ## CHAPTER III.

### That Chemistry was attributed by the first practitioners not to Hermes, but to other inventors; and further, that Chemistry itself is not a very ancient thing.

If, however, there was no Hermetic medicine in the past, it clearly appears ridiculous that certain people now assign this name to the doctrine of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), was a radical physician who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often claiming a lineage of secret ancient wisdom.</note> and trace back to that author a medical art which he did not actually cultivate in ancient times. Nevertheless, they still have a claim to make: namely, that Hermes was surely the inventor of Chemistry, and therefore the "Chemical Medicine" currently in circulation is rightly attributed to him. 

Truly, even if we were to grant that Chemistry came from Hermes Trismegistus, who among the ancients ever mentioned *chemical medicine*? Certainly, not even a trace of it appears in the ancient records. Indeed, under the name of "Chemia" (for so I speak, not "Chymia," following the example of all the Greek chemists who are the most ancient in this field) <note>Renaissance scholars debated the spelling of the word; "Chemia" was thought to link the art to "Khem" (the ancient name for Egypt), whereas "Chymia" suggested a Greek root meaning "juices" or "infusions."</note>—under the name of "Chemia," I say—you would hardly read that anything else was signified in the past than the **art of gold-making** <note>original Greek: χρυσοποιητικὴν (chrysopoiētikēn)</note> or indeed that **transformation** <note>original Greek: μετασχηματισμὸν (metaschēmatismon)</note> which promises the changing of cheaper metals and stones into something better. 

One cannot even read that the first professors of chemistry spent any effort on preparing medicines; they were so far from establishing an entire sect of the medical art. To be sure, it was only after Chemistry began to be cultivated among the Arabs <note>This refers to the "Islamic Golden Age" (roughly 8th–14th centuries), during which scholars like Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) and Al-Razi (Rhazes) significantly advanced the techniques of distillation and alchemy.</note> that several remedies for diseases were worked out in the chemical manner...

...were worked out; and yet even then the name of chemical medicine had not been heard. We shall demonstrate this more fully below.

Since these matters are indeed so, we may deservedly leave this point. However, so that the truth may be protected in every respect, we shall also demonstrate regarding Chemistry itself—that <term>venerable art<note>original Greek: $τ\tilde{\eta}\ \sigma\epsilon\beta\alpha\sigma\mu\tilde{\eta}$ (tē sebasmē), meaning venerable or august.</note></term>—that it is by no means owed to Hermes as its author, even though we admit it was first born and raised in Egypt. In the first place, we believe this is manifest from this one fact: although the ancient Egyptians said many things in praise of their Hermes and attributed many things to him as the inventor, nevertheless, among those praises and those inventions, no mention of chemistry occurs. Who would have omitted so great a benefit—they who were so diligent in extolling and worshipping that divinity? Indeed, they who valued Chemistry so highly that they boasted of it as the <term>sacred and great art<note>original Greek: $ἱ\epsilon\rho\tilde{\alpha}\varsigma\ καὶ\ μεγάλ\η\varsigma\ τέ\chi\nu\η\varsigma$ (hieras kai megalēs technēs).</note></term> and called its practitioners by the name of "philosophers." Yet, it is already clear from what was brought forward a little earlier that in the ancient eulogies of Hermes, there was a deep silence concerning chemistry.

The same point is confirmed by the most ancient monuments of the Egyptians themselves, in which they reveal anything concerning the origin of chemistry. For although they do not agree among themselves, they nevertheless praise authors of the art who are very different from Hermes. There exists among those works circulated today under the name of Hermes a small book titled *Minerva Mundi* <note>Latin: *Minerva Mundi* (Minerva of the World), also known by the Greek title *Kore Kosmou* ("The Virgin of the World"), a significant Hermetic text preserved by Stobaeus.</note>, described by Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved many fragments of ancient literature that would otherwise be lost.</note>, which is truly full of ancient Egyptian wisdom. There, it was handed down by Isis that the souls of men behave differently according to the position of the places from which they are sent into bodies; and hence some souls are "royal" because they fell from the royal zone, and these are superior either in their souls, or their bodies, or their arts...

“O woman, <note>Addressing Theosebeia, a female student of Zosimus to whom he addressed many of his alchemical writings.</note> know that there is a certain race of demons that makes use of women. Hermes also mentioned this in his *Physics* <note>original: "ἐν τοῖς Φυσικοῖς" (en tois Physikois); likely referring to a lost Hermetic work on nature</note>; and almost every doctrine, both manifest and secret <note>original: "ἀπόκρυφος" (apokryphos)</note>, has mentioned this. So the ancient and divine scriptures said that angels lusted after women, and descending, they taught them all the works of Nature. Because of this, they were cast out and remained outside of heaven, because they taught men all things that are evil and which in no way benefit the soul. From these same beings, those same scriptures say that the Giants were born. Thus, their first tradition regarding these arts is called *Chema* <note>original: "ΧΗΜΑ͂"</note>; and they called this book *Chema*. From this, the art itself is called Chemistry <note>original: "ΧΗΜΙΑ" (Chemia)</note>.” *The sacred scriptures or books say, O woman, that there is a certain race of demons that makes use of women. Hermes also mentions this in his Physics: and almost every doctrine, both manifest and secret, records it. Therefore the ancients and divine scripture say: that angels lusted after women, and arriving, taught them all the works of nature. Having caused offense by this, they remained outside of heaven, because they had taught men all evil things, and those which do not help the soul. From them, the same scriptures tell that the Giants were born. Therefore, their first tradition concerning these arts is Chema. Moreover, they called that book Chema. From this, the art of Chemistry itself is named.* These are the words of Zosimus.

From these words, it is clear that this Egyptian from Panopolis <note>Zosimus of Panopolis was a prominent Greco-Egyptian alchemist and mystic who lived around the late 3rd and early 4th centuries AD.</note>—a chemist as ancient as he is great—did not attribute the origin of the art to Hermes, but to evil spirits. Indeed, he attributes it to those who are believed to be meant by the holiest Moses under the name "sons of God" in <term>Genesis 6:2</term> <note>This biblical passage describes the "sons of God" taking the "daughters of men" as wives, a passage traditionally linked to the origin of forbidden knowledge.</note>. And truly, Zosimus is so far from wanting this art to have come to Hermes from the Angels, that he clearly pronounces that the female sex was taught it first of all by their impure demon lovers. Perhaps the story went that the art came down to <term>Imuth</term> <note>original: "Ἰμΰθ"; a name often appearing in Zosimus's texts, sometimes identified with a specific woman or a personification of the art itself.</note>, a woman who was either the only one or the leader of that kind: and for that reason, Zosimus placed the name <term>Imuth</term> at the head of his work.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument from page 18, where he examined Zosimus of Panopolis's account of the origins of chemistry. ### CHAPTER III.

I certainly do not doubt that there is no truth in either of these stories, whether it be that of Isis or that of Zosimus. Nevertheless, it is clear enough from this that the ancient Egyptians did not attribute the invention of chemistry to Hermes Trismegistus, even in their myths; this is sufficient to refute the opinion that currently prevails. In passing, it is worth observing that those today are mistaken who think the word <term>chemistry</term> <note>original: "χημείας" (chēmeias)</note> is derived from a certain Egyptian prophet named Cheme, or from the Greek word for "a thing poured" <note>original: "χύμα" (chyma)</note>; for Zosimus himself has taught us its true origin, however much he relied on fables. And indeed, that prophet they refer to is consistently called *Chimes* <note>original: "χίμης"</note>, not *Chemes* <note>original: "χήμης"</note>, in the Greek records of that art.

<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.</margin>
Certainly, others more plausibly derive the name of the art from the region where it was born. For if we believe Plutarch, Egypt itself was called *Chemia* <note>original: "Chemia"</note> in the sacred language of the priests. But perhaps it should be read as *Chamia*. It is well known in the Psalms of David and elsewhere that Egypt is called the "Land of Ham," and Jerome says: *The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> write "Cham" <note>original: "χὰμ"</note> for Ham, expressing the double aspiration of the Hebrew letter Heth with the Greek letter Chi <note>original: "χῖ"</note>; from which Egypt is still called Cham today in the language of the Egyptians.* But this is by the way. One may see that other Greek chemical writers do not differ much from Zosimus. For although there survives a commentary by Olympiodorus of Alexandria *on the actual work of Zosimus, regarding all things said by Hermes and the Philosophers* <note>original: "εἰς τὸ κατ' ἐνέργειαν Ζωσίμου ὅσα ὑπὸ Ἑρμῆ καὶ τῶν Φιλοσόφων ἦσαν εἰρημένα"</note>, and even then certain chemical works circulated among the Greeks under the name of Hermes, nevertheless, the invention of the art is not attributed to him. Instead, it is counted among other "philosophers," as they call them—that is, the practitioners of the chemical art <note>original: "τῆς χημευτικῆς" (tēs chēmeutikēs)</note>.

Furthermore, the very novelty of that art shows that it did not originate with Hermes, since in the accounts of the Egyptians, Hermes lived in the most ancient times, either before the Deluge <note>The Great Flood.</note> or not long after.

<meta>This page continues the historical investigation into the origins of the word "Chimia" (Chemistry/Alchemy). # ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

However, the surest proof of the art's novelty, in my judgment, is that since the Greeks and Romans were most greedy for gold and silver, and ruled all of Egypt for many centuries, they were nevertheless entirely ignorant of both the name of the art and all its attempts—to say nothing of the works, which were either always non-existent or very rare. To whom will it truly be proven that the Egyptians were able to hide for so long that which was so greatly desired by their masters? Indeed, that all things were unknown is evidenced by the clear and persistent silence on this matter by all Greek and Latin writers alike, almost until the fourth Christian century, even though Egypt had been subject to the Greeks and Romans for more than six hundred years. Moreover, it is not common for something that appeals to almost everyone among the common people, and is thus held in great esteem, to be passed over in silence by everyone without reason.

And yet, the first to mention the name of the art was Julius Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer whose work *Mathesis* is one of the most complete handbooks on ancient astrology.</note> during the reign of Constantine the Great, as far as can be learned from surviving books. *“If,” he says (in Book 3 of the **Mathesis**, chapter 15, discussing the decrees of the Moon through the individual stations of the sky, and specifically concerning the ninth place from the horoscope), “this house should be of Mercury, it will give astronomy; if of Venus, songs and joy; if of Mars, the work of arms and instruments; if of Jupiter, divine worship and knowledge in the law; if of Saturn, the knowledge of Alchemy.”* This is the first record of the word Alchemy. There is no reason why we should change it in this place against the evidence of the manuscripts by discarding the Arabic article **Al** to make it *Chimia* <note>The author argues that the word should be left as "Alchemy," resisting attempts by other scholars to strip away the Arabic prefix "Al-" to make the word appear more Greek or ancient.</note>. *“We observe many Arabic words in the ancient monuments of the Egyptians: almenicha <note>original: ἄλμενίχα</note>, oasis <note>original: ὄασις</note>, and others which do not come to mind,” writes Joseph Scaliger in his notes to Eusebius.*

<margin>Note on page 248, column b.</margin> If Africanus, the author of the *Cesti* <note>original: τῶν κεστῶν (tōn kestōn). Julius Africanus was a 3rd-century Christian traveler and historian.</note>, was Julius Africanus—an opinion held by Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar.</note> in codex 34 and by the most learned Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a prominent 17th-century Dutch scholar.</note> in Book 2 of *Greek History*, chapter 15—that word was already known to Alexander...

### CHAPTER III.

...was mentioned in the third Christian century during the reign of <insert>the mother of Emperor Alexander Severus,</insert> Mamaea. However, the lexicographer Suidas calls that man Sextus Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240 AD) was a Christian traveler and historian; the author is debating whether a "pious Christian" could have written a book filled with magic.</note>; and the fact that those *Cestoi* <note>original: "cestos"; the *Kestoi* or "Embroidered Girdles" was a multi-volume encyclopedia of miscellaneous knowledge, including medicine and magic.</note> were not the work of a Christian man is sufficiently betrayed both by the fragments of the work—which are filled with magical superstition and survive in various places, especially in the *Geoponica* attributed to Constantine <note>The *Geoponica* is a 10th-century collection of agricultural lore compiled for Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus.</note>—and by the very subject matter of the work itself. This is because it contained **a treatise on medical, physical, agricultural, and chemical matters involving natural powers** <note>original Greek: "πραγμάτειαν ἰατρικῶν καὶ Φυσικῶν καὶ γεωργικῶν καὶ χημικῶν περιέχουσαν δυνάμεις"</note>. Indeed, it is no secret to any learned person what is usually meant by the term <term>natural powers</term> <note>original Greek: "Φυσικῶν δυνάμεων"; here implying occult or magical properties rather than modern physics.</note>. 

Nor is it truly credible that those passages which Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous Renaissance scholar known for his work on chronology.</note> inserted on page 70 of his *Greek Eusebius* are from the hand of Eusebius himself—as if Africanus had written the books of the *Cestoi* specifically for Alexander, the son of Mamaea. This is especially doubtful since Jerome, who was certainly a diligent reader of Eusebius's works, makes no mention of this work, the *Cestoi*, among the writings of Africanus. Furthermore, to those who attend a little more carefully to all those Greek fragments of Eusebius, it is easily apparent that many parts of George Syncellus, Panodorus, and others are read as if they were by Eusebius; this occurred because Scaliger selected those "Eusebian" passages from the records of Syncellus mostly by mere conjecture.

Not only is the name of the art of such recent memory, but you will perhaps not even find any <term>chemical</term> <note>original: "χημικὸν"</note> work mentioned before these times. At last, toward the end of the fifth century, during the reigns of the Emperors Zeno and Anastasius, Aeneas of Gaza <note>A Neo-Platonist philosopher and convert to Christianity.</note>—in the latter part of his dialogue *Theophrastus*—endeavored to prove that the mortal body can be perfected for the better through the resurrection. He used the example of a statue-maker who restores a broken bronze statue, and indeed, so that by his art the bronze is turned into gold, and he who was previously a bronze Achilles returns as a golden one. He adds: *“Even among us, those who have skill in matter take silver and tin, and once the former appearance is abolished, they turn it into...”*

...have been refuted by the most learned men. This is not even to mention that although there is much talk in the apocryphal books of Enoch concerning those spirits and the arts they bestowed upon the mortal race, there is nonetheless a deep silence in them regarding chemistry. Indeed, you will read nothing of these things in that clear fragment of those apocryphal works which Joseph Scaliger <note>Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609): A leading scholar of the Renaissance known for his works on chronology and his editions of ancient texts.</note> cites in his notes <margin>Scaliger's notes p. 243.</margin> on the Greek chronicles of Eusebius, taken from the unpublished works <note>original: "ἀνεκδότοις"</note> of George Syncellus, <note>George Syncellus (died after 810): A Byzantine chronicler and ecclesiastic whose work preserved many fragments of ancient texts that would otherwise be lost.</note> as far as can be conjectured; rather, he says only this: *And they taught themselves and their wives sorceries and incantations. First, Azael, the tenth of the leaders, taught how to make swords and breastplates, and every instrument of war, and the metals of the earth, and how they should work gold to make ornaments for women, and silver. He also taught them the art of polishing and beautifying, and the use of choice stones.* These things this apocryphal book says regarding the first arts communicated by the Watchers: <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν ἐγρηγόρων" (from the Watchers). In the Book of Enoch, the Watchers are fallen angels who reveal forbidden heavenly knowledge to humanity.</note> I confess that in some respect these are not unlike chemical matters, insofar as they certainly pertain to metallurgy; <note>original: "μεταλλεργικά"</note> however, they say nothing of the art of making gold. <note>original: "χρυσοποιητικῇ" (chrysopoeia)</note>

...had taken root, and for that reason, even then—more than thirteen hundred years ago—medical books, and likewise for more than a thousand years, chemical <note>In this context, "chemical" refers to alchemy, the precursor to modern chemistry</note> books had been circulated under the name of Hermes. For if even then many pamphlets falsely bore that author's name, and if even then there was a great discordance of doctrine within them, it is clearer than the sun that the testimony of that age carries no weight.

Thirdly, it deserves to be noted that in no Greek or Latin writer who preceded the time of Christ is there any record of a Hermetic book that was handled by anyone other than Egyptian priests. ## ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...born: undoubtedly by the unique craft of an evil demon <note>original: "mali dæmonis arte"</note>, so that the successful progress of Christian doctrine might be hindered, and a new color might be added to that impure demon-worship—which, consisting of the far too foul fables and fictions of the Greeks and Latins, could not fail to collapse—by a certain theology dressed in the cloak of antiquity and appearing more plausible and secret. Just as many other works of the same sort first came forth for a similar reason, while the Christian heretics whom we call Gnostics <note>Gnostics were members of various early religious movements who claimed that salvation came through secret, mystical knowledge (gnosis) rather than through faith or the established Church.</note> were working toward the same end with great effort. In that climate of study, who could doubt that many things were published under the name of Hermes which were foreign to the ancient Hermetic doctrine itself, as long as they served the intended goal?

*Fourthly*, it is furthermore established that among the Egyptians there was the greatest disagreement regarding the worship of the gods and other major institutions of human life; and yet, nearly all of them praised Hermes as the author of their teachings. From this, it is manifest that not everything the Egyptians themselves attributed to Hermes truly belongs to one person; rather, the various inventions of priests and others were already commonly assigned to that name long ago. Because of this, even in ancient times, the reliability of the Hermetic doctrine—even when drawn from the most secret and sacred Egyptian writings—could not have been anything but questionable.

*Fifthly* (to say nothing of the fact that it is not even sufficiently certain whether there ever was a Hermes such as the Egyptians describe), this especially deserves to be considered: that it is not safe to believe a writing is by Hermes simply because it was produced by the Egyptians. Certainly, we have shown elsewhere that nothing was more vain than Egyptian stories in the past, and that their priests destroyed all credibility with monstrous lies <note>The author reflects a common early modern skepticism toward Egyptian history, viewing their claims of extreme antiquity and secret wisdom as fabrications meant to overshadow Greco-Roman and Christian traditions.</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

Sixthly and finally, the Egyptians themselves have made the entire reputation of the Hermetic books highly suspicious; for, as they themselves testify, in the age of Hermes and even in the following period, the Egyptian custom was to engrave doctrine not upon papyrus <note>An early form of paper made from the pith of the papyrus plant.</note> but upon columns.

<margin>Book 1, *On the Mysteries*</margin>

Pythagoras and Plato learned from the columns of Mercury. These columns are filled with the teachings of Mercury.* <note>The author uses "Mercury" as the Roman equivalent for the Egyptian Thoth or the Greek Hermes Trismegistus.</note>

For the Egyptians, even past events are always kept fresh through memory. ### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

Mercurius <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Hermes. The text refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a mythical figure seen as the founder of alchemy and "Hermetic" philosophy.</note>, if we believe Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) who wrote a history of Egypt.</note>, wrote no book, but rather carved his teachings upon stone columns. Regarding the other claim—that he translated the doctrine of his grandfather into Greek, and did so after the Great Flood—this is not only refuted by the truly sacred history of the Hebrews, but is even self-evidently far from the truth. This is because, at that time, the Greek nation was obscure, undistinguished, and possessed no reputation for learning; indeed, they were entirely ignorant of all letters. How, then, could this sacred and most ancient doctrine have been translated into their language back then by Hermes himself, the father of Tat <note>In Hermetic dialogues, Tat is the son and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>—that is, by Mercury Trismegistus himself? Furthermore, for a long time, the Egyptians barred all foreigners, including the Greeks, from entering their land. At such a time, who would believe that Mercury or anyone else wrote in Greek?

<margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin>
Indeed, Herodotus <note>A Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note>, who lived near to those times, relates that Psammetichus <note>Psamtik I (reigned 664–610 BCE), a Pharaoh who famously employed Greek mercenaries and opened Egypt to Greek trade.</note> was the first to admit men of foreign speech—specifically Greeks—into Egypt, and that only from that time forward did the Greeks establish commerce with the Egyptians.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, chapter 67.</margin>
Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> testifies to the same in his first book: *for those who held power before Psammetichus made Egypt inaccessible to foreigners, punishing those who landed with either death or slavery.* Yet Psammetichus lived barely a hundred years after the start of the Olympiads <note>The ancient Greek system of dating starting in 776 BCE. This places Psammetichus around the 7th century BCE.</note>. Indeed, these facts are so certain that one cannot even admit what Philo writes <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who attempted to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> in his

<margin>Philo, Life of Moses.</margin>
*Life of Moses*, namely that Moses was steeped in Greek disciplines, with teachers summoned from Greece by Pharaoh's daughter with great rewards. For in the age of Moses, there was no glory of learning among the Greeks, as they had perhaps not yet even received the first characters of the alphabet from the Phoenicians.

### CHAPTER V.

#### *It is demonstrated regarding the individual books today usually attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, that they are either of no credibility or of uncertain credibility, and not very ancient; therefore, Hermetic doctrine cannot safely be sought from them.*

Furthermore, perhaps enough has been said to many regarding what should be thought of the books of the Egyptian Hermes in general. Nor indeed is it now unclear to anyone that even those books circulated under this name long ago were of very uncertain credibility; since they contained inconsistent doctrine, true Hermetic wisdom could not safely be drawn from them even then. Next, it is necessary that we inquire more specifically into the individual Hermetic books currently in circulation. Indeed, some of them still survive today, while many others have perished. ...at least those which he mixed into his collections from Isidore of Gaza, Damascius, Simplicius, and Agapetus. <note>These are late antique and Byzantine philosophers and authors, suggesting the sources used for these "ancient" texts were actually much later.</note> But this testimony of Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved many fragments of Greek literature.</note> alone is of little weight in proving the authenticity <note>original: γνησιότητα</note> of that Hermetic booklet. Yet none of the ancients—not only among the pagans, but not even among the Christians—mentions this little work: so it is necessarily a very recent offspring. In the *Fifth* book, many things are found from Job and other sacred books of both Testaments, but nothing of the Egyptian dogmas is to be found, except for what is called the "most excellent god of the celestial gods." This discourse, too, is devoid of any testimony from antiquity: so it is not difficult to say how much value should be placed on it. The case is similar for the *Sixth* and *Seventh* books. That the *Eighth* book came forth from the Platonic school is proven by, among other things, the mention of "ideas"; for Plato was the first to fashion these, as Aristotle says more than once. The *Ninth* book seems to be an appendix to that dialogue commonly known as *Asclepius*, which we discussed near the beginning. This is indicated by the first words of the discourse: "Yesterday, O Asclepius, I delivered the Perfect Discourse; now I consider it necessary to provide the sequel to that, concerning sensation—" <note>original: "χθὲς ὦ Ἀσκληπιὲ, τὸν τέλειον ἀποδέδωκα λόγον. νῦν δ' ἀναγκαῖον ἡγῆμαι ἀκόλουθον ἐκείνῳ καὶ τὸν περὶ αἰσθή-" (Chthes ō Asklēpie, ton teleion apodedōka logon. nyn d' anankaion hēgoumai akolouthon ekeinō kai ton peri aisthē-)</note>

<meta>The final Greek word "αἰσθή-" (aisthē-) is completed by the catchword "σεως" (seōs) to form "αἰσθήσεως" (sensation).</meta>

The tenth treatise, or *The Key*, also seems to have come from the same author as the ninth. For it begins: *The discourse of yesterday, O Asclepius, I dedicated to you, but it is right to dedicate today’s to Tat* <note>In Hermetic literature, Tat is the son and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> *since it is an epitome* <note>a summary or condensed version</note> *of the "General Discourses" spoken to him.* Namely, the *Perfect Sermon* is consecrated to Asclepius with an appendix. Thus, it is fashioned as if this discourse of Hermes were held the next day for the benefit of his son, Tat. The sentiments of the booklet certainly agree with the doctrine contained in the *Perfect Sermon* (or *Asclepius*), and for that reason they truly "taste" of Egypt rather than Greece, and much less of Christianity. Furthermore, those *General Discourses* <note>original: γενικὰ (genika)</note>, of which this little work promises a summary, are also listed among the Hermetic works in the Greek chronicle of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century historian of the early Church.</note>. We shall provide those very words shortly hereafter; it follows that this booklet is of the same "offspring" as the *General Discourses*. 

It certainly seems this was also read by Lactantius. For in the first book of the *Institutes*, chapter 11, he says: *It appears, therefore, that Saturn was not born from heaven (which is impossible) but from a man whose name was Uranus. ...[Mercu]ry <note>original: *Mercurius*. The word "rium" from the previous page likely completed the name *Mercurium*</note> (perhaps, *Mercury*) named his kinsmen. Moreover, in *The Key*, *Hermes* speaks in this way: <note>original Greek: οἱ δυνάμενοι πλέον τι ἀρύσασθαι τῆς θέας κατακοιμίζονται, πολλάκις ὑπὸ τοῦ σώματος εἰς τὴν καλλίστην ὄψιν· Ὥσπερ Οὐρανὸς καὶ Κρόνος οἱ ἡμέτεροι πρόγονοι ἐντετυχήκασιν.</note> "Those who are able to draw a little more from the vision are lulled to sleep, often [carried] by the body into that most beautiful sight; just as Uranus and Saturn, our ancestors, encountered it." Johannes Stobaeus <note>A 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts, essential for preserving fragments of lost works.</note> undoubtedly used this text, as he inserted six quite large fragments into the first book of his *Eclogues*, taken *From the Discourses to Tat* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν πρὸς Τὰτ</note>, which nevertheless appear in this very *Key* in so many words.

The *eleventh* treatise was perhaps in the hands of only a few ancients. However, St. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444), a major figure in early Christian theology who cited Hermes to demonstrate that even "pagans" recognized the divine nature.</note> uses its testimony in the second book of *Against Julian*: <note>original Greek: προσποιήσει δὲ τούτοις ἃ γέγραφέ ποτε ὁ Τρισμέγιστος Ἑρμῆς πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ υἱὸν. ὀνομάζεται γὰρ ὧδέ τὸ βιβλίον. Εἶτα, Φὴς, ἀόρατος ὁ Θεὸς ; εὐφήμησον, καὶ τὶς αὐτοῦ φανερώτερος ; διὰ αὐτὸ τοῦτο πάντα πεποίηκεν, ἵνα διὰ πάντων τὶς αὐτόν βλέπῃ. τοῦτο ἔστι τὸ ἀγαθὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, τοῦτο ἡ αὐτοῦ ἀρετὴ, τὸ αὐτὸν φαίνεσθαι διὰ πάντων.</note> "And he will add to these things what Hermes Trismegistus once wrote to his own son; for that is the title of the book. Then he says: 'Do you say God is invisible? Speak well, I pray; for who is more manifest than He? For this very reason He made all things, so that through all things one might see Him. This is the goodness of God, this is His virtue: that He appears through all things.'" To these I shall add what Hermes Trismegistus wrote to his own mind <note>Referring to the *Poimandres* or "Mind" as a teacher.</note>. For so the booklet is named. "Is God then, you ask, invisible? Speak well, I pray. Who is more visible than He? For that reason He created all things, so that through all things one might contemplate Him. This is that goodness of God, this is His very virtue: that He is discerned through all things." These words are found toward the end of the booklet, and we have learned at the same time how it was once titled.

Truly, the doctrine savors more of the Platonic school than the Egyptian. The *twelfth* treatise is of the same mark; for immediately at the beginning you may see that Platonic doubt as to whether God has *substance* <note>original Greek: οὐσίαν (*ousian*), referring to "essence" or "being."</note>. Indeed, both the subject matter and the method of treatment are the same as the previous one. However, nothing occurs to me now from elsewhere that was taken from this text. That it was not written by the most ancient Hermes is indicated by even a single mention of the Persians and Greeks, peoples who were once quite unrefined.

[[page number: 46]]

And for this reason, none of the ancient writers mention it, even though it displays a thoroughly Christian faith regarding holy regeneration <note>The concept of being "born again" spiritually, central to Christian theology</note>, and its wording is made up of terms from the New Covenant <note>original: "novi fœderis" – meaning the New Testament</note>. Thus, this little book clearly originated from someone not ignorant of Christian doctrine during these most recent centuries, no less than the *Crater* and *Poimander* <note>Two significant texts in the Hermetic Corpus; the *Crater* is also known as "The Mixing Bowl"</note>, which are mentioned before the sacred hymn. *The fourteenth discourse to Asclepius likewise seems to be the work of a Christian author rather than a pagan one, since it condemns the depiction of God through images—a practice which the Egyptians, more than other nations, recommended, and indeed perhaps were the first to bring into use. Even though it argues in favor of Christian doctrine, one cannot find any testimony quoted from it by an ancient Christian writer. This is the most certain proof that this book is a recent work and dates to after the era of the early Church.*

From all this, what we have said becomes clear: those works which the leading scholar Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Italian priest and scholar (1433–1499) who translated the Hermetic writings during the Renaissance</note> published and translated into Latin under the single title of *Poimander* are of varying quality and by various writers. Some appear to be forged by Christians, others by Platonists, and invented under the name of Hermes; very few truly reflect the ancient Egyptian doctrine. For although Plato himself perhaps owes his theology to the Egyptians (since one cannot easily say from where else he received those ideas which rely on no formal proof <note>original: "ἀποδείξει" (apodeixei) – a Greek term for logical demonstration or mathematical proof</note>), Egypt nevertheless possessed many unique elements in its sacred rites that do not seem to have appealed to Plato.

Yet even those few parts which we have noted as being more "Egyptian" than the rest are not by the most ancient Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth</note> himself, nor by any ancient writer at all. <margin>Casaubon, in the place cited.</margin> For Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), the scholar who famously proved the Hermetic texts were late forgeries rather than ancient Egyptian wisdom</note> says most correctly regarding all the short works in that book: *If this book were truly the work of Mercury, it would be necessary that either he himself wrote it in Greek, or that someone had translated it from the Egyptian language.*

### CHAPTER IV.

We most firmly deny that either of these things occurred. First, because the style of this book is completely foreign to the language used by the Greeks who were contemporaries of Hermes. That ancient language possessed many words, many phrases, and indeed an entire character of expression very different from that used by later Greeks. Here, there is absolutely no trace of antiquity, no "bloom" <note>original Greek: χνοῦς (*chnous*)</note> or "breath of antiquity" <note>original Greek: πνῶς της αρχαιότητος (*pnos tēs archaiotētos*)</note>—the subtle "downy" quality of age which the most excellent of the ancient critics observe even in Plato, let alone in Hippocrates, Herodotus, and other older writers. On the contrary, there are many words here that were not even recognized by the older "Hellenism" <note>The form of the Greek language used during the classical period versus the later Roman period</note> that flourished around the birth of the Lord. What ancient Greek used the word *authentia* <note>αὐθεντία</note> to mean "power"? Who ever employed those dithyrambic <note>Highly ornate or exaggerated</note> terms like *archikē prophaneia* <note>αρχικὴ προφάνεια</note>, that is, "imperial preeminence"? Who among the earlier writers said *hylotēs* or *hosiotēs* <note>υλότης, ὁσιότης</note>, meaning "materiality" or "substantiality," and other things of that kind? I also deny that these works were translated from another language. I maintain that they are original <note>original Greek: αὐτοφυῆ (*autophye*), meaning native or genuine</note> and were originally written in Greek. No translation was ever so successfully executed that it did not reveal its foreign origin or demonstrate it through certain signs. Here there is nothing of the sort. Everything is genuinely <note>original Greek: γνησίως (*gnēsiōs*)</note>—that is, purely or authentically—Greek; and throughout the work, the style remains consistent with the "Hellenism" of the age I have identified.

<margin>
Bulenger, *Discourse V* on Chapter XI of Casaubon’s *First Exercise*.
</margin>

These and many other things were noted by Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a scholar famous for proving the Hermetic Corpus was written in the 2nd or 3rd century AD rather than ancient Egypt</note>. These facts are so true that they even drew these words from his opponent and the defender of Baronius, Julius Caesar Bulenger: *"Many among the ancients and moderns approve of Baronius's judgment concerning Hermes Trismegistus. However, I do not reject your own view. I believe that author was more recent, as he mentions Phidias and Eunomius the Locrian musician, and records trophies through which he mentions prophecies of the Prytaneum <note>A public hall in ancient Greek cities; the mention of such specific historical figures and institutions suggests a later Greek context</note>."* However, these references to Phidias and others are found in the books of *Asclepius*, not in those of *Mercury* <note>The Latin name for Hermes</note>; in this matter, even Casaubon’s memory failed him.

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE <note>Hermetic Medicine refers to a philosophical and medical system attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus, blending Egyptian, Greek, and early Christian ideas.</note>

But perhaps more than enough has been said regarding the fourteen small works published by Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian scholar and priest who was central to the revival of Hermeticism in the Renaissance.</note> under the name of *Poimander*. To these, Francesco Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a philosopher who sought to replace Aristotelianism with a "pious" philosophy based on Hermetic and Neoplatonic texts.</note> added six or rather seven booklets in his Ferrara edition of Hermes, which appeared in the year 1591: one of which, entitled the *Sacred Book*, he reports was found by him in Cyprus, in a monastery named Enclistra. He admits that the others were compiled from Joannes Stobaeus <note>A 5th-century compiler who preserved extracts from many ancient Greek authors whose original works are now lost.</note>, as well as from a few fragments surviving both in Cyril’s <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century bishop who quoted Hermetic texts to argue against the Emperor Julian the Apostate.</note> books *Against Julian* and in the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia and dictionary.</note>, though he does not indicate the specific places from which he took them. It seems, however, that the booklet found in Cyprus is the one which Patrizi placed in the **first position**, *On Piety and Philosophy*. From the *Physical Eclogues* <term>Eclogues: a term used for a collection of selected passages or extracts from various authors.</term> of Stobaeus was collected the fourteenth Patrician booklet, *On the Soul*, and the **sixteenth**, *On Energy and Sense*, except that one or two sentences were copied from the *Moral Discourses 13 and 117*. From this source also were taken the passages concerning Providence and Fate which are found after the thirteenth booklet, though they did not count among the number of books in Patrizi's edition. Indeed, the entire **thirteenth booklet** was stitched together from two large fragments of the *Hermetic Sacred Book* which are contained in chapter 40 of those same *Physical Eclogues*. The **seventeenth** booklet of Patrizi is found in Stobaeus, in the *Moral Eclogues*, *Discourse 11*, of the Gesner edition <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss scholar who published an influential edition of Stobaeus.</note>. The **twentieth** of the same Patrizi is composed entirely of fragments cited by Cyril of Alexandria.

The condition of almost all of these is nearly the same as the previous ones, except that all of them have at least some testimony from the Middle Ages, and thus they are not of the most recent origin. To be sure, some display almost nothing Egyptian but rather smack of Plato; others seem to be copied from the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments; finally, others [Egyptian...]

Egyptian doctrines, containing quite a lot. In the first category, one might place those which Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), who organized the Hermetic works into different "orders" of philosophical importance.</note> cast into the fourteenth and seventeenth booklets, or those concerning providence which he gathered from Stobaeus. ...of the Republic of Augsburg [[note: likely "Augustanæ reipublicæ," referring to the city-state of Augsburg]]. Since no mention of this little book is made not only in Ptolemy [[note: Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer]], but also in Julius Firmicus [[note: Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman who wrote on astrology]], a most diligent student of Egyptian Astrology (who nevertheless praises the works of Aesculapius, Petosiris, Necepsos, Abraham, and others)—indeed, since its memory is found nowhere else—it is sufficiently clear from this that this work was also substituted by someone or other after the times of the best Greek and Latin astrologers. Added to this is the fact that the doctrine does not agree with those things which Firmicus brings forward in good faith throughout from Petosiris, Necepsos, and Aesculapius, or with those which survive today in the fragments of Hephaestion of Thebes, Dorotheus of Sidon [[note: Astrologers from the 1st and 4th centuries CE]], and others.

Much less (to say nothing of the *Aphorisms*) are the two books *on the revelations of nativities* the work of Hermes. These were translated from an uncertain Greek author and were somewhat emended by Hieronymus Wolf [[note: A 16th-century German humanist scholar]]; they were produced in Basel from the workshop of Henricus Petri [[note: A prominent Swiss printer]] in the year 1559 [[note: CIƆ IƆ LIX is an archaic way of writing 1559]]. For (to pass over other points now), in Book 1, Chapter 3, Ptolemy’s *Compilation* [[note: original: *σύνταξις* (*Syntaxis*), referring to the *Almagest*]] is clearly brought forward as evidence; in Book 2, in the "Firdaria of Venus" [[note: <term>Firdaria</term> is a system of planetary periods in medieval astrology]], Hermes himself is cited as a witness. Throughout the work, the astrological observations of the Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, and Indians are discussed as if they have already been proven by the use of many centuries.

The book of the *Cyranides* [[note: A famous ancient text on the magical and medicinal properties of plants, animals, and stones]] ought more justly to return by right of recovery into the number of Hermetic works. This book is commonly attributed to some "Kyrannus," King of the Persians, as if the name were derived from that author; not so long ago, it appeared in print in a Latin version. Indeed, Thomas Reinesius [[note: A 17th-century German physician and philologist]] has learnedly noted that the name of the booklet is of Arabic (I would prefer to say Egyptian) origin, and was already ascribed to Hermes by Olympiodorus, the Theban alchemist [[note: A 5th-century commentator on alchemy]], in the age of the Emperor Theodosius. # CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Various Readings, Book 1, Chapter 2</margin>
The words of Olympiodorus [[note: A late-antique scholar or alchemist, likely referring here to his commentary on alchemical works]], brought forth from a manuscript, are these: "Again in the *Cyranides*, Hermes, speaking figuratively, says the rooster [[note: original Greek: *ἀλεκτρύονα* (alektruona)]] is truly a holy thing to the Sun and a proof of the Moon." Indeed, we have observed a similar testimony in the Greek writings of Eusebius [[note: Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian]] edited by Scaliger [[note: Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading 16th-century scholar of historical chronology]]. The complete words in the first book of his *Chronicles* are as follows: "These things, being analyzed or divided into these very years twenty-five times, reveal the restoration of the zodiacal myths according to the Egyptians and Greeks—that is, from the same point to the same point, which is one minute of the first degree of the equinoctial sign called Aries among them, just as it is said in the *General Matters* of Hermes and in the books of the *Cyranides*."

<margin>Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, page <unclear>7</unclear></margin>
Perhaps, however, those are not the words of Eusebius himself, but rather of George Syncellus [[note: A 9th-century Byzantine chronicler]] or Panodorus [[note: An Egyptian monk and chronicler around 400 CE]], from whose chronicles Scaliger excerpted his Eusebian material. Be that as it may; it is clear that already long ago, and indeed by the fifth Christian century, the short works of the *Cyranides* [[note: A famous Greco-Egyptian compilation of magical and medicinal properties of plants, birds, and stones]] were ascribed to Hermes. Therefore, they were perhaps translated into Greek not from Arabic as some would have it (for Arabic works in that age were not of such importance that you would translate them), but perhaps from the Egyptian language. Those *Cyranides* which survive today seem to be altogether of the same character as those mentioned by the ancients, except that perhaps they have not reached us in their entirety.

<margin>See the words of Syncellus in the notes of Scaliger, page 246.</margin>
It is uncertain who translated it into Latin: Schenck [[note: Johann Georg Schenck von Grafenberg, a medical bibliographer]] indeed testifies that Gerard of Cremona [[note: The most prolific translator of the 12th century, who turned Arabic scientific works into Latin]] translated four books of the *Cyranides*, though I do not know with what reliability. Reinesius [[note: Thomas Reinesius, a 17th-century German physician and philologist]] deserves thanks, for he successfully cleansed that extremely faulty text in many places; even if it is still not entirely sound, nor of much significance.

<margin>Schenck in the *Medical Library*. Reinesius, Various Readings, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin>
Furthermore, there appeared not long ago in the library of Thomas Erpenius [[note: A famous Dutch Orientalist and professor of Arabic]] an Arabic booklet titled *Hermes on Precious Stones*, written in the year 749 of the Hegira [[note: Approximately 1348 CE]]: which you might rightly say was translated from Greek, but not from the ancient Egyptian language, since the author is expressly called by the Greek name of Hermes, not the Egyp—

Finally, several alchemical works are circulated today under the name of Hermes. Among these is the treatise on the *secret of the philosopher’s stone* <note>The "philosopher’s stone" was the legendary substance sought by alchemists for its supposed ability to transmute base metals into gold and provide the elixir of life.</note> found in the fourth volume of the *Alchemical Theater* <note>original: "Theatri Chemici". This was a massive multi-volume compendium of alchemical writings published in the 17th century.</note>, but most notably the *Table* called the *Emerald Tablet*. However, it has already been demonstrated that these works falsely claim that name of Mercury <note>The author uses 'Mercury' here as the Roman equivalent of the Greek 'Hermes'.</note>.

## CHAPTER VI.

***The lost Hermetic writings mentioned by the ancients were likewise all counterfeit.***

Since no other writings besides those we have mentioned so far are usually attributed to Mercury, it is clear that our earlier assertion was correct: no certain Hermetic doctrine can be learned from the works believed to be by Hermes today. It is indeed clearer than the sun that some of those writings do not even have an Egyptian flavor, while others have very little; all are of recent origin <note>original: "recentis monetae", literally "of recent coinage," a metaphor for works that are not ancient but modern forgeries.</note> and falsely boast an ancient and magnificent title. It is, moreover, very likely that those works of which only the names remain in ancient writings were no better. Indeed, let no one believe that the world of letters suffered a great loss because many Hermetic works have perished, or be distressed that...

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

<margin>Justin's *Exhortation*, near the end.</margin>
Saint Justin Martyr writes that Hermes said: "To conceive of God is indeed difficult, but to express Him is impossible." <note>original Greek: Θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν δὴ χαλεπὸν φράσαι δὲ ἀδύνατον</note> Saint Cyprian looked toward this same sentiment in his book *On the Vanity of Idols*: *Hermes Trismegistus also speaks of one God and confesses Him to be inexpressible and beyond measure.* These words of the most holy martyr are recited by Saint Augustine in *Book 6 against the Donatists*. Saint Cyril of Alexandria has all these matters at much greater length in *Book 2 against Julian*, as does John Stobaeus in his *Moral Sermon 78*, and specifically in the section *from the discourses to Tat*. <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν πρὸς Τατ; Tat was the son and disciple of Hermes in the Hermetic dialogues.</note> However, this fragment is not found elsewhere, except that this—along with other pieces sought from Cyril—was cast into the twentieth book by Francesco Patrizi. <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597) was a Renaissance philosopher who compiled Hermetic texts to prove they were compatible with Christian doctrine.</note> Indeed, no one fails to see that this <term>maxim</term> <note>original: γνώμην (gnomen)</note> was as if copied from Plato, whose words in the *Timaeus* are these: "To find the maker and father of this universe is a task, and having found him, it is impossible to speak of him to everyone." <note>original Greek: τὸν μὲν οὖν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς εὑρεῖν τε ἔργον, καὶ εὑρόντα λέγειν εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον</note> Consequently, whoever authored that discourse of "Mercury to Tat," they must have had a Platonic source. But concerning the fragments which remain in Stobaeus, Cyril, and others, it has already been discussed above, and there is no reason why we should repeat what has already been done.

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*, last book.</margin>
Iamblichus mentions that a hundred books were written by Mercury *on the empyrean gods*, <note>The 'empyrean' refers to the highest, most fire-filled part of heaven, believed to be the dwelling of God or the highest deities.</note> just as many *on the ethereal gods*, and a thousand *on the celestial gods*. These were undoubtedly recorded in no less a fabulous manner than what Seleucus and Manetho narrated—according to the same witness—concerning the immense number of Hermetic volumes; we have already brought forward the words of Iamblichus on this matter above.

Certainly, Clement of Alexandria is a witness that the Egyptian priests themselves carried and displayed no more than forty-two books of Hermes in their sacred rites. Who would deny that Clement is a substantial and worthy source of trust? For he was of distinguished piety and learning, and being an Egyptian by nation, he spent his life in his homeland. All of his narration on this matter deserves...

...they contain information about laws, gods, and the entire discipline of the priests. For among the Egyptians, the Prophets are also in charge of the distribution of taxes.
