## CHAPTER VII.

->*That the ancient books of other authors do not survive today from which Hermetic doctrine might be safely sought: indeed, it seems that Hermes himself was merely a mythically invented figure.*<-

What should be thought of the books which—whether in antiquity or even today—are usually attributed to Hermes himself, is clearly evident from the evidence we have presented. It follows that we should see if any ancient monuments by other authors remain from which one might safely learn Hermetic doctrine. Indeed, it is well known that certain works of this kind were commonly circulated in the past, just as they are today. However, unless I am very much mistaken, it is not difficult to prove that none of those can be accepted as genuine. We shall trace this matter back from the most ancient records.

Regarding Sanchuniathon <note>A Phoenician author whose works are lost but were said to predate the Trojan War; his history was supposedly translated into Greek by Philo of Byblos</note>, Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note> says: *Sanchuniathon of Tyre, a philosopher who lived during the time of the Trojan War, wrote about the Natural Philosophy of Hermes.* <note>original Greek: Σαγχωνιάθων Τύριος φιλόσοφος, ὃς γέγονε κατὰ τὰ Τρωϊκά, ἔγραψε περὶ τῆς Ἑρμῆ Φυσιολογίας</note>

## CHAPTER VII.

->*That the ancient books of other authors do not survive today from which Hermetic doctrine might be safely sought: indeed, it seems that Hermes himself was merely a mythically invented figure.*<-

...of the discourse <note>original: "λογίας"</note> which was translated into the native dialect of the Tyrians or Phoenicians, [entitled] *Egyptian Theology*, and certain other things. <note>original: "πατρία τυρίων τῇ (l. ἤ) φοινίκων Διαλέκτω, Αἰγυπτιακὼ θεολογίαν, καὶ ἄλλα τινά"</note> Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia</note> was perhaps mistaken regarding the *Egyptian Theology*, since he should have said the *Theology of the Phoenicians*: which indeed we still possess today in no small part, described by Philo of Byblos <note>A scholar of the 1st–2nd century AD who claimed to translate the works of the ancient Phoenician priest Sanchuniathon</note> in the writings of Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD)</note> in *Book 1, Chapter 10 of the Preparation for the Gospel.* However, this "theology" has perished just as that "physiology" <note>In this context, the study of the laws of nature</note> has; though from the fragments preserved by Eusebius, it is easily apparent that those works of Sanchuniathon consisted of monstrous lies, trifles, and fables.

<margin>Eusebius in Scaliger's *Greek Chronicle*, page 6</margin>
It is also clear from the preface of the work he titled *Sothis*, addressed to Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II (r. 283–246 BC), the great patron of the Library of Alexandria</note>, that Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote in Greek</note> also professed that he would explain the affairs of the world "from the sacred books written by our forefather Hermes Trismegistus." <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν βιβλίων γραφέντων ὑπὸ τοῦ προπάτορος τρισμεγίστου Ἑρμοῦ"</note> He undoubtedly made the same claim in his *Epitome of Natural Philosophy* <note>original: "ἐν τῇ τῶν φυσικῶν ἐπιτομῇ"</note> mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> in his *Proem*, and in his *Egyptian Theology* mentioned by Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD)</note> in the *Miscellanies*, Book 1, and by Theodoret in his second oration *Against the Greeks*. <note>original: "πρὸς ἕλληνας"</note> But in truth, all these things have long since been lost, and the "lying speech" <note>original: "mendaciloquentia"</note> of this man is elsewhere sharply criticized by us.

<margin>page 30, Paris edition</margin>
Furthermore, Saint Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> in his first book *Against Julian* <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman Emperor</note> is a witness that a certain Athenian attempted to encompass all Hermetic doctrine in fifteen books, called the *Hermetica*. But perhaps these were no other than those which Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> calls the *Salaminian Books*: so named because they were written in Salamis, a place near Athens opposite Eleusis. This suspicion is owed to Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar who proved the Hermetic texts were written in the Christian era, not deep antiquity</note>. Regarding the *Salaminian Books*, <margin>Casaubon on Baronius, page 55 of the German edition</margin> Iamblichus says: *The doctrines contained in the Salaminian Books comprise but a very small part of the Hermetic arrangements.* Even if they were extant, they would not fully instruct us; yet not even a slight trace of them appears anywhere anymore.

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

Long before all of these, the prophet Bytis <note>Bytis was a legendary Egyptian priest mentioned by later Neoplatonists as a translator of Hermetic wisdom.</note> had explained the Hermetic doctrine, if Iamblichus spoke the truth. We have already cited Iamblichus's words above regarding the "way of Hermes" <note>original: Ἑρμῆν</note>, which was explained by Bytis for the benefit of King Ammon. Indeed, the same Iamblichus mentions this Bytis again in these words near the end of his work *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*:

> *The Egyptians consider one kind of "good" to be divine—namely, the God who is perceived by the intellect alone—and another to be human—namely, the union with that same Lord—just as the prophet Bytis explained from the books of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurialibus," referring to Mercury/Hermes.</note>.*

However, since Ammon is numbered among the most ancient kings, it is not likely that any written book survived from that age. Therefore, that work too must have been a forgery. Certainly, it does not survive today, but perished long ago.

Let us proceed to the students of Hermes themselves. There is just as little support to be found in the monuments <note>In this context, "monuments" refers to the surviving written records or literary remains.</note> attributed to them. <margin>Justin Martyr, First Apology for the Christians.</margin> For regarding Ammon, from whose alleged booklet Saint Justin cites a small portion (for the name is wrongly read as Ammon for Ammon <note>The original Greek text likely contained a subtle misspelling or a distinction between the Egyptian deity and a human king that the author finds philologically suspicious. Indeed, that same second booklet touches upon the fable of Eunomius of Locri, the cithara player <note>A legendary musician whose broken string was said to have been replaced by the song of a cicada during a competition.</note>, mentioned by Strabo, Clement of Alexandria, Antigonus of Carystus, and others. It uses the Greek terms *prytanis* <note>original: πρύτανις; a presiding official in Greek government.</note> and *prytaneia* <note>original: πρυτανεῖα; public buildings or administrative terms.</note>: it alludes to the *palamnaios* <note>original: παλαμναῖον; a Greek term for an avenging spirit or one stained with blood.</note> and explains the etymology of the word *basileus* <note>original: βασιλεύς; king.</note>. All these things show more clearly than the sun that the author was not Egyptian but Greek, and certainly not particularly ancient. ...elaborate and ornate diction, and should strive for logical demonstrations. However, this kind of philosophy only began to be like that among the Greeks in the age of Socrates and Plato. Perhaps the small books from which those maxims were transcribed by Al-Mubashshir ibn Fatik <note>original: "Mebsiro Fatikide." He was an 11th-century Arab scholar famous for his collection of philosophical sayings.</note> shortly before the year 1000 AD—which Elichmann <note>Johann Elichmann (1601–1639) was a physician and orientalist who studied Arabic manuscripts for Greek philosophical remnants.</note> recites on his authority—were no better.

<margin>Elichmann's letter to Beverovicius.</margin>
For there is no reason for us to expect monuments from the Arabs that precede the times of the Greek sages. Certainly, up to now, nothing has come to light written in that language that truly tastes of antiquity; on the contrary, one might almost say that what was translated from Greek or Latin into Arabic was corrupted by the Arabic translators, to such an extent did they strip away the ancient and genuine character in that version. Indeed, the historians of the Arabs are almost like children regarding more ancient matters, at least as far as one can gather from published writings. But this is said in passing. It is more likely that works once believed to be by Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius is the Latin name for Asclepius, the god of medicine, often associated with Hermes in Hermetic literature.</note> regarding astrological subjects could be sold as "Hermetic" writings. Julius Maternus Firmicus, in Book 3, Chapter 1, writes concerning Petosiris and Nechepso <note>Petosiris and Nechepso were legendary Egyptian figures to whom many foundational Hellenistic astrological texts were attributed.</note>:

> *They wished this to be the "birth of the world," following Aesculapius and Anubis, to whom the most powerful divinity of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij numen," referring to Hermes/Mercury as the source of wisdom.</note> entrusted the secrets of this science.*

Pliny says of the same:
<margin>Book 7, chapter 49.</margin>
> *The sect of Aesculapius says that fixed spans of life are received from the stars, but how much it attributes at most is uncertain. They say, however, that longer durations are rare, since a huge crowd is born during the notable moments of the hours of the moon or of the seven and nine days (which are observed by night and day) by a climbing law of years, which they call climacterics <note><term>climacteras</term>: critical years in a person's life, traditionally thought to be multiples of 7 or 9, where one was at high risk of death or major change.</note>, generally not exceeding the fifty-fourth year of that race.*

But perhaps even in Pliny's age, no astrological work of Aesculapius was in public circulation, but all those things were drawn from the monuments of Petosiris and Nechepso—who, nevertheless, with what degree of faith they handled the Hermetic and Aesculapian teachings...

## CONCERNING HERMETIC MEDICINE

...[the] doctrine they professed is unknown today, although many of their opinions may be sought from Dorotheus of Sidon, Manilius, Julius Firmicus, and Hephaestion of Thebes, who all followed Egyptian Astrology as closely as possible, rarely mixing in anything from the "barbaric sphere" <note>original: "sphæræ barbaricæ"; this refers to astronomical systems or star maps of non-Greek origin, such as those of the Babylonians</note> or Chaldean doctrine; unlike what was done by Claudius Ptolemy and, before him, Hipparchus and others.

Before we depart from this subject, we neither should nor can conceal that not only are all the writings attributed to Hermes, and the Hermetic doctrine itself, of suspect reliability, but it cannot even be safely believed that there was ever any "Hermes Trismegistus" among the Egyptians who was the author of the great wisdom attributed to them. I shall not use the arguments of Goropius Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572) was a physician famous for his eccentric theory that a dialect of Dutch was the original language of humanity.</note> derived from the Cimmerian language, for they are inept and full of foolishness. But truly, first of all, the ancient writers do not agree among themselves regarding his place, his time, or many other things pertaining to the life of Hermes—which is certainly a sign of great uncertainty. 

For instance, Sanchuniathon <note>A semi-legendary Phoenician author whose work survives only in fragments quoted by later writers.</note> makes him a Phoenician and a counselor to Saturn, the king of Byblos, as Philo of Byblos reports in the works of Eusebius. Many others, on the contrary, hand down the tradition that he was born in Egypt, and was there a counselor to King Osiris, and that he instructed Osiris's wife, Isis. Others report that he lived in Greece and performed entirely different deeds, which are well known from the common Greek myths. Furthermore, anyone with even a little prudence must admit that the stories Sanchuniathon relates concerning the first men and the first inhabitants of Palestine and Coele-Syria <note>A region of the Levant, literally "Hollow Syria."</note> are foul and "old wives' tales." 

Nor can it be concluded by any evidence that the things interspersed regarding Taautus <note>A Phoenician deity associated with the invention of writing, often identified with the Egyptian Thoth and the Greek Hermes.</note> are any better. Moreover, how mythical is the claim that the first Egyptian Thoth <note>original: "Thoyth"</note> inscribed the sciences upon columns before the cataclysm <note>the Great Flood</note> in hieroglyphic letters, but in a sacred language...

### CHAPTER VII

...or Egyptian [doctrine], and that after the Flood this doctrine was translated into Greek and once again transcribed into books using hieroglyphic signs by Agathodaemon, the second Mercury and father of Tat! <note>Tat, often identified as a son or disciple of Hermes Trismegistus, is a frequent interlocutor in the Hermetic dialogues.</note> Was the Egyptian language in use before that Great Flood? Are not hieroglyphic letters signs for things rather than sounds? How, then, could anything be written in either Egyptian or Greek through hieroglyphic letters? Certainly, the writing of the Chinese <note>original: "Sinensium"; the author compares Egyptian hieroglyphs to Chinese characters, which were understood by early modern scholars as "real characters" representing concepts directly rather than phonetic sounds.</note> is not something you can translate into this or that language, since they too use characters that are indicators of things, not sounds. 

Now truly, that Agathodaemon, the father of Tat, is none other than Hermes Trismegistus himself, the teacher of Isis; yet the claim that he wrote in Greek is a ridiculous fabrication, as we have already demonstrated above. I will not even mention how improbable it seems that pillars survived from the Flood which contained written doctrine, although this was also reported by Josephus <margin>Book 1 of *Antiquities*, chapter 3.</margin> regarding a certain pillar in Syria. All these things are reported from Manetho <note>Manetho was an Egyptian priest of the 3rd century BCE who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek.</note> by Eusebius in his *Greek Chronicles*. <margin>Eusebius, page 6.</margin> 

On the other hand, in the little book attributed to Aesculapius, it is strongly advised that the sacred doctrine of Hermes should not be translated into the Greek language. However, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended the antiquity and authenticity of the Egyptian mysteries.</note> relates that it was translated into Greek by men who were not unskilled in philosophy—specifically Greek philosophy. Furthermore, in the Isiac book, it is taught that Hermes created human bodies into which souls were confined through divine indignation; unless the discussion there is not about Trismegistus (who is affirmed there to have been a man himself), but about Mercury, one of the planets, which I confess seems more likely to me. 

Be that as it may: the stories told about Isis and Osiris and the other Egyptian gods are such that no one would rashly claim there is any true history underlying them. Therefore, long ago, all the wiser men began to [interpret] everything through various allegories <note>original: "ἀλληγορίας"; the practice of interpreting myths as symbolic representations of physical or moral truths.</note>...

To this point, the ancient author Artapanus <note>Artapanus of Alexandria was a historian of Jewish origin who lived in the 3rd or 2nd century BC; he sought to show that Egyptian culture was actually derived from Jewish figures.</note>—according to Eusebius, who seems to have copied his words from Alexander Polyhistor—records that Moses was called "Hermes" by the Egyptians. For where he has narrated many benefits provided to the Egyptians by Moses, Artapanus adds: <note>original Greek: "Διὰ ταῦτα οὖν τὸν Μώϋσον ὑπὸ τῶν ὄχλων ἀγαπηθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἱερέων ἰσοθέου τιμῆς καταξιωθέντα προσαγορευθῆναι Ἑρμῆν διὰ τὴν τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων ἑρμήνειαν."</note> "Because of these things, therefore, Moses was loved by the masses and, judged worthy of divine honor by the priests, was addressed as Hermes because of his interpretation <note>The author identifies a pun here: the Greek word for interpretation, *hermeneia*, sounds like the name *Hermes*.</note> of the sacred writings." However, Moses is not that Trismegistus who was the companion and advisor to Osiris: even if perhaps he was known by this name to the Egyptians, a superstitious people who accepted the idea of <term>metempsychosis<note>The transmigration of souls, or the belief that a soul can move from one body to another after death.</note></term>, as if the soul of Hermes had somehow insinuated itself into Moses. Just as that doctrine of "transanimation" has elsewhere caused many people to be regarded under the same name simply because of a similarity in their character. It would be very easy to illustrate this with examples if the situation required it. Truly, it does not seem that we would be making good use of our time if we did so: especially since it is already clearer than the sun that the entire Egyptian history concerning Hermes is of doubtful reliability.

If those Egyptian matters are so, it is much less likely what Elichmann <note>Likely Johann Elichmann (1601–1639), a physician and orientalist known for his studies of Eastern languages.</note> wished to convince us: that even the Persians, Chaldaeans, and Indians attributed the beginnings of wisdom to Hermes. You certainly would not read this in the records of the ancients; furthermore, it is established that the Chaldaeans worshipped a certain Oannes by that name, whose history is entirely different from the Hermetic one. Certainly not, even if the word "Hermes" is also used by the Persians...

### CHAPTER VII.

...was in use, it can be gathered from here that those Egyptian fables also pleased the Persians. For the word Hermes <note>original Greek: "Ερμης"</note> was born among the Greeks, not among the Egyptians; it clearly descends from the Greek word *ereo* <note>original Greek: "ερεω"</note>, which means "I speak." If the same name was in use among the Persians, it happened by chance, as often occurs. Undoubtedly, it also meant something quite different to the Persians, assuming it was a word intended to signify anything at all. Even *Hermon* is the name of a mountain mentioned in our own sacred scriptures. 

From the most ancient memory, the names *Irmin*, *Ermin*, or *Armin*—or even *Hirmen*, *Hermen*, or *Harmen* with an added breathing sound and an "e" replacing the final "i"—have been frequent among the Germans. The origin and meaning of these names are unknown today. For it is a recent invention to claim that the word originated from the German *Man* <term>man</term> and *Her* <term>lord or army</term>, as if it meant "Lord Man," or as others prefer, "Lord of the Army." 

<margin>See Meibom, *On the Saxon Irminsul*, chapter 6.</margin> <note>Heinrich Meibom (1555–1625) was a German historian who wrote about the Irminsul, a sacred pillar-like object or "world pillar" worshipped by the pagan Saxons.</note>

Indeed, perhaps no one heard the name *Herman* among the Germans before Hermannus Contractus <note>Hermann of Reichenau (1013–1054), a celebrated scholar and monk known as "Hermann the Lame."</note>. This etymology is refuted by the very sound of those two small words, which is far different from the popular pronunciation of the name *Hermin* or *Hermen* used throughout the centuries. To suggest that the name reached us from the Greeks is ridiculous. Truly, in ancient times, it was common to combine it with various other words.

Hence we find not only *Hermin*, but also *Herminburc, Herminfrid, Hermingard, Hermingaus, Hermingund, Herminhild, Herminhold, Herminhulf, Herminrath, Herminric, Herminfind, Hermintrud, Herminvvar, Herminvvit*, and similar names. Certainly, to hunt for historical truths based solely on a slight resemblance of words is exactly like trying to attribute a bark and four feet to the "Celestial Dog" <note>The constellation Canis Major.</note> simply because it shares the name "dog" with the animal that barks. You might more plausibly say that the *Margemah* mentioned by Solomon, or the *Merkolim* of the Hebrews, refers to Mercury, and that the name "Mercury" arose from some such origin. For it agrees with the rites of Mercury...

One thing deserves to be added: even in ancient times, the Egyptians were unable to persuade those who were a little more sensible of their fables concerning Hermes and the wisdom proceeding from him. I will not bring up the Greeks, who preferred to claim the glory of that discovery for themselves. However, <term>Nicolaus Damascenus<gloss>A Greek historian and philosopher from the 1st century BC, a friend of Herod the Great.</gloss></term>, a great man, wrote expressly that Arithmetic and Astrology first reached Egypt from <term>Abraham<gloss>The biblical patriarch.</gloss></term> and thus from the Chaldeans; his words are recited by <term>Josephus<gloss>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</gloss></term> in Book 1 of his *Antiquities*. <term>Eupolemus<gloss>An early Jewish historian who wrote in Greek.</gloss></term> and <term>Artapanus<gloss>An author of Jewish history, likely living in Alexandria in the 2nd century BC.</gloss></term> told the same story, as witnessed by Alexander Polyhistor in <term>Eusebius<gloss>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop often called the "Father of Church History."</gloss></term>, Book 9 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. Even <term>Proclus Lycius<gloss>Proclus (412–485 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher.</gloss></term> testifies that the Assyrians cultivated Astrology before the Egyptians. I shall not cite other witnesses today.

<margin>
Eusebius, page 3, 6.

# CHAPTER VII.

The Egyptian grammarian Hellanicus, as cited by <term>Photius<gloss>Photius I (c. 810–893 AD), a Byzantine scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople whose 'Bibliotheca' preserves summaries of many lost ancient works.</gloss></term> in volume 279, calls Ioannes by the name "Oën." The words of Hellanicus (or perhaps Photius himself) are: <note>original Greek: Ὡ̈ην μυθολογεῖ ἄνδρα τινὰ ὠνομασμένον Ὡ̈ην... "The legend says that a certain man named Oën came up from the Red Sea; while the rest of his limbs were those of a fish, he had the head, feet, and hands of a man. He taught both astronomy and writing. Others say he was born from a first-born egg, and that his name testifies to this. Though he was entirely human, he appeared to be a fish because he was clothed in a whale-like skin."</note> <term>Scaliger<gloss>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a titan of Renaissance scholarship known for his work on chronology and philology.</gloss></term> believes that in the text of Hellanicus, "Oën" was written instead of "Oannes" by a scribe’s error, and "egg" <note>Greek: ὠὸν (oon)</note> instead of "Oannes." But perhaps Scaliger is mistaken; for "egg" seems to be a common noun here rather than a proper name, and the passage is clearly discussing a specific egg. Certainly, in the works of <term>Arnobius<gloss>Arnobius the Elder (died c. 330 AD), an early Christian author who wrote against pagan practices.</gloss></term>, the Syrian gods are said to be the offspring of eggs. <term>Nigidius<gloss>Publius Nigidius Figulus (c. 98–45 BC), a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero known for his interest in the occult.</gloss></term> also writes (as quoted in the commentary on <term>Germanicus<gloss>Refers to the 'Scholia' on the 'Aratea' of Germanicus Caesar.</gloss></term>) that the Syrian Venus was born from an egg, as does Lucius Ampelius in his book dedicated to Macrinus. Ampelius’s words are as follows: *It is said that in the river Euphrates, a dove sat upon a fish's egg for many days and hatched a goddess, kind and merciful to humans, leading them to a good life.* Some have passed down the tradition that Oën, or Ioannes, was born from the first of such mythical eggs. However, these matters are beyond our current purpose.

## CONCERNING HERMETIC MEDICINE
-> I <-

...writings or opinions that are attributed to Hermes, but rather about all of them, because of the similarity of the subject matter, and so that no lack of diligence may be found in us. Now, as if none of the things we have said were demonstrated, but that the genuine Hermetic doctrine of the ancient Egyptians can and should be sought from those monuments, we shall see of what kind those things are which occur in those monuments relating in any way to the medical art: then what may be achieved by conjecture concerning that Hermetic medicine, from the narrations of the ancients about Hermes and from the surviving Hermetic doctrine which is circulated.

Among the medical books ascribed to Hermes, those six which Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who recorded much about Egyptian pagan customs</note> mentions were sacred to the *shrine-bearers* <note>original Greek: "τοῖς παστοφόροις" (the pastophoroi); these were a specific class of Egyptian priests who carried the sacred shrines in processions</note> of the Egyptians, would undoubtedly be our primary consultation if they still existed. But these, along with that book which Pamphilus the Botanist <note>A 1st-century writer on the medicinal properties of plants</note> praised—as Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman era</note> testifies—concerning the thirty-six herbs of the horoscopes, have long since perished. Only the *spiritual medical matters* <note>original Greek: "ἰατρικὰ πνευματικά" (iatrika pneumatika)</note>, the *Books of the Kyranides* <note>A compilation of ancient lore regarding the magical and medicinal uses of animals, plants, and stones</note>, and those things which are circulated concerning Gems, can teach us something of Hermetic medicine. From the titles of the books which those *shrine-bearers* once held in their secret archives, it can be gathered that Hermes was involved with the <term>Physiology</term> <note>original Greek: "Φυσιολογίαν"; in this context, it refers to the study of the nature and functions of the human body</note> of the human body, with the nature of diseases, with surgical instruments and various medicines; but he seems to have worked with particular care on those things pertaining to the conditions of the eyes and of women. For individual booklets on each of these existed in the possession of those *shrine-bearers*. What was actually accomplished in these books, however, we are ignorant of today.

The title of the book which Pamphilus mentioned signifies that Hermes favored that doctrine once familiar to the Egyptians concerning the thirty-six gods or demons of the horoscopes...

...[guar]dians of the parts of the human body. It was believed, of course, that just as many herbs were sacred to them. Concerning these demons, Celsus—the man who drew his pen against Christian piety—speaks as follows in the works of Origen:

<margin>Origen, Book 8 *Against Celsus*</margin>
The Egyptians say that thirty-six demons, or certain ethereal gods, have divided the body of man among themselves, which is partitioned into that many parts—though some say there are many more. Each spirit is appointed to provide care for a different part. They know the names of these demons in their native tongue, such as Chnoumen, Chnachnoumen, Knat, Sicat, Bio, Eru, Erebiu, Ramanor, Reianoor, and whatever other names they use in their own language. Indeed, by calling upon these spirits, they heal the ailments of the specific body parts. <note>original Greek: "Αἰγύπτιοι λέγουσιν, ὅτι ἄρα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ σῶμα ἓξ καὶ τριάκοντα διειληφότες δαίμονες..." This passage is from Origen’s *Contra Celsum*, quoting the pagan philosopher Celsus to illustrate Egyptian beliefs in "Decans"—astrological spirits ruling segments of the body.</note> We have quoted these very words in Greek because the Latin translator, Christophorus Persona, translated this passage quite carelessly, completely omitting the "barbarous" names of the demons.

We learn from this text, however, that the human body was divided by the Egyptians into thirty-six parts. According to their view, an equal number of demons or celestial gods undertook the care of these parts, with individual parts committed to individual gods. Therefore, for the sake of health, any one of them must be invoked for the cure of his specific part. This was believed to be effective only if one held their proper names, which was a knowledge granted only to the Egyptian priests and <term>Magi</term><note>Here referring to the learned priest-magicians of ancient Egypt, rather than the Persian Magi</note>. Origen hints that to appease these spirits, certain secret <term>incantations</term><note>original Latin: "carmina," which can mean songs, poems, or ritual chants</note>, herbs, stones, and <term>seals</term><note>original Latin: "signacula," referring to engraved talismans or amulets</note> of stones were employed by the Egyptians. Teaching shortly after the quoted words of Celsus, Origen notes: *The greatest and best God approves rather of the conduct of those who pray to Him alone, than those who fix their attention on the names, powers, and deeds of demons.* Furthermore, he notes that they place great value on incantations and herbs pleasing to demons, as well as stones and the engravings upon them, which—as others have handed down—bear the likeness of a demon's form or some other figure. If that true divining astrology comes from Hermes, then undoubtedly medical astrology should also be credited to the same author; for the latter is like a branch growing from the former. Furthermore, if Aesculapius owes his secrets to Mercury—as Firmicus says—then perhaps he also owed to him his wonderful doctrine regarding the <term>climacteric years<note>Critical points in a human life, historically thought to occur in cycles of seven or nine years, believed to be times of great physical or spiritual risk</note></term> of human life, which we have already briefly mentioned above from the works of Pliny.
<margin>See page 61.</margin>

Far beyond what is believable, many things are also attributed to the power of stones and engraved sigils with Hermes as the author, as recorded by Albertus Magnus in his work on metals. If these are truly Hermetic, it is clear to everyone what sort of thing Hermetic medicine once was.

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

No medicine prepared by the chemical art in the name of Hermes was praised by any of the ancients. Furthermore, we will demonstrate elsewhere that whatever medical knowledge is attributed to that art <note>The "chemical art" or early alchemy.</note> only arose after all the ancient doctrine of the Egyptians had been extinguished and the affairs of the Arabs were flourishing.
<margin>Book 3, Antidotary, § 6.</margin>
Conversely, Johannes Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue the Younger (925–1015 CE) was a famous Persian physician whose works on purgatives and "antidotaries" (books of remedies) were fundamental to medieval European pharmacy.</note> lists two descriptions under the name of Hermes for pills <note>original: *catapotiorum*</note> made from colocynth <note>A bitter desert fruit used as a powerful purgative.</note> or *alhandal*, as the Arabs call it; a certain *Hiera* <note>A "hiera" (holy remedy) was a traditional bitter purgative powder or electuary.</note> also bears his name. These compositions contain nothing out of the ordinary; they certainly differ greatly from chemical preparations. Even if these texts falsely claim Hermes as their author, this itself confirms what we have said: that not even in legend was any chemical medicine once ascribed to Hermes in ancient times. Nowhere do you read that Hermes favored what today's chemists claim regarding the origin of things from the "three principles"—salt, sulfur, and mercury. Instead, it is taught everywhere in the ancient texts that bodies are born from the four things called elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Regarding the human body, the doctrine is especially clear 
<margin>Stobaeus, page 85, Plantin edition.</margin>
in Stobaeus <note>Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved fragments of lost Greek and Hermetic literature.</note>, Book 1, *Physical Eclogues*, chapter 35. This very thing was observed by Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 CE) was an early Christian author who often cited Hermes Trismegistus as a "pagan prophet" of monotheism.</note>, who consequently wrote: 
<margin>Lactantius, Book 2, Divine Institutes, chapter 13.</margin>
*Empedocles established four elements, perhaps following Trismegistus, who said our bodies were constituted by God from these four elements.*

Furthermore, although what was once called Hermetic medicine cannot rightly be called chemical, it was entirely magical. This is clearly shown by what we have already said, and it can be gathered from the fact that both the Phoenicians and the Egyptians worshiped Hermes alone as the master and prince of their <term>eidōlomania <note>original: είδωλομανείας; literally "idol-madness," referring here to the practice of animating statues or using physical images for magical purposes.</note></term>. Indeed, Sanchuniathon <note>A legendary Phoenician writer; our knowledge of him comes via Philo of Byblos.</note> (or rather Philo of Byblos) [recorded] the Phoenician myths regarding the origin of the world and the first men—

The records concerning men who were consecrated into the number of the gods are said to be taken from the monuments of a single man, Taautus <note>Taautus is the Phoenician name for the Egyptian god Thoth, often identified with the Greek Hermes.</note>. # ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

<margin>Eusebius, in the place cited.</margin>
In Philo's book titled *On Phoenician Elements* <note>original: "περὶ τῶν Φοινίκων στοιχείων" - Philo of Byblos claimed to have translated the works of Sanchuniathon, a Phoenician author</note>, Eusebius relates: "Taautos <note>The Phoenician name for Hermes or Thoth</note> himself deified the nature of the Dragon and of serpents, and after him, the Phoenicians and Egyptians did so likewise." Although Philo indeed brings forward certain arguments for the divine nature of dragons and serpents, no one fails to see that they are unsuitable for proving such a thing. Undoubtedly, therefore, Hermes was believed in this way because a demon <note>original: "daemon" - here used in the early modern sense of a supernatural spirit or fallen angel</note> frequently presented himself under the appearance of that animal, or even within that animal, which is very well known to us from the sacred history of Moses <note>A reference to the Serpent in the Garden of Eden</note>.

For those animals were held sacred and divine by the Egyptians and other peoples above all others, whose appearance or bodies the evil spirits <note>original: "mali dæmones"</note> had misused.

But it is clear enough what kind of religion the Phoenicians once professed to have been handed down to them by Hermes. It is certain that the Egyptians also recognized Hermes as the teacher of their religion. Diodorus Siculus writes from the mouths of the Egyptian priests in *Book 1, Chapter 16* concerning Hermes: <margin>Clement, Book 6 of the Stromata.</margin> *he ordained the worship of the gods and sacrifices.* From Clement of Alexandria, we have also already learned that in the so-called sacred processions, various books were carried around concerning the entire worship of the gods, as if they had originated from Hermes. Concerning Osiris separately, Diodorus says: <margin>Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 20.</margin> *Having returned to Egypt, he brought back with him the most excellent gifts from every place, and on account of the magnitude of his benefits, by the common consent of all, he obtained the reward of immortality and honor equal to the celestial gods. Then, after he was translated from men to the gods, Isis and Mercury <note>Hermes</note> deemed him worthy of sacrifices and other most distinguished honors among the gods. These two also instituted the ceremonies of his initiations, and other things to be performed according to the mystical rite concerning him, to magnify the power of this god.*

If we believe these things, the veneration of men as gods must be accepted as having been brought about by Hermes alone, as well as the [fabrication] of idols

## CHAPTER II.

...construction. For the Phoenicians and Egyptians seem to have first established these things; the latter, indeed, attributed the glory of the invention to their own Taautus or Thoth. It is very likely that these practices flowed from the Phoenicians and Egyptians to other peoples.

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 1, Chapter 9.</margin>
Philo of Byblos <note>A Phoenician scholar who claimed to translate the ancient history of Sanchuniathon</note> testifies to this sufficiently in the works of Eusebius: *“This we must first of all establish: the most ancient of the Barbarians, especially the Phoenicians and Egyptians—from whom other nations subsequently received the custom—held in the place of the greatest gods all those who had found things necessary for the conduct of life, or who had conferred some benefit upon the human race. These they worshipped with divine honors because they were convinced they were the authors of many goods. They turned the use of temples, which had already been built, to this service and duty; moreover, they consecrated columns and wooden statues in their names. Having followed these with a special religious cult, the Phoenicians also dedicated to them very famous feast days. In this practice, it was particularly notable that they gave the names of their kings to the elements of the entire universe and to certain things to which they attributed divinity. Furthermore, they recognized only the natural gods—the sun, the moon, and the other fixed stars—along with the elements and those things joined to them by affinity. Thus, they had some gods who were mortal, and others who were immortal.”* All this is from Philo. Although lengthy, we have recited these things here so that the character of the Hermetic religion of the ancient Egyptians and Phoenicians might be made apparent (at least in part) to the less experienced. We know—not only from Philo's testimony but also from others and indeed from the Greeks themselves, as will be discussed elsewhere—that the worship of idols and men was first brought from them into Greece, together with the sacred orgies <note>In the ancient sense: secret rites or festivals, particularly those of Dionysus</note> and mysteries.

In those Hermetic books that are circulated today, it is indeed indicated that the construction of idols [began] even before Hermes...

> *The wonder of all wonders surpasses admiration: that man was able to discover nature and to bring it about. For because our ancestors erred greatly, being unbelieving toward the discourse of the gods and not paying attention to divine worship and religion, they discovered an art by which they might create gods. To this discovery they joined a power appropriate to the nature of the world, mixing it in; and, since they were unable to create souls, by summoning the spirits of demons or angels, they placed them into their images and divine mysteries, through which alone these idols could have the power of doing both good and evil.*

Already before in the same discourse he had said:

> *Understand the power of man, O Asclepius, and his strength. Just as the Lord and Father—or that which is supreme, God—is the creator of the celestial gods, so man is the creator of the gods who are in temples, joined to man by proximity; and he is not only illuminated by them, but he also illuminates them; nor does he only advance toward God, but he also confirms the gods.*

Likewise, with several remarks of the same kind interjected:

> *Do you speak of statues, O Trismegistus? Then he replied: Statues, O Asclepius (do you see to what extent you yourself doubt?), statues animated with sense and full of spirit, performing such great and marvelous things; statues with foreknowledge of the future, predicting things which perhaps every prophet is ignorant of, foretelling in many and varied matters, bringing infirmities upon men and curing them, bringing sadness and joy according to merits.*

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 8, Chapters 23 and 24.</margin>

# CHAPTER IX.

...intervened, as one who not only used magical incantations—as Philo <note>Likely Philo of Byblos, who wrote on Phoenician religion and the origins of culture</note> expressly writes—but who, as a new teacher, taught the worship of demons. By an abominable art, he summoned spirits into statues and established that men should be worshipped as gods. For he could not have learned that first <term>image-making art</term> <note>original: *εἰδωλοποιητική* (eidōlopoiētikē), the magical practice of drawing spirits into idols to animate them</note> from anywhere else than from the evil spirits themselves; for that art surely consists solely of their will and whim. Nor is it likely that he was led, or that others were led by him, to worship dead men in a new fashion, unless the demons had provided some credibility to such unusual impiety through certain apparitions and miraculous works. Furthermore, from a magician—and indeed such an abominable teacher of <term>demon-worship</term> <note>original: *δαιμονολατρεία* (daimonolatreia)</note>—the medical art could certainly not have originated unless it were steeped in that same essence. 

Experience certainly teaches us that men of this sort practice medicine not by a method or reason whose causes the human mind can understand, but through <term>amulets</term> <note>original: *περίαπτα* (periapta), charms worn around the neck or body to ward off disease</note>, through incantations, and through characters and signs full of vanity and superstition. Nor can it happen that a mind so occupied by evil spirits could perceive what is true or not in the effects of natural things; this is because the power of demons mingles itself with the things of nature, so that it is not easy even for another person—one less subject to the devil's deceptions—to discern what belongs to nature and what to the demon. Concerning this matter, we shall speak more extensively elsewhere.

...Suidas <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> remarked on this, writing under the entry for **sacred scribes**: *namely, among the Egyptians, they were skilled even at speaking the truth about future events.* <note>original: "ἥτοι παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις ἦσαν δεινοὶ καὶ περὶ τῶν μελλόντων τὴν ἀλήθειαν εἰπεῖν"</note>

But it is clear enough from what we have said that the medical art was always held in high honor by the Egyptians and was cultivated by the care of both the kings themselves and the priests. Before we explain what that art was like, however, this especially deserves to be noted: from the time Egypt came under the power of the Greeks, just as philosophy and other arts flourished, so too did a certain **Greek-style Medicine** thrive in the heart of Egypt, particularly in Alexandria. Indeed, it was eventually so preferred over the ancient Egyptian discipline that the latter, held in contempt by all, finally fell into decay. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (129–c. 216 CE) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note> concludes that **Herophilus** <note>An Alexandrian physician (c. 335–280 BCE) often called the "father of anatomy."</note>—certainly that great light of the medical art—lived in Egypt
<margin>Galen, *On Anatomical Procedures*, Book 2, last chapter.</margin>
based on the fact that he compared the **vermiform body** <note>A structure in the cerebellum of the brain.</note> to a pen-nib, noting it was similar to an **Alexandrian pen**. It is also evident from the fact that he wittily handled **Diodorus Cronus** <note>A Greek philosopher famous for his dialectic paradoxes, including arguments that motion is impossible.</note> when the latter was suffering from a dislocated shoulder and yet was denying that motion is possible, as Sextus Empiricus <note>A physician and philosopher (c. 160–210 CE) who recorded the arguments of the Skeptics.</note> testifies. 
<margin>Sextus, *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*, Book 2, chapter 22.</margin>
Furthermore, Diogenes Laërtius teaches that Cronus lived in Egypt at the court of **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>The King of Ptolemaic Egypt (283–246 BCE) who famously promoted the Library and Museum of Alexandria.</note>. From that master, Egypt undoubtedly received many followers of the Herophilean sect. According to the author of the *Medical Definitions* (which are wrongly attributed to Galen), Herophilus's student was **Apollonius of Memphis**; however, the author of the *Introduction* or *The Physician* counts him among the followers of **Erasistratus** <note>Another famous Alexandrian physician and contemporary of Herophilus.</note>. It is known from Suidas that **Dioscorides Phacas** <note>A physician at the Alexandrian court; "Phacas" means "lentil-shaped," likely referring to a mole or birthmark.</note> practiced medicine for **Cleopatra** and **Mark Antony**; indeed, we have shown elsewhere that he was Alexandrian by birth and a Herophilean by sect, and thus a different person from our most noble writer on *materia medica* <note>Referring to Pedanius Dioscorides, the author of the most famous ancient herbal.</note>. Around the same time, **Serapion** and **Leonidas** also flourished, both of them Alexandrians; the former gained a famous name among the **Empiricists**, the latter among the **Methodists** <note>The Empiricists and Methodists were two of the primary competing "sects" or schools of ancient medical thought.</note>.
<margin>Author of the *Introduction* or *The Physician*, chapter 3.</margin>

<margin>See Galen’s commentary on Hippocrates’ *On the Nature of Man*, note 2.</margin>
<margin>Suidas, under the entry <term>Asclepiades</term> <note>original: "Ασκληπιάδης"</note>.</margin>
That same Dioscorides <note>Not the famous herbalist, but an editor of medical texts who lived during the 2nd century AD.</note> seems to have been from the same country; he published the works of Hippocrates after his relative Artemidorus Capito during the reign of Hadrian Caesar, as we discuss elsewhere. Asclepiades also, once a teacher of medicine of great renown, lived at first in Alexandria, if we believe Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>: but Suidas, by a shameful error, confuses Asclepiades of Myrlea (who flourished during the reign of King Philopator) with the Asclepiades of Prusa, who was a contemporary of Pompey.

It is certain from our Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician in the Roman Empire; his writings dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> that in Galen's own time, the Alexandrian medical school was famous. Among its teachers, Julianus flourished; there remains a defense written by Galen on behalf of Hippocrates against this Julianus. Galen accuses that entire school of being <term>sophistical</term> <note>original: "σοφιστικὴν" (sophistikēn); here Galen implies the teachers were more interested in clever arguments and rhetoric than in practicing medicine.</note> (*Commentary 1 on the 6th book of Epidemics, part 2*). Perhaps he seized this opportunity for criticism because those Alexandrians taught the medical art for a public salary, and boasted of the title of <term>iatrosophists</term> <note>original: "ἰατροσοφιστῶν" (iatrosophistōn); literally "healer-philosophers," a title for a formal professor of medicine.</note>, that is, professors of the medical art. Certainly, the "Sophists" whom Galen criticizes seem to have been none other than the doctors of the art appointed with a public stipend. This practice had begun at that time through the generosity of the Emperors Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius, both in other places and especially in Alexandria. We shall speak more extensively on this matter elsewhere. Indeed, the young Galen himself had traveled to Alexandria for the sake of his medical studies, because he had heard that Numesianus lived there, as he writes in *On Anatomical Procedures*, book 1. There, he was on familiar terms with Heraclianus, as he reports in *Commentary 2, part 2 on Hippocrates’ "On the Nature of Man."* However, although in Galen's age that "sophistry"—and indeed what seems to have been the sect of Asclepiades—had infected that school, it flourished most greatly in the fourth Christian century with the better doctrine of Galen himself.

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22.</margin>
Hence Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian.</note>, recounting all the good things of the city of Alexandria, wrote during the reign of Valentinian Caesar: "Medicine, however—which is much needed in this life of ours, which is neither frugal nor sober—"

### CHAPTER IX.

...[those cano]nical <note>original: *canonica*; likely referring to standard or authoritative medical rules or texts</note> studies were preferred. <margin>Herodotus, Book 3, near the end.</margin> When Darius, son of Hystaspes <note>Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BCE), King of Persia</note>, was suffering from a dislocated hip, the most famous physicians he had brought with him from Egypt treated him poorly. However, he was eventually healed by Democedes of Croton <note>A renowned Greek physician known for his travels and service to various rulers</note>; Herodotus tells the story at great length of how much the King valued Democedes in the book titled *Thalia* <note>The traditional title for the third book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>. Ctesias of Cnidus served first as the physician for Cyrus the Younger, and then for his brother Artaxerxes; this is well known to the public through various testimonies of the ancients. Our own Hippocrates of Cos was also sought after by Artaxerxes, if any credit can be given to the letters that are circulated under his name and the biography written by Soranus <note>Soranus of Ephesus, a 2nd-century physician whose *Life of Hippocrates* contains many legendary elements</note>.

Among the Macedonians <note>The Ptolemaic dynasty (305–30 BCE), the Greek-speaking rulers of Egypt following Alexander the Great</note> who ruled Egypt, one can find no record that either Egyptian philosophers or physicians were held in any high esteem. Indeed, they allowed all that discipline to fall into such decay that by the time of Augustus’s reign, all that once-praised zeal of the priests of Heliopolis for cultivating wisdom <margin>Strabo, Book 17.</margin> had already perished. This is according to the testimony of Strabo, who viewed those places alongside Aelius Gallus <note>A Roman prefect of Egypt; Strabo was a Greek geographer whose *Geographica* provides a vital record of the Roman world</note>. After that time, it seems that all that ancient learning failed more and more, unless perhaps it received some small measure of help again through the Emperor Hadrian, as he was a quite diligent follower of Egyptian superstition <note>Hadrian was famous for his fascination with Egyptian culture, even deifying his companion Antinous in an Egyptian style</note>.

In the fourth Christian century, once the Egyptian temples were closed or destroyed, all the learning of the priests seems to have been completely extinguished at the same time. And truly, even though Egypt later fell under the power of the Muslims, only Greek philosophy and medicine remained in high regard. The Arabs themselves sought the medical art from the writings of the Greeks—and especially those of Galen—translated into their own language. That this custom has not ended even now is well known from the accounts of many who travel through those lands with care, and it is abundantly clear from the excellent work of Prosper Alpini <note>An Italian physician and botanist who published *On Egyptian Medicine* in 1591</note> concerning the medicine of the Egyptians. Regarding the Arabs...

From these things we have said, it is clear that not all medicine that was once used in Egypt was truly Egyptian; rather, another newer Greek-style medicine was held in the highest esteem there for many centuries—indeed, since the time of Alexander the Great—over the ancient medicine itself. Now, however, we have no business with that Greek medicine, but only with the one that is ancient and truly Egyptian. This alone, in fact, can be considered Hermetic, as it was the only one proper to the Egyptian priests, some of whom (as we have said) worshipped Hermes <note>The mythical Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian science and magic</note> as the first master and author of medicine, just as they did for their other arts.

...to believe, as I did when I saw those priests whom they call **Prophets** in the temple around the altars of the gods, that they smear this finger with prepared perfumes. For that finger, when folded, represents the number six, which is in every respect full, perfect, and divine. <note>The author refers to the ancient belief that a "nerve" or vein ran directly from the ring finger to the heart, and to the symbolic numerology associated with hand gestures.</note> This is indeed Egyptian doctrine; however, it is known even to beginners in the field of Anatomy that it deserves laughter rather than a serious refutation.

Also quite crude is that division of the human body into the head, hands, chest, and legs, which the author of the *Introduction* or *The Physician* <margin>Introduction, chapter 10.</margin>—a book counted among the forged works of **Galen** <note>Galen was the most influential physician of antiquity; many later texts were falsely attributed to him to grant them authority.</note>, though it may perhaps be by **Herodotus**—attributes to the Egyptians. Furthermore, the division of our body parts into thirty-six rests on no foundation, whether one is discussing "similar" or "dissimilar" parts <note>In ancient medical terminology, "similar" parts were uniform tissues like bone or skin, while "dissimilar" parts were complex organs like the eye or hand.</note>. Truly, the idea that there are exactly as many demons <note>The author uses "demons" here to mean spiritual entities or minor deities assigned to oversee specific bodily functions.</note> who each have care over a single part is a completely impious invention. We have already shown in chapter eight <margin>See page 69.</margin> that this was a common teaching among the Egyptian priests.

There seems to be more than one reason for their meager progress in medical science, despite the very frequent cutting open of bodies. First, all that anatomy <note>original: *ἀνατομὴ* (anatomē)</note> seems to have been established only for the purpose of preserving corpses <note>The author is referring to the process of mummification.</note>. For you will not find that the Egyptians dissected bodies minutely in our modern fashion—which is the only way the size, shape, position, and composition of individual parts can be understood. Rather, to prepare the corpses for burial, there were specific laws for cutting that defined which parts were to be removed, which were to be kept, and which were to be incised. This is what **Herodotus** and **Diodorus** <note>Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus were Greek historians whose accounts are the primary Western sources for ancient Egyptian customs.</note> tell us; consequently, many parts were not even touched by the iron blade. Those parts that were removed from the belly and chest were soon stored away again elsewhere...

...were offered, and indeed by a certain unique rite, which **Porphyry** relates on the testimony of **Euphantus** in Book 4 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: περὶ ἀποχῆς τῶν ἐμψύχων</note>. <margin>Porphyry, page 379, Lyon edition.</margin> Next, it appears that the physicians themselves did not preside over the dissection of bodies, but rather the *taricheutae* <term>taricheutae: from the Greek word for "one who salts or preserves"; these were the embalmers responsible for mummification</term>. For although in the age of the **Patriarch Jacob** the physicians and the embalmers <note>original: pollinctores; those who prepared the dead for burial</note> were one and the same—as is clear from our own sacred history <note>A reference to Genesis 50:2, where Joseph commands "the physicians to embalm his father."</note>—nevertheless, this changed in subsequent centuries. Truly, those embalmers do not seem to have been suited for the philosophy of the human body or for medical observations. 

Evidently, it is not within everyone's power to gather the fruit that one ought to—and otherwise could—from the dissection of bodies. For though you may learn without much difficulty those things which are obvious to the senses, it is not permitted to deduce anything further of certainty from those sensory perceptions, nor to investigate the function of the parts or the causes of diseases and death, unless you are skilled in demonstration—that is, unless you have an exact grasp of *The Analytics* <note>original: τὰ ἀναλυτικά; a reference to Aristotle’s logical works, which established the rules for scientific deduction and proof</note>. This is the very art that the Egyptian, who wrote a short book titled *On the Sun and Daemons* <note>original: περὶ ἡλίου καὶ δαιμόνων</note> under the name of **Aesculapius**, dared to attack with words. Furthermore, all the Egyptians were excessively devoted to superstition; once this has settled in the mind, it can hardly struggle out toward the knowledge of truth. And indeed, those notions concerning the thirty-six body parts and as many demons <note>The Egyptians believed different deities or spirits governed specific parts of the body.</note> are owed to superstition; just as those ideas about the weight of the heart and the nerve of the ring finger <note>discussed on the previous page</note> are owed to vanity.

# CHAPTER X.

Although I think little progress was made by the Egyptians in the philosophy of the human body <note>This refers to anatomy and physiology, the study of how the body functions.</note>, I would not say, however, that they held none of this teaching. For since butchers learn something of what pertains to the bodies of beasts through constant use, why shouldn't these embalmers <note>original: *pollinctores*; those who prepared the dead for burial</note> have learned something too? Thus, that Egyptian doctrine is deservedly to be praised: *the heart is the enclosure of the soul* <note>original: περιίϐολον (*peribolon*) animæ</note>; *likewise, the soul is nourished by blood*, if by the word "soul" you understand the "innate heat" <term>innate heat: a vital warmth believed by ancient scientists to be the fundamental source of life and movement in the body</term>; *furthermore, that the active principle of generation is from the male, and the passive from the female*, and several other things of this sort.

<margin>Horapollo, Book 1, Hieroglyphics, 9.</margin>
To the philosophy of the human body also belongs that doctrine concerning the influence of the stars upon our bodies: regarding which we have Egyptian opinions in the records of **Dorotheus of Sidon** (the ancient Greek poet), **Manilius**, **Julius Firmicus**, and **Hephaestion of Thebes**. But that [doctrine] truly contained nothing sound, to such an extent that **Claudius Ptolemy** himself rejected it throughout his *Tetrabiblos* <term>Tetrabiblos: literally "Four Books," the foundational 2nd-century text on the influence of the stars on human affairs</term>. Certainly, there is no need to refute it today, especially since **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**—truly the "phoenix of geniuses" of his age—did so laboriously in that admirable work he wrote against divinatory astrology.

<margin>Firmicus, Book 3, preface.</margin>

Firmicus's words are: *God, that craftsman of man, with nature showing the way, perfected the form and state and the whole substance of man according to the image and likeness of the universe. For He composed the body of man, just like that of the universe, from a mixture of the four elements—namely fire, water, air, and earth; and the balanced conjunction of all these presented the living creature in the form of the divine craftsmanship,*

Truly, the futility of this doctrine is apparent to everyone. For if man is a "small world" simply because his body is composed of the four elements...

# CHAPTER XI.

[It seems that] these things first profited the Egyptians in maintaining their health, especially since they consumed vegetables and other less-than-healthy products of the earth as food, drank beer <note>original: "zythum," a fermented barley drink common in ancient Egypt</note>—the faults of which Galen and others have noted—and lived for the most part a sedentary life. That these habits did not hinder their health is evidenced by the fact that these same Egyptians were, of all those whom <margin>Herodotus, Book 1</margin> Herodotus once saw (and he saw many throughout Asia, Africa, and Europe), by far the most excellent and, after the Libyans, possessed of the healthiest bodies. However, I would agree with Herodotus that this health was chiefly due to the air, which in Egypt is not so subject to the changes of the seasons <note>original Greek: "αἱ ὧραι" (hai horai); referring here to the seasonal shifts or "hours" of the year</note>, *from which diseases otherwise chiefly arise in humans:* <margin>Hippocrates, Book 3, aphorism 1</margin> an opinion which is also held by Hippocrates.

Furthermore, since the Egyptians believed the parts of our bodies were composed of the elements, they undoubtedly believed that diseases likewise arose from the qualities of those elements. In addition to this, they felt that certain diseases were inflicted by the power of demons, as can be gathered from many sources. In this matter, they entirely surpassed the skill of the Greeks, since almost none of the latter acknowledge diseases of this kind; yet we are convinced by experience that they do occur, as will be demonstrated by us elsewhere in a separate work. Nothing else pertaining to the Egyptian doctrine on pathology <note>original Greek: "παθολογίαν" (pathologian); the study of the causes and nature of diseases</note> has reached us.

However, I fear greatly that the medical art of the *Egyptians* was very far from perfection. Among those laws was undoubtedly the one mentioned by *Aristotle*, saying: <margin>*Aristotle, Politics, Book 3, Chapter 11, Giphanius edition.*</margin> *In Egypt it is permitted for physicians to move <note>original: "κινεῖν" (kinein); in a medical context, this refers to "moving" the humors or initiating a treatment like purging.</note> [the treatment] after the fourth day, but if they do so sooner, it is at their own risk.* *Aristotle* uses this as an example to prove how foolish it is to attempt to define everything by laws. Indeed, the law itself is flawed, whether the discussion is about cutting a vein <note>Bloodletting.</note> or about evacuating the body through a drug (for both can be understood by that word *to move*). For experience teaches that sometimes in acute diseases, when the humor is surging, both opening a vein and giving a drug at the very first moment brings remarkable benefit to health. Sometimes, I say: for often the nature of the disease allows for neither at the beginning; which surely commands us *to medicate and move those things that are ripened, but not those that are raw, nor...* <note>original: "τὰ πέπονα φαρμακεύειν καὶ κινέειν, μὴ ὠμὰ, μηδὲ"; this is a fundamental principle of ancient medicine (often attributed to Hippocrates), suggesting that one should only attempt to purge "concocted" or "ripe" fluids, not those in the early, "raw" stages of illness.</note>

# CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Hippocrates, Book 1, Aphorism 22.</margin>
"In the beginning [of diseases], unless they be in their prime <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀρχῇσιν, ἢν μὴ ὀργᾷ. This refers to the Hippocratic concept that one should not interfere with a disease until the "humors" are ready to be expelled.</note>," as has been most excellently observed by our Hippocrates. Other more universal precepts of healing by the Egyptians are nowhere to be found; and therefore, it is not permitted to affirm anything about them in either direction.

If we believe Aelian—who claimed that men were taught the use of clysters <note>A clyster is an early term for an enema used for internal cleansing.</note> by the Ibis—the invention of such a useful thing seems to be attributed to the earliest Egyptians, since the Ibis is a bird unique to Egypt. However, either Diodorus has deceived us, or those clysters and vomits were in too frequent use among the Egyptians in Diodorus's time. <margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, ch. 82.</margin> *To forestall diseases,* he says, *they treat their bodies with clysters and certain drinkable purges, fasts, and vomiting, and they repeat this either every single day, or they leave a gap of three or four days.* So says Diodorus. <margin>Herodotus, Book 2.</margin> Herodotus, however, recounts that *the Egyptians purged themselves for only three days in each month by vomiting and rinsing out their intestines.* The latter account can be tolerated as a reasonable way of living; but the former reported by Diodorus, no prudent physician would recommend. Therefore, those Egyptians who established their lives in the manner [Diodorus describes] could not have been endowed with the health for which Herodotus praised them. Either Diodorus was wrong, or as the Egyptians moved away from the lifestyle practiced in the age of Herodotus's ancestors, they eventually lost that ancient reputation for health. Nor indeed could this [excessive purging] fail to be harmful to health; just as, on the other hand, Asclepiades of Bithynia abstained from every drug to the detriment of health, as Cornelius Celsus testifies. <margin>Celsus, Book 1, cap. 3.</margin> And indeed, even in the age of Socrates, the Egyptians abstained from all more violent drugs, and therefore at that time not even the <term>syrmaismos</term> <note>original Greek: συρμαϊσμὸς; a technical term for the Egyptian practice of internal cleansing using emetics and enemas.</note> was undoubtedly frequent among them. Isocrates testifies to this in *Busiris*: *Living with these [customs], they discovered a medical aid for their bodies, not using risky drugs, but such as have a safety similar to daily food, but [the benefits...]*

# CHAPTER XI.

Crito, in the works of the same Galen, records plasters under the name of Isis. Galen recites various *Egyptian* remedies from various writers in the sixth book of that same work. Similar examples occur frequently among ancient writers. For us, it is enough now to have brought forward these few testimonies to make it clear that the ancient Hermetic Egyptians did not once use remedies that were laborious and dissolved by **chemical means** <term>chemica ratione</term> <note>The author is distinguishing between "Galenic" medicine (using whole plants and minerals) and "Chemical" or "Chymical" medicine (using distillation and extraction), which some of his contemporaries falsely claimed originated with the ancient Egyptians.</note>, but plainly those which today are called **Galenic** <term>Galenica</term> by the crowd of chemists.

<margin>
*Homer, Odyssey, Book 4.*
</margin>
One can hardly observe that metals were much in use among the Egyptians. Much less can one read that they attributed the power of healing primarily to gold and gems. It is abundantly clear from Pliny, Galen, and others that they sought remedies for diseases mostly from plants. By what names the Egyptian common folk and, separately, their **Prophets** <term>Prophetae</term> <note>In an Egyptian context, these were high-ranking priests responsible for sacred knowledge and the interpretation of texts.</note> called herbs can still be learned today from certain volumes of Dioscorides, to which a collection of names is added, and from Pamphilus, an ancient botanist, as far as can be gathered from what Galen says in the preface to his sixth book *On Simple Medicines*. Even then, the soil of Egypt was praised by Homer for its fertility and indeed for its drugs:

> Where the life-giving earth bears the most medicines, 
> many good when mixed, and many baneful.

We see that those medical compositions of the Egyptians which are circulated consist of almost no other material.

Furthermore, that Pamphilus transcribed his own works from the Egyptians is indicated by what Galen narrates shortly thereafter, concerning both other matters and the sacred herbs of the <term>thirty-six horoscopes</term><note>These refer to the "Decans," 36 groups of stars used in Egyptian astrology to divide the zodiac; each was believed to govern specific parts of the body and specific plants.</note>, which Pamphilus claimed were taken from the book of **Hermes the Egyptian**.

To the same Pamphilus, and thus to the Egyptians, also belong these words of Galen: *“Who is so wretched that—passing over the writings of Dioscorides, Niger, Heraclides, Cratevas, and countless others who grew old in the art itself—would endure the <term>grammatical books</term><note>Galen dismisses Pamphilus’s work as "grammatical" because it focused more on the names and linguistic origins of herbs than on their actual medical properties.</note> (for such were the books of Pamphilus, as was said before by Galen) of a man writing about incantations, transformations, and the sacred herbs of the <term>decans</term> and demons?”* It is certainly established that the Egyptians recognized certain herbs as sacred to demons and decans. ### CHAPTER XI.

[Egy]pt, although the soil of the Egyptians is particularly fruitful compared to other lands, yet it does not seem to have anciently abounded in a wealth of truly natural medicines. This is evident even from Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD, author of "De Materia Medica"</note>, who shows that the **medical matter** <note>original: "ὕλην ἰατρικὴν" (hylēn iatrikēn)</note> was sought from Egypt in only a very small part. Indeed, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "Father of Botany"</note> himself also testifies in Book 6 of *On the Causes of Plants* that most things growing in Egypt are odorless. <margin>Book 6, *On the Causes of Plants*, ch. 27.</margin> *“For in Egypt, the flowers and the plants used for garlands are, so to speak, of the poorest quality, because the air is misty and dewy; and in such regions, fragrance does not generally develop, because ripening <note>original: "πέψιν" (pepsin) — in ancient science, this referred to the "concoction" or ripening of a plant's juices by the sun's heat</note> does not occur, but rather it happens in very dry places; for in these, plants are fully ripened.”* Those things which are odorless also tend to be less flavorful; and consequently, it is necessary that they are also less effective for healing, since the medicinal power resides chiefly in the flavor and scent.

And indeed, the nature of the Egyptian soil remains the same today. For neither Prosper Alpinus <note>An Italian physician and botanist (1553–1617) who wrote "The Medicine of the Egyptians"</note> nor Johann Veslingius <note>A 17th-century German anatomist and botanist who worked in Padua and traveled to Egypt</note>—that great current ornament of Saxony among the Italians—could describe many medicinal plants to us, even though they, more than others, investigated Egyptian herbs with great care. 

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History"</note> also shared this same opinion with me regarding Homer. For after he had discussed the writers who recorded the benefits of herbs in *Book 13, Chapter 2*, and had praised the diligence of Antonius Castor in the final place (after which some words have been lost from Pliny’s manuscript due to the ravages of time), and had already begun to discuss something of the magical powers of herbs, he says: *“What have Medea of Colchis and others not filled with fables, especially the Italian Circe, who was even ranked among the gods? ### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE.

Pythagoras and Democritus were the first to celebrate these [magical arts] in our world, having followed the path of the Magi. These are the words of Pliny. In this, he is mistaken, as if Orpheus himself had not committed some things concerning herbs to writing. Aristotle speaks more cautiously about the Orphic songs, calling them <term>the so-called Orphic verses <note>original: "τὰ λεγόμενα Ὀρφικὰ ἔπη"</note></term> both in other places and in his first book <term>On the Soul <note>original: "I. de animà"</note></term>. <margin>Sextus Empiricus, Book 3 of the *Pyrrhonian Outlines*, chapter 4; [and] Book 8 *Against the Mathematicians*, chapter on the body.</margin>
<term>to speak of the "so-called" [verses]: that the poems do not seem to belong to Orpheus, as [Aristotle] himself says in his work *On Philosophy*. For while the doctrines are [Orphic], they say that Onomacritus set them down in verse. <note>original: "λεγομένοις εἰπεῖν: ὅτι μὴ δοκεῖ Ὀρφέως εἶναι τὰ ἔπη, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ περὶ Φιλοσοφίας λέγει. αὐτὸ γὰρ εἰσὶ τὰ δόγματα, ταῦτα δὲ φάσιν Ὀνομάκριτον ἔπεσι καταθεῖναι."</note></term> In the same manner, Sextus Empiricus, when using the testimony of the Orphic songs, praises Onomacritus regarding the Orphic works. Onomacritus, moreover, was that Athenian interpreter of the prophecies of Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and poet of early Greece</note> who lived during the time of Xerxes,
<margin>Herodotus, Book 7, near the beginning.</margin>
whom Herodotus mentions in <term>Book 7</term>. It is also likely that that Pythagorean book on herbs contained Pythagorean doctrine, yet was not written by Pythagoras himself,
<margin>Diogenes Laertius in the *Life of Pythagoras*.</margin>
as much as can be gathered from the things narrated by Diogenes Laertius. Furthermore, Pliny himself admits
<margin>Pliny, Book 24, chapter 17.</margin>
that this book was attributed by others to the physician Cleemporus, even if he himself disapproves of that view. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that Orpheus, Onomacritus, Musaeus, Pythagoras, and even Empedocles were most devoted students of Magic, and for that reason, they practiced a certain "Magical Medicine." Hence, concerning Orpheus, besides Pliny, Pausanias writes in <term>Book 9</term>: <term>he was believed to have discovered the sacred rites of the gods, purifications for unholy deeds, cures for diseases, and the turning away of divine wrath. <note>original: "πιστευόμενος εὑρηκέναι τελετὰς θεῶν, καὶ ἔργων ἀνοσίων καθαρμούς, νόσων τε ἰάματα καὶ τροπὰς μηνιμάτων θείων."</note></term> How much Homer also valued the magical arts is abundantly clear from the *Odyssey*; for as
<margin>Pliny, Book 30, chapter 1.</margin>

<margin>Odyssey, Book 10 (kappa). Odyssey, Book 19 (tau).</margin>
by means of an incantation <note>specifically referring to the scene where Odysseus's wound is staunched by a chant</note> is entirely magical. That Hesiod also was either a magician or certainly fashioned himself as such, even if...

## CHAPTER XI.

Even if [Orpheus’s] magical books on herbs have perished, it is made clear even today by those things which he sings in the *Theogony* <note>A poem describing the origins of the gods; while Hesiod is the most famous author of a Theogony, many such works were attributed to Orpheus</note> regarding his first encounter with the Muses. Indeed, one egg is no more like another than those poetic encounters are to the meetings of magicians with unclean spirits that are still practiced today. In fact, generally speaking, a certain singular familiarity with demons existed among the most ancient of poets; certainly, their own songs do not merely suggest, but loudly proclaim, that they wished the common people to regard them as such. That all this magic first arrived from Egypt is proven by the fact that it began most notably with Orpheus <margin>Pausanias, Book 6</margin>, whom Pausanias claims was of Egyptian origin; among others, there is a constant tradition that he brought all his teaching from there. The Egyptian prophet Calasiris, in the third book of Heliodorus’s *Ethiopian Story* <note>An ancient Greek novel, also called the *Aethiopica*; the author uses its characters as historical authorities</note> <margin>Heliodorus, Book 3, page 149, Commelin edition</margin>, even claims that Homer was an Egyptian. That Homer received many things from Egypt is correctly proven by that collection of Egyptian priests mentioned in the first book of Diodorus <margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, chapter 97</margin>. Regarding Pythagoras, Democritus, and others, this fact is known to everyone.

Furthermore, it is perhaps unnecessary to prove that some form of magical medicine was held in the highest esteem in Egypt, given the customs of the Greeks who received their teaching from there. This is sufficiently established by this single fact: that already in the time of Moses, Magic was universally and solemnly practiced by the Egyptian priests and numbered among the sacred arts. Indeed, the treatment using sea water, through which Plato recovered his health from the priests in Egypt <margin>Diogenes Laertius, in the *Life of Plato*</margin>, was certainly magical in nature. For the natural power of that water to cure diseases is not particularly great; however, its use among magicians and <term>idolaters <note>In this context, a term used by the author for practitioners of non-Christian ancient religions</note></term> was frequent for all purifications and <term>expiations <note>Rituals of spiritual or physical cleansing</note></term>. To this end, that little verse of Plato’s is relevant:
> The sea washes away all the evils of men. <note>original Greek: "θάλασσα κλύζει πάντα τ' ἀνθρώπων κακά"</note>

They write that Acron, the leader of the Empiric sect <note>Acron of Agrigentum (5th century BCE) was a physician. Furthermore, it is not immediately clear how fire could have restrained the heat of Sirius <note>The "Dog Star," the brightest star in the sky.
