Indeed, we have heard that the people of Ceos <note>An island in the Aegean Sea.</note> are accustomed to watch the rising of the Dog Star diligently every year and to form a conjecture (*as Ponticus Heraclides writes*) as to whether the coming year will be healthy or pestilential. For if the star appears somewhat faint or misty, they believe the sky is thick and dense, so that its breath will be heavy and pestilential. But if the star appears bright and translucent, it signifies that the sky is thin and pure, and therefore healthy. Nevertheless, it is hardly likely that such defects of the air were "burned away," as it were, by Iachenes <note>Likely referring to a specific Egyptian priest or sage mentioned in the preceding context.</note> through the use of fire. It is more likely that fire was used for the sake of expiation <term>expiatio</term> <note>A ritual cleansing or atonement intended to remove religious or physical impurity.</note>; for this purpose, fire was once adopted by almost all nations throughout the whole world. It is certain that among the priests in Egypt, fire and frequent fumigations were used for the same goal. Nor would one rashly accept the claims reported by Plutarch, as if these practices were instituted solely for the sake of physical health and for purifying the air.

Thus says Plutarch. These explanations will not be easily accepted by anyone who is aware of the ancient frequency of fumigations in all sacred rites. It is ridiculous to claim that these were instituted among all nations solely for the purpose of correcting the air from natural defects, especially since it is clear that everywhere on earth, men expected much greater and more divine benefits for the soul from those fumigations. However the use of fire stood among the Egyptians—both that which was commonly accepted and that which was first praised by Iachene <note>Iachene (or Jachas) is a figure mentioned in the Suda encyclopedia as a master of medical magic</note>—it is abundantly clear from the words of Suidas cited above that Iachene, relying as much as possible on magical powers, made medicine easier.

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 25.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus reports, based on the faith of the Egyptians: *that she [Isis] discovered a "medicine of immortality" <note>original Greek: Φάρμακον ἀθανασίας (pharmakon athanasias)</note>, by which she not only restored the soul and brought back to life her son Horus—who had been overcome by the snares of the Titans and found dead in the waters—but also made him a sharer in immortality.* This report undoubtedly moved the common Egyptians to believe that some drug of this kind truly exists in the nature of things, and thus it stirred many to search for it. It is indeed not unlike the truth that, perhaps on this occasion, a certain Egyptian philosopher <margin>Galen, *On Wasting*, chapters 2 & 4.</margin> attempted to teach the method of "not aging" <note>original Greek: ἀγερασίας (agerasias)—the prevention of old age or preservation of youth</note>, whom our Galen ridicules in his *Book on Wasting* <note>Latin: *liber de marcore*</note>.

Finally, it must also be observed that in Egypt there were formerly frequent cures of diseases through remedies indicated by the gods to sick people as they slept <note>This refers to the practice of "incubation," where the sick slept in temples hoping for a dream-vision from a god providing a cure</note>. For we have already mentioned at the beginning of this small book that the shrines of Isis, Horus, and Serapis were held in great renown for this. In that same place <margin>See above, chapter 2, pages 8 & 9.</margin>, it is also told from the Hermetic *Perfect Discourse* <note>Latin: *Sermo Perfectus*, an important Hermetic philosophical text also known as the *Asclepius*</note> that in the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine, often used here to refer to the Egyptian deity Imhotep</note>, which was near the "Crocodile Coast," the sick recovered their health. That the same occurred <margin>Galen, Book 5, *On Medicines According to Kind*, chapter 1.</margin> in the *Hephaesteum*, or Temple of Vulcan <note>The Egyptian creator-god Ptah was identified by the Greeks and Romans with Hephaestus and Vulcan</note>, near Memphis, is clear from the medications which Heras of Cappadocia, according to Galen, recited as having been received from that temple. At the very least, those remedies which Heras lists forbid us from doubting that in this way remedies were sometimes revealed to the sick that were equal in natural power to curing the disease. Moreover, all those things which they once heard from the voice of Isis seem to have been handed down in a similar manner; they are found not only in Galen but also in the works of Celsus, Aëtius, [Paulus] Aegineta, and others. Galen relates <margin>Galen, Book 9, *On Simple Medicines*, chapter 2.</margin> that some were warned in their sleep to use rich Egyptian mud with success, while others, relying only on their own judgment, experienced the same benefit. Although truly not—

### CHAPTER XI.

...this never happened in such a way, it is nevertheless mostly likely that those things indicated, which could only serve as symbols, were given the power of healing by demons <note>The author uses "demons" here in the Renaissance sense—spiritual entities, often associated with pagan gods, who could manipulate the natural world to perform "miracles" that were not truly divine.</note>. For it is clear from the sacred volumes of both testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments of the Bible</note> that something similar was observed even by the Best and Greatest God; it is a common habit for demons to emulate His works in a truly wretched crime. Let those four marble inscription tablets found in the Temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; his temple in Rome was located on the Tiber Island</note> at Rome testify to this, which the most learned Mercurialis reports in the first book of <margin>*Mercurialis, Book 1, Chapter 1.*</margin> *On the Art of Gymnastics*. For none of those things, by which those four sick persons are written to have recovered their health, had any power to cure diseases. Indeed, similar stories are read everywhere.

By this very fact, the lie of those who accuse the excellent Hippocrates of Cos <note>Often called the "Father of Medicine," Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) moved medicine away from the supernatural toward observation and logic.</note> is made manifest—as if, after the Temple of Aesculapius was burned, he stole for himself the recorded remedies and thereby acquired such a great name for himself. For, to say nothing now of the fact that skill in pharmacology <note>original Greek: τῆς ὕλης ἰατρικῆς (tēs hylēs iatrikēs)—literally "of medical matter"</note> was the smallest part of Hippocrates' glory, what could he have achieved with those remedies of Aesculapius, most of which lacked any natural healing power? Furthermore, since the nature of those sacred medicines was undoubtedly the same as those which the Egyptian demons once revealed to sick people sleeping in the temple, it is manifest that this mode of healing was also supernatural <note>original Greek: ὑπερφυσικὸν (hyperphysikon)</note>, and for that reason, it did not advance the medical art with true, certain, and natural remedies.

These are nearly all the things that remain in the most ancient monuments concerning the whole of the medicine of the ancient Egyptians. It is not difficult, however, to pass judgment once these have been weighed. First, therefore, since the medical art [cannot exist] without an accurate knowledge of the human body and its unnatural afflictions...

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...since it could not be established by fixed laws, and that of the Egyptians was very unrefined and partly absurd, it was certainly far from true that this art reached any particular perfection through the care of the Egyptians. In this respect, it must have been much inferior to the Greek tradition <note>original: "Graecanica"</note>. 

Furthermore, given that nation's superstition and their praise of the magical arts, it was hardly possible for many natural remedies for diseases to be discovered through honest experimentation. For it almost always happens where magic is held in high regard that the things nature provides are despised; nor can those natural remedies easily be distinguished from others, since the power of demons so thoroughly mingles with nature that their deceptions <note>original: "ludibria," implying mocking tricks or illusions</note> very frequently creep into its place. 

Nor is there any reason to attribute that magical medicine to the secret forces of nature <note>original: "arcanis naturae viribus"</note>, as Johannes Langius <note>Johannes Lang (1485–1565), a German physician who published "Medicinal Epistles" exploring the history of medicine</note> and others do. For it is abundantly clear from what we have said that the Egyptians themselves attributed it to their own gods. 

And indeed, it is certain that neither incantations, nor offerings to demons, nor engraved figures, nor inscribed characters can add any natural power to herbs or stones. They are clearly effective only as symbols, based on a pact—whether silent or expressed—with guardian spirits <note>original: "geniorum"</note>, or simply with supernatural spirits <note>original Greek: ὑπερφυσικῶν; meaning those existing above or beyond nature</note>. Therefore, if those spirits withdraw their power, such things are worthless and are, as it were, mere mockery. 

No one will doubt that it was not good spirits but evil ones that lent their labor to the Egyptians, unless they are unaware that the Egyptians were the most superstitious worshipers of demons among all men. And indeed, among the pious who are faithful to the one Creator God, the reason why all those once-praised Egyptian remedies have no power today, now that the cult of demons has been destroyed, is none other than that the demons are no longer able to bestow power upon their former symbols. Indeed...

<margin>Aëtius, Book 1, Chapter 2, Tetrabiblos 1</margin>

For no other reason, it seems, did the reputation of Egyptian medicine immediately decline among the Greeks. For that nation <note>the Greeks</note>, persuaded by their own philosophers, so thoroughly despised the commonly accepted religion of demons <note>original: "religionem dæmonum," referring to the worship of intermediary spirits or lesser deities</note>—especially from the age of Alexander the Great onward—that in the end few seemed to remain, and then only among the common people, who still heartily approved of the public rites inherited from their ancestors. Offended by this contempt, the demons themselves seem to have ceased being beneficial. For this very reason, Egyptian medicine could not help but collapse at the same time, as it was poorly equipped with remedies established within the limits of nature. 

Certainly, even that medicine of Nechepsos <note>Nechepsos: A legendary Egyptian Pharaoh to whom many early astrological and medical texts were attributed</note>, which might be considered to rely on the powers of the stars, if it had any value, it was only through the aid of demons. This is clear from what we have already presented regarding the decans <note>term: decans <gloss>36 groups of stars used in Egyptian astronomy to divide the sky and represent various spiritual influences over the body</gloss></note> and their worship. Nor would I say that he handed down nothing in the way of natural medicines, since I see some of that kind cited by Aëtius <note>Aëtius of Amida: A 6th-century Greek medical compiler</note> regarding chamomile, "Jewish stone" <note>term: Jewish stone <gloss>Lapis Judaicus; a fossilized sea-urchin spine used historically to treat kidney stones</gloss></note>, and the "Armenian stone" used by painters <note>term: Armenian stone <gloss>Lapis Armenius; a blue mineral pigment, likely azurite, used medicinally as a purgative</gloss></note>. But this is a small amount, almost nothing. I do not doubt that Athanasius Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher: A famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar known for his attempts to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, a man most outstanding in intellect and learning, will bring forth little of this sort in his "Hieroglyphic Medicine," which he recently did not hesitate to promise to posterity.

However, these matters are not of such weight that you should rightly doubt the truth of what we have said. This truth will become most evident if we look a little more deeply into all the ancient wisdom of the Egyptians. Therefore, it is certainly true that in that nation there was once great value and authority placed upon learning. For just as by the institution of God Himself among the Hebrew people, an entire tribe <note>The Tribe of Levi.</note> of a very numerous nation was dedicated to the care of sacred things—remaining immune from agricultural labor, taxes, and other burdens—so in Egypt, the occupation concerning sacred matters was hereditary among many priestly families. Their authority was so great that, while all the lands of the entire region were divided into three parts, *the order of Priests claimed the first portion for themselves; they were constantly present with the king as the leading members of the senate, assisting him with their effort, counsel, and learning; moreover, being immune from all burdens, they held the first rank of honor and power from the king*, as witnessed by Diodorus Siculus; a view in which Herodotus, Strabo, and others concur. In that state of leisure, authority, and abundance of all things, it likewise cannot be denied that some of the priests devoted their minds to the study of wisdom; especially since this is consistently testified by many authors...

It is likely that it was Hecataeus of Miletus, the son of Hegesander. For **Herodotus** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note> testifies that this man spent time in Egypt with the priests during the age of Darius Hystaspes. **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> agrees regarding his era; thus, those most learned men are mistaken who claim that he described the war of the Greeks against Xerxes, since he only dealt with the war that Darius waged against the Greeks, as is clear from Herodotus himself. **Suidas** is also the authority for the fact that Sanchunathon, Philistus, and Palaephatus committed Egyptian Theology to writing. **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop, essential for preserving fragments of lost ancient works.</note> writes in the second book of *On Principles* <note>original Greek: *peri archōn*</note> that **Manetho** <note>An Egyptian priest who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek in the 3rd century BCE.</note> did the same, both "in the Sacred Book" <note>original Greek: *en tē hiera biblō*</note> and in other commentaries; as does **Theodoretus** in his second book *Against the Greeks*. Although all these works are lost, it is nevertheless possible to form an opinion about the wisdom of the Egyptians from certain other remains: just as the lion is revealed by its claws, so the ass is revealed by its ears. <note>A proverbial expression meaning that a small part can reveal the true nature of the whole.</note>

<margin>
*Diodorus, Book 1.*
*Eusebius, Book 2 of the Preparation, chapter 1.*
*Eusebius, Book 3 of the Preparation, chapter 3.*
*See Eusebius, Book 3 of the Preparation, chapters 4, 7, 11, 12, and 13.*
</margin>
To begin, therefore, with theology—at least as it was commonly known to the public—**Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> related it quite extensively at the beginning of his historical work, which **Eusebius** later condensed into an epitome. For with few exceptions, those things found in **Herodotus** and others of that kind can be read in **Diodorus**. The more arcane <note>Hidden or secret.</note> doctrine of the Egyptians is not presented in the same way by everyone. Indeed, **Diodorus** delivered it in summary form (according to the mind of **Manetho**, as **Eusebius** indicates elsewhere); however, **Chaeremon**, the Egyptian priest and scribe, explained it differently in *Porphyry’s Letter to Anebo*; **Plutarch** differently in his book *On Isis and Osiris*; **Porphyry** differently in the works of **Eusebius**; and **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> has several other views in his work *On the Mysteries*, not to mention the interpretations of others. ...they argued that these were not true gods but evil demons who had feigned some divine appearance. Nor indeed was Iamblichus equal to resolving the doubts of Porphyry; he was, of course, forced to admit that impure demons frequently present themselves in sacred rites in place of good gods, and that those whom Porphyry criticizes are of such a nature. <margin><unclear>Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, Book 2</unclear></margin> But in truth, it was not just some, but all of them—even the greatest: I say Osiris himself, Isis herself, Pan himself, Ammon himself, and other credited gods—who, when petitioned by their worshipers, inflicted injury, aided illicit intercourse, and incited shameful lusts, which Porphyry recognized as being inconsistent with the nature of gods. <margin><unclear>Ibid. n. 3</unclear></margin> Nor were they any different who allowed themselves to be driven by the threats of puny men <note>Latin: *homuncionum*, a disparaging term for "little men"</note> to perform certain tasks. <margin>Porphyry, cited in Eusebius, Book 5, ch. 10</margin>
> *What is most absurd of all is that not merely against some common demon or the soul of a deceased person, but against the Sun itself—the prince of the stars—against the Moon, and the rest of the celestial Gods, a man from the very dregs of the people intends threats, and to compel them to speak the truth, he displays a false terror. For he threatens to announce the future by shaking the very heavens, or by revealing the secrets of Isis, or by bringing to light the unspeakable mystery hidden at Abydos <note>A sacred city in Egypt, the mythical burial place of Osiris</note>, or by halting the course of the Egyptian ship <note>likely referring to the solar barque</note>, or by scattering the limbs of Osiris for the sake of Typhon <note>The Greek name for Set, the antagonist of Osiris</note>. I ask, what remains but the height of stupidity and madness for the one threatening these things (which he neither knows how to do nor can achieve)? And for the Divine Powers, whom this fictitious and empty terror strikes like little children, what remains but the depth of humiliation?* 

And yet, all these things Chaeremon, that sacred scribe, wrote down as if they had long been spoken by the mouths of all Egyptians.

### CHAPTER XII.

*...which indeed, like others of the same kind, they say are most powerful for compelling the gods by force.* <note>original: Latin – *ad vim diis afferendam*</note> All these things Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who often critiqued traditional religious practices</note> relates: which indeed clearly show what kind of beings the supreme gods of the Egyptians themselves were. Because mention is made of this so frequently in the Hermetic books, many have been deceived into thinking they speak of true piety, when nevertheless, beneath that fair-sounding voice lurks a most impious **demon-madness**. <note>original Greek: *daimonomania*</note>

That the world was created by God, and that it would one day perish, was indeed an opinion held by the ancients and the Egyptians. However, not even in this matter did the Egyptians deserve the praise of wisdom above others. For the fact that the world indeed once had a beginning does not seem to have been unknown to any nation of old. ...from body to body, and specifically from the human body into bodies of every kind of brute animal. For **Herodotus** <note>A 5th-century BC Greek historian, often called "The Father of History."</note> speaks well of them:

<margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin>
> *They were the first to appear who said that the human soul is immortal, and that it would continually migrate from a dead body into another and another as they are born; and when it had moved through all creatures of the land, sea, and air, it would again enter into some newly born human body, and from this, a cycle would be completed within three thousand years.*

<margin>Stobaeus, Book 2, *Physical Eclogues*, page 202, Plantin edition.</margin>
I will not touch upon how absurd it is to say that souls first fell from heaven into punishment, and that for them, the inhabitation of bodies is a form of penalty. We find this opinion throughout our **Hermetic books** <note>The *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, but it is found most fully in those fragments of **Porphyry’s** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of early Christianity.</note> small book *On what has been said [about the soul]* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν εἰρημένων (peri tōn eirēmenōn)</note> which **Stobaeus** <note>A 5th-century compiler who preserved extracts from many lost Greek works.</note> preserved. Thus far, certainly, no traces of "great wisdom" appear among the Egyptians; and yet they formerly acquired a great name for themselves, especially for their skill in sacred matters.

<margin>Origen, Book 1, *Against Celsus*.</margin>
How much more correctly **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note> speaks! *But let Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and critic of Christianity.</note> *be persuaded by the fable of conflagrations and floods, since he considers his own most wise Egyptians as its authors: traces of whose wisdom are found in the animals they worship, and in the commentaries of those who provide a more hidden reason for this kind of mystical cult. Those men are considered wise while they extol their own theology concerning animals; but he who agrees with the Law and the Lawgiver of the Jews, if he refers everything to God alone as the creator of the universe, will—in the judgment of Celsus and his like—be considered more unlearned than the one who, asserting the fabulous migrations of the soul from body to body, leads it not only into rational and mortal animals but even into those lacking reason.*

<meta>This page continues the critique of Egyptian intellectual tradition, moving from their beliefs about the soul to their natural philosophy and medical foundations. # ON HERMETIC MEDICINE.
<meta>catchword: doubts and (Latin: dubiaq.)</meta>

Since the medical art is, as it were, a branch of natural philosophy, and since that philosophy among the Egyptians labored greatly under vanity and magical superstition, it is already clear what sort of philosophy this was of the Egyptians; namely, of the very same character as their medicine. Indeed, one may seek many signs of its vanity and superstition from other sources as well. How foolishly infected with fables the natural history of the Egyptians truly was is shown abundantly by the two small books on hieroglyphs by Horapollo <note>Horapollo was the purported author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs that interpreted them as purely symbolic allegories rather than a phonetic script.</note>, to say nothing of the *Kyranides* <note>The *Kyranides* is a famous ancient compendium of magico-medical lore, traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, detailing the "virtues" of plants, stones, and animals.</note> and others. For no history of any plant or animal is free from old wives' tales—or rather, monstrous lies—as is manifest to those who weigh these things and are knowledgeable of the truth. I remain silent regarding phoenixes, sphinxes, and other animals of that kind, born entirely from Egyptian fictions.

Furthermore, how unsuccessful they were in explaining the causes of things is best proven by their teaching on the rising of the Nile. For Egypt owes a great part of its prosperity to this river, and every year the inhabitants were struck by its rising; and yet, far more certain explanations were brought forward by the Greeks than could be produced by the priestly order over long intervals of centuries.

<margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin> Herodotus relates in *Euterpe* <note>Euterpe is the traditional title of the second book of Herodotus's *Histories*, which focuses extensively on Egypt.</note> that in his age, the Egyptian priests were able to discuss nothing regarding the causes of this phenomenon.

<margin>Strabo, Book 17</margin> Strabo also records that before the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 283–246 BCE), a patron of the sciences who funded expeditions to find the source of the Nile.</note>, neither any of the kings nor the Egyptian priests knew the true cause of the river's rising. He marvels at this, *since the priests would quite carefully record in their sacred books and confirm those things which possessed some measure of more subtle knowledge.*

<margin>Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 37</margin> Diodorus Siculus seems to have encountered some who attempted something in this matter, though foolishly. *The Egyptian priests,* he says, *asserted that the Nile is born from the Ocean that flows around the earth.* But they record nothing sound.

<summary>The author critiques Egyptian natural philosophy and medicine as being rooted in superstition and "monstrous lies," citing their inability to explain the flooding of the Nile as proof of their scientific failure compared to the Greeks.</summary>

<margin>The same, Book 1, chapter 40.</margin>
and when he had refuted it, he adds: *“While the authors of opinions that cannot easily be disproven interpose an uninhabitable part of the world, they think that in this way they will escape the arguments of a solid refutation.”* But it is only right that those who assert anything certain about any matter should either bring forward the thing itself as testimony or assume demonstrations granted from the start. What indeed so great a number of priests, swollen with the reputation of wisdom, could not achieve over so many centuries, was already easily discovered by Aristotle. For he too, on the testimony of Posidonius, attributed the annual rising of the Nile to rains falling in the farthest reaches of Ethiopia during the summer; whether he was taught by some Thrasyalces <note>Thrasyalces of Thasos was an early Greek thinker who theorized about the winds and the Nile.</note> or other, or relied on the powers of his own genius. And indeed, mention of those rains is made in our surviving work, the *Meteorology*, *book 1, chapter 12*; just as the source of the Nile is said to be from what is called the Silver Mountain <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ Ἀργύρου καλουμένου ὄρους</note> in the chapter immediately following. So that subsequently, 
<margin>Strabo, Book 17.</margin>
taking Aristotle as their leader, Eratosthenes (as cited in Strabo), and 
<margin>Diodorus, Book 1, chapter 17.</margin>
Agatharchides of Cnidus (as cited in Diodorus), as well as Posidonius the Stoic and others followed him, agreeing with the same opinion after the truth of the matter had been explored by King Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE) sponsored expeditions to the interior of Africa to find the source of the Nile.</note>. For as to the fact that the Egyptian priests also partially approved of this, as Horapollo states in *Hieroglyphics*, *Book 1, chapter 21*, it undoubtedly reached them at last from the teachings of the Greeks. For they seem rather to have attributed everything to the powers of Sirius <note>The "Dog Star," whose rising coincided with the Nile's flood.</note>, just as the word "Sirius" itself seems to have arisen from *Siris* <note>original Greek: Σίεις</note>; which is how Dionysius the Voyager <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a geographer of the 2nd century CE.</note> states the Nile was named by the Ethiopians.

There is no evidence that the Egyptians’ investigation into other natural matters turned out more successfully; indeed, it lacks all probability, especially since it is already well-established that they spoke nonsense regarding natural history. And truly, it could not have happened otherwise than that they stumbled everywhere in the investigation of natural causes, being so deeply entangled in superstitions and exposed to the delusions of demons. For this reason, in nearly all things, they recognized something <term>supernatural<note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ φυσικὸν (hyper physikon). The author argues that instead of looking for physical causes, the Egyptians immediately jumped to mystical or divine explanations.</note></term> to which they ascribed their effects; they also attributed many powers to nature that far exceeded its capacity, as if such powers were inherent to it. Nor did they convince themselves of this only regarding the celestial bodies,

<margin>Herodotus, Book 3.</margin>
but even regarding those things which are right here among us. *Thus, as Herodotus testifies, it was believed that Fire was a living beast that devoured everything that is born, and after it had been filled by devouring, it died along with the very thing it had consumed.* <note>The Greeks often contrasted their own "rational" view of elements with the Egyptian view of elements as living, divine entities.</note> In all Waters, they recognized something divine,

### CHAPTER XII. 135

*...or the earth, or the nature of things underlying the sun: for this reason, the whole body of the goddess is made dense with continuous breasts, because the universe is nourished by the earth or by the deep nature of things.* <note>The author is likely quoting a description of the "Many-Breasted" goddess, often identified with Isis or Cybele, representing the nurturing power of Nature.</note> I omit other testimonies on the rest.

<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*</margin>
Those who have philosophized about the elements in this way undoubtedly spread the same errors into the doctrine of things formed from the physical mixing of those elements. Of such a kind, indeed, is that doctrine regarding **Salt**: which it was a sin for Egyptian priests to bring to the table, because they said it was the foam of **Typhon** <note>In Egyptian mythology, Typhon (the Greek name for Set) represented chaos, the desert, and the sterile sea, as opposed to the life-giving Nile.</note>, as Plutarch is the authority. It was as if, forsooth, something malignant and <term>supernatural<note>original Greek: ὑπερφυσικὸν (hyperphysikon)</note></term> lay hidden in salt.

From the same source comes their abstinence from eating **fish**. For thus Herodotus says in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note>: <gloss>it is a sin to taste of fish</gloss>. The cause was undoubtedly no other than that at least sea fish were believed to belong to Typhon, while those of the Nile were perhaps sacred to **Osiris**.

<margin>Horapollo, Book 1, Hieroglyphics 42.</margin>
For as Horapollo says: <gloss>every fish is a "maker of emptiness" and a "devourer of its own kind,"</gloss> <note>original Greek: κενοποιὸν ἰχθὺς πᾶς καὶ ἀλληλοφάγον. This refers to the belief that fish were either nutritionally useless or inherently violent because they eat one another.</note> perhaps this is not from the doctrine of the Egyptians; yet if it is, it proves their utter vanity beyond their superstition. For a fish is not more of an "emptiness-maker" or "cannibal" than other animals; and even if it were, the reason for their abstinence from eating them is not apparent.

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 15. See also Herodotus, Book 2.</margin>
Furthermore, it is clear from **Juvenal** that our conjecture is more likely; seeing as he teaches that some of the Egyptians worshipped the fish of the river, or the Nilotic fish: so that, consequently, not every fish was <term>forbidden or an abomination<note>original Greek: ἀθέμιτον ἢ μῦσος (athemiton e mysos)</note></term> to the Egyptians. By a similar madness, it seemed to the Egyptians:

> *It is a sin to violate a leek or onion and to break them with a bite.*

For the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal, known for mocking Egyptian customs.</note> confirms that they recognized something divine in these plants in that mocking little verse immediately following:

> *O holy nations, for whom these divinities grow in the gardens!*

### CHAPTER XII.

...we shall speak, and in predicting they made more use of these fallacious dreams than of stars and planets. *Heliodorus* writes that *Mercury Trismegistus*, who first discovered the *Lots* <note>original: *Partes*, referring to the Arabic Parts or Hermetic Lots—mathematical points in a horoscope calculated from the distances between planets</note> of the planets, opened the way so that through those *Lots* alone, with no other thing being considered, judgment could be pronounced about all things equally. It is remarkable how much they attribute to *Monomeria* <note>the doctrine that each individual degree of a zodiac sign has its own specific planetary influence</note> and *Dodecathemoria* <note>original: *Dodecathemoriis*, a system where each 30-degree zodiac sign is subdivided into twelve parts of 2.5 degrees each</note> in every prediction. Whence *Ptolemy*, the most prudent of astrologers, noting them indirectly, says that he will hand down his teachings "not by means of lots and numbers without cause" <note>original Greek: μὴ διὰ κληρῶν καὶ ἀριθμῶν ἀναιτιολογήτων</note>: which are all "superfluously babbled about by the many and possess no persuasive reason," <note>original Greek: περιττῶς ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν φλυαρούμενα καὶ μὴ πιθανὸν ἔχοντα λόγον</note> *that is, not through parts and ineffective numbers, which have no rational cause, and which many people tell as fables without any reasoning to convince.* 

When he mentions numbers, he is noting both the *Dodecathemoria* <note>the twelvefold divisions of signs</note> which we criticize, and those who determine *Climacteric* <note>critical periods in a person's life thought to be governed by specific number cycles</note> years from the observation of numbers alone, such as the *enneadics* <note>years occurring in multiples of nine</note> and *hebdomadics* <note>years occurring in multiples of seven</note>. From this comes the superstition, troublesome to many old men, concerning the sixty-third year <note>Known as the "Grand Climacteric" (7 x 9 = 63), it was historically feared as a year of great peril or death</note>, which they dread worse than a snake or a tiger. Thus says *Pico* <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a 15th-century philosopher whose "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology" heavily influenced later skepticism</note>. It seems that even *Chaeremon* himself, a sacred scribe of the Egyptians, recognized the 
<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*, near the end.</margin>
vanity of his own astrology, as one who—according to the testimony of *Porphyry* in his letter to *Anebo*—said that the rules of astronomy and astrology are *incomprehensible and uncertain*; *Porphyry* agrees with this pronouncement, while *Iamblichus* barely dared to offer a slight resistance.

It does not escape me, however, that the Egyptians once achieved a great reputation for the faculty of divination. *Diodorus Siculus* <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote a monumental universal history</note> speaks thus: *"They have eagerly and at great expense recorded the motions and circuits and stations of the planets, and the powers of each concerning the birth of living things—what good or what evil they may effect—and predicting the occurrences of life that will often happen, they pre-signify those things that will fall upon men or cattle. They also [predict] earthquakes and floods, and the rising of comets, and all such things the knowledge of which is commonly thought to exceed human capability, from the observation of a long time..."*

...Indeed, that Egyptian astrology was much like the study of portents, about which Herodotus wrote: <margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin> *Furthermore, more portents have been discovered by them than by any other people. For when a portent occurs, they record it, observing how it turned out. And if something similar happens again later, they expect it to turn out according to the previous example.* <note>The author is quoting Herodotus's *Histories* (2.82), where the historian describes the Egyptian habit of meticulous record-keeping to predict the future based on past coincidences.</note> And although Herodotus seems to have believed this Egyptian doctrine was of great value, it was actually quite empty, as is shown more fully elsewhere. Indeed, divination among the Egyptians was considered a gift of the gods, and therefore their oracles were consulted by those eager to know the future; however, their prophets <note>original: "vates"—referring to the human speakers or priests who interpreted the divine will.</note> were not listened to in the same way—unlike the custom that prevailed everywhere else. Herodotus also reported this very thing: <margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin> *Divination,* he says, *is so established among them that the skill of it is not claimed by any mortal, but only by certain gods.*

Since theology, natural philosophy, and astrology were conducted in this manner among the Egyptians, it is clear to everyone what kind of thing their much-celebrated Magic was. It was certainly not truly "natural," since their magical effects far exceeded the forces of nature; they themselves even recognized a power **beyond nature** <gloss>original Greek: ὑπὲρ φύσιν [hyper physin]</gloss> within natural things. We should certainly not agree with Origen <margin>Origen, Book 1, *Against Celsus*</margin> when he says that there are certain **efficacious** <gloss>original Greek: ἐνεργῆ [energe]</gloss> names used by the Egyptian sages, or by the chief Magi among the Persians, or by the Brahmans and Samanaeans <note>The Samanaeans were ancient Indian ascetic philosophers, often identified by Western writers with Buddhist monks or wandering practitioners.</note> who philosophized among the Indians. Nor did they perform such great feats by the help of good spirits; for they were solely occupied in the worship of evil demons, however much they believed they were dealing with good gods. Indeed, the Egyptians even seem to have used some of the sacred ceremonies of the Hebrews for magical use. For also...

<margin>Clement, Book 4 of the *Recognitions*</margin>
It is far from likely that the magical arts first began in Egypt, even though the Egyptians were those magicians whose earliest mention appears in our sacred histories <note>A reference to the magicians of Pharaoh's court who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus</note>. Indeed, several points in the same vein are reported in the books of the *Recognitions*, which are attributed to Clement of Rome <note>The *Recognitions* is a 4th-century Christian philosophical novel falsely attributed to Pope Clement I; it was a popular source for legends about the early Church and its enemies</note>. The words themselves deserve to be read here:

> *They taught men that demons could be made to obey mortals through certain arts—that is, through magical invocations. Like a furnace or a workshop of malice, they filled the whole world with the smoke of impiety, after the light of piety had been withdrawn. For these and several other reasons, a flood was brought upon the world, and all who were upon the lands were destroyed, except for the family of Noah, who survived with his three sons and their wives. One of these sons, named Ham, passed on this ill-discovered discipline to one of his own sons called Mizraim, from whom the race of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians is derived. The nations that existed then called him Zoroaster, admiring him as the first author of the magical art; many books on this subject are still held in his name.*

Thus writes that author, though by what authority I do not know; perhaps by none truly worthy of belief. For it is not likely that historians can be found who are able to narrate such things with certain reliability. Furthermore, while it is indeed certain that the Egyptians originated from Mizraim <note>Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt and its legendary progenitor in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10)</note>, it is hardly probable regarding the Babylonians and Persians, so far as we can gather by conjecture from what is read in the eleventh chapter of Genesis. Whatever the truth of this may be, it remains clear that magical arts once flourished in Egypt. We have already established above that their medicine was also magical for the most part, and that Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary "Thrice-Great" Egyptian sage credited with the foundation of alchemy, magic, and astrology</note> was a magician. But more on these matters elsewhere. It is clear from what we have said so far how full of impious superstition those branches of wisdom were in which the Egyptians most boasted—namely, *Theology*, *Physics* <note>In this period, "Physics" referred to "Natural Philosophy" or the study of nature, rather than the modern laboratory science</note>, and the *Magical Art*. They seem to have earned better praise in the mathematical disciplines: *Arithmetic*, *Geometry*, and especially *Astronomy*. Indeed, Aristotle is also an authority for the claim that mathematics was first established in Egypt, and there is hardly any witness more reliable than he. 

Yet they are not equally commended by everyone for their skill in *Arithmetic*. In fact, Strabo expressly writes that while *Geometry* was invented by the Egyptians, *but logistics and arithmetic were invented through the Phoenicians, for the sake of their trade* <note>original Greek: "τὴν δ' λογιστικὴν καὶ Ἀριθμητικὴν διὰ τῶν Φοινίκων, Διὰ τὰς ἐμπορίας." Strabo argues that while the Egyptians needed geometry to redraw land boundaries after the Nile flooded, the Phoenicians needed arithmetic for their vast merchant shipping networks</note>. Nevertheless, Diogenes Laertius testifies that the Egyptians themselves boasted of being the first authors of *Arithmetic* no less than of *Geometry* and *Astrology* <note>The term *Astrologia* at this time often encompassed what we now call Astronomy</note>. 

Undoubtedly, the Egyptians also scrutinized the nature of numbers more subtly, since they handled *Geometry* and *Astronomy* with such diligence; they were invited to this partly by necessity and partly by the kinship of these studies, since the courses of the stars cannot be accurately handled without the science of numbers, and the investigation of lines is very closely related to the doctrine of numbers. Diodorus also testifies most clearly that the children of the Egyptian priests were extensively trained by their parents in the studies of *Geometry* and *Arithmetic*, *since Arithmetic served them both for the other affairs of life and for the speculations of Geometry.* How much progress they made...

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...for <note>The catchword from the previous page 'enim' (for/indeed) is integrated here to complete the transition.</note> what the Egyptians once knew regarding this science of numbers is uncertain. For it is not established whether the Pythagorean philosophy of numbers originated in Egypt, or even that system which **Euclid** left behind. It is certain that the <term>Cossic doctrine</term> <note>The "Cossic" art refers to early algebra (from the Italian 'cosa' for "thing," used to represent the unknown variable 'x').</note> is more recent and is not owed to ancient Egypt. Indeed, **Diophantus**, who seems to have been the foremost to refine it, was an Alexandrian, yet of Greek rather than Egyptian origin, and he lived long after the glory of ancient Egypt had been extinguished.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1</margin> It has been passed down by many that the Egyptians cultivated Geometry, and specifically because the Nile River disturbed the boundaries of the fields every year. **Diodorus**, writing on the education of the sons of the priests, states: *They exercise them quite extensively in the studies of Geometry and Arithmetic. For because the river, overflowing every year, transforms the fields in various ways, it excites many controversies of every kind among neighbors regarding their boundaries, which it is not easy to settle exactly unless the truth is demonstrated through the skill of Geometry.* 

<margin>Strabo, Book 17</margin> **Strabo**, having said that Egypt was divided into <term>nomes</term> <note>original Greek: "νόμους"; the major administrative districts of Egypt</note>, <term>toparchies</term> <note>original Greek: "τοπαρχίας"; smaller local government sectors</note>, and after other sections into <term>arouras</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀρούρας"; a standard unit of land area used in Egypt</note>, adds: *There was a need for such diligent and subtle division of places because of the continual confusion of boundaries which the swollen Nile caused, adding to some and taking away from others, changing the shapes and burying the markers by which one's own property was distinguished from another's. Therefore, it was necessary to measure the land repeatedly; and hence they believe Geometry was invented by the Egyptians.*

<margin>Iamblichus, Book 1, Chapter 29, page 144, Commelin edition</margin> **Iamblichus** teaches exactly the same in *Book 1 on the Life of Pythagoras*: except that in place of the word "Nile," the printed volume mistakenly contains the word "Ninus" <note>Ninus was the legendary founder of Nineveh; the author notes this as a typographical or scribal error</note>, which deceived the translator to such a degree that he wrote that Geometry began in Egypt under the authority of Ninus.

### CHAPTER XII.

...for <note>original: "enim"; this word completes the thought from the previous page.</note> an accurate science of geometry is necessary for the proper measurement of places, but the aforementioned **geodesy** <note>original: "γεωδησία"; referring to the practical art of measuring land rather than theoretical geometry.</note> alone suffices, yielding much to the subtlety of true Geometry. <margin>Iamblichus, in the place cited</margin> However, we would not deny what **Iamblichus** writes: that "many problems of geometry" <note>original: "πολλὰ προβλήματα γεωμετρίας"</note> were in use among the Egyptians; and perhaps for that reason they made some worthwhile effort in that science. Certainly, they practiced in this field before the Greeks. Nevertheless, an argument that they were far below the subtlety of **Archimedes** and **Apollonius of Perga**, and indeed other Greeks, is that nowhere can one read that the Greeks received any exceptional doctrine of this science from the Egyptians, even in the times of the Ptolemaic kings themselves; on the contrary, all praise for geometric skill belonged to the Greeks alone, from the age of **Pythagoras**, or certainly from the time of **Eudoxus** and **Plato**. 

<margin>Diogenes Laërtius, *Life of Pythagoras*</margin> Regarding **Pythagoras**, Diogenes cites Apollodorus as the authority: that he sacrificed a <term>hecatomb</term> <note>A massive public sacrifice, traditionally of one hundred oxen.</note> upon "discovering that in a right-angled triangle, the side subtending the right angle is equal in power to the sides containing it." <note>original Greek: "εὑρόντα ὅτι τοῦ ὀρθογωνίου τριγώνου ἡ ὑποτείνουσα πλευρὰ ἴσον δύναται ταῖς περιεχούσαις"; this describes the Pythagorean Theorem.</note> Moreover, this is the forty-seventh proposition of **Euclid’s** first book. Therefore, either the Egyptians had not progressed this far, or they concealed this wisdom of theirs from Pythagoras. The latter is hardly likely, since he lived intimately with the priests, devoting himself to Astronomy and Geometry for twenty-two whole years, as **Iamblichus** is the authority.

One could easily bring forth similar praises of the Egyptians from other writers, but to pile them all up would perhaps be a waste of effort. For it seems so certain that the Egyptians achieved much in this field that no one can call it into doubt. And indeed, they deservedly earn praise above other peoples of the world thus far; specifically because they were, if not the first, at least among the first to investigate the courses and positions of the stars and the whole system of the heavens with diligent study and a certain curiosity. If, however, the truth must be confessed, they have not earned all the praise that is usually attributed to them by some, or which they once arrogated to themselves. First, it is not sufficiently clear whether they were the very first to be occupied with the stars or not. It is likely—based on what Josephus reports from Berosus and others, and what Alexander Polyhistor reports from Eupolemus and Artapanus in the works of Eusebius—that this type of learning first reached Egypt from the Patriarch Abraham, and thus from the Chaldeans <term>Chaldeans: a people of Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) famous in antiquity for their pioneering work in astronomy and astrology</term>. Concerning Abraham, Berosus says that he was "a great man and skilled in heavenly matters." <note>original Greek: "ἀνὴρ μέγας καὶ τὰ οὐράνια ἔμπειρος"</note> Eupolemus, speaking even more eloquently of Abraham, writes: "who indeed discovered both astrology <term>astrology: in this context, it refers to the general science of the stars, including what we now call astronomy</term> and the Chaldean art." <note>original Greek: "ὃν δὴ καὶ τὴν ἀστρολογίαν καὶ τὴν χαλδαϊκὴν εὑρεῖν"</note> Likewise, he writes that the Phoenicians learned the system of the sun's and moon's motion and other astrological matters from Abraham; and furthermore, that Abraham lived in *Heliopolis*, a city of Egypt, with the priests, and that they were taught by him...

## CHAPTER XIII.
### Our critique of Egyptian wisdom is defended against several objections.

Our judgment concerning the wisdom of the **Egyptians** has been established, unless I am mistaken, with such reasoning and weight of argument that we might safely leave this topic behind—especially since we only entered into it as the occasion arose. However, I fear that some may still be fascinated by the authority of those who think otherwise, whom we mentioned at the start of the previous discussion. Perhaps some may even be troubled by the things we ourselves brought forward there in praise of the Egyptians. Therefore, let all these matters be cleared away before we proceed, so that no material for doubt remains.

The opinion of **Francesco Patrizi** <note>Francesco Patrizi da Cherso (1529–1597) was a philosopher who sought to replace Aristotelianism with a "new philosophy" based on the Hermetic traditions, which he believed predated the Greeks.</note>, therefore, is certainly not something that should move anyone. He was indeed a man of extensive reading and varied learning, yet he possessed a less refined sharpness of judgment, especially when indulging his passions. For when he was commending **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the "Hermetic" corpus of Egyptian-Greek wisdom was attributed.</note>, he was entirely focused on birthing a "new philosophy" and was burning with hatred for the teachings of **Aristotle**...

None of the **Church Fathers** <note>The early influential Christian theologians who established the intellectual foundations of the Church.</note> approved of **Egyptian** wisdom; many, in various places, criticized its vanity. Indeed, **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), who wrote extensively on the relationship between Greek philosophy and Christianity.</note> and **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260 – 339 AD), a historian and bishop known for his "Preparation for the Gospel."</note> did so most vigorously. Nor did any of them intend to suggest that the **Greeks** owed all their erudition to the Egyptians and other barbarian sages. Rather, they were merely attempting to blunt the arrogance of the pagans of their own age, who boasted that the possession of all learning had always belonged to the Greeks alone and laughed at Christians as followers of a "barbarian" doctrine. The Fathers showed that every kind of wisdom had been cultivated by those barbarians long before the Greeks, and indeed, that the first wise men of Greece had sought many things from the Egyptians, **Phoenicians**, and others.

<margin>Eusebius, book 9, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 3.</margin>
> *As the path is more and more prepared,* says **Eusebius**, *for that greatest usefulness which flowed to the Greeks from the writings of the **Hebrews**, I thought it would be a necessary and worthwhile labor if I were to show that all that doctrine and philosophy of the Greeks, which is so greatly boasted about—as well as each of their primary disciplines and the weightier points of the art of logic—were collected by them from Barbarians everywhere. This is so that none of them may dare any longer to cast it as a reproach upon us, that we follow a religion and philosophy drawn from Barbarians within their narrow [limits...]*

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...we have held the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" here refers to sacred or hidden knowledge of the divine and nature.</note> as more important. Thus says Eusebius, and indeed most correctly. For it is truer than truth itself that those whom the Greeks called "Barbarians" <note>In this context, "Barbarian" is not an insult but a technical term for anyone who was not Greek, such as the Egyptians, Persians, or Phoenicians.</note> pursued the study of wisdom a long time before the Greeks, and that these things finally reached the Greeks from them. Indeed, this is so certain that the Greeks received their first characters for writing from the Phoenicians by way of Cadmus <note>In Greek mythology, Cadmus was the Phoenician prince who introduced the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>. And truly, this is the very thing that once the most prudent among the Greeks themselves freely confessed; it is with their own testimonies that Tatian, Clement, Eusebius, and others successfully fight their battle on this argument. Furthermore, we heard above that even Aristotle himself admitted that the mathematical arts were first established in Egypt, and that the motions of the stars had already been observed for many centuries by the Egyptians and Chaldeans; this was a type of discipline that had only just begun in Greece yesterday, so to speak.

*Some assert (these are the words of Diogenes Laërtius) that philosophy took its beginnings from the Barbarians. For there were the Magi among the Persians, the Chaldeans among the Babylonians or Assyrians, the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked wise men," referring to ancient Indian philosophers/ascetics.</note> among the Indians, and among the Celts or those called Gauls, the Druids and the Semnothei, just as Aristotle says in his "Magicus," and Sotion in the thirteenth book of his "Succession." Furthermore, they say Ochus was a Phoenician, Zamolxis a Thracian, and Atlas a Libyan.* The rest of the discourse may be sought from the preface of his work *On the Lives of the Philosophers*.

And indeed, Diogenes attempted to refute that claim quite ridiculously: <note>original Greek: "λανθάνουσι δὲ αὐτούς τὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων κατορθώματα, ἀφ’ ὧν μὴ ὅτι γε Φιλοσοφία ἀλλὰ καὶ γένος ἀνθρώπων ἦρξε, Βαρβάροις προσάπτοντες. ἰδὲ γοῦν παρὰ μὲν Ἀθηναίοις γέγονε Μουσαῖος, παρὰ δὲ Θηβαίοις Λίνος."</note> "They overlook the achievements of the Greeks—from whom not only philosophy but even the human race began—by attributing them to Barbarians. Behold, for instance, Musaeus was among the Athenians, and Linus among the Thebans."

I say Diogenes says these things ridiculously. For there was surely very little wisdom in either Linus or Musaeus; this is a fact admitted by all the Greek philosophers, for they never earned the title of "sages" among their own people. And so that they might be...

### CHAPTER XIII.

...it was said that a Jewish woman had substituted her infant, whom she first named Moyses; later, however, the Greeks called him Musaeus once he had reached manhood. <margin>Strabo, Book 17.</margin>

However, we must carefully observe both that specific time period and what the Greeks actually brought back with them from Egypt. The last men recorded to have gone there are **Plato**, **Eudoxus of Cnidus** <note>A famous Greek astronomer and mathematician.</note>, and **Euripides**. From that point on, however, Egyptian discipline seems to have fallen into such contempt among the Greek people that, under the reigns of the Ptolemaic kings themselves, it collapsed for the most part—even though those kings cultivated the study of literature by offering the most generous rewards. The things written by the most learned Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian whose "Geographica" is a key source for ancient history.</note> concerning **Heliopolis**—a city once especially famous for its reputation for wisdom—are worthy of mention:

> In Heliopolis we saw spacious houses where the priests used to live. For they maintain that this was formerly the residence of priests—men devoted to **Philosophy** and **Astronomy**. It is well established among the learned that Eudoxus of Cnidus learned much of the science of the stars in Egypt. *Pamphila reports that Thales of Miletus, having been taught the precepts of Geometry by the Egyptians, was the first to describe a right-angled triangle within a circle, and for that reason sacrificed an ox*; though others attribute this to Pythagoras, according to Diogenes Laertius. <margin>Diogenes Laertius, in his *Life of Thales*.</margin> It is certain, as Laertius also relates, that Thales associated familiarly with the Egyptian priests. So that it should not be doubted that he was instructed in astronomical matters by the Egyptians. And indeed, since he is the leader of astrology among the Greeks...

To those weighing all these things accurately, it is certainly clear that what we said before is true: only those things pertaining to religion, magic, civil laws, and mathematical disciplines reached the Greeks from the Egyptians. The same reasoning applies to Egyptian Magic, which some likewise brought in part into Greece. But when both the impiety and vanity of it were perceived by the wiser Greeks, almost no one from then on did not despise and cast all these things aside.

However, we have demonstrated above that the doctrine of the Egyptians was not free from errors. Consequently, along with the truth, errors also passed from Egypt into Greece. Indeed, it was by the instruction of the Egyptians that **Thales of Miletus** <note>Considered the first Greek philosopher (c. 624–546 BCE), he is famous for predicting a solar eclipse.</note> learned that the solar year is completed in 365 days; this seems to have been the accepted belief in Greece until the time of **Eudoxus** <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BCE), an astronomer and student of Plato.</note>. Eudoxus was led into another error by the "Prophets" <note>Referring to high-ranking Egyptian priests who managed sacred and scientific knowledge.</note> of his time, as if beyond those 365 days a whole quarter-day ought to be added, and thus every fourth year a full day must be intercalated <term>intercalation</term> <note>The insertion of a leap day into the calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar year.</note>. from these words of **Pliny**: *Eudoxus thinks that, if one chooses to observe even the smallest cycles, the same patterns return after exactly four years—not only for the winds, but also for most of the other seasonal weather.* And the beginning of his four-year cycle always occurs in a leap year, at the rising of the **Dog Star** <note>original: "caniculae ortu." Whether the Greeks learned anything else of great importance from the Egyptians regarding the calculation of solar or lunar motion is quite doubtful. ## CHAPTER XIV.
### The reasons why the Egyptians made so little progress in the studies of wisdom.

<margin>Pico, Book 12 against Astrology, chapter 2.</margin>
Furthermore, perhaps enough and more than enough has been explained regarding the nature of Egyptian wisdom. However, I believe I see more than one reason why, despite that scholarly leisure, that abundance of all things, and that great number of people, education made such meager progress among the Egyptians. For although I would not dare, along with Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who argued against the validity of astrology.</note>, to attribute a "native stupidity" to them; being aware that it often happens solely by reason of education that one and the same people might now excel in genius and now be plainly unrefined—which is certainly evident from the single example of the Greeks, who lost all their ancient vigor of mind along with their fortune—nevertheless, other causes are at hand to which one might deservedly ascribe Egyptian unrefinedness. 

The *first* and chief of these is the immense superstition of the people. For this truly snatches away the mind's freedom and reduces it to slavery, so that it does not dare to use its own strengths or spread its wings. Among the Egyptians, indeed, almost every doctrine of the priests was immediately called "sacred" and held as if it had proceeded from a divinity; and therefore, it was a sin to even whisper <note>original: "hiscere," meaning to gape or open the mouth to speak.</note> against those things which had been handed down. By this, every correction of errors, or the perfection of science, could not help but be hindered.

I judge the second cause to be of no less weight: that hieroglyphic <term>hieroglyphica</term> <note>The author views the complex Egyptian writing system not as a tool for clarity, but as a barrier to the widespread advancement of knowledge.</note> system of writing, in which, nevertheless, every superior doctrine among that nation was recorded.

### CHAPTER XIV.

The unrefined nature of their writing was even more burdensome than it should have been because the scribes used figures that had no actual resemblance to the things they signified, or because they harbored erroneous ideas about those subjects. For in those days, no matter how industrious or sharp-witted a person might be, they could not guess the meaning of these symbols without the help of a living teacher. The records of Horapollo <note>An author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics, which was the primary source for Renaissance attempts to decode Egyptian writing before the discovery of the Rosetta Stone</note> and others clearly prove that Egyptian hieroglyphics suffered from these defects. Indeed, it is only rarely possible to find anything truly symbolic <note>original: "συμβολικὸν" (symbolikon)</note> in those hieroglyphics that relates to the thing being signified. Furthermore, it appears that what the Egyptians believed about both the symbols and the things they were meant to indicate was entirely removed from the truth. 

This makes it clear how much effort is wasted by those who—going beyond the explanations of hieroglyphics drawn from Egyptian sources by Horapollo, Clement of Alexandria, Ammianus, and other ancients—attempt to devise new interpretations of their own. <margin>Ammianus, Book 22, Chapter 39.</margin> These letters are, and will perpetually remain, *unknowable to the Latins* <note>original: "Latinis ignorabiles"</note>, to use the words of Ammianus. Nor will the riddles of those sphinxes be solved, I am certain, by Athanasius Kircher <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar (1602–1680) who claimed to have deciphered hieroglyphics in his work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, though his translations were later proven to be entirely fantastical</note>, who did not hesitate to promise a "new Oedipus" <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the one who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher used this name to frame himself as the one who finally cracked the Egyptian code</note>. I do not doubt that Kircher—given his great talent—will invent many things that are more plausible in appearance than those produced by Johann Georg Herwart <note>Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622), a Bavarian scholar and statesman who also attempted to interpret ancient symbols</note> and others. However, that entire *Treasury of Hieroglyphics* which the elder Herwart collected with such zeal, the famous Bembine Tablet <note>A bronze tablet of Roman origin decorated with Egyptian-style figures, once owned by Cardinal Bembo and long thought to be a key to ancient wisdom</note>, and whatever else survives of hieroglyphic literature, will not yield any solid teaching even with a "new Oedipus." Based on what we can gather from Horapollo and others, it is simply unlikely that any better, hidden knowledge lies buried there.

The *third cause* of Egyptian unrefinement may rightly be called the fact that the Egyptian teachers [processed] those things perceived by the senses...

...they taught without demonstration those things that ought to have been demonstrated and were capable of being demonstrated. This is confirmed by that complaint found in the first book of *Asclepius* <note>Also known as the *Perfect Sermon*, a famous Hermetic dialogue.</note> concerning the Greeks who use demonstration. For Asclepius is depicted asking King Ammon not to allow that discourse to be translated into Greek, or to reach the Greeks: because the phraseology of the Greeks is proud and ornate, and it would render the <note>original Greek: τὸ σεμνὸν καὶ στιβαρόν (*to semnon kai stibaron*)</note> solemnity and solidity of the Egyptian doctrine weak. It is added: <note>original: "Ἕλληνες γὰρ, ὦ βασιλεῦ, λόγους ἔχουσι κενοὺς ἀποδείξεων ἐνεργητικούς. καὶ αὐτὴ ἐστὶν Ἑλλήνων φιλοσοφία λόγων ψόφος. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ λόγοις χρώμεθα, ἀλλὰ φωναῖς μεγίσταις τῶν ἔργων."</note> **"For the Greeks, O King, have words that are empty of effective proofs. And this is the philosophy of the Greeks: a noise of words. But we do not use words, but voices that are most powerful in their works."** Thus says that author, whoever he may have been. However, these claims are very far removed from all reason. For the unique principle of true human science is demonstration; and indeed, without demonstrations, no one can arrive at science.

Finally, that custom of training only the sons of the priests in the more accurate doctrines seems to have hindered progress and the growth of the arts in no small measure. For these men did not excel others in natural talent; rather, by this law, the most select talents in other classes of men—who would otherwise have been most suited for philosophy—were prevented from bearing any fruit. Furthermore, it generally happens in common practice that unless you apply your mind to an art of your own accord, and if there is plenty to live on and the path to honors is open without learning, most will handle literary matters quite lazily. Indeed, the children of the Egyptian priests were sufficiently provided for in terms of livelihood and honors, even if they possessed no exceptional training in doctrine. Nor, truly, is there any reason for us to approve of their method of instruction,

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Was Paracelsus a Hermeticist?</margin>
*That Paracelsus did not wish to be considered a Hermeticist, nor was he skilled in the ancient Hermetic wisdom; furthermore, that the writings circulated in his name are of doubtful authenticity, and that he does not agree either with himself or with his disciples.*

We have so far pursued at length the nature of what was once not only the medicine but the universal wisdom of the Egyptians—which one might rightfully call "Hermetic." It remains for us to contemplate Paracelsian medicine <note>The medical system of Paracelsus (1493–1541), which emphasized chemistry and minerals over traditional herbal humorism.</note> as well, so that it may finally be clear whether it claims the title "Hermetic" by right or by error. To the extent that his system agrees much or little with that ancient wisdom of the Egyptians, it either deserves that name well or poorly; and therefore, a comparison of the two must be undertaken. 

But before all else, it must be observed that neither Paracelsus himself nor his first disciples used the name...

### CHAPTER XV.

It is also truly to be noted that neither Paracelsus nor his disciples, who seek to claim the name of "Hermetics," possess any actual skill in ancient Hermetic medicine. Certainly, nothing is found in their writings of those things which we have commemorated above, collected from various sources. For that reason, they have no other pretext for using the Hermetic name than the fact that they believe **Chemical Medicines** <note>Medicamenta Chemica: Medicines created through laboratory processes like distillation or sublimation, rather than simple herbal preparations.</note> originated with Hermes as their author—a claim by which this class of men most highly boasts of itself. However, it is already manifest from our previous disputes that they are vehemently mistaken in this matter, and it will be revealed even more clearly shortly hereafter.

In the third place, a warning must also be given: although many writings exist today under the name of Paracelsus—which **Johannes Huser** <note>Johannes Huser (c. 1545–1600) was a physician who spent years collecting and editing Paracelsus's scattered manuscripts for the first "complete" edition (1589–1591).</note> published as a single collection at the request of **Ernest of Bavaria, Elector of Cologne**—not all of them undoubtedly proceeded from that man. *Firstly*, the works Huser published are much different from those which **Adam von Bodenstein**, **Dorn**, and others had published previously; this is clear at first glance to anyone comparing them. In such a variety of copies, it is certainly very difficult to declare what is truly "Paracelsian"—unless Huser deserves greater trust simply because he claims to have transcribed most of them from Paracelsus’s own original manuscripts. But the reliability of that man is deservedly suspect.

*Secondly*, many of Paracelsus's books themselves are perhaps spurious. **Johannes Oporinus** <note>A famous Swiss printer and scholar who served as Paracelsus's secretary and assistant for two years. His testimony is often cited by critics to debunk Paracelsus's reputation.</note> himself, who accompanied Paracelsus as a servant for nearly two years when he departed from Basel, long ago wrote to the most distinguished physicians **Reiner Solenander** and **Johann Weyer** in these very words: *I am often accustomed to wonder when I see so many things brought forward which are affirmed to have been written by him and left to posterity, of which I never, even in a dream, [saw] him...*

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...nature and all the disagreement of both the ancient and new Hermetic schools, we will first survey the medical art separately, and then briefly the rest of the Paracelsian philosophy.

In the business of the Art, we first encounter the study of Anatomy. That the ancient Hermetics were practiced in this, <margin>See chapter 10, page 89.</margin> even if they may have performed little of it, has been stated above. They clearly saw the use of anatomical study, both for understanding the natural constitution of the body and for uncovering the secrets of diseases. Paracelsus and his followers, however, despise all of this. They do not hesitate to condemn our anatomy to the slaughterhouse, calling it "local anatomy" <note>By "local," the Paracelsians meant an anatomy that only looks at the physical location and shape of dead organs, rather than their "living" spiritual functions.</note>—as if we shared this knowledge in common with butchers. In its place, they recommend another which they call *Vital, Essential, and Formal* Anatomy, by which they mean a more intimate and secret knowledge of all the parts. 

For Paracelsus himself taught this, both in various other places and in *Book 1 of the Origin of Diseases from the Three Primary Substances, chapter 6*, as well as in *Part 2, Book 2 of Tumors, Pustules, and French Ulcers* <note>original: "ulceribus Gallicis." This is an early name for syphilis, which Paracelsus studied extensively.</note>*, chapter 11*. Truly, no one with even a little skill fails to see that in this matter, the Paracelsians not only fail to deserve the name of "Hermetics," but are also most shamefully mistaken. Even granted that the knowledge produced by anatomy might be common to both physicians and butchers, it would still be a foul thing for a physician to be ignorant of what a butcher knows. 

And indeed, you may see that most Paracelsians are more ignorant than the butchers themselves; for this reason, they discuss the position, shape, and connection of the body's parts as if they had never even stepped inside a meat market. For example, Paracelsus himself writes in his *book Azoth* that the sutures of the head, in the part where they resemble the letter <term>τ</term> <note>The Greek letter "tau." Paracelsus is referring to the lambdoid and sagittal sutures of the skull.</note>, are found in an opposite way in women than in men; he even went so far as to write that it was the work of the devil. To claim that the skill of anatomists does not extend beyond the slaughterhouse, or that it can be learned in a meat market, is a foul calumny indeed, or even ma—

### CHAPTER XVI.

...ignorance or malice of the Paracelsians. Nor is there a need for us to prove here the remarkable utility of Anatomy in the medical art; we consider it worth noting only that the truth of it is so clearly perceived here that Paracelsus himself, driven by its force, attempts to rely on the support of anatomical teaching. In *Book 1 on the Plague, chapter 1*, <note>original: "l. quidem 1. de peste c. 1."</note> he argues that the brain is not purged through the ears, nor the heart through the <term>emunctories<note>Emunctories are organs or ducts that carry off waste; in traditional medicine, it was believed certain glands "cleared" the major organs.</note></term> under the armpits, nor the liver through the groin. Elsewhere, in *Book 1 on Tartar, treatise 1, chapter 4*, he claims the intestines do not receive nourishment from the liver. No learned man thinks he should stop at only that "local anatomy"—to use their own phrasing—as if it were sufficient for a knowledge of the parts of the body. Therefore, everyone proceeds further to those things which the Paracelsians attribute to "vital anatomy." Yet, one hopes in vain to learn the latter if the former is not thoroughly understood. On this account, it is most certain that the Paracelsians rightly fall far short of the praise given to the ancient Hermetics.

We have already demonstrated that there is a profound silence in all ancient monuments regarding the composition of things from salt, sulfur, and mercury. It will be clearly revealed shortly that this new doctrine of Paracelsus is removed from any likeness to the truth.

For if the nature or essence of all things lies hidden in man, then all bodies are also actually contained there. For some bodily magnitude belongs to the essence of all natural bodies; in dissimilar or "organic" bodies—such as celestial things and those of plants and animals—the constitution is also partly fulfilled by the position and shape of the parts. For a dog, a wolf, or a lion cannot be of just any size, no more than can a house or any other set of tools. Now indeed, to claim that all the bodies of the greater world are found in man is more absurd than any absurdity. ### CHAPTER XVI.

[...to appear] <note>This word completes a sentence from the previous page, likely "to appear" or "to flow."</note>, the cypress, the beech, wheat, the vine, gold, and the emerald: but anyone who seeks the properties and radical tinctures <term>radical tinctures: in alchemy, these are the fundamental, deep-seated essences or "dyes" that give a substance its specific nature</term>, which are the sources of actions—of grapes, wheat, barley, gold, emerald, roses, and violets—finds them. Indeed, even Severinus <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), a Danish physician and influential proponent of Paracelsian "Idea Medicine."</note> talks nonsense. For the sources of the actions of wheat, barley, roses, and violets are, in part, the very tangible bodies of the plants: since their specific actions are germination, fruit-bearing <note>original: καρποφορία (*karpophoria*)</note>, and the like; these certainly cannot be performed without physical bodies.

The same reasoning applies to stones and metals. Surely nothing is more foolish than to ascribe all power of acting to some sort of "spirits" within bodies, whatever those may be. Furthermore, the properties of these things cannot exist where the essences <term>essentia: the fundamental "being" or nature of a thing</term> themselves are absent, since properties are nothing but the consequences of those essences. 

Besides, perhaps there is no reason to attack that dogma with logic, as it is enough simply to reject it because it relies on no argument. For not even the slightest proof is brought forward by its defenders to justify such a great paradox. Much less do they even attempt to teach that analogy <note>A comparison based on similar functions or structures rather than literal identity.</note> of the greater world with man, or even to show what becomes gold, silver, or iron in man; or what becomes a wolf, a lion, a cat; or this or that star—whether fixed <note>original: *inerrantium*, referring to the stars that appear not to move relative to one another.</note> or wandering <note>original: *vagantium*, referring to the planets.</note>. 

Consequently, if he alone ***is a true physician who can say, this in man is sapphire, this is mercury, this is cypress***, as we just heard Paracelsus boast, then no one from that flock deserves the title of Physician. What of the fact that the Paracelsians themselves explicitly deny that existence of the macrocosm within man when they use the word analogy <note>original: ἀναλογίας (*analogias*)</note>? For things that agree only analogically <note>original: ἀναλογικῶς (*analogikōs*)</note> are not truly the same, but different. Therefore, if the things of the great world are found in man only analogically, they are not actually present there. Furthermore, even that very analogy...
