...of the greater or lesser world <note>The Macrocosm (the universe) and the Microcosm (man)</note> can be either conveniently explained or shown by any argument by the Paracelsians. Hence, in their writings, there is great disagreement in explaining that famous **analogy** <note>original Greek: ἀναλογίᾳ (analogia)</note>; yet never does even the slightest demonstration appear. This is proof of their vanity and folly.

For example: they want seven principal parts of the human body (as they think of them) to correspond by analogy to the seven wandering stars in the heavens <note>The seven traditional "planets" of the ancient world: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon</note>, yet they do not show in what respect that analogy is situated, if you except the resemblance between the heart and the sun. And indeed, it is clear that all this is a hollow fiction, since we have no such analogy between the stars and the internal organs discovered by the senses nor demonstrated by reason.

Furthermore, it is now established for us that there are companion stars to Jupiter in the heavens <note>A reference to the Galilean moons, discovered in 1610, which increased the known number of celestial bodies</note>; it is also very likely that sunspots are formed by stars wandering beneath the sun, and thus there are more than seven planetary bodies. It follows, therefore, that in order to defend their analogy, our **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of the Hermetic tradition, which sought hidden spiritual truths in nature, often associated with alchemy and Paracelsus</note> must find even more organs for us.

But let us imagine it were so; since the organs (and thus the planets) constitute a large part of our body, what, finally, will correspond to the infinite variety of all other things that remain in the great world? I will not mention that the gallbladder is numbered among the principal parts, though it is established to be surely less noble than the stomach.

This deserves to be observed: that according to Paracelsus’s doctrine, not just man alone, but whatever nourishes the human body, ought to be considered a **microcosm** <note>original Greek: μικρόκοσμος (mikrokosmos)</note>, however much elsewhere he and his disciples deign to grant this title to man alone. The reason for this is that they believe the things which are nourished are actually contained within the food, and thus by the "native heat" <note>The innate warmth of the body believed to drive digestion and life</note> no transformation occurs, but only a separation. Two in the feet are attributed to Saturn and Jupiter; two in the neck to Venus and Mars; two in the temples to the Moon and Mercury; the pulse of Jupiter is on the left side under the heart. From this it follows that if the pulse moves faster than it ought, the seven principal members suffer: the heart, brain, liver, gallbladder, kidneys, spleen, and lungs; hence the pulse is irritated or stirred to anger. If, however, any principal member is overcome by disease, the pulse moves weakly; and it generally happens that when the pulse moves weakly, the air or vital spirit <note>original: "spiritus vitæ." ...for how are we to recognize that which is said to consist not of nourishment, but of the excrements of all the parts of the body? We have elsewhere, unless we are mistaken, <margin>Book on the Fire of the Soul, chapter 11.</margin> made it seem probable that this saltiness <note>original: *salsuginem*</note> arises from the combustion of the thin parts of the blood by the power of the innate fire. Nor indeed is there any weight to what some object: *that the volatile salt of urine is produced without burning, and indeed from that part of the urine which distills in the first place; for we do not say that the urine itself is burned into salt by the force of flame, but we recognize that this saltiness is produced within the body.* But it is also said—though without any argument—that only the waste products of the stomach, liver, and kidneys are present in urine; this is merely to invent fictions. On the contrary, it is well known that the **concoction** <term>concoction: in ancient medicine, the process by which "raw" humors are "cooked" or matured by bodily heat into a healthy state</term> of humors of every kind is indicated to us by urines; indeed, the Paracelsians themselves dare to divine anything and everything from urine with a great abundance of foolishness, which nevertheless simultaneously shatters the Paracelsian doctrine concerning urine.

# CHAPTER XVI.

...that this [doctrine] agrees very little with the ancient one, and is indeed much worse. The same logic applies to the teaching on diseases. For one may read more than once in the Hermetic monuments <note>The "Hermetic monuments" refers to the corpus of writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, which formed the foundation of Western alchemy and "chemical" philosophy.</note> that many kinds of diseases arise from the elemental qualities <note>The four primary qualities of traditional Aristotelian and Galenic medicine: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>. In those same works, there is a profound silence regarding salt, sulfur, and mercury—as if diseases originated from them. 

Conversely, the Paracelsian school attributes nothing to these elemental qualities in the origin of diseases, but assigns almost everything to that salt, sulfur, and mercury. Yet even here, the strength of the truth shows itself; you may see them promising everywhere that they will cure an affliction—now a hot one, now cold, now moist or dry—with their medicines. Paracelsus’s own words are: *“from heat and cold, leprosy and other diseases are generated.”* And rightly so: since the force and efficacy of those tactile qualities in producing diseases is so well known to the senses, that anyone denying it or calling it into doubt deserves to have winter cold or flaming fire attack them until a confession of the truth is squeezed out of them.

Certainly no one before Paracelsus was so solemnly insane. Indeed, Petrus Severinus <note>Peder Sørensen (1542–1602), a Danish physician who wrote "Idea medicinae philosophicae," the most influential defense of Paracelsian theory in the 16th century.</note> is wasting his time when he tries to prove the agreement of Hippocrates with us by bringing forward certain testimonies from the book *On Ancient Medicine*. For besides the fact that the book reveals itself in many ways to have come from the Empirical school—and thus is not truly by Hippocrates—it does not strip all power from the hot and the cold. Instead, it only denies that the primary importance should be granted to those qualities, as they should rather be attributed to others, namely: harshness, bitterness, sharpness, acidity, and the like. <note>original: "acerbitati, amaritiæ, acrimoniæ, aciditati"</note>

Yet how far even that doctrine departs from the truth is clear to everyone, at least to anyone attending to the power of fire; which can certainly reduce the entire body of a man to ashes—something granted to no other capacity. It is well known that man is also killed by cold, and that this or that part of the body dies away from it. Who can rightly doubt that a tempered heat is supremely necessary for all living things to sustain life? But now indeed, sharp, bitter, and acidic bodies do not truly harm except insofar as they are composed of those primary tactile qualities <note>The "tactile qualities" are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, so called because they are perceived through touch.</note> in their temperament. For bitterness, acidity, and sharpness are species of tastes, and thus are only suited to affect the sense of taste; but their inner effects are actually the result of the innate heat of certain bodies, tempered by a mixture of the moist and the dry.

### CHAPTER XVI.

But indeed, mixture produces that extraordinary and wonderful power of flavorful things, even by reason of their tactile faculties; <term>tactile faculties: the primary physical qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, which are felt through touch</term> which, when adhering in simple bodies, are far more mobile and more uniform. This matter led even the highly acute <margin>Cesalpino, *Medical Questions*, Book 2, question 4.</margin> **Andreas Cesalpino** <note>original: "Andreas Cæsalpinus" (1524–1603), an Italian physician and botanist who helped bridge the gap between ancient Galenic medicine and modern science.</note> into the error of teaching that the powers of medicines consist more in secondary qualities than in primary ones: even though those secondary qualities <note>Secondary qualities refer to sensory perceptions like taste and smell.</note> are nothing other than species of the primary ones, with the primary qualities holding the place of the genus. 

Truly, the argument by which that author of the *book on ancient medicine* <note>original: *libri de veteri medicina*, a famous treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus.</note> tries to prove to us that no account should be taken of the hot, cold, moist, and dry is of no worth. His argument is this: that the first inventors of the medical art did not pay attention to these things. For it is well known that arts are first discovered through experiments, by which "the fact" is established; <note>original: "τὸ ὅτι" (to hoti), a Greek philosophical term referring to the observation that something is true, without yet knowing why.</note> from there, the investigation of "the reason why" usually follows; <note>original: "τὸ διότι" (to dioti), the Greek term for the underlying cause or explanation of a fact.</note> furthermore, once the causes are now understood, then in turn those things which became known through demonstration serve as a hypothesis for the subsequent investigation of things. 

Certainly, the main point of that little book is centered on this: that the art was first discovered through experience alone, and therefore one should not argue about matters of the art from a certain hypothesis: but also that this very hypothesis itself suffers from falsehood. But to treat these matters with the dignity they deserve is outside my current purpose. It is enough now that we have shown that the author of that book is wrongly drawn into suspicion by **Severinus**, as if he too denied all efficacy in producing diseases to the tactile faculties.

How many ways, furthermore, that doctrine of **salt, sulfur, and mercury** <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus, which he believed were the three fundamental substances of all matter, replacing the four elements of the ancients.</note> labors under error will appear clearly not long from now, when we turn our attention to the Paracelsian philosophy. Here, I wish only to observe in passing the inconsistency of the doctrine. For indeed, they teach that in man...

...all things are found, and so there is an infinite multitude of things that can cause harm; yet they <note>The Paracelsians, or followers of the chemical medicine of Paracelsus.</note> attempt to trace the causes of diseases back to those three alone <note>The "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, which are certainly a far cry from the infinite variety of mixed things. Indeed, through their own lack of skill, they do not see that it is impossible for the human mind to grasp the causes of diseases if they are infinite in number. **For the infinite is unknowable** <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ ἄπειρον ἄγνωστον</note>, as Aristotle rightly objected to Anaxagoras. Certainly, since the same symptoms can arise from different causes, if these causes are infinite in number, it will be impossible for us to know the certain cause of a disease. This very fact would strip away all certainty from the medical art, insofar as medicine consists of either the certain prevention or the removal of disease-causing agents, and thus requires a prior knowledge of those causes.

Furthermore, Paracelsus himself writes in the *Paramirum*, treatise 2, number 1:

> *The body was given to us without poison, and in it there is no poison; but that which we give the body in the place of food, in that there is poison: the body was created perfectly, but other things were not so.*

By these words, he seems to attribute the cause of all diseases to food. Although this is consistent with the opinions of the ancient Egyptians (as is clear from what we proposed above from Herodotus), it nevertheless departs significantly from those myths about the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The idea that the human being is a "miniature world" containing all the elements and forces of the universe.</note>, which establish a complex of every kind of poison within man himself. These words are also quite foreign to the doctrine of the origin of diseases from those three celebrated principles of our body; and they differ most of all from the things discussed in chapter 11 of *The Labyrinth of Wandering Physicians* concerning the **double seedbed of diseases, the iliastrum and the cagastrum** <note>original: iliastro & cagastro. In Paracelsian theory, *iliastrum* refers to the primordial matter of life, while *cagastrum* refers to diseases arising from external seeds or corruption.</note>. Indeed, it is also obvious to everyone that diseases are born not from food alone, but from very ma-

# CHAPTER XVI.

...from many other causes, circulating both within and outside our bodies.

Certainly, Paracelsus trifles with more plausibility in that same work, the *Paramirum*, concerning the "five beings" (for so he calls the efficient causes) of diseases. The first is the **Divine Being** <note>original: Ens Deale</note>, or God Himself; for from Him many diseases are sent down individually. The second is the **Astral Being** <note>original: Ens Astrale</note>: because many diseases proceed from the stars—not only those in the heavens, but also those found within the human body. The third is the **Natural Being** <note>original: Ens Naturale</note>, which produces diseases by the power of those three principles: salt, sulfur, and mercury. They call the fourth the **Spiritual and Mental Being** <note>original: Ens Pagoycum; Paracelsus used "pagoyum" to refer to the soul or mental world</note>: from this, all diseases are produced by the power of the imagination, whether one's own or another's; and from this origin come those diseases brought on by magical sorceries. The fifth is the **Being of Poison** <note>original: Ens Veneni</note>, and it encompasses within its scope all poisons, both those found in nature alone and those created through human art <note>i.e., chemical alchemy or refinement</note>. These, I say, are far more plausible than those other theories; and for that reason, this doctrine—among many others which Paracelsus babbled out with his usual inconsistency—was embraced by Croll <note>Oswald Croll, a prominent Paracelsian physician</note>, Scheunemann, and many others of that school.

And indeed, these ideas agree in part even with the ancient **Hermetic dogma**, by which it was believed long ago that diseases proceed likewise from the stars and their governing spirits, as we have shown above.

Truly, however, they agree **only in part**. For neither the theology of the Egyptian Decans <note>The 36 stars or deities that ruled over specific parts of the body in Egyptian astrology</note>, nor even the astrology of Nechepso, Aesculapius, or Petosiris <note>Famous legendary figures associated with early Greco-Egyptian astrological and medical texts</note>, was known to the Paracelsian school even in a dream. Indeed, from that entire sect, you could praise no one as being even slightly skilled in the commonly accepted astrological doctrine, so far are they from understanding those ancient and long-buried matters. In truth, if we examine <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "spectemus"</note> this Paracelsian doctrine itself...

...gives us, yet even this doctrine rests upon no probability at all. For while it is certainly true that diseases are sent by God, they are sent in such a way that their immediate cause is natural; therefore, those diseases truly depend on their own natural causes. Similarly, by what sign or argument, I ask, can they prove that diseases are produced by the stars without any intervention from earthly things? These are merely fictions, foreign to all reason. Certainly, nothing is more absurd than that philosophy of Paracelsus which he professes in that same work, the *Paramirum*:

<margin>*Paramirum*, treatise 1, chapters 8 and 10.</margin>
He claims that the **Astral Entity** <note>original: *Ens Astrale*</note> which transforms our bodies is a breath, vapor, odor, or sweat of the stars mixed into the air; likewise, that some stars release arsenic, others mercury, others sulfur, and others various poisons into the air, and thus infect mankind. If anything is an absolute **impossibility** <term>original: ἀδύνατον (*adynaton*); a Greek term used here to describe something fundamentally contrary to the laws of nature</term>, it is the idea that eternal bodies [the stars], which are subject to no change, could breathe out sweat, vapors, or breaths into these lower regions. It was stated a little earlier how much this contradicts Paracelsus's own doctrine—namely, his claim that the natural causes of diseases act only through the power of those three principles they call [salt, sulfur, and mercury]. Furthermore, it is an impious opinion that diseases produced by magical power originate from the imagination; as if, forsooth, the works of demons should be attributed to the imagination. However, this impious claim must be criticized more at length elsewhere. Finally, "poison" is foolishly separated from the natural causes of diseases. This folly is especially conspicuous if you consider that by the word "poison," Paracelsus refers to any slimy waste products of the bodily fluids <note>original: *humorum*; the "humors" or vital fluids of ancient and medieval medicine</note> hiding in the secret recesses of the human body. Yet these are mostly free from great harm and are certainly not **deadly poisons** <term>original: δηλητήρια (*deleteria*); things that are destructive or fatal</term>, at least not according to the meaning of the word accepted by common usage throughout the world.

For the rest, it is likewise necessary that he should disagree with this doctrine...

### CHAPTER XVI.

...would be the opinion of the school of Paracelsus, if they wish to defend what they teach elsewhere. For they commonly establish, following the lead of their master Paracelsus, that all transformations of things are carried out by a certain **seminal power** <note>original: *vi seminali*</note> lurking within a unique spirit; and thus, whatever happens is achieved by the help of spirits. It would therefore be necessary for diseases to be produced from their own seeds.

And indeed, this was observed by **Petrus Severinus** <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602) was a Danish physician and a major proponent of Paracelsian ideas; his work *Idea Medicinae Philosophicae* (1571) attempted to systematize Paracelsus's theories</note>, and for that reason, in chapter 13 of his *Idea*, he assigns to each individual disease its own seeds. Indeed, you may find this dogma scattered throughout the writings of Paracelsus himself. There is no doubt, however, that such a notion was completely unknown to the ancient Hermetic school of the Egyptians. In the surviving writings, not a "hide nor hair" of it appears, as they say <note>original: *nec vola... nec vestigium*, literally "neither the palm of the hand nor a footprint," a Latin idiom meaning not a trace exists</note>; their doctrine stays close enough to the commonly accepted views of the time.

This doctrine might instead seem somewhat related to the dogma of **Athenaeus of Attalia** and the **Pneumatic** <note>original: *πνευματικῆς* (*pneumatikēs*); a medical sect that believed a vital "pneuma" or spirit was the primary force behind health and disease</note> sect, as it was once called. They believed in a spirit inherent in all bodies as a "fifth principle" alongside the four elements, which penetrates all things and by which all things are contained and governed: *for by this spirit alone do natural things exist and are governed, and all diseases are created when this spirit is first harmed.* The author of the *Introduction*, or *The Physician*—a booklet appearing among the works of Galen, though it is perhaps by Herodotus <note>Referring to Herodotus the Physician, a practitioner of the Pneumatic school, not the famous historian</note>—taught us this opinion of that school.

And truly, the Paracelsians must also say that in all diseases, the spirit implanted in the parts is suffering; and some of them recognize this spirit—which they call the **balsam of nature** and the **archeus** <term>original: *archæum*; the "internal alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believed directed the life-functions of an organ</term>—as the source of all health. Yet it is not easily apparent how this doctrine fits with the ideas we have already cited from their school, especially if that spirit is something different from those three principles of bodies [Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury], as I see most of them believe. But that these ideas do not agree will appear without much difficulty...

->### CHAPTER XVI.<-

...to agree to some extent with the ancient Hermeticists. To some extent, I say; for I would not say [they agree] entirely. It is certainly not clear whether the Egyptians believed the Isiac **medicine of immortality** <note>original: *Pharmakon athanasias* — a legendary elixir or "drug of immortality" associated with the goddess Isis.</note> <margin>*See above, chapter 11.*</margin> was effective against all diseases. Indeed, he who taught the **art of youthfulness** <note>original: *agerasias* — the practice of preventing the effects of old age.</note> <margin>Galen, *On Marasmus*, chapters 2 & 4.</margin> in Egypt, according to Galen, did not profess to cure all diseases so much as to offer **preventive medicine** <note>original: *prophylaktikēn*.</note>. For this reason, he wanted everyone to be educated according to the laws of his art from earliest infancy, lest they become subject to old age and death once corrupted by diseases. 

Yet Paracelsus, in *Book 1* of his *Paramirum*, *Chapter 8*, and elsewhere, did not hesitate to assert that all diseases already formed, without exception, could be cured. You might hear others of that discipline speak with equal rashness everywhere. However, this is so lacking in probability that a confession of the truth was wrung from Paracelsus himself elsewhere. One can read many of the man’s sayings, collected from various places into one, in the works of **Erastus** <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his systematic refutation of Paracelsian alchemy and medicine.</note>. <margin>Erastus, part 3, *Against Paracelsus*, p. 208.</margin> 

And lest you argue, as some do, that he called certain diseases "incurable" not by the inherent power of the disease but by accident, he wrote expressly in the *Book on the Womb* <note>original: *l. de matrice*.</note>: *certain diseases are incurable because of the weak nature of the body.* In the book *On Contractures* <note>original: *Libro de contractis* — likely referring to diseases that cause the stiffening or shortening of muscles.</note> he says: *not all those with contractures are cured, because they either have a dead spirit of life, or it is fatal for them to be sick in this way. Neither can be known for certain unless the remedies do no good.* 

In his notes on *Book 2, Chapter 3* of *On Urines*, he lists the signs of an incurable disease. In his *Book on Dropsy, Chapter on Prognostics*, he pronounces as "incurable" those sufferers of **dropsy** <note>original: *Hydropicos* — a condition of swelling caused by excess fluid, now known as edema.</note> who are exhausted by a continuous cough, who are marred by easy discoloration, for whom breathing is difficult, whose upper parts waste away, and whose urine is scant and thick. In the *Paragranum*, he admits that **leprosy** is incurable when small ulcerations of the skin—which he calls "hailstones"—become ulcers; likewise when the flesh is lost in the thigh and hips, just as usually happens between the thumb and fingers.

Furthermore, Petrus Severinus <note>A Danish physician and leading advocate of Paracelsian medicine (1542–1602).</note> asserts that neither gout, nor dropsy <note>original: *hydrops* — an old term for swelling caused by fluid retention, often related to heart or kidney failure.</note>, nor leprosy, nor epilepsy are incurable, whether they arise from heredity or diet, and whether they are mild or severe, incipient or well-established. # CHAPTER XVI.

...they boast that diseases universally agreed by all to be incurable—namely dropsy <note>original: *hydropem* — an old term for swelling caused by fluid retention, often related to heart or kidney failure.</note>, gout, leprosy, and epilepsy—have been cured by them. Even if we imagine that these diseases were both believed by everyone to be incurable and were indeed cured by the Paracelsians, this still does not prove their point. For there are many other lethal diseases which none of them has ever cured. It is also false to say that all those diseases are commonly held to be simply incurable; rather, they are only considered so in certain circumstances. Indeed, to the extent that they have been regarded as incurable until now, no Paracelsian has yet succeeded in healing them. To be sure, some diseases simply resist all treatment, while others allow for healing at times, yet at other times they overcome the power of medicine for various reasons. This argument was excellently pursued in a specific book titled *On Incurable Diseases* <note>original: *de morbis incurabilibus*</note> written by Bruno Seidel <note>Bruno Seidel (c. 1530–1591) was a German physician and poet known for his cautious, empirical approach to medicine.</note>.

Furthermore, the line of reasoning by which some attempt to establish their opinion is foolish. They argue that if diseases were truly incurable, the cause would lie either with nature or with God. Since nature seeks its own preservation, and God loves mankind and therefore wishes them well—and since He is certainly capable of making all diseases curable—He must undoubtedly have decreed them to be so. However, we acknowledge that the reason why diseases are not simply curable, but that man must necessarily succumb to certain ailments, is situated in the very nature of things and is therefore from God. Even though the whole of nature desires its own preservation, this does not prevent it from willing that some diseases be incurable. Indeed, by this same logic, one might deny all corruption <term>corruption: in the philosophical sense used here, this refers to the natural process of decay, breaking down, and death that affects all physical matter.</term> of things. For the very perfection of the universe requires that while the species of things should endure, most individual bodies remain subject to change—

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *The same is shown separately regarding every method of healing, especially regarding that which is expected from a universal remedy for all diseases.*

Therefore, although the Paracelsians agree to some extent with the ancient Egyptians, it is clear that even in this area there is a disagreement, and that the teachings of the Paracelsians are even less tolerable than those of the ancients. The matter is much the same regarding the entire method or "way" of healing. For we mentioned above that the Egyptians once observed the laws of healing prescribed by their ancestors even to the point of superstition; however, in the Paracelsian writings, one can see almost every rule of healing discarded, even those strengthened by the consensus of many centuries. They have gone so far because they believe that every disease arises from a certain unique "seed," and that for every disease there is an opposite <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: *arcanum*; in Paracelsian medicine, a "secret" or "inner essence" of a substance that acts as a powerful, specific remedy.</note>...

### CHAPTER XVII.

...a medicine, whose power is situated *in the consubstantial properties of a Chironian nature <note>original: "cherioniæ." In Paracelsian thought, "Chironian" (referring to the centaur Chiron) often denoted diseases or remedies of a particularly high or occult grade, or those requiring special surgical or alchemical insight.</note>, endowed with the knowledge and predestination of health*, to use their words. Indeed, they speak about medicines as if they possessed intelligence and operated by deliberate choice. Hence, they place all skill in healing within the knowledge of secret remedies <term>arcana: From the Latin 'arcanum' (secret), these were the hidden, powerful chemical or spiritual essences that Paracelsians believed were the true agents of cure.</term> of this kind; for them, the very word "medicine" signifies nothing more than a physical drug. Furthermore, that empty fiction regarding the seeds of diseases <note>The Paracelsian theory that diseases grew from internal "semina" like plants, rather than being caused by humoral imbalances.</note> has already been rejected by us. Nothing is more certain than that individual diseases, and the individual symptoms of those diseases, are produced by diverse causes. From this it follows that no "specific" remedy <term>specific: A medicine believed to have a unique, almost magical power to cure a particular disease regardless of the patient's individual constitution or the disease's underlying cause.</term> (as they call it) can be found for any disease whatsoever that is able to remove the illness always and in everyone. Daily experience itself demonstrates this very fact.

For no matter what the Paracelsians <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who rejected traditional Greek medicine in favor of alchemy and chemistry.</note> or others of that same ilk may boast, no remedy has yet been discovered that is effective in any given disease with always the same success; even the best and most praised remedies often deceive every hope.

<margin><unclear>sh. d. 1</unclear></margin>
Nor is there any reason for you to pretend that some remedies have deserved to be called Cephalic, Stomachic, Hepatic, or Cardiac <note>original: κεφαλικὰ (head), στομαχικὰ (stomach), ἡπατικὰ (liver), καρδιακὰ (heart). In the first place, none of these is so dedicated to a single part of the body that it can do nothing in others. Secondly, much less does any remedy have such power over one part as to be suitable for all its various afflictions. Certainly, those who persuade themselves of such a thing are utterly deceived; but Experience—the teacher of fools <note>Refers to the Latin proverb *experientia est magistra stultorum*, suggesting that those who ignore reason must learn the hard way through failure.</note>—will easily refute them if they will only admit logic. Therefore, nothing is simply Cephalic or Cardiac in an absolute sense; nevertheless, certain things are called so in preference to others only because they have great power in several (and indeed the more frequent) afflictions of those parts. <margin>Angelus Sala in his Censure.</margin>

Therefore, both **Paracelsus** and his first followers, who used them indiscriminately in every kind of disease, practiced butchery <note>original: "carnificinam"</note> rather than medicine. But whether those **Crollian** preparations made from antimony, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and vitriol <note>sulfate minerals</note> have truly been rendered harmless, we have already heard from **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who sought to bridge Galenic and Paracelsian medicine.</note>. **Hartmann**, the commentator on **Croll**, writes that this caution regarding mercury and antimony is well worth noting:

Hartmann 
on Basil

These words clearly testify that those purges are not always safe and harmless, even if there may occasionally be some use for them.

Indeed, I have no certain grounds to assert it, yet I would say that what our modern Hermetics profess—that the cure of diseases is effected not by contraries but by similars <note>The principle of "Similia similibus curantur," the idea that a substance that causes symptoms in a healthy person can cure those symptoms in a sick person.</note>—did not please the ancient Egyptians. For it is too far from probability that such a thing could occur to anyone’s mind, unless they wished to play with words. As indeed the **Paracelsians** do in this business, clearly confusing the preservative part of the art with the curative part; as is especially clear from those things discussed by **Quercetanus** near the end of the defense he published for Hermetic medicine.

Those things which agree more correctly with the opinions of the Egyptians...

### CHAPTER XVII

# 209

Now, our modern Hermeticists <note>Followers of the alchemical and philosophical traditions attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, who sought to bridge chemistry and medicine.</note> are so enamored by the belief that there is one single remedy capable of curing all diseases. It is evident that the ancients attributed such power to the <term>medicine of immortality</term> <note>original: τῷ τῆς ἀθανασίας Φαρμάκῳ</note> belonging to **Isis** <note>The Egyptian goddess often associated in alchemical lore with the discovery of life-giving medicines.</note>. However, it is not easy to say whether any other among the **Egyptians** after **Isis** attempted to find something of this kind. Truly, the school of **Paracelsus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who revolutionized medicine by using minerals and chemicals.</note> has labored strenuously in this pursuit; indeed, some have not hesitated to claim possession of so great a thing. Yet, any prudent person rightly wonders how there could be those who either hope for or claim this for themselves, since neither experience nor any reason provides even the slightest credibility to the matter.

If we are to stand by experience, this paradox is surely already cut down. For the myths of **Isis** do not deserve to be counted among historical facts. As for what some bring forward from the middle of the medieval period concerning **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> and **Raymond Lull** <note>Major 13th-century philosopher and polymath; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.</note>, as if they were privy to this secret, it is not at all likely. For even if I would not deny that they aspired to that goal, it cannot be proved by any sign or testimony that their hope was ever realized.

The surviving papers of **Arnold** speak of him using various remedies. **Lull’s** own "fifth essence" <note>The "quintessence," or the purest and most potent medicinal extract of a substance.</note> varies according to the diversity of diseases. For to his "heaven"—or what they call the spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol, distilled repeatedly.</note> prepared through many circulations <note>The process of repeated distillation or refluxing in a sealed vessel.</note> in a Hermetic vessel—**Raymond** adds various and different "stars" (that is, remedies for diseases), according as one disease or another is to be cured. This is clear from **Lull’s** two books *On the Fifth Essence*, which are in circulation today, even if they reveal the entire art clearly enough. The same must be said of **Johannes de Rupescissa** <note>John of Roquetaillade (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan friar who wrote extensively on the medicinal use of distilled alcohol.</note>, who likewise did not hesitate to profess such a remedy in a specific little book. ...into that, he especially recommends the lime of gold <note>Gold that has been calcined or reduced to a fine powder through chemical processes.</note> prepared with mercury, dissolved in the "vinegar of the philosophers" <note>original: "aceto philosophorum"; an alchemical term for a powerful solvent, often a distilled acid or mercurial substance.</note> or aged urine. ### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>Billich in *Assertions*, no. 24.</margin>
...would have drawn away <note>The text begins mid-word, completing a verb from the previous page likely meaning "drawn away" or "exhausted"</note>: because it consumed the substance of the body and the **primigenial moisture** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, this "innate moisture" was thought to be the fuel for the body's life-force; exhausting it led to aging and death</note>, which it ought to have restored, most ruinously through diaphoresis <note>sweating</note>, diuresis <note>urination</note>, and **insensible perspiration** <note>original: *ἀδηλον διαπνοὴν* (adelon diapnoēn)</note>. A patient with **tertian fever** <note>A fever recurring every third day, typically associated with malaria</note> who, overflowing with thick and raw humors, began the use of this remedy without first purging his body, brought upon himself a continuous fever from an intermittent one, an incurable disease from a curable one, and a lethal state from a benign one, as his humors were melted and precipitated.

Johann Wolfgang Dienheim achieved no reputation among the common people through any actual work, even though he did not hesitate to profess knowledge of this secret and wonderful remedy in a specific book. Indeed, in that very book, he undermined his own credibility; in chapter 7, he teaches that different remedies must be applied to different diseases, and his "universal" remedy is only to be given as a companion—this is the same way that **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic often associated with early alchemy</note> and **Rupescissa** <note>Johannes de Rupescissa (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan friar who wrote on the "quintessence"</note> formerly rambled on. But even so, Dienheim’s universal remedy provided nothing worthy of praise. It was clearly of the same character as the **universal solvent** for all bodies, or the **menstruum** <term>menstruum: a powerful solvent used in alchemy, believed to be capable of reducing any solid matter into its primary liquid essence</term> as the chemists call it, which that vain man was likewise not ashamed to promise.

There are those who assert that Johann Montanus, a Silesian of the chemical order, recovered the blackness of his hair in his old age by means of that famous remedy. But Johann Francus rightly noted in his *Chemical Letters* that the same thing happened to **Postel** <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a famous French polymath and mystic</note> and others without the use of any chemical medicine. I myself, this past summer, cured a patient suffering from an abscess in the chest in such a way that his baldness and grey hair of several years were simultaneously corrected with a thick and black growth of hair. I do not doubt that the same has happened to others. 

Thus, that belief in a single remedy for all diseases is so thoroughly refuted by daily experience that the more sensible **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of the tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, seeking spiritual and physical perfection through alchemy</note> only dare to promise a cure for diseases arising from internal causes through such a thing. And yet, not even so far [have they been] favor...

->### CONCERNING HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...they can claim experience for themselves, since no one has yet been found who has cured all those diseases with a single remedy.

This Hermetic opinion suffers equally from its reasoning. It is held as most plausible that the nature of the human body is the **healer of all diseases** <note>original: "natura... medicatrix"; a reference to the Hippocratic concept *Vis medicatrix naturae*, the healing power of nature.</note>, and that nature can be preserved whole or restored to health by some single, excellent remedy. But in truth, many things are encompassed here by that word "nature": certainly, that term embraces the entire essence of the human body, which is different in each of its parts. To preserve this whole essence or to restore it when weakened with a single remedy is **impossible** <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (*adynaton*)</note>; and thus, there is a **begging of the question** <note>original: "petitio... in principio"; a logical fallacy where the premise assumes the truth of the conclusion it is trying to prove.</note> in the argument. It does not escape me that by that word "nature," the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine and sought the "life force."</note> mean the indwelling **vital spirit**, which they wish to call the <term>quintessence</term><note>original: "quinta essentia"; literally the "fifth essence," thought by alchemists to be the purest form of matter and the source of life.</note>. But first, that spirit hardly deserves the name of "nature" exclusively, nor is it the sole healer of diseases. For the actions of our body do indeed flow from the nature of the body; at the same time, besides that common vital spirit which the parts receive from the heart, it is necessary that the **specific constitution of the individual parts** be in good condition. Therefore, just as diseases do not belong to that single spirit alone, neither is that single spirit sufficient for curing diseases.

<margin>
*Book on Animal Fire*.
</margin>
Furthermore, they wrongly assume that this spirit is some kind of "fifth essence"; we have demonstrated at length elsewhere that it is nothing other than a certain **mobile fire**. Let us imagine, however, that it is not of an elemental nature; how would they prove, at the very least, that all the defects of that spirit can be cured by a single medicine? Certainly, a flaming fire is a single body of very powerful virtue, yet we see it affected in various ways and by various causes,

# CHAPTER XVII. 215

...so that it may not frequently be assisted in more than one way. In truth, the reasoning which the **Hermetics** <note>Followers of the Hermetic tradition, an ancient philosophical and religious system often associated with alchemy and the search for secret knowledge.</note> believe deserves the praise of a demonstration is futile. It is of the same character as those three arguments that are likewise usually brought forward. 

The first of these is: if fire burns all things, and **antimony** <term>antimony</term><note>original: "antimonium"; a semi-metal used in alchemy, known for its ability to "purify" gold by consuming other metals in a melt.</note> is fit to consume all metals except **gold** <note>original: "aurum"</note>, then there must be something that removes all diseases. The second: there are **poisons** <note>original: "venena"</note> lethal to all men; therefore, something also exists which benefits all men. The third: there are remedies opposed to the defects of individual parts, which are called **specifics** <term>specifica</term><note>Medicines intended to treat a specific organ or a particular disease rather than the whole body.</note>; why then should there not be found something that is advantageous to the whole in general? 

One can indeed reject these three in a single blow, since they suffer from a **flaw in logic** <note>original: "vitio consequentiæ"; a failure in the logical sequence where the conclusion does not follow from the premises.</note>, such that they cannot be forced into any legitimate **syllogism** <term>syllogismum</term><note>A formal logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note>. I add: neither fire nor antimony is capable of correcting all the defects of those bodies which can be corrupted and consumed by them. And just as a body, and thus an animal, perishes if even one of its essential parts is destroyed, so it is necessary for all parts to be intact for it to be preserved. Therefore, although all life can be taken away by a single poison, it does not follow that life can likewise be preserved by any single thing. Furthermore, we have already discarded those specific remedies for individual parts; even if they were granted, you would still foolishly conclude from this that a remedy common to all diseases could be found.

With no less folly, the **chemists** <note>In this context, early modern alchemists or "iatrochemists" who sought to replace traditional herbal medicine with mineral-based chemical cures.</note> are accustomed to hawk now this, now that, as a universal remedy. For **Lully** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1316), a major medieval philosopher to whom many alchemical texts were later attributed.</note>, **Rupescissa** <note>John of Rupescissa (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan alchemist who pioneered the idea of "quintessences" extracted from wine and other substances to prolong life.</note>, and others, recommend for this purpose what they call the **quintessence** <term>quinta essentia</term><note>The "fifth essence" or ether; alchemists believed it was the pure substance of the heavens and the key to medicinal immortality.</note> of bodies, because they believe that corruptibility is [overcome] only by that which is **incorruptible** <note>original: "incorruptibile"</note>...

He specifically critiques the alchemical theories of Raymond Lully and John of Rupescissa regarding the "quintessence."</summary>

->ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...[so that corruption] can be warded off, but that the **fifth essence** <term>Also known as the "quintessence"; in ancient and medieval philosophy, it was the pure, celestial element that made up the stars and planets, distinct from the four earthly elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</term> alone is incorruptible. Furthermore, to find some incorruptible body here in these **sublunary regions** <note>The realm below the moon, which in the science of the time was the only place where things were believed to change, decay, and die.</note>, or anything worthy of the name of "fifth essence," is a mere fabrication. Certainly, the "heaven" of *Lullius* <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher whose name was often attached to later alchemical writings.</note> and *Rupescissa* <note>Johannes de Rupescissa (c. 1310–1362), a friar who wrote extensively on the "quintessence" as a medicinal alcohol.</note> is nothing but the thinnest spirit of wine <note>original: "vini liquor"; a reference to distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note>, reduced by art to the highest degree of thinness. Their "stars," meanwhile, are merely the flavorful and fragrant juices of plants, or metals dissolved—either entirely or in part—by the sharpest liquids. Not one of these things is immune to corruption. <margin>Chapter 6 of the same work</margin> Indeed, *Rupescissa* himself confesses the corruptibility and "lightness" of his "heaven"—that is, the natural weight by which it is carried upward. <margin>Chapter 16, book 1.</margin> 

Furthermore, even if some celestial thing did exist here among us, it does not follow that it could preserve us from corruption. This is especially true since it cannot even keep the very body in which it is hidden whole and intact. For the spirit of wine has no such power over the wine itself. Indeed, the sun, which possesses the greatest power in our world, does not prevent corruption; in certain things, it even promotes it. How much less, then, would be the power of a "fifth essence" imprisoned within earthly bodies! Finally, who will prove that health cannot be preserved in its entirety until the natural end of life by the power of "corruptible" things <note>Meaning ordinary, natural medicines rather than alchemical "miracle" substances.</note>? This certainly requires a demonstration; yet these men assume its impossibility as if it were a established fact.

Even more ridiculous are the conclusions by which most of that "flock" <note>A dismissive reference to the followers of Hermetic or Paracelsian medicine.</note> ascribe this universal healing power to gold, or to their much-celebrated **philosopher’s stone**. This is because the stone is believed to transmute all imperfect metals into gold; and gold itself is known as the "sun" among the metals, and is consumed by no fire and no passage of time.

### CHAPTER XVII. 217

<margin>
Book on Animal Fire, chapter 10.

For no form of **syllogism** <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> can be constructed from this to prove such great power, even if you were to grant the premise. Are the parts of our body metallic, or must they be changed into a single, nobler, and incorruptible mass? Can gold do what the sun can do? And even if it could: would it therefore be fit to correct any defects, a power which is not even granted to the true sun? Can that which is incorruptible—and thus incapable of being acted upon—also immediately act upon anything else? Truly, that which is immutable cannot nourish and perpetually preserve our **native heat** <term>In ancient and early modern medicine, "native heat" (calidum nativum) was the vital warmth within a living body that drove digestion and life processes.</term> (as they imagine for themselves), since nothing provides nourishment unless it is capable of being changed by our internal fire into its own nature, as we have shown elsewhere. By this argument, one can certainly dismiss all those who try to provide, through some **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence" or a supposed pure, celestial substance.</note> of things, the same benefits that others seek to provide through gold.

Moreover, that opinion regarding the universal medicinal power of gold or the **philosopher's stone** <note>The legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note> is perhaps characteristic of the new Hermetic school. One can nowhere find that the ancient Egyptians believed any such thing; indeed, we have already proved that they used plants in healing rather than metallic substances.

It is strange indeed that those "new Hermeticists" do not likewise seek that power in plants, since the **Tree of Life** <note>The biblical tree in the Garden of Eden whose fruit conferred immortality.</note> shown of old to our first parents in Paradise could provide a pretext for their folly. But if that power resides in gold, or in some "fifth essence" of wine and other bodies, then our first parents were kept from plucking the fruit of the Tree of Life by the Angel in vain, for the earth would everywhere supply that

## CHAPTER XVIII.

->Showing that more errors are committed today than in the past regarding the<-
->magical remedies for diseases used by both Hermetic schools, and<-
->likewise that the Weapon Salve belongs to the<-
->magical category.<-

Truly, enough has been said of these things. We must proceed to those matters which are used for healing in both Hermetic schools, setting aside those imaginary remedies. Indeed, in several of these, both sects agree wonderfully with each other, yet in some they differ in their customs. There is the greatest agreement in the magical cure of diseases. I refer here to that healing which is established through words, through characters <note>In this context, "characters" refers to mystical symbols, sigils, or astrological signs believed to hold power.</note>, through images, and through the open invocation of demons and other spirits. Regarding these, Paracelsus did not hesitate <margin>Book 1 of *Sage Philosophy*, chapter 6.</margin> to write: *Nature places its powers into words: just as into herbs and roots, so also into gamahaos.* <note>original: "gamahaos"; these are stones or talismans naturally or artificially marked with figures believed to contain celestial influences.</note> And a little later: *Images and characters are boxes in which the Mage preserves the powers of the stars.* He treats this matter at length in the book he wrote on *Occult Philosophy* under the title *On Characters*, teaching that diseases can be thoroughly healed by characters which neither drinkable gold nor the fifth essence of antimony could cure. In the same place, he prefers two above all other characters and seals: one with the name **Adonai** <note>A Hebrew name for God, translated as "Lord."</note>, the other with the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>The "four-letter" name of God in Hebrew (YHWH), considered most holy and powerful in mystical traditions.</note> marked along with a certain fixed figure. Nor did he hesitate to write in the same place these very words: *A foot or hand, or another limb, must be manufactured or fashioned in the form of that which is sick and in pain, or even an image of the whole body, and that image must be anointed and bound, not the suffering man.* If a man [loses] through incantation the use of speech, hearing, or virility...

### CHAPTER XVIII.

if he has lost <note>The word "amiferit" completes a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to a patient losing a limb or vital force.</note>, an image of the whole man should be made from wax, with strong faith and a fixed imagination, and that image must be cared for in the proper way. In his book *The Magic Archidoxis* <note>original: "Archidoxeos magicae"; one of Paracelsus's most famous works on talismans and sigils.</note>, he teaches how to form various characters <note>mystical symbols or sigils</note> suitable for healing diseases. In Book V of *Invisible Diseases*, he writes: *God gifted the Devil with this art, and placed him as one very skilled in the light of nature, though this art can be snatched away from him. The art is to be used, but the Devil is to be abandoned. We dwell in this world so that the lesser may learn from the greater; thus, the use of the art as it is in itself is not a transgression of the law or a sin.* Likewise: *We must be most fully persuaded that God established medicine and placed it before our eyes for our consideration. Therefore, if something good happens to us through characters, they should be held in the same regard as plants. Indeed, even if they belonged to the devil, they should still be treated as if they were jars from a pharmacy. If the devil,* he says, *uses a word instead of an herb, let it be like an herb to us. Words are his ingredients; characters are his compounds and syrups.* From here, he openly taught in the school of Basel: *if God’s help fails, let the devil’s succeed.* <note>original: "si Dei deficit auxilium diaboli succedat"; this was one of the most scandalous statements attributed to Paracelsus by his enemies.</note>

->### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...[ex]treme and sad wage that the devil was accustomed to pay to his servants: he used to respond that he would not long after sound the retreat. Furthermore, since Paracelsus believed that beyond good and evil angels, there was found a third kind of spirits, <margin>See book 1 to the Athenians, ch. 13.</margin> called by him *Evestra* <note>original: "Evestrum" — in Paracelsian philosophy, an "Evestrum" is a kind of shadow-being or prophetic spirit that links the physical and spiritual worlds</note> (of which sort are those who show themselves in water, mirrors, crystals, and fingernails, and appear to those sleeping and waking alike: Salamanders, Sylphs, Melusinae, Diemii, Durdales, Neufarinae, Lorindae, Nesderae, Gnomes, Lamiae, Nymphs, and Sirens), he undoubtedly judged that we could lawfully use their help as well. Indeed, he also commends the *homunculus* <term>A "homunculus" is a "little man," an artificial human-like being that alchemists believed could be created in a laboratory through the putrefaction of biological materials.</term>, whose construction he teaches in *Book 1 of On the Generation of Things*, for its expertise in all matters, and <margin>Book on Images, ch. 11.</margin> he advises that the arts and power be expressed through what he calls *Ascendants* <note>original: "Ascendentibus" — here referring to astrological influences or planetary forces captured in physical objects</note>. Moreover, he pursues every kind of Magic everywhere with the highest praise, except that he contends one must deal with evil demons not with flatteries or any covenant, but with threats and force; because all magical things are within the limits of nature. And for that reason, he explicitly writes in *Chapter 9 of the book titled The Labyrinth of Errant Physicians*: *Magic is the art of arts, and the inventress of all occult things; and from it, rather than from Galen, Avicenna, or similar men, medicine must be learned.* <margin>Book on Occult Philosophy.</margin> Elsewhere he writes: *Magic is in itself the most occult art, and the highest wisdom of supernatural things: and whatever cannot otherwise be recognized by human reason, can be investigated by Magic. Which of the theologians,* he asks, *without magic has either cast out a demon, or called a spirit to himself, or driven one away? Who, unskilled in magic, has ever healed a sick person, or accomplished anything similar, let alone moved mountains?* In the second treatise of the *Book on the Plague*, he advises the physician to learn Magic and its related arts, *pyromancy, chiromancy, and hydromancy* <note>pyromancy (divination by fire), chiromancy (palm reading), and hydromancy (divination by water)</note>: *for he claims that John the Evangelist, Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Enoch, [and David]...*

I pass over extracting other things written to this effect from Paracelsus’s books, for they are innumerable. Nor did he profess himself a follower of Magic obscurely; not only is this manifest from what was cited before, but it is also established by the single testimony of Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a major Swiss Reformer and successor to Zwingli</note>, who knew the man in Zurich <note>original: "Tiguri"</note>, which Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a physician and theologian famous for his critiques of Paracelsus</note> inserted into his disputations: <margin>Erastus, part 1, p. 239.</margin> *“I conferred with him,”* he says, *“once and again about various matters, including Theological or religious ones. # ->CHAPTER 18.<-

...to those things which we taught above. In that same place, we showed that the Egyptians attributed a natural power to words, characters, and images—and even to plants and stones—for the purpose of compelling spirits <note>original: "genios"</note> to perform this or that task, even against their will, or certainly to drive them toward it if they were willing; for this reason, they considered that type of magic to be "natural." We also showed that they sought remedies for diseases from these same spirits or geniuses. However, I doubt whether they sought remedies for diseases from those spirits they knew to be evil and perverse. Certainly, I do not recall ever reading such a thing. And so, I would say that in this matter, the Paracelsians differ somewhat from the customs of the ancient Hermeticists. Furthermore, it is established that the Egyptians used drink offerings <note>original: "libaminibus"</note> and supplications to obtain the help of spirits or gods; yet it does not appear that Paracelsus or all his followers recommended these same things to soothe even those spirits of the middle order. Thus, even in this regard, there are certain discrepancies between them. Finally, you will nowhere find any mention in the magical volumes of any nation of the Paracelsian <term>homunculus: a miniature human-like creature supposedly created through alchemical processes</term> produced by the chemical art; thus, this too is unique to the Paracelsian school alone.

I do not wish at this time to remark at length upon these magical matters of either the ancient or the modern Hermetic school, since many excellent arguments have been made by others on this subject, and I intend to expose the vanity of what they call "Natural Magic" in a separate work, pointing out both the limits of nature in its actions and the hidden workings of spirits among natural things. It is also clear that images, characters, and words or incantations (to the extent they lack power by their very nature) have either no efficacy or so little that they cannot rightly be used as remedies for diseases...

# CHAPTER XVIII.

...or what the Paracelsians <term>Paracelsici</term> promise concerning the power of physical objects over those spirits, it is evident from this very fact to be vain and empty. As for the things that spirits <term>genii</term> <note>In this context, *genii* refers to guardian spirits or supernatural entities, not necessarily "geniuses" in the modern sense.</note> do regarding the use of characters, images, words, or other natural things, they do them because it has pleased them to act in that way; they themselves have established that they would effect this or that upon the presentation of those symbols.

Furthermore, if all those spirits are substances more spiritual than man himself—as was said before—it is necessary that they also be placed within the order of Angels. And indeed, since they are endowed with will no less than with intelligence, they must be of either good or evil character, so to speak. By this it again becomes manifest that the Paracelsian doctrine is worthless and erroneous when it claims that the *Evestra* <note>original: "Evestra"; a term coined by Paracelsus to describe a type of prophetic spirit or an "astral body" that reflects future events.</note> or those spirits (which they say show themselves in mirrors, crystals, fingernails, and elsewhere) are below the angelic order and therefore not to be counted among either the good or the bad angels.

Certainly, it is a sin to doubt that those who present themselves to men as *incubi* and *succubi* <note>Demons believed to have sexual encounters with sleeping humans.</note>, or who serve sorcerers in every kind of crime, are of a depraved mind.

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

[[page number: 226]]

Just as evil demons imposed themselves upon the Egyptians under the guise of gods, so too it is easily shown by their actions that all the Paracelsian **Evestra** <term>Evestra</term><note>In the system of Paracelsus, these are "astral twins" or prophetic spirits that emanate from people or objects.</note> belong to that same most wicked order. The "Spirit" that Paracelsus taught how to produce through the chemical art is likewise demonstrated—by the very works attributed to Paracelsus himself—to be either a demon or a demonic mockery. Yet, perhaps all of that is merely a fabrication.

Furthermore, if those spirits are as beneficial toward the human race as the Paracelsians claim, and not evil; and if it is within their own will to help or to harm, then they would have to be enticed into obedience through some form of honor and worship. Since the ancient Egyptians did this, and the **Magi** <term>Magi</term><note>Ancient practitioners of "high magic," often associated with Persian or Egyptian wisdom.</note> teach that it should be done, it is clear that they tend to defend their hypothesis more correctly than some Paracelsians (I say *some*, for some indeed think and act differently). One might even say the Egyptians were more cautious than the Paracelsians regarding the use of demons whose malice was well known to them. For it does not appear that they expected any benefit from them; although it is manifest from both Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrio"</note> and Iamblichus <note>original: "Iamblicho"</note> that the Egyptian Magi knowingly and willingly used their assistance for sorcery and crimes. 

<margin>
Porphyry, *On Divination and Demons*; 
Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*
</margin>

Yet we have heard that Paracelsus recommended the aid and labor of the devil in many places throughout his writings. But it is evident—not only from our own divine Christian scriptures but also from other sources—that all those demons possess a most hostile spirit toward mankind, and because of this, they do everything in their power to deceive humans and cast them into every kind of evil. Is it not, therefore, exposing one's entire well-being to the whim of mortal enemies to commit one's health, life, and fortune to their labor?

<margin>
Slander against the Prophets and Apostles
</margin>

Furthermore, what a great and impious slander it is to claim that the most holy Hebrew Prophets, as well as the Apostles, practiced those magical arts praised by Paracelsus!

...[to have been]! <note>The text begins mid-word, concluding a thought from the previous page: "to have been believed" (original: "...cuisse").</note> How horrifying it is—indeed, equally wicked to speak or to hear—that Christ used the same magic as those Egyptian adversaries of Moses! ### CHAPTER XVIII.

(as they call the moss grown on the heads of bodies long suspended from the gallows) <note>original: *muscum*. The patient must also take care not to commit any error in diet, by which wounds are otherwise usually adversely affected.

From these things we have said, it can be gathered that the healing of only those wounds inflicted on the flesh without any serious bruising is attributed to the powers of this Ointment. Truly, in bodies of good health, if those things we last mentioned are properly observed during this treatment by the "Weapon Ointment" <term>Armarium unguentum</term>, such wounds are usually healed by the natural benefit of the body, entirely without the aid of any ointment. However, it cannot be denied that certain things sometimes happen regarding that treatment which the natural power of the wounded—unaided by any helps—is not accustomed to, nor able to, perform. Such are the things we noted in the third place as being confirmed by experience. But if it were true what some report—that any wounds whatsoever are healed in this way without distinction—then that too should not be attributed to the nature of the sick alone. Yet I have found nothing of the sort to be certain, nor is it recorded by authors worthy of trust; on the contrary, others as well as myself have known very many for whom that method of curing turned out badly.

It is evident that those things which happen not from the innate faculty of the sick should by no means be attributed to the virtue of the Ointment. This seems not difficult to prove by this single fact: that all these things do not happen to everyone or always, but only to the superstitiously credulous or to those who have some commerce with demons <note>original: "daemonibus commercij." ### CHAPTER XVII

[[page number: 231]]

...[na]ture acts, they usually work in one way or another according to human persuasion, but they always conduct themselves in one and the same way. Most authors indeed attribute almost every effect to the **Usnea** <note>original: "Vsneae"; a type of moss or lichen found growing on the skulls of criminals who had been executed, usually by hanging. It was highly prized in 17th-century "sympathetic" medicine.</note> of a hanged man. 
<margin>Regarding Oswald Croll’s *Royal Chemistry*, page 485.</margin>
These are the words of Hartmann <note>Johannes Hartmann (1568–1631), a German physician and the first professor of chemistry in Europe, who edited and commented on Oswald Croll’s *Basilica Chymica*.</note>: *We say that the base of the Martial Ointment is Usnea, or a coagulated, corporeal animal spirit. For when people are strangled, the vital and natural spirits are driven upward, and there, because no exit is open due to the solid hardness of the human skull, they are trapped during the suffocation along with the animal spirits, and are confined as if in certain prisons until, with the passage of time, they coalesce into one and break out to the outer surface of the skull.*

But truly, in the first place, it is clear from what was said above that this kind of Ointment is prepared by some without *Usnea*; Johannes Wittichius <note>Johannes Wittich (1537–1596), a German physician known for his works on chemical medicine.</note> also follows this method, and thus it should not be considered the base at all. Moreover, we have heard it solemnly promised that the same healing occurs with a piece of ash wood alone, without any ointment. Secondly, that fabrication of Hartmann’s regarding the origin and substance of *Usnea* is ridiculous. Not only does it lack all reason and is simply made up at will, but it is also impossible for "spirits" <note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> to thicken into a dense body of that kind. I add that the vital spirit loses all power once the natural heat is extinguished; the remaining spirits are nothing other than the vital spirit tempered in one way or another, as we have taught elsewhere at length. 
<margin>Disputation on Innate Heat.</margin>
How, then, could the power of the spirit reside in the *Usnea*? Surely, you would much rather look for such a coagulated body (if one exists) in the heart immediately after death than in the head—and indeed in the brain, the seat of the animal spirits, rather than around the bones, through the whole body...

...already putrefied. Imagine indeed that such a growth is **Usnea** <note>A lichen found on the skulls of the dead, believed by Paracelsians to contain the "vital spirits" of the deceased.</note>; could it exert its power further than the spirits themselves can when they are intact? And yet, it is certain that the spirit of one man has no power over another. Even if they could exert some influence, the spirits of one healthy man are not able to heal another, as is well known to everyone. The same logic applies to human blood or fat. For even without these ingredients, the Ointment is often believed to be effective. Moreover, in these substances—which have by then been separated from the living body for a long time—nothing of the **vital spirits** <note>The "spiritus vitalis," thought to be a subtle substance that animated the body.</note> remains, and therefore nothing of the **animal spirits** either. Nor do those substances, when existing intact within living bodies, contribute anything to health elsewhere; thus, they contribute even less when they are already dead and their powers are diminished.

Nor is there any truth in the excuse some make: that these ingredients can exert their power only through the medium of spilled blood—as if, forsooth, that blood were finally the vehicle for that **sympathy** <note>original Greek: *συμπαθείας* (sympatheias); the occult principle that "like affects like" across a distance.</note> of the blood. For if that spilled blood possessed such a capacity for communication, the power of all things that are sprinkled with blood ought to be transferred to the wounds, or at least into the blood; yet this does not usually happen. Certainly, nothing prevents other things from being carried in this way, if the ingredients from which that ointment is constructed can be moved thus.

Furthermore, it is universally true that every action is beyond the forces of nature unless the agent is in some way joined with the "patient" <note>The "patient" refers to the object being acted upon by an external force.</note>. Truly, the Ointment is so far distant from the wound that there is actually nothing to unite them. Some defenders of the Ointment have seen the force of this objection, and they have fled to the **World-Spirit** <note>The *Spiritus Mundi*, a concept in Neoplatonism and alchemy describing a universal "breath" or substance that connects all parts of the cosmos.</note> as if to a **sacred anchor** <note>A Latin idiom (*sacra anchora*) meaning a final refuge or last resort.</note>; claiming, of course, that through the intervention of that spirit, all the power is carried to the wounds. Pietro Servio <note>Petrus Servius (died 1648), a Roman physician and scholar known for his defense of the weapon salve.</note>, currently the ornament of the physicians of the City of Rome, could devise nothing else in that most learned dissertation on behalf of this Ointment, which he even [sent] to me...

# CHAPTER XVIII.

Rome, with its characteristic kindness, has passed this on. No prudent person can admit its existence unless led by the strength of arguments. But suppose it were so. Yet if that Spirit transferred the powers of the Ointment to distant places, it would also transfer the powers of all other things. It is certain that this does not happen; otherwise, there is nothing that would not affect the human body. Indeed, all things would act upon all things without distinction, and thus there would always be a confused disturbance of all things. This would occur most especially if this communication were not restricted by certain limits, but occurred across any undetermined space, so that what is in the **Indies** <note>Used historically to refer to distant lands in Asia or the Americas.</note> would be capable of affecting Germany. And yet, the defenders of the salve are accustomed to affirming even this, failing to pay attention to those things which are most obvious in the nature of things and clearer than the midday sun. They would be driven to this point by the force of their own thesis, even against their will: for since that "carrier Spirit" is diffused through all things, nothing could hinder its work.

## CHAPTER XIX.

### That the Paracelsian school has labored much in metallic medicines compared to the ancient Hermetic school; yet in their use, they commit dangerous errors.

Truly, we have perhaps discussed the magical remedies of the Paracelsian sect more at length than the plan of this work requires. ...of those who followed the customs of the Arabs, as the writings of Pliny, Dioscorides, and Galen teach us; not to mention others.

Our Paracelsians <note>Followers of the 16th-century physician Paracelsus, who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> furthermore recommend metallic remedies above all others, not only for external applications but also for those taken internally. However, it is likely that the ancient Hermetics <note>Followers of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus; the author distinguishes these "true" ancients from the "modern" Paracelsians.</note> acted differently, both because this is nowhere mentioned and because of the contrary custom of all the Greeks. Indeed, to those surveying all the Greek records, it appears they very rarely used metallic substances except among those they call topical <note>original: "τοπικὰ"; meaning local applications like ointments or plasters.</note>; such things served that branch of medicine which heals by hand—surgery—for wounds, ulcers, and fractures.

Indeed, you would see almost no other minerals applied internally in the past than <term>burnt copper<gloss>aes ustum; likely copper oxide used for its drying properties</gloss></term>, "flower of copper" and copper scale, iron rust and <term>scoria<gloss>slag or metallic dross</gloss></term>, sulfur, <term>sandarac<gloss>here referring to realgar or red arsenic sulfide</gloss></term>, <term>vitriol<gloss>chalcanthum; a sulfate of copper or iron</gloss></term>, and even then only for a few conditions. Antimony mixed with elaterium <note>A potent purgative derived from the squirting cucumber.</note> to induce a bowel movement is found barely once in Dioscorides; nor can one find the internal use of <term>split alum<gloss>alumen scissile; a variety of the mineral alum</gloss></term> praised more than twice or thrice.

<margin>Hippocrates, *On the Nature of Women* and Book 1 of *Diseases of Women*.</margin>
One can read only in Hippocrates that <term>misy<gloss>a metallic sulfate mineral, similar to vitriol</gloss></term> was sometimes drunk by some in the quantity of a bean to prevent conception, though in vain. Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> is the sole witness that <term>quicksilver<gloss>Hydrargyrum; mercury</gloss></term> was customarily given in his age for colicky conditions; yet Dioscorides reports it as being counted among poisons, and Paul himself did not dare to praise the practice. 

After salt, however, one may learn from Dioscorides alone that the Greeks used <term>nitre<gloss>nitrum; in antiquity, this usually referred to natron (sodium carbonate) rather than modern saltpeter</gloss></term> quite frequently; he mentions in several places scattered throughout his work that it was mixed with other things. Pliny is witness 
<margin>Pliny, Book 31, Chapter 10.</margin>
that it was added to bread in place of salt, and likewise to radishes, side dishes, and vegetables. Galen's words in Book 13 of his *Method of Medicine*, Chapter 9, are: "Vitriol is among the primary astringents, as are also misy, sory, chalcitis, diphriges, burnt copper, and its scale and..." <note>The author lists several copper-based minerals (sory, chalcitis, diphriges) used in ancient pharmacology for their caustic or drying effects.</note>
