...flower <note>original: "flos", referring to the "flower of copper" mentioned on the previous page.</note>. However, these medicines are harmful if swallowed; for this reason, it is not safe to mix them for patients with stomach ailments, as something from these substances occasionally flows down into the belly. Therefore, whether there is some disagreement in this matter between the new **Hermetic sect** and the ancient one—if it is not certain, it at least appears highly probable.

It undoubtedly departs from the decree of the **old school** that the ***Paracelsians*** teach that those metallic substances are endowed with a **nourishing virtue**; for you would not easily find this written by any man of the ancient era.
<margin>Paracelsus, *Book on Leprosy*</margin>
**Paracelsus** indeed states: *Gold and Tartar <note>term: Tartar (Tartarum), the potassium bitartrate deposits found in wine casks, which Paracelsians believed caused "stone" diseases like gout.</note> are diaphoretic <note>term: diaphoretic, a substance that induces sweating.</note> foods*; and in his Aphorisms, he writes elsewhere: *It must be known that the internal organs are sustained and nourished by potable gold.* Likewise: *Every human contains within themselves a **Balsam** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, the "internal balsam" is a semi-mystical preservative force in the body that maintains health and prevents decay.</note> which lepers lack. Therefore, when **potable gold** is in the stomach, it distributes its powers from there into the rest of the body, from which a humidity is born that causes the balsam to grow.* The followers of Paracelsus speak in this same manner very frequently.

Finally, our new **Paracelsian school** undoubtedly departs most from the old school in the use of **metallic preparations**. For those ancients did not use remedies prepared chemically <note>original: "chemice paratis", referring to the process of laboratory distillation or sublimation.</note>, just as they did not use other metallic ones, as we have shown above. These men, however, value these alone, while others that are not so prepared are nearly cast out of the medical forum. Consequently, regarding metallic remedies, there is much disagreement between the ancient and this new school.

**TRULY**, however, if those ancient **Hermetics** had judged that one should abstain entirely from remedies of a metallic nature, they would certainly have erred gravely. For there is no evidence by which that could be proven; on the contrary, it is today most well known to everyone by experience that some of them are by far the most useful, whether used internally or externally. But it is not right to burden them with this suspicion...

### CHAPTER XIX.

...one can easily cite the consensus of the entire world regarding that excellence of **plants** in healing. For you will find few **metallic substances** brought into the practice of medicine among all nations; indeed, from the foundation of the world, almost everyone has provided medicine for the sick from plants alone. However, in that our **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine against the traditional herbal Galenic system.</note>, following the example of their master, have begun to apply metallic substances again to external ailments more often than was common, they deserve total praise in this regard. Truly, if I judge correctly, **Paracelsus** himself owed a better-than-usual cure for malignant and old ulcers to this one thing: for we shall show below that he was most effective in that area, and it is well known that, beyond the accepted custom of that time, he used very strong metallic substances for that kind of ulcer, both externally and internally. 

And indeed, besides him, others at that time noticed the flaw in the accepted custom. For clearly, when Paracelsus first became famous at Basel, **Georgius Agricola** <note>1494–1555, known as the "Father of Mineralogy." Though a contemporary of Paracelsus, he was more grounded in traditional scholarship.</note>—that great and incomparable light of Germany—wrote these words in the first book of his works on metals, titled *Bermannus*: <margin>*Bermannus*, chapter 2.</margin> *Is it any wonder if we do not heal certain **ulcers** which might otherwise perhaps be cured, when we can prepare so few complete plasters, especially those composed of metallic substances, which the ancients used with the greatest benefit to mankind and their own highest praise?* Likewise: *Who today can point out to us **molybdena**, **pyrite**, **chalcitis**, **misy**, **sory**, **pompholyx**, **spodos**, **diphryges**, and certain residues of metals, and many other things?* <note>These are technical terms from ancient Greek and Roman mineralogy. Chalcitis, misy, and sory refer to various copper and iron sulfates; pompholyx and spodos are types of zinc oxide residues from smelting; diphryges is a byproduct of copper refining.</note> *For besides **antimony**, **litharge** <term>litharge: a lead-based mineral (lead monoxide)</term>, **arsenic**, **white lead**, and a few other things, neither do the workshops <note>Apothecaries or pharmacies.</note> in which medicines of every kind are made have anything today, nor do the doctors know them.*

Similarly, our **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of the "Hermetic" or alchemical tradition, who sought the secrets of nature through chemical experimentation.</note> must not be cheated of the praise for their diligence, even regarding the internal use of metallic substances.

For they have indeed taught the advantages of a greater number of metallic substances than were formerly used, as well as various previously unknown preparations of those that were already in some use, which are nevertheless extremely beneficial for certain diseases.

Nor, indeed, should we listen to those who think all these substances should be excluded from the medical class of internal remedies, as if they were either plainly hostile to our body, or, due to their hardness and dryness, unfit to produce any effect. Daily experience teaches us how far both claims are from the truth. If all metallic substances were hostile to the body when taken internally, surely a long period of time would have already discovered this; and yet, from the time of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> until today, quite a few of them have consistently earned praise from the finest practitioners of the medical art. The latter claim is so false that—with the possible exception of gold and raw silver—all metals and metallic substances, even those that have undergone no chemical processing, often demonstrate their power when taken by mouth, sometimes causing great harm, but occasionally resulting in improved health. Regarding metallic substances and the so-called <term>chyta</term> <note>original: χυτῶν (chytōn). A Greek term referring to "cast" or "molten" materials, specifically metals that can be liquefied and poured.</note>, the matter is clear.

Indeed, mercury was once counted among the poisons; today we have discovered that if it is taken in such a quantity that it can quickly find a way through the bowels by its own weight, it is actually harmless; otherwise, it can afflict the body with many very serious conditions. <margin>Jean Fernel, *On the Venereal Disease*, ch. 3. Indeed, gold especially is of such a solid substance that not even the most violent flaming fire is able to dissolve it; how much less, then, would the gentler heat of living creatures accomplish this? If this is impossible, then no essence can be drawn from it into the veins, nor would the substance of gold itself perform anything extraordinary, since it does not possess any outstanding quality in itself. Rather, since it is of heavy weight, it is very likely to remain in the intestines; this is especially clear since it is established that gold leaf, even when eaten by chickens—whose stomachs are hotter than a human's—is excreted whole with the waste. 

However, although this is the case for raw gold and silver, it is completely false to say that the same metals, prepared by chemical art, can do nothing for our body. I am certain that the gold called *fulminating* <note>Aurum fulminans: a volatile gold compound. ...melting and dissolving. Furthermore, it seems common to almost all—or at least nearly all—metallic remedies that their power and nature cannot be entirely overcome or transformed by our bodies. ->### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<- [[page number: 248]]

...that gold and silver itself could be converted into the substance of an animal body, and that a trial of this should be conducted in a hen—as a certain **Franz Wendler** <note>original: "Franciscus VVendlerus"</note> did not hesitate to profess at length, as if he had performed the experiment—yet in reality, this "hot invention" <note>An idiomatic way of describing a baseless or overly imaginative claim.</note> is refuted. **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a prominent German physician who attempted to reconcile traditional Galenic medicine with the newer chemical theories of Paracelsus.</note>, who had inserted the man’s words into the preface of the first edition of his work *On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chemists with the Aristotelians and Galenists* <note>original: "Consensu & dissensu Chymicor. cum Aristotelicis & Galenicis"</note>, repeated them indeed in the nineteenth chapter of the second edition. At the same time, however, he testifies that he had provided silver to be devoured by a hen according to Wendler’s prescription in vain. And indeed, when Wendler himself was addressed by letter, he affirmed the deed, but only hesitantly—which is surely the custom of those who have been convicted of a fabrication.

<margin>Observations on the Aphorisms of Sala, 21.</margin> <note>Likely referring to the work of Angelo Sala (1576–1637), a pioneer in chemistry who was skeptical of alchemical transmutations.</note> **Peter Lauremberg** <note>Petrus Laurembergius (1585–1639), a German physician and polymath.</note> recounts that he attempted the same thing with silver with a similar outcome. Nor, indeed, is there any reason to think, as our Sennert does, that perhaps things would succeed more correctly with gold. For it is well known that gold is far less suited to be dissolved than silver, whether by the force of a most intense flame or by corroding liquids. How then should gold be dissolved by our animal heat, when its strength has no power over silver?

And truly, however much of what they call **gold leaf** <note>original: "foliati auri"</note> you give to be devoured by a hen or any other animal, the burned remains of their excrement will return just as much to you, if you collect it carefully, as has been tested more than once.

<margin>Eichstadt, *On Apple Alkermes*, no. 20.</margin> <note>Lorenz Eichstadt’s work on "Alkermes," a popular medicinal cordial often containing pearls or gold.</note> **Lorenz Eichstadt** <note>Laurentius Eichstadius (1596–1660), a physician and astronomer.</note>, outstanding in learning as both a physician and an astronomer, attests to this fact; in a **Calicut hen** <term>gallina Calecutiensi</term> <note>In this period, this often referred to a turkey or an exotic breed of poultry.</note>, after it had devoured two **books** <note>original: "libellos"; here referring to the small packets or booklets containing sheets of gold leaf.</note> of gold leaf, as they call it, he could detect no gold at all, whether pure or mixed with any part of the body. On the contrary, it is certain that nothing is lost from pure gold by **animal fire** <note>The innate heat of a living body, thought to be the engine of digestion.</note> if it is devoured.

<margin>Sennert, chapter 29, *On the Agreement...*, page 430.</margin> Indeed, the story brought forward from Zacharias Puteus <note>Zacharias Pasqualigo (1512–1594), an Italian physician known as Puteus.</note> by our colleague Sennert does not prove the contrary; for Puteus did not claim that the earring in question was made of pure gold. Perhaps, in truth, it should be counted among fables. It is no less a myth than that saying of 
<margin>Pliny, book 29, chapter 4.</margin>
Pliny: *“If the parts of a hen are mixed with molten gold, they consume it into themselves; thus, this is the poison of gold.”* <note>original Latin: "Si auro liquefacto gallinarum membra misceantur consumunt hoc in se: ita hoc venenum auri est"</note> Or consider instead the claim of Leonardo Fioravanti <note>An influential and controversial Italian physician and alchemist (1517–1588).</note>, most famous by reputation among the chemists of Italy: that if gold leaf is inserted into the flesh of a hen, the gold is dissolved into a liquid. I do not deny, however, that when almost all other metals are swallowed, something is gradually worn away by the power of the "animal fire" <note>The "innate heat" or vital energy believed by early physicians to drive digestion and life.</note>, just as happens with stones. But indeed, it is by no means to be inferred from this that these metals turn into nourishment. Even if one of these things is sought out by an animal—as they say the **ostrich** <note>original: "struthiocamelum"</note> eats iron—it should be considered that it is sought as a medicine rather than as food. In truth, if metallic substances provide nourishment, they must nourish either the animal fire, or what they call the "spirits," or the solid parts of the body. They certainly do not nourish that fire; for this fire is light and demands matter for its fuel that is easily suited to be changed into fire. Metals, however, are heavy and do not cast off their weight except with extreme difficulty. If you except sulfur and bitumen, almost none of them feed a flame. Those which today are called metals **par excellence** <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἐξοχὴν" (kat' exochēn), meaning pre-eminently or in the highest sense.</note> are all entirely unfit for feeding a flame: alum, vitriol <note>original: "chalcanthum," a term for metallic sulfates like copperas.</note>, and all the chemical liquids prepared from these metals actually extinguish fire. There are those who affirm that the **innate heat** <note>original: "calidum nativum"</note> is nourished by metallic substances because that heat is sometimes revived by metallic remedies. But in fact, many things assist any kind of fire without actually serving as fuel; and thus, the animal fire is revived by things other than food alone. Similarly, it is not even possible for the spirits of the living body (if there are such things) to arise from metallic substances,

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...is possible, is disproven by the natural weight, density, and difficulty of transformation of metallic substances. For all these qualities are vehemently opposed to spirits of this kind. It is truly foolish that some claim gold is very similar to the spirits because both participate in the nature of the **fifth essence** <note>Also known as "quintessence," this was believed by alchemists to be a pure, celestial element beyond the four earthly elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. For all of this is a mere invention, proven by not even the slightest piece of evidence. Furthermore, metallic fumes or spirits are dry, and cannot be inhaled through the nostrils without danger to life; they are far from being suitable for conversion into the spirits of a living body. Indeed, the same density, hardness, and unfixable dryness of metals proves that metallic things cannot be changed into the solid parts of our body, since most of these parts must be soft and juicy. Even for bones, the hardness and dryness inherent in metals is unsuitable, as they otherwise could not properly contain the **animal fire** <note>A historical medical term for the internal heat that drives digestion, circulation, and life.</note> which requires moist nourishment. 

And truly, what need is there for words? Since it is well known that no animal feeds on anything metallic except very rarely and perhaps as a seasoning or a remedy for disease. Moreover, no living thing is generated from the decay of any metallic substance; finally, stones, metals, and metallic juices are not gnawed by any animal as wood is by the woodworm. It is no wonder, however, that the **Paracelsian** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a physician who famously incorporated chemistry and minerals into medicine, often using obscure or mystical terminology.</note> sect thinks and speaks otherwise, as they are accustomed to playing with words and asserting whatever comes into their minds during a dream or whatever comes out of their mouths. Thus, they attribute nutritional power to all medicines insofar as they are medicines. 

<margin>Paracelsus in *The Surgical Physician*</margin> 

Paracelsus, in his book *On Tartar* <note>original: "de Tartaro." Paracelsus used the term "Tartar" to describe stony or mineral deposits in the body that he believed caused diseases like gout or stones.</note>, says: "Only nourishment pervades the whole body, and by that alone are diseases cured everywhere." Elsewhere he writes that the art of curing wounds consists in offering the appropriate nourishment to the wound. Likewise: "My natural **balsam** <note>In this context, an internal healing force or "vital honey" that Paracelsus believed existed within the body to repair damage.</note> is that which heals; for this, it needs a double nourishment;"

### CHAPTER XIX. 251

...one provides *food and drink*, the other *a remedy applied to a wound. Therefore, an ointment or medicine is the suitable nourishment of the Balsam <note>original: "Balsami"; in Paracelsian medicine, the "internal balsam" was a theoretical healing force within the body that maintained health and repaired tissues.</note>; wherefore a good doctor ought primarily to strive to choose appropriate nourishment.* To have recited these things is to have refuted them.

In preparing metallic remedies according to the chemical manner, the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a physician who famously broke with traditional Greek medicine to advocate for the use of minerals and chemicals in cures.</note> of our time have truly expended so much industry, so much labor, and so much expense, that they have left far behind not only those ancient **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of the mystical and alchemical traditions attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, but also the chemists of the Middle Ages. Nor indeed has luck entirely failed them, since in this way quite a few things have come into the workshop of the medical art which can be of the greatest benefit for taming certain most stubborn diseases. 

But truly, if one examines everything accurately, this *first* point must be confessed: the discovery of those remedies should be attributed not so much to any art as to chance and luck. For all the work of the chemists tends toward this: that they may elicit from metals what they call the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; also known as the "quintessence," this was believed by alchemists to be a celestial, incorruptible element distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>, which is supposedly the unique source of all latent virtues. This they hope to achieve partly by fire and partly by dissolution through corrosive liquids. 

Now, however, it will be clearly demonstrated shortly that everything concerning that "fifth essence" of **sublunary bodies** <note>original: "corporum sublunarium"; refers to objects on Earth, beneath the moon, which in ancient cosmology were thought to be changeable and corruptible, unlike the eternal stars.</note> is a mere fable and an empty invention. Certainly, from metals as from other things, the chemists have so far produced nothing that does not reflect the nature of elementary bodies in every respect; nothing that truly deserves the name of "spirit," however much they are commonly sold by Paracelsians under such ambitious and proud titles. Furthermore, no reason indicates that if any fifth essence exists within metals, it could be drawn out either by the force of the most violent fire or through corrosive liquids—

...to be drawn out. On the contrary, it seems more likely that in this manner those very essences, if any exist, are either driven away or corrupted. Gluckradius—or rather Johannes Hartmann <note>Johannes Hartmann (1568–1631) was the first professor of chemistry in Europe, though he published some works under the pseudonym Gluckradius.</note> himself—seems to have acknowledged this to some extent, writing in these words: 

<margin>In the notes to Beguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum* <note>Jean Beguin's "Chemical Beginner's Guide," a highly influential 17th-century chemistry textbook.</note>, page 4.</margin>

> *It is certain and established that the pseudo-chemists <note>original: "chymicastros," a derogatory term for amateur or fraudulent chemists.</note>, without true and natural reasoning, through the violence of Vulcan <note>A poetic reference to the intense heat of the forge or furnace, named after the Roman god of fire.</note>, various sublimations and reverberations, and likewise through burning and eroding solvents <note>original: "menstruis," a term used by chemists for liquids capable of dissolving solids.</note>, in some way change, destroy, and pervert the natures of things. They do not extract true essences from them as they foolishly claim, and much less do they separate that solar and healing balsam <note>In alchemy, the "balsam" refers to the internal preservative or medicinal soul of a substance.</note>.* 

Even Angelus Sala <note>An Italian physician (1576–1637) who was an early critic of alchemy and a pioneer of chemical analysis.</note> did not hesitate to write thus in his *Aphorisms*:

<margin>Sala, section 1, aphorism 15.</margin>

> *All things treated in fire undergo alteration, and they must necessarily be cast down in some way from the state of their natural temperament. This is especially true if they are forced to endure either the most vehement heat or a longer duration; it is less so if the fire is milder and the time spent in it shorter.*

However, almost all metallic preparations are made through the force of vehement fire. These are also the words of the same Sala: 

<margin>Section 1, aphorism 43.</margin>

> *Those who calcine <note>To heat a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note> precious stones in a most vehement fire layered with sulfur, saltpeter, or other such things, and thereafter strive to separate their substances or reduce them to a liquid, are shamefully deluded in two ways. First, by this calcination they strip away all tincture <note>original: "tincturam," the inner quality or color that alchemists believed held the medicinal power.</note> from them, and by altering their natural temperament, they plunder their specific properties. This can be seen in the magnet, which, once calcined, entirely loses its attractive power, etc.* 

The same logic that applies to gems applies to most metallic substances. While gold and mercury are not dissolved into parts by fire or corrosives, they nevertheless take on a different nature in this way, one far removed from their native state, as is very well known. They certainly do not provide a <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or purest medicinal extract of a substance, supposedly free of the impurities of the four elements.</note> since they are insoluble. Indeed, it cannot be by the chemists...

### CHAPTER XIX.

...opponents who have the audacity to deny that whatever chemically prepared metallic substances are commonly available differ greatly from the nature and powers of whole metals. Therefore, those remedies that the school of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> has prepared for us from metals are certainly not the result of the Art—for the Art performs all things with right reason and prudent, prior consultation. Instead, it is only because experience has proven them—constructed as they are by I know not what design—capable of being beneficial to health.

From this it follows, furthermore, that most of that Paracelsian school incorrectly judge the powers of chemically prepared substances based on the nature of metals that have not undergone such violence. They act as if these chemical products differ from the whole metals in no way other than having a greater power of penetration. Yet **Crollius** <term>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), an influential follower of Paracelsus who codified many chemical recipes</term> defames raw **Chalcanthum** <term>original: "Chalcanthum," a term for vitriol or copper sulfate, often used as a caustic</term> as a poison, while he hawks its "spirit" as a **Theriac** <term>original: "Theriaca," traditionally a complex herbal "all-cure" antidote, here used for a chemical distillate</term>. When this same man had described the virtues of the whole salt, he indeed wrote: *Since these virtues are present in the raw salt, how much more powerful will they be in its suitably prepared spirit?* nonetheless, a little earlier he had said: *It is a marvel that this spirit has a singular antipathy and a contrary nature to common salt.* Paracelsus himself, in *Book 1 on Natural Things, chapter 9*, counted **arsenic** prepared with **niter** <term>original: "nitro," or saltpeter</term> among medicines. **Quercetanus** <term>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who advocated for the chemical "Harmonious" medicine</term> and others dare to promise the most noble **antidotes** <note>original Greek: "ἀλεξιφάρμακα" (alexipharmaka), medicines intended to ward off poison or disease</note> from arsenic. I will not say now with what sincerity they do this; the substance praised by Paracelsus is surely a most potent poison. Yet if, by their own admission, arsenic is turned from a poison into an **antidote** <note>original Greek: "ἀλεξιφάρμακον"</note> through preparation, it is clear from this one example alone how much metals are changed by chemical preparations.

Furthermore, since these chemical preparations are not made without violent fire or corrosives, they wrong-

Thus we know the boast of a **sweet spirit of vitriol**; we know that some attempt to make it using iron and other materials, while others use coral crushed into powder. CHAPTER XIX. 255

...[he] said [it was] of the sweetest scent, and wrote that the spirit of salt was **bittersweet** <note>original: *γλυκύπικρον* (glykypikron)</note>. Hartmann, his commentator, more correctly adds—where he had ordered a certain sweet oil of **vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid</note> to be prepared from iron: *"But by these **procedures** <note>original: εγχειρήμασι (encheirēmasi)</note>, the virtues of the oil itself are greatly diminished, and no medical effects are hoped for from them."* He writes the same regarding the "sweet oil of salt" <note>hydrochloric acid neutralized or mixed with alcohol</note> which is likewise commonly boasted of: *"There is a quite glorious display among the Chemists concerning sweet oil of salt, but it can never be demonstrated. Therefore, it is the spirit of wine alone that procures this sweetness: whether it is joined with the salt for distilling from the beginning, or whether the spirit of salt is distilled afterward by frequently **redistilling** <term>cohobando: the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid from its solid residue to concentrate it or extract more essence</term> with the same. In this way, and no other, does it remove all sharpness from the spirit of salt and make it somewhat sweet, effecting the same in other spirits in a similar manner."* **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne, a prominent Paracelsian physician known for his chemical remedies</note> affirms that his "sweet crystals of salt" have the power to dissolve even that which is most fixed; whether such a thing is consistent with a sweetness rivalling sugar is not difficult to judge.

I confess there is no lack of those of the Paracelsian order who promise solutions of metallic bodies without fire or corrosives, through tasteless and sweet **solvents** <term>menstrua: a term for solvents used in alchemy, believed to 'extract' the soul or essence of a substance</term>. <meta>This page continues the author’s critique of chemical medicines. ### ->ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...[no] body under the sun from that triple kingdom <note>The "three kingdoms of nature": animal, vegetable, and mineral.</note> is destitute of it.

<margin>See chapter 17, page 212, and Hartmann, page 389, on Basil <note>Referring to the works of alchemist Basil Valentine.</note>.</margin>
We have already warned above that **Francis Anthony** <note>Francis Anthony (1550–1623) was an English goldsmith and physician famous for his "Aurum Potabile" or drinkable gold, which he claimed was a universal cure-all made without corrosives.</note> falsely boasted of the calcination and solution of gold without corrosives, and no less falsely denied the possibility of reducing that dissolved gold back to its original state. Even **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a prominent Paracelsian physician and alchemist.</note>, a most expert and yet most superstitious investigator of these matters, admits that such solvents of gold are commonly and fabulously invented by all other chemists. Crollius himself foolishly places all his hope in what they call the **universal solvent of the philosophers** <term>menstruum universale<gloss>the "Alkahest" or mythical universal solvent capable of dissolving any substance</gloss></term>, which both reason and experience demonstrate to be no less fabulous. Truly, Crollius is just as foolish in this matter—if not more so—when he promises that vitriol <term>vitriol<gloss>a sulfate of a metal, here copper or iron</gloss></term> is to be made from **Venus and Mars** <note>Alchemical symbols for copper and iron.</note> without a corrosive, yet at the same time orders sulfur to be burned with a most vehement fire; as was correctly noted also by **Angelo Sala** <note>Angelo Sala (1576–1637) was a pioneer of chemistry who criticized the more mystical claims of alchemy.</note>. Suppose indeed that some tasteless solvent could be found for a metal: it is nonetheless well-known that corrosives are commonly used, and therefore a corrosive faculty commonly adheres to all metallic substances dissolved in that way.

If, however, all chemically prepared metallic substances contain an **empyreuma** <term>empyreuma<gloss>the "burnt" smell or harsh quality resulting from the use of extreme heat in distillation</gloss></term> or the power of eroding, it is certainly manifest that physicians must proceed with far greater caution in their use than in raw materials. Much less can they be administered indiscriminately in all diseases, as the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus who favored chemical and mineral medicines over traditional herbal remedies.</note> are accustomed to boast. Neither truly can any of these find a place in cases of **hectic fevers** <note>A chronic, wasting fever often associated with tuberculosis.</note> or ulcerated internal organs.

<margin>Aphorism 26, section 2.</margin>
Wisely indeed, Sala himself denies that the so-called **magistery of pearls** <term>magisterium perlarum<gloss>a preparation of pearls dissolved in an acid (usually vinegar or lemon juice) and then precipitated</gloss></term> is suitable for those with hectic fever or consumption, because of the sharp spirits of vinegar that adhere to the pearls. How much more will metallic substances cause harm, if to their native power is added either vehement fire or a corroding

...a liquid far more pungent than the spirit of wine vinegar. In some consumptive patients who abound with much phlegm <term>pituita<gloss>phlegm or mucus, one of the four traditional humors</gloss></term> (for consumption sometimes arises from this, as Fracastoro <note>original: "Fracastorius"; Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553) was an Italian physician known for early theories on contagious diseases.</note> correctly observed) and who are free from all hectic heat, I would not deny that some such metallic preparation might occasionally do good. However, for others suffering from this disease, both reason and <margin>Basil, page 423.</margin> practice prove that none of these things are beneficial, except in the rarest of cases. For Crollius is by no means to be listened to when he recommends the flowers of sulfur <term>flowers of sulfur<gloss>a fine yellow powder produced by heating sulfur until it turns to vapor and then cooling it back to a solid</gloss></term>—having undergone a fierce fire two or three times—indiscriminately for all ailments of the lungs, for pleurisy, and for all fevers and pneumonia. <margin>Basil, page 369.</margin> He likewise attacks what remains of health by praising milk of sulfur <term>lac sulphuris<gloss>a white precipitate of sulfur, named for its milky appearance when in suspension</gloss></term>, as if it were a balsam for the radical moisture <term>radical moisture<gloss>the vital fluid or "innate heat" thought to sustain life and be depleted by disease</gloss></term>, as if it were a specific remedy for the lungs, and as if it were uniquely beneficial when administered with cinnamon water to those who are parched and suffering from hectic fever, helping all consumptives indiscriminately by acting upon the radical moisture. 

It certainly acts upon it, but *like a hidden fire*; with which phrase Crollius himself does not exactly express the power of that "milk" in a "milky" way <note>The author makes a pun on the Latin "lactè," meaning "clearly" or "smoothly," in contrast to "lac," meaning "milk."</note>. More correctly, Sala <note>Angelo Sala (1576–1637), a pioneer in chemical medicine who advocated for more cautious applications than the Paracelsians.</note> adapts those flowers of sulfur to <margin>Aphorism 32, section 2.</margin> *infirmities proceeding from a cold and moist cause*. And indeed, they induce sweating in all diseases, as <margin>Hartmann on Crollius.</margin> Hartmann <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631) was the first professor of chemistry in a European university.</note> notes; who, forced by the weight of truth, warns that such a fiery thing as milk of sulfur is not suitable for all hectic patients. Truly, the ancients cautiously preferred native sulfur <term>sulphur vivum<gloss>naturally occurring sulfur that has not been processed by fire or sublimation</gloss></term> for consumption and other internal ailments. Hippocrates has nothing else on his lips but "unfired" sulfur <term>apyron<gloss>original Greek: ἄπυρον, meaning "without fire" or "unprocessed"</gloss></term>. Dioscorides explicitly testifies that the "unfired" kind is considered the best. <margin>Pliny, Book 35, Chapter 5.</margin> These are the words of Pliny: *of all kinds of sulfur, physicians use only the native sulfur.* Nor indeed did they employ sandarac <term>sandarach<gloss>in this context, likely "realgar," a red arsenic mineral used in ancient medicine</gloss></term> except very rarely, and then primarily for an old cough;

likewise: Hippocrates gave sulfur only in the weight of one or two obols <note>original: *obolus*; a small ancient Greek unit of weight, roughly 0.7 grams</note>, whereas Croll prescribes a whole drachm <note>roughly 3.9 grams—a significantly higher dose</note> of his "flowers" <term>flowers of sulfur<gloss>a fine powder produced by the sublimation of sulfur</gloss></term>.

Indeed, they commonly extol their gold-based preparations almost to the heavens, and yet so far no one has prepared gold without corrosives; that it cannot be done otherwise, despite what triflers commonly boast, **Angelus Sala** <note>a 17th-century physician and chemist known for his skeptical approach to alchemy</note> clearly showed in his *Chrysologia* <note>a work on the nature of gold</note>. Truly, Croll's bombastic claims <note>original: *ampullas*, literally "flasks" but used here to mean "puffed-up language"</note> regarding the powers of **potable gold** <term>aurum potabile<gloss>a legendary alchemical "liquid gold" panacea</gloss></term>, prepared "philosophically" as he says, are mere absurdities. The proof is that he himself admits he has never seen such a thing, even though he tried various ways, and after using nearly a hundred recipes in a futile effort, he suffered a loss of time and expense, and thus he rejects all the preparations of common Alchemists. Indeed, he asserts that this gold cannot be prepared "philosophically" (that is, without corrosives) except by the benefit of a **universal solvent** <term>menstruum universale<gloss>the "alkahest," a mythical substance capable of dissolving any matter into its primary elements</gloss></term> (an opinion which the commentator **Hartmann** also approves), which is nonetheless impossible to find. It is very clear that he spoke of a matter unknown to himself. He likewise attacks all gold prepared through corrosives. **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315); here referring to alchemical texts falsely attributed to him</note> says (these are Croll's words):

> *It is better to eat a blazing fire with the eyes of a basilisk <note>the mythical king of serpents whose gaze was lethal</note> than to apply poison in the place of potable gold: because sophisticated gold <note>falsified or chemically altered gold</note> is entirely full of impurity from the fire against nature <note>ignis contra naturam; a term for corrosive acids or chemical heat used in alchemical processes</note> with which the Sophist works: for immediately through these sharp things of the 'fire against nature,' the natural heat is killed, and the spirits of the heart, in which natural heat is preserved, are dissolved.*

For the rest, I certainly do not [agree] with Lull and Croll...

### CHAPTER XIX.

...and others, to such an extent that I dread the power of every corrosive. I am well aware that excellent remedies are given, prepared from gold and other substances through corrosives; indeed, **Croll** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a disciple of Paracelsus and author of the influential *Basilica Chymica*</note> himself filled almost his entire *Basilica* with remedies of this kind alone. Yet this is truer than truth: such a gold preparation is not to be administered always, nor in all conditions of the heart. Certainly, it cannot be regarded as a universal medicine without committing a crime against the patient. **Sala** <note>Angelus Sala (1576–1637), a pioneer in chemistry who bridged the gap between alchemy and modern science</note> ingenuously confessed the same, and in the seventh deduction of his *Chrysologia* <note>a treatise on gold</note> he wrote: *“There is no mastery <term>magisterium<gloss>a high-level alchemical preparation where the 'essence' of a substance is extracted</gloss></term> of gold that may not at times harm as much as it may help, if its manifest qualities, dosage, and correct use are neglected.”*

<margin>Sala, section of aphorisms 24, 31, 32, and 25.</margin>
A greater sin is commonly committed by our **Paracelsians** <note>followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, known for using minerals and chemicals in medicine</note> in the use of **metallic vinegars** <term>acetum metallicum<gloss>strong acids derived from minerals, used as solvents</gloss></term>, and indeed the sin is greater where there is more acrimony and corrosive power in them. Nor is it unknown that these substances are so boasted of—not only by the common people but by the leaders of the Paracelsian sect themselves—as if no danger were to be feared from them, and as if they possessed the same mildness as lemon juice, mineral waters, or garlic. Croll promises the cure of internal ulcers and the renovation of man from the **spirit of salt** <term>spiritus salis<gloss>hydrochloric acid</gloss></term>. **Hartmann** <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631), the first professor of chemistry in Germany</note> promises the restoration of the essential humidity of our bodies. **Vitriolated tartar** <term>tartarus vitriolatus<gloss>potassium sulfate, often used as a purgative</gloss></term> is a "universal digestive" according to Croll. **Spirit of vitriol** <term>spiritus vitrioli<gloss>sulfuric acid</gloss></term> is everywhere commended as a **panacea** <note>a universal cure-all</note>. According to **Paracelsus** himself, it is: *“the fourth part of the pharmacy and the cornerstone in the shops of pharmacists.”* But the actual use and the fatal outcomes have forced Angelus Sala himself to express quite different views. Concerning the spirit of salt, he says: *“It requires a prudent and circumspect physician who knows how to administer it cautiously and appropriately.”* Concerning the spirit of vitriol: *“It must be used with no small amount of accurate judgment, and applied according to medicinal rules. For it is not a panacea, as some have persuaded themselves, but rather because...”*

No one is ignorant that this crime was slanderously ascribed by **Hartmann** <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631), the first professor of chemistry in Europe</note> to **Thomas Erastus** <note>A famous physician and critic of Paracelsus</note>, unless they are equally unaware that no other physician more detested or more frequently attacked metallic remedies of this kind. # CHAPTER XIX.

...you would certainly wait in vain [for it to mix], because on account of its inherent weight it easily separates from that [fluid], especially if it is liquid, and seeks the bottom of the stomach itself. How easily it detaches itself from the very juices and companion fluids with which it was mixed is indicated by their more vibrant color at the bottom. Therefore, it easily causes harm whenever it does not encounter humors <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenic medicine believed governed health</note> capable of warding off that corrosive power from the bare internal membranes of our body; although this harm might be washed away if it is not frequent or large. The nature of acidic mineral waters is certainly far different; yet even they are drunk with greater danger the sharper they are. For first, how small is that sharpness which is diluted by a large quantity of water! Then, how light and volatile that is, compared to how heavy those **metallic vinegars** <note>original: *metallicorum aceta*; a term used by early chemists for concentrated mineral acids like sulfuric or hydrochloric acid</note> are! In vain, therefore, are the evils of those vinegars masked by the benefits of acidic mineral waters by **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and diplomat who championed "Chymical" medicine</note>, **Beguin** <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620), author of the highly influential *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, the first chemistry textbook</note>, and others. Nor is the difference obscure between the power of lemon juice, garlic, and vinegars of that sort, provided the judgment is left to the tongue and daily experience. It is very well known that the tongue tolerates whole ounces of lemon and garlic juices better than one or two drops of **spirit of vitriol** <note>original: *spiritus vitrioli*; concentrated sulfuric acid</note>.

Finally, the most serious offenses are committed by the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, who rejected traditional herbal medicine in favor of minerals and alchemy</note> in their use and praise of both **emetics** <note>original: *emeticorum*; medicines that induce vomiting</note> and **purgatives** <note>original: *purgantium*; medicines that induce bowel movements</note> prepared from metallic bodies in the chemical fashion. However, this error has already been noted above; and the nature of this undertaking does not allow us to examine everything down to the bone <note>original: *ad vivum resecare*; literally "to cut to the quick," meaning to analyze in exhaustive or painful detail</note>. For that reason, we shall now leave this entire topic, to deal briefly in the next section with every other kind of remedy.

## CHAPTER XX.

->The same is demonstrated concerning medicines derived from stones, animals, and plants.<-

Whether the ancient practitioners of Hermetic medicine made any use of stones is not easily said, except that it is certain that various images were once engraved upon them according to the teachings of **Nechepso** <note>original: *Nechepsi disciplinâ*; Nechepso was a legendary Egyptian Pharaoh to whom early texts on astrology and medical magic were attributed</note>. Today, certain followers of Paracelsus likewise employ them in a similar fashion. However, this belongs to the realm of Magic. Furthermore, the Paracelsians, following the doctrine of the **Arab physicians** <note>Medieval Islamic physicians like Rhazes and Avicenna, who frequently included crushed gemstones in their pharmacopeia</note>, are accustomed to recommend the administration of powdered gems, especially for ailments of the heart. Yet, they do so after a preparation performed in the chemical manner, which it is not likely was used by the Arab physicians.

Moreover, that raw gems can provide what the Arabs believed they could has certainly not been established by any experiment to date. Even less tolerable, it seems, are the chemical attempts of the Paracelsians. For here, as elsewhere, they have hoped to separate the **fifth essence** <term>Fifth Essence: also known as the "quintessence," it was believed to be the purest, most potent spiritual core of a substance, distinct from the four physical elements</term> of the gems—that is, the source of all their powers—from the thicker, material body. To achieve this, they are accustomed to **calcine** <term>Calcine: to reduce a mineral to a fine powder or ash by applying extreme heat</term> the gems in a most violent fire, having "stratified" them (as the chemists say) with sulfur, nitre, and other salts. Soon after, they separate a part of that ash or reduce it into a liquid, and whatever is thus separated and dissolved they distinguish with the name of "oil," "salt," or the "essence of gems." However, that entire notion of the fifth essence of bodies—and thus of gems as well—is nothing but a feverish fabrication.

<margin>See Sala, section 1, aphorism 43.</margin> <note>original: *Vide Salam.*; a reference to Angelo Sala (1576–1637), a pioneer of chemical medicine who advocated for more rational, laboratory-based evidence</note>

### CHAPTER XX.

...essence. For it would be just as if you searched for the complete essence of a house within the ashes of a house that had been burned down. To this end, those substances which are separated and dissolved from the **lime** <term>Lime (calx): the powdery residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined" at high heat</term>, if you judge the matter truly, are nothing but the burnt salts of niter, sulfur, and others, which adhere to the tasteless lime of the gemstones. Even if these were the actual salts of the gems themselves, they are certainly far from being worthy of being held in the place of **quintessences** <term>Quintessence: the "fifth essence," or the most purified, spiritualized core of a substance that remains after its physical elements are stripped away</term>. Indeed, all of that material is no less sharp and corrosive than the calcined lees of wine <note>original: *fæx vini calcinata*; likely referring to potash or potassium carbonate, which is highly alkaline and caustic</note>, as the taste reveals. 

From this it is simultaneously clear that, while gemstones may have some value in protecting the heart, nothing of that sort can be expected from those common preparations of the Paracelsians; rather, those preparations are harmful instead of useful for that purpose. Not even Paracelsus himself could always hide that sharpness of the **magistery** <term>Magistery: a concentrated medicinal preparation supposed to contain the full power of a substance</term> of gemstones. *Do not fear* (he writes in Book 5 of the *Archidoxis* <note>The *Archidoxis* (The Archidoxes of Theophrastus) was one of Paracelsus's most influential works on the preparation of chemical medicines</note>) *to administer it because it is sharp and partakes of the nature of lime: for its sharpness only acts against resistance.*

A similar effort, and no less unhappy a success, has been seen among these same Paracelsians thus far regarding shells, corals, and pearls. Likewise, the primary praise for all these in medical matters seems to be owed to the **Arab physicians** <note>such as Avicenna and Rhazes, who used crushed precious materials in their remedies</note>, though it is destitute of any certain experiment or reason that might persuade one of it. For the argument some take from their luster—proposing a correspondence between our vital spirits and this shine—is ridiculous. For what does luster do for the spirits, if such things even exist? Certainly, their powder has lost its original luster; yet the Arabs were only accustomed to give them to the sick when crushed into a fine dust. Now truly, all these things (unlike gemstones) provide a tiny amount of liquid, water, and oil when subjected to the violence of an open fire, with a certain tasteless lime remaining. But these products do nothing for medical use; they are far from containing anything of the fifth es- <meta>catchword: sence (sentia)</meta>

...essences or of extraordinary virtues. Commonly, these bodies are changed into a **false powder** by the benefit of distilled vinegar, which they call "Salt," ascribing the pure virtues of the whole, original substances to the powder itself. Furthermore, all that saltiness is derived from the vinegar, as Angelus Sala <note>Angelus Sala (1576–1637) was an early chemist and physician who was skeptical of some extreme alchemical claims.</note> rightly warned: <margin>Section 1, aphorism 40</margin> that powder cannot always be safely administered; certainly, the sharpness and corrosive power it immediately leaves on the tongue proves it is very far from the nature of corals and pearls.

Indeed, Oswald Croll <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) was a prominent follower of Paracelsus and an advocate for "spagyric" or chemical medicine.</note> fights against the senses, declaring that powder (as long as it truly deserves the name of "Salt") to be free from all sharp acidity. I am not ignorant of its excellent uses, but they should not be ascribed to the corals and pearls so much as to the remnants of the vinegary spirit. Both reason and experience prove that the praises of Croll and others are vain. 

For what is more vain than to claim that *this salt of pearls preserves a healthy body, restores a damaged one to its original health, improves a woman's milk, increases the semen of both sexes, and dries up and consumes all evil humors existing in the body?* They claim it works *against wasting, dryness, and the decay of old age; that it renews, increases, and strengthens the **radical moisture*** <term>Radical moisture: In medieval physiology, the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid of the body that was thought to be consumed by the "fire" of life as one aged.</term>, *so that it is of the highest benefit even to those weakened by old age; and that it fortifies the humor of life and the internal nature in all limbs!* 

What is more foolish than the claim that the **salt of corals** possesses such power and nature as to *cleanse and renew the blood in the whole body, so that—all diseases and conditions arising from corrupt blood having been removed and healed in a short time—the vigorous health of the former state is restored to the body as if it were made whole again; that it stops all immoderate female fluxes and all fluxes of the belly; and that it cleanses and renews the blood.* I pass over the remaining grand[iose...] <note>The text cuts off mid-word "am-pul-", likely "amplitudines" or "ampullas," referring to the grandiloquent or pompous claims of the alchemists.</note>

# CHAPTER XX.

...Crollian trifles <note>original: "pullas Crollianas"</note>, which are equally futile for the most part. For who, being a little more prudent, would dare to expect such results from powders full of a most biting salt, which therefore entirely reflect the nature of salt? These claims are certainly so far from all truth that **Angelus Sala** <note>Angelus Sala (1576–1637) was an early chemist and physician who was skeptical of some extreme alchemical claims.</note> could not help but openly protest against those praises of the "salt of pearls"—or "magistery," as he more correctly calls it in the Paracelsian manner.

*As for the claim,* he says, *that it confers any help to those suffering from consumption <term>Phthisis: A historical term for pulmonary tuberculosis or wasting diseases.</term> and hectic fevers, specifically regarding the fever and dryness, by moistening the brain, restoring the radical moisture <term>Radical moisture (humidum radicale): In ancient and medieval medicine, the innate fluid within the body that sustains life and heat.</term>, and extinguishing preternatural heat—and doing so like moist things, which some vainly imagine pearls to be, even though they are pronounced "cold and dry" by the unanimous voice of all physicians—that is simply nothing. Rather, they are harmful to these sick patients: not by reason of the pearls themselves, whose quality is temperate, but by accident—namely, because of the sharp spirits of the vinegar itself which adhere to the pearls. So far are they from moistening or restoring that they produce the opposite effects: they "cut" through phlegm and cause sweats, through which the consumed nutritional fluid is lost, which instead ought to have been kept sound and protected.* 

Thus says Sala, who writes elsewhere that the power of the "magistery" <term>Magistery (magisterium): In alchemy, a substance prepared from another by removing its external form, supposedly concentrating its essence.</term> or salt of corals is equal to that of pearls; therefore, by this judge’s standard, **Croll** must again be condemned.

As if, indeed, the medicinal powers of corals were contained solely in their color, or as if that tincture were worth more than the corals themselves. Certainly, if you consult both reason and experience, you will find the Paracelsians as vain in their methods of preparation as they are in their medical use.*

### # ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...[skull oil] can be used while it lasts; but in truth, since nature has produced an abundance of remedies endowed with the same powers as these oils, it will be wiser to use those. For it is admitted that these [animal] oils, which most heavily disturb the **spirits** <note>In this context, 'spirits' refers to the 'vital spirits' or 'pneuma'—the subtle fluids early modern doctors believed circulated through the nerves to animate the body.</note> and often cause no small harm to the sick, should be ordered to go into total and permanent exile. So says Angelus [Sala] regarding those oils.

As for the **Salts** <term>In alchemy, 'salts' were the solid residues left after a substance was burned (fixed salts) or the vapors collected from it (volatile salts).</term> — whether volatile or fixed — that are prepared from animal parts, since they are in no way better than the salts of plants, what necessity could there be to seek them from animals with such a great stench and joyless labor? Regarding the so-called **Extracts** of the heart, spleen, liver, testicles, flesh, and other parts, it is certainly not yet established by any trustworthy experiment that they possess any exceptional value in the practice of medicine.

There is also no reason at all why the so-called **Western Civet** <note>original: "Zibetha occidentalis." This was a euphemism used by Paracelsians for human excrement, which they processed through long digestion (heating) to create medicines.</note> should be prepared from foul human dung, and indeed through a long process of digestion. All that labor is therefore useless, especially since its failure to work proves its vanity. Only the **spirit of Blood** is worth the expense of the effort. Yet it is sought from humans out of superstition, since experience teaches that deer, pig, and even calf blood possess the same powers.

The ancient Hermetics <note>Followers of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, associated with alchemy and magic.</note> used human blood among their magical rites, both for other things and for the cure of **elephantiasis** <note>In the ancient and early modern world, this term often referred to a severe form of leprosy.</note>. From this, our modern [Paracelsians] prepare **biolychnia** <term>A "lamp of life"—an alchemical candle or lamp made from human blood believed to flicker or go out if the person from whom the blood was taken became ill or died.</term>, philtres, antidotes for philtres, the transplantation of diseases, and **magnetic cures** <note>A theory that diseases could be drawn out of a person and 'transplanted' into an animal or object through a 'magnetic' or sympathetic attraction.</note>. These are done through no other power <margin>Tertullian, *The Apology*, chapter 14.</margin> than a magical one, as we teach more extensively elsewhere. These (to use the words of **Tertullian**) are the deceptions of demons, whom the Magi, their priests, know to be delighted by human slaughter and the shedding of blood; who for that reason instituted medicines and sacrifices from human blood. But more on these matters elsewhere.

In my judgment, the followers of Paracelsus have nowhere labored more successfully until now than regarding **PLANTS**. Yet not in every...

In the extraction of **Medicinal Waters**, they have followed the old custom of the chemists and commonly praise them as if the sincere and entire **virtue** <note>In early medicine, the "virtue" of a plant referred to its specific healing power or essential properties.</note> of the plants were contained within them. Indeed, we are taught by both sense and experience that most waters lack both the taste and smell of their original plants, and therefore the powers of purging, binding, or thinning <note>In the Galenic system, medicines were categorized by their "actions," such as "astringents" (binding) or "attenuants" (thinning the bodily humors).</note> do not pass into the waters. Indeed, there seems to be no other reason why this preparation of waters was so rarely adopted for medical use in the past, and why common **decoction** <term>Decoction is the process of boiling plant material in water to extract its medicinal chemicals, as opposed to distillation, which collects the steam.</term> was preferred to them by the **Arabs** <note>The "Arabs" refers to the medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes, whose texts dominated European medicine for centuries.</note> and other doctors following in their footsteps, even though this art of distillation was already very well known then. ### CHAPTER XX. 271

[most full of par-]ticles; and thus, they reflect the force and nature of fire in every way. They do not even deserve the name of the "essence" of those plants from which they are made. For they are certainly not present in the whole plants, nor in their juices or parts, but only after fermentation has taken place. Such fermentation occurs not only by art but also by nature in the seeds and fruits of plants when they are committed to the earth and germinate; this happens because they then especially require a certain internal fire, greater than they need later when they have already grown and are permitted to enjoy the heat of the surrounding air produced by the sun. Hence, in all spirits of this kind, one and the same temperament is found, except that they differ somewhat in smell and taste. Certainly, they do not reflect the native temperament of the plants at all, such as it is outside the time of that first germination. Therefore, it is vain to expect I know not what secret powers of the plants from these spirits, as the common crowd of **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed "spagyric" or chemical medicine over traditional Galenic herbalism.</note> does.

The Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who advocated for the use of chemistry in medicine.</note> seem to me to have placed even greater value on their labor regarding the oils of plants—at least those prepared without burning, namely by a certain boiling alone. There is hardly any reason why we should use them even for external uses. Certainly, we can perform our duty quite well without them. However, other oils prepared without burning are, by their own right, most worthy of all praise—especially if there is a need for warming. <margin>Defense, book 1, chapter 1.</margin> To be sure, **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and prominent advocate of Paracelsian medicine.</note> sins gravely when he says: *Chemists know how to draw out cold essences and oils by their art: namely by macerating the **four cold seeds** <term>Traditionally: cucumber, gourd, melon, and watermelon seeds.</term> in water, from which and from poppy seeds they extract those oils or essences which you would not dare to deny are cold.* But indeed, these claims are so far from the truth that those oils are actually the vital fire of the plants...

...things, having acquired a certain fixity from the viscous substance of the oil. Indeed, in animals, this **fire** <note>original: *ignis*; referring to "vital heat" or the internal energy believed to sustain life.</note> is completely mobile; in plants, while they are sprouting, it is likewise mobile but to a lesser degree, while it is more fixed in them at other times. For this reason, spirit of turpentine is changed over time into something oily, and depending on different fermentations, more or less oil or spirit can be drawn out; moreover, when vinegar is added, some spirits display an oily quality. Truly, the native fire of plants is, as it were, a concentrated essence within such oils. Therefore, they must be used with great caution, especially internally, lest they burn too much or, because of their thinness, fail to meet expectations. For some delay is necessary for them to take effect; thus it happens that sharp substances are less effective at **cutting** <note>original: *incidendum*; in Galenic medicine, this meant breaking down and thinning thick or stagnant bodily fluids.</note> than bitter ones, as was also observed by **Galen** <note>A Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose medical theories were the standard for centuries.</note> in book 4 of *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*.

<margin>
Section 2, aphorism 12.
</margin>
**Sala** <note>Angelo Sala (1576–1637), a physician and chemist who advocated for the careful, experimental use of chemical remedies.</note> himself says best: "Anyone who is about to administer those oils internally must first and foremost be concerned about the dosage, since the body is inflamed and heated more violently by a single drop of **oil of cinnamon** <note>original: *olei cinnamomini*</note> taken incorrectly than by a whole **drachm** <term>a unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</term> of the powder of the same substance. Then, he should provide a suitable **vehicle** <note>original: *vehiculo*; a substance like water, wine, or syrup used to dilute or carry a potent medicine.</note> for it, not only to temper their immoderate heat, but also to break their excessive penetrating power, and to moderate everything according to the differences of the oils themselves. For they do not all have the same penetration, heat, sharpness, and subtlety—qualities which are easy to distinguish by smell and taste. The same caution must be observed in external use: namely, that they be mixed with an appropriate oily vehicle, lest they heat too much, or 'cut,' or inflame, or even strip the skin." Thus says he. It is all too well known how little these things are commonly observed by the followers of **Paracelsus** <note>Followers of the 16th-century physician Paracelsus, who were often criticized for using harsh chemical "cures" without sufficient caution.</note>.

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

However much they may err in their practical use, the technique for preparing those oils is nevertheless remarkable and excellent.

The practice of condensing the juices of plants, extracted by various means, so as to preserve them for a long time, was already frequent in ancient times—as can be learned primarily from **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist whose *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note>. Yet a later age, following the custom of the **Arabs** <note>Refers to the influential medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes who introduced new pharmaceutical forms.</note>, preferred to reduce those juices into the form of syrups using honey and sugar. However, it is certain that the potency of most of these is greatly weakened and altered by this method; therefore, the chemists certainly deserve praise for once again bringing those unadulterated, thickened juices back into use. It is also to their credit that they more frequently extract what remains of the moisture from drier herbs than the ancients did, and that they employ **spirit of wine** <term>Spirit of Wine: An early term for ethanol or highly distilled alcohol, prized by chemists for its ability to dissolve resinous substances that water could not.</term> for that purpose—a substance unknown to the ancients, yet nothing is more suited for dissolving resinous juices. Our modern practitioners are also accustomed to purifying their juices, or **extracts** (for they prefer to use that term), far more correctly than the ancients. Truly, while this is indeed more pleasing to the eye, it is often associated with a great loss of potency. 

<margin>
Fernel, Book 4, *Method of Healing*, chapter 11.
</margin>
**Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who introduced the term "physiology" and was a major authority in Renaissance medicine.</note> correctly states: *The most effective of all is the juice which is fresh and cloudy; however, that which has already become clear and has been rendered purer, though it may be more pleasing and more agreeable, has nevertheless deposited its portion of power along with its dregs.* <note>original: "Omnium efficacissimus succus est qui recens ac turbidus: qui autem jam inclaruit, puriorque redditus est, licet gratior iucundiorque sit, ut tamen fæcem ita & facultatis portionem deposuit."</note> Furthermore, use and experience have long since corrected the error of the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who advocated for "chemical" medicine over traditional Galenic herbalism.</note>, as if everything of this kind could be contained within Extracts; for almost all purgative medicines have failed to meet expectations. ### CHAPTER 20

...the deficiency of the **mercurial solvent** <note>original: "menstrui Mercurialis." In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent used to extract the essence of a solid. Mercurial solvents were highly prized for their supposed ability to dissolve substances without destroying their "life force."</note>, since even those preparations called "Mercurials" do not preserve their purgative power intact when made into extracts. It is well established that this quality is best drawn into a liquid through simple infusion. Furthermore, the acidic juices of barberries, lemons, and currants turn bitter under even a gentle fire, while others easily turn rancid. Consequently, not all things can be successfully converted into extracts, contrary to what many of the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often breaking with traditional herbal practices.</note> have been persuaded to believe.

There is also little doubt that the great effort of the Paracelsians in producing what they call the "tinctures" of plants should be regarded as **futile meddling** <note>original: "περιεργία" (periergia). A Greek term used here to describe excessive or useless labor that yields no real benefit.</note>. Indeed, they put the greatest effort into this task, relying on the opinion that in this way they finally possess the entire **secret power** <term>Arcanum: From the Latin for "hidden" or "secret." In alchemy, an arcanum is the most concentrated, potent essence of a substance that contains its true healing power.</term> of the plants. Yet no one would deny that this color is merely pleasing to the eyes. How it might assist in medical practice is not at all clear, since color has no efficacy in the art of healing.

Just as our **Hermetic** <note>The "Hermetic sect" refers to the school of chemists and alchemists who traced their wisdom back to the mythical figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note> sect has departed significantly from the ancients in all these matters, it still retains something of that ancient vanity regarding the gathering of plants. For even if you do not see every old superstition employed today, they still believe that the various positions of the stars must be diligently observed. However, if you except the Sun and the Moon, we have no certain experimental evidence that the remaining stars have much power in this matter. Therefore, the rising, setting, and positions of the stars can indeed be used as markers for various harvest times—much as annual feast days are commonly used as guides—but to anxiously seek their medicinal power in plants seems a vain superstition. The same logic applies to that distribution by which some, following the decrees of the **Astrologers**, divide all plants into seven classes, ruled by as many **Planets**. For this too is

...an empty fiction supported by no experiment and no reason. I pass over the fact that it is now well established that more than seven planets have been discovered <note>A reference to recent astronomical discoveries, likely Galileo’s discovery of the moons of Jupiter in 1610, which debunked the ancient belief that there were only seven wandering celestial bodies (the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets) corresponding to various earthly systems.</note>.

For no trace of this appears in any ancient era. I truly marvel that this doctrine has found approval among anyone outside the Paracelsian sect. Indeed, if color and shape were supposed to prove themselves as certain signs of medicinal powers, then that rule would surely hold true always and in all cases.

Yet now, countless things correspond to the parts of the body they heal in neither color nor shape. Conversely, things that do correspond are often unable to heal. For do only yellow things, or all yellow things, benefit yellow bile? Do only or all black things benefit black bile, or only or all white things benefit phlegm? <note>Referring to the "Four Humors" of ancient medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Paracelsians often argued that yellow plants cured jaundice/yellow bile, etc.</note> The same logic applies to all shapes. 

For example, the **Palma Christi** <note>original: *Palma Christi*, literally "Palm of Christ." This refers to the castor oil plant (*Ricinus communis*), so named because its lobed leaves resemble a human hand.</note>, which is so called because it represents a hand quite beautifully; and yet, it does not notably benefit ailments of the hands—indeed, it hardly helps at all. Truly, the argument is empty which claims that if those shapes and colors were not established to signify those powers, then they were created by nature in vain. 

Just as plants themselves, however many they may be, are natural bodies created primarily for the fulfillment of the whole world, but for the use of man only secondarily and in part; so too did these same plants receive their colors and shapes not so much for human use as for the sake of their own purpose. Therefore, the fact that some similarity to man exists in them is entirely accidental and a matter of nature's chance.

### CHAPTER XXI. 281

Certainly, just as one method of seasoning and cooking food makes it more suitable than another, that fact does not in itself make the food useless or harmful. It is also evident—since every disease known until now has been cured without these chemical remedies—that chemical preparations are not strictly required for the act of healing. Indeed, one cannot name any disease or condition which cannot be healed without these chemical aids.

I myself would not praise the mixing of medicines into **compounds** <term>Medicines made of multiple ingredients, as opposed to "simples" consisting of one herb or mineral</term> unless necessity demands it. That saying of Arnald of Villanova <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note> certainly pleases me: *He who is able to heal with **simples**, seeks compounded remedies either deceitfully or in vain.* Nor does the ancient law of healing always recommend lengthy jumbles of ingredients; in fact, it usually disapproves of them. Yet it does not follow from this that one must always abstain from compounding. On the contrary, it has been most clearly demonstrated by many that compounding is frequently very useful and sometimes plainly necessary. It is not relevant to repeat those arguments here, since the Paracelsians themselves not only call for compounds from common pharmacies for medical use, but also mix their own substances together in various ways. What of the fact that all those things they call **masteries** <term>original: *magisteria*; refined chemical substances thought to retain the full power of the source material</term>, as well as many spirits and most extracts, are not simples but compounded?

...but especially those [potencies] which are in a thinner substance; those, however, which are in a thick and earthy substance are not equally strong. Likewise: by boiling <term>elixatio: the process of thorough boiling to extract medicinal properties</term>, the potency (which resides especially in thicker matter) is more clearly called forth and transferred into the broth itself, while that which consists in thinner matter is for the most part entirely dissipated and destroyed. For very often, the potency that exists in either the thin or the thick substance alone is sufficient for use; and in such a case, a single infusion or boiling is equal to the physician's desire. Furthermore, although sometimes neither infusion nor decoction <note>A medicinal preparation made by boiling plant material.</note> provides all that is sought, what is missing can nevertheless be supplied by adding certain other things. To this end, it is now accepted by the more prudent to perform decoction in closed vessels and in a double-boiler <term>diploma: a double-walled vessel used for gentle heating</term> or "bath" <term>balneum: a water-bath or bain-marie</term>, as they call it; both so that too much does not exhale, and so that the more intense heat of the fire does not change the strength of the medicine more than is right or cause it to vanish. Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), a famous Italian physician and botanist who preceded the "modern" chemical school.</note>

had already praised that use of the bath: lest anyone think the art of pharmacy owes this to the leader Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), known as Quercetanus, a French physician and key advocate for Paracelsian "chemical" medicine.</note>. # CHAPTER XXI.

...are [effective], as shown by many foods which likewise rot in a short time, yet they nourish our body, provided they are eaten in time. But it is also well established, as Fernel himself <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician who sought to harmonize ancient Greek medicine with modern observations.</note> advises, that the power of cooling, moistening, and softening flourishes most fully in green plants; therefore, if you seek these effects, you should certainly boil <term>elixanda: substances prepared by thorough boiling</term> them while they are as green and succulent as possible.

It is falsely claimed that pleasantness is absent from all commonly prepared medicines. It is also false to attribute pleasantness indiscriminately to all chemical remedies, even if they are small in volume. For what is pleasant about **vitriolated tartar** <term>potassium sulfate, often used as a laxative</term>? What pleasantness do the **salts of plants** have? What of **oil of tartar** <term>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term>? What of **Paracelsus's gilla** <term>zinc sulfate, commonly used to induce vomiting</term>? What of the **liquors of the human skull** <note>In the 17th century, "Spirit of Human Skull" was a recognized pharmacological preparation, often used to treat epilepsy.</note>? What of the oils drawn from fat or grease? It must be admitted, however, that many chemical preparations are more pleasing to the palate than the common ones, both because of their small size and their not-unpleasant flavor. But what wise person would discard things that displease the mouth, provided they safely restore health?

Indeed, if one speaks generally, it is most certain that the use of those common remedies is far safer than that of the chemical ones. I will not emphasize now that those ancient remedies have been proven through the long course of centuries; whereas most of these chemical ones are praised only by a few, some of whom are plainly unskilled in the method of healing, while others have ruined their credibility through a passion for lying. Thus, on this account, the use of the ancient remedies is undoubtedly safer than that of the modern chemicals. I will not even use the excuse now that since most chemical preparations are **most active** <note>original: "δραστικώτατα" (drastikōtata) — extremely potent or "drastic" in their physiological effect.</note>, a slight error in dose or weight becomes very dangerous; in this regard as well, the use of the ancient remedies is safer. The chemical preparation itself makes it so that you cannot use them with as much security. For how easily a mistake is made in some laborious preparation! # ON HERMETIC MEDICINE
