Now truly, since you cannot be certain whether something has been prepared correctly or not, and since you must fear lest some desired virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the medicinal power or essence of a substance.</note> has been removed, or some harmful quality added, the use of the medicine itself is certainly not free from danger. These things are to be especially feared because most chemical preparations act more violently. In contrast, the common <note>original: *vulgaris*; referring to the traditional Galenic methods based on herbal mixtures.</note> method of preparation is neither very laborious, nor is it so powerful in its effect on the materials in either direction; therefore, error is not easy, nor, if one is committed carelessly, will it do much harm.

Just as no learned man would deny that in the old method of preparation there remains something which deserves to be corrected and perfected; so, on the other hand, it is certain that until now no **Paracelsian** <term>Paracelsians: Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed "spagyric" or chemical medicine over traditional herbalism.</term> has handed down any true and certain art of preparation. Instead, all of that **Chemistry** <note>original: *Chemiam*; in the 17th century, the boundary between alchemy and chemistry was fluid.</note> has until now consisted of various exercises, labors, and experiments. These are indeed so numerous today—since workers have left almost nothing untried—that it is no longer very difficult to establish a formal art from those things which experience has taught. Nevertheless, the Chemists themselves stumbled upon diverse methods of preparation and remedies for diseases—not so much by some prior deliberation as by risks blindly taken through various attempts, and certainly not by any plan undertaken as was proper—which is proven by the manifold errors in those preparations, from which no one has yet been able to guard himself. # CHAPTER XXI.

...a systematic method is possible, when both the material to be prepared—what it is in actuality and what it is in potentiality—and the method of preparation itself, including how much it affects any given thing being prepared, are exactly understood. Indeed, the goal of every preparer is to render the medical material <term>materia medica: The raw herbs, minerals, and animal products used to create medicines.</term> more suitable for healing than it was in the state it was left in; however, this cannot be done by art unless you hold an exact understanding of both the subject material and the means by which the preparation is established, at least as much as is required for the intended purpose. For this is the nature and condition of all arts.

In these two matters, however, so many errors are committed by the **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsians: Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed "spagyric" or chemical medicine over traditional herbalism.</term> that it is manifest from what has been said before, and easy to show briefly, that they are as far as possible from the true art. For *firstly*, they undertake to prepare everything in their own fashion, as if there were always something present that hindered the power of healing. On the contrary, however, the desired power is often so situated in the whole substance of the thing that if you violate it, the medicinal power either perishes entirely or is weakened. In such cases, no preparation is the best, and things in their natural state <note>original: *sponte nata*; literally "born of their own accord."</note> are to be preferred over all prepared ones. Hence Jeremiah Barth himself wrote to Beguin:

which we see happen in the case of pepper; for when the stomach is distressed, a few of its swallowed grains achieve more than if a large quantity of the oil of that same spice is administered. [...of the whole substance] of the crude human skull to its oil; in **aphorism 17**, he prefers the dust of raw pearls to their "mastery" <term>magistery: a concentrated medicinal extract or chemical precipitate produced by dissolving a substance and then reclaiming it</term> or their salt, in **aphorism 27 of the second section**.

*Secondly*, they base all preparation upon separation; and yet, it is repeatedly better to add something, either to correct a substance or to increase its strength.

*Thirdly*, they claim that all medical power lies hidden in a certain "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the "quinta essentia," or the purest and most concentrated part of a substance, believed by alchemists to be a spiritual element beyond the four physical ones (earth, air, fire, water)</term> and thus in a spiritual and thin substance; consequently, they believe this must be separated from all "coarser" parts. However, that entire idea of the fifth essence is a mere fiction, as will be demonstrated below. Furthermore, the power of binding <note>original: *adstringendi*, meaning to contract tissues or stop bleeding</note> and drying is found more in a dense substance than in a thin one. Sometimes, even if the power resides in the thin part, it is better for it to remain mixed with the dregs <note>original: *crassamento*</note>, so that once separated it does not penetrate too quickly or even vanish. For a proper delay is needed for a medicine to act; hence, bitter things are found to break up humors <note>original: *incidere*, literally "to cut," a medical term for breaking down thick fluids like phlegm</note> more effectively than sharp things, even though sharp things are "thinner" than bitter ones.

By a similar *fourth* error, they have persuaded themselves that a treasure of power lies hidden in what they call "Tinctures," and for that reason, they strive solely to transfer the color of whole things into their remedies. Now, in truth, color itself has no power of action; and it is often prone to change, even while the temperament, mixture, and proportion of powers remain exactly the same. Consequently, all that effort of transferring colors serves the delights of the eyes rather than medical utility.

*Fifthly*, while they attempt to dissolve everything and divide it into parts, they certainly waste their labor on gold, silver, and mercury <term>hydrargyro: "liquid silver," the traditional name for mercury</term>, as these cannot be broken down into further parts at all. Not to mention that they also labor in vain on the remaining four metals, shells, corals, pearls, and others: whose separated parts provide what medical use...

However, such separation is often more rightly managed within the human body itself; just as we see that the nature of our own bodies distinguishes the useful juice of our food from the waste products much more effectively than any human Art could.

By these many errors—indeed, by far more—concerning **medicinal materials** <note>original: *materia medica*</note> alone, and thus regarding the pharmaceutical subject itself, our **Paracelsians** <term>Paracelsians: followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who advocated for the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine rather than traditional herbalism</term> are entangled even today. Nor are they held by fewer or lesser errors regarding the **means** by which they strive to achieve their desired separation. Indeed, since they study to perform that separation partly through fire and partly through some **solvent** <note>original: *menstruum*, a technical term in alchemy for a liquid used to dissolve or extract substances</note> (to use their own word) endowed with the power of dissolving, they very often fail in both respects. 

Yet there is one common error: the belief that **Separation** cannot or should not be performed for medical use except by those two means. This is despite the fact that many excellent juices flow spontaneously from wounded plants—which are commonly called **tears** <note>original: *lachrymae*</note>—while others are squeezed out from crushed plants. But there is another common error, more serious than the first: the idea that everything produced by the power of fire and solvents was already actually present in the whole bodies beforehand. They believe that through fire and those solvents, there occurs nothing but a separation of things that were previously joined. The cause of this error is that they believe the production of things from matter consists only in **composition** <note>original: *συγκρίσει* (synkrisei), the assembly of pre-existing parts</note> and **division** <note>original: *διακρίσει* (diakrisei), the breaking apart of substances</note>. it must be assumed that true separation occurs only when the qualities of the separated parts are either entirely the same as, or nearly similar to, the whole substance. Other qualities existed in the whole substance only as a potential, not in actual reality or effect. But regarding that matter, I shall speak more correctly and at greater length elsewhere.

<margin>1.</margin> In preparations indeed *performed by fire*, the Paracelsians <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who favored chemical and mineral treatments over traditional herbal remedies.</note> err by far the most seriously of all, thinking that through the intervention of calcination <term>calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to ash or a powdered "lime."</term> a power or faculty can be drawn out that is identical to what exists in the whole substances. We have already heard Johannes Hartmann <note>A German chemist and the first professor of chemistry in Europe (1568–1631).</note> and Angelus Sala <note>An early 17th-century chemist and physician who was critical of some Paracelsian claims (1576–1637).</note> <margin>*See ch. 19, p. 252.*</margin> confessing to this above. <margin>Section 1, aphorism 15.</margin> 
> *All things treated in fire undergo an alteration, and it is inevitable that they are somewhat cast down from the state of their natural temperament. This happens even more if they are forced to endure either a very intense fire or a longer duration; it happens less if the fire is milder and the time spent in it shorter. Yet it is not always a matter of **empyreuma** <note>original: ἐμπύρευμα; a burnt or smoky smell and taste resulting from the overheating of organic substances</note> that you might find fault with; rather, sometimes a portion of the inherent virtue <note>The specific medicinal power or life-force of a substance</note> perishes through the force of the fire. For some things do not endure even the gentlest fire without change.*

Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), an Italian physician, philosopher, and botanist</note> says most correctly: 

<margin>Caesalpinus, Book 2, *On the Medicinal Faculties*, chapter 18.</margin> 
> *There are very few fragrant flowers that yield fragrant water through distillation <note>A process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling the vapor to collect the condensed liquid</note>. This is either because, due to the delicacy of the scent, the fragrant part exhales before the water rises—as in the violet—or because they cannot bear the force of the fire lifting them, as is the case with most spices. For the exhalation is burned when it is not protected by moisture. For this reason, a most fragrant water is drawn from green cinnamon in India; but among us, it can only be obtained from dry cinnamon when water is added, or, what is better, if the water receives the vapor in the upper vessel which they call an **alembic** <note>original: elambica; an early chemical apparatus used for distillation</note>; for the fragrant part is dissolved by the fire and the rising vapor into the water.*

Regarding the so-called <term>menstrua <note>In alchemy, these are solvents used to dissolve solids, named because some were thought to take a "philosophical month" to work</note></term>, the Paracelsians first make the ridiculous promise of a liquor that can dissolve absolutely everything <note>A reference to the "Alkahest," the mythical universal solvent</note>. Experience, however, refutes that error. Nor has this century, in which the greatest labor has been spent on chemical matters, seen such a liquor thus far. In that [liquor], gold indeed...

**Franciscus Antonius** <note>Francis Anthony (1550–1623), an English physician and goldsmith famous for his controversial "Aurum Potabile" (potable gold), which he claimed could cure all ills</note> claimed that his gold was dissolved, and he did not blush to boast much of its possession. However, he has long since been proven a liar, for the preparation of that "potable gold" is now common knowledge. Similarly, the vanity of **Dienheim** <note>Johann Georg von Dienheim, an alchemical author of the early 17th century</note> has returned to the underworld from which it emerged.

And truly, to wish to dissolve all things with a single liquid seems just as foolish as wanting to use a single degree of fire for every purpose. Therefore, names like "Water of Wisdom," "Hyleal," "Celestial," "Raymundine," "Universal Solvent" <term>Menstruum universale|A hypothetical liquid sought by alchemists that could dissolve any substance into its primary matter</term>, "Philosophers' Mercury," "Bath of Diana," "The Philosophers' Magnetic Key," and any other such chemical evasions <note>original: διευλαβήσεσιν (*dieulabēsesin*); referring here to the deceptive or cautious linguistic tricks used by alchemists to hide their failures</note> are empty titles. **Secondly**, the attempt to dissolve metals and stones using liquids entirely lacking in acidity or the distilled oils of plants contradicts experience. **Angelo Sala** <note>An Italian physician (1576–1637) who was a pioneer in chemical medicine but remained a critic of alchemical mysticism</note> confessed as much in his *aphorisms 23 and 25 of the first section.*

**Thirdly**, the entire nature of most bodies is changed no less by corrosive liquids than by calcining fire; therefore, the followers of Paracelsus <note>Adherents of the medical system of Paracelsus, which relied heavily on chemistry</note> are certainly mistaken when they attempt the separation of active virtues using such liquids.
<margin>Hartmann on Beguin, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
Indeed, **Hartmann** <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631), the first professor of chemistry in Europe, who often edited and commented on the works of Jean Beguin</note> himself was forced to admit that *the natures of things are in a way changed, destroyed, and perverted by burning and eroding solvents* <term>Menstrua|Solvents used in chemical extraction</term>, *rather than the true essences being extracted—much less a healing balsam.*
<margin>Barthius on Beguin, Book 2, Chapter 17.</margin>
**Jeremias Barthius** <note>A 17th-century physician who provided extensive commentary on Beguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum*</note>, writing on the salt of corals prepared with thrice-distilled vinegar, asks: *Who would not suspect that its most noble powers are corrupted and destroyed by such calcination* <term>Calcination|The process of reducing a substance to powder or ash by heating it or treating it with acid</term>, *since corals—even when merely worn to treat fevers and other diseases—very easily lose all their saturated tincture and color?* **Fourthly**, a separation is wrongly expected through those solvents which have the power to dissolve and soak into the entire body. Indeed, it is impossible for something to separate one part from another if it...

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

[[page number: 294]]

...one ought to know [what sort of substance] it resides in, whether earthy or watery; thick or thin; in the juice or in the body. For many things have their powers so diffused through all their parts that they lose them entirely, or for the most part, if they are separated. Many possess their powers in their juice; yet in water extracted from them by whatever ingenuity, they hardly retain a trace. Many do not require the industry of Chemistry; indeed, they are despoiled of their strengths by it; from these, the virtues are easily extracted by **maceration** <note>The process of soaking a substance in a liquid to extract its medicinal properties without using high heat.</note>.

One must know, therefore, which things release their powers more easily through **ascent** <note>Distillation where the vapors rise up into a condenser.</note>, which through **descent** <note>A method of distillation where the heat is applied from above and the extract flows downward.</note>, which through **expression** <note>Squeezing or pressing out the juices.</note>, which through **coction** <note>Boiling or cooking.</note>, and which through **maceration**. For some can be cleansed of useless parts, or dregs, by one of these methods, others by several; by other means, they cannot. Those things which cool <note>In the Galenic system of medicine, drugs were classified by "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note> have obtained this power in almost all their parts; if separated and changed by the heat of fire, they lose a good portion of their strength. Those things which can and should warm the body acquire greater strength when changed by fire. Those things which must either sink deep themselves, or penetrate to more remote parts of the body, or carry other substances with them, need to be thinned and made more subtle by fire. If these are stripped of their earthy and thicker parts, they will become more effective.

Those who desire to make impure medicines purer ought to look toward these and similar goals. Indeed, it is not rare that a whole medicine is most beneficial, which, once certain parts are separated, becomes a poison. For this reason, there is need for great caution <note>original: "limitatione"</note> if we do not wish to err in this matter at the peril of the sick. All these things are the words of **Erastus**.

Now, having properly weighed what we have presented so far, what should be thought concerning the common pharmacy—or rather, that once accepted by even the ancient Hermeticists—and what of the "new" **pharmaceutics** <note>original: "φαρμακευτικῇ" (pharmakeutikē)</note> of the Chemists, can no longer remain hidden. Doubtless, this new method is by no means to be preferred to the old; indeed, it is not at all necessary to the Medical Art, as if it were not permitted to practice medicine without it; furthermore, the greatest benefit of this...

### ARTICLE CHAPTER XXI.

...[they] seem to be ardent spirits <note>original: *spiritûs ardentes*; likely referring to distilled alcohols</note>, and oils of plants prepared with a gentler fire, since you could desire nothing more ready or better than these for warming and strengthening the vital fire <note>The internal heat believed in ancient medicine to be the fundamental source of life and health.</note>.

In a word, something must be added regarding that controversy which the Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a physician who rejected traditional Galenic medicine in favor of chemically-prepared remedies and often attacked the medical establishment.</note> stir up against public pharmaceutical shops <note>original: *Officinis publicis pharmaceuticis*</note>.

Indeed, for many centuries the medical art <note>original: *Ars medica*</note> lacked these, as the physicians themselves prepared their medicines at home. This same custom still prevails today throughout all of Asia. In Africa, it seems physicians first cast this duty from themselves onto others more than five hundred years ago; at which time the most noble kingdoms of Tunis <note>original: *Tunetanum*</note> and Morocco <note>original: *Maroccanum*</note> flourished there under the kings of the Lamtuna <note>original: *Luntuniæ*; a Berber tribe associated with the Almoravid dynasty.</note> and Almohad <note>original: *Almohavidicæ*</note> families.

It seems there is no doubt that this custom prevailed in Africa in the time of Avenzoar <note>Abu Marwan ibn Zuhr (c. 1094–1162), a renowned physician from Islamic Spain who emphasized practical experience and pharmacy.</note>. From there, along with every kind of doctrine and art, it passed first into Spain and soon into the rest of Europe. Truly, this institution holds no disadvantage that might not also be feared if a physician were to have his medicines prepared by his own servants at home; for it is not possible for him to make everything with his own hand.

Why, indeed, should an apothecary <note>original: *pharmacopæus*</note>—to whom this office is entrusted under oath by a magistrate after the man’s integrity and skill have been proven—not apply the same diligence and good faith as the physician’s own domestic servant? Conversely, through those public apothecary shops <note>original: *pharmacopolia*</note>, two great evils are prevented: first, that a physician might not dare or be able to commit some rash error, since he can be called to justice if it is known what remedy he used; second, that remedies may be sold at a fair price, which might otherwise be sold at the highest cost to the sick by greedy men. the master of this new school prefers to be heard, not hesitating to call himself a *philosopher by fire* <note>original: "philosophum per ignem"; a title adopted by alchemists who believed that chemical processes involving heat revealed the true essence of matter.</note>, as if he became a philosopher through its benefit alone. <margin>*Introduction to Natural Philosophy*</margin> Truly, this philosophy certainly requires experience of every kind, as we have taught elsewhere, yet Chemistry helps only a certain part of this: namely, that which deals most specifically with tangible things—I mean heat and cold and their operations, as well as the moist and the dry and all their distinctions; in a word, those things which **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose works on the natural world remained the standard university curriculum in the 17th century.</note> once intended to teach in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorology* (Meteorologica) dealt with the elements and the transformation of physical substances; Book IV was often considered the first manual of chemistry.</note>. The *Paracelsians* <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often claiming their knowledge came from ancient "Hermetic" secrets.</note> depart far more significantly from the *Egyptian Hermetics* <note>Followers of the mystical and philosophical traditions attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure from ancient Egypt associated with alchemy and magic.</note> in Natural Philosophy itself. *First*, one might not rashly say that they also seemed to hold what the *Chemists* <note>Early chemical practitioners and alchemists.</note> commonly assert today: that in all natural bodies, something celestial is found, worthy of the name **quintessence** <note>original: "quintæ essentiæ"; the "fifth essence" or element, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water, believed to be the substance of the stars and a source of healing power.</note>, and that this is contained in a certain spirit which is likewise of a more divine substance. For it seems that whatever this doctrine is, it was born initially in the **pneumatic** <note>A school of ancient medicine that emphasized the "pneuma," or vital breath/spirit, as the primary force of life and health.</note> school of *Archigenes* <note>A prominent Greek physician of the 1st and 2nd centuries AD.</note>, as one which recognized in individual bodies a certain fifth principle, *a spirit penetrating all things and by which all things are contained and governed* <note>original: "spiritum cuncta penetrantem & à quo omnia contineantur ac gubernentur"</note>, as witnessed by *Herodotus* <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-Herodotus or a specific medical commentator of the time.</note>, or whoever else was the author of the *Introduction* <note>original: "εἰσαγωγῆς" (isagōgēs); a common title for introductory textbooks in the ancient world.</note> or the book titled *The Physician*. This idea then flowed to nearly all proponents of hidden natural powers, among whom the *Chemists* have almost always held the first place. Indeed, even *Johannes Mesue* <note>A 9th-century Persian physician (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh) whose pharmaceutical works were standard in Europe for centuries.</note> praises the celestial virtues of bodies in his rules for purgative medicines; and *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the most influential medical text in the medieval world.</note> elevated the forms of natural bodies so far above the nature of the elements that he dedicated their generation to a certain unique divine power, namely the **cholcodea** <note>original: "cholcodeam"; a term used in medieval translations of Arabic philosophy to describe the "Giver of Forms" or an intelligence that bestows life and shape upon matter.</note>. Many also of that *Latin* school of philosophers which liked to call itself **Peripatetic** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, known for walking about while teaching.</note>, even if they believe their "forms" of natural bodies are drawn out from elementary matter, they nonetheless attribute a far more divine nature to them. In the writings of the *Chemists* of a later age, however, long before *Paracelsus*, that tenet regarding the quintessence and celestial spirit lurking in **sublunary** <note>original: "sublunaribus"; things "below the moon," meaning the earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay.</note> things was most clearly expressed. ## CHAPTER XXII.

...claim. Clearly, however, **Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who introduced the term "physiology" and sought to reconcile Galenic medicine with hidden, "occult" causes in nature.</note> attempted to support this very dogma of the Chemists with many arguments in his books *On the Hidden Causes of Things*, and **Sennertus** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), an influential German physician and chemist who attempted to harmonize the theories of Aristotle, Galen, and Paracelsus.</note> followed in his footsteps.

<margin>In the book *On the Origin of Things*, chapter 3.</margin>
Furthermore, we have already warned elsewhere against those Latins that the term **substantial form** <term>original: "formæ substantialis"; in Aristotelian philosophy, this is the internal principle that gives a thing its specific essence and makes it what it is.</term> is being taken to mean some more "noble" part of the essence, contrary to the usage of the old **Lyceum** <note>The school founded by Aristotle in Athens; the author is arguing that contemporary writers are distorting Aristotle's original definitions.</note>. Thus, even if something celestial or more divine than the elements were present in every natural body, it would not be worthy of the name "form," as that term properly signifies the entire essence of a thing, of which that celestial element is only a part. Nevertheless, we admit that the current widespread misuse of the word "form" is such that the name might not undeservedly be applied to a **fifth substance** <note>Also known as the quintessence or ether, supposedly distinct from the four earthly elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note> of this kind, if any such thing exists.

But truly, there is no sign, not even the slightest, from which to conclude that any celestial substance exists within **sublunary** <note>Referring to the region of the universe below the Moon, i.e., the Earth, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the "incorruptible" heavens.</note> bodies. For granted that all things may possess virtues or faculties not composed of the sensible qualities of the elements, it does not follow from this that they are celestial in nature or located in some celestial spirit. For why should these and those sensible faculties not reside in the very same subject? Just as we see colors, tastes, and smells clinging to the same place as tactile qualities, and arising from the same matter, even if not from the same potentiality of that matter. 

To be sure, **Aristotle** confessed that in every seed there is a certain nature and power **analogous** <note>original: "ανάλογον"; corresponding or comparable to.</note> to the heavens, and thus more divine than the elements; yet he did not acknowledge any matter or subject for it other than elementary bodies.

...the spiritual subject of more divine powers, a claim derived from their supposed dignity: as if that which is superior to elementary qualities could only arise or exist within a matter that is equally noble. For beyond being asserted without any proof, this argument destroys itself; if this were the case, nothing celestial could exist within a non-celestial body. And yet, no other argument more plausible than this paradox is available for proof. Now, indeed, it has certainly not been established—neither by experience nor by any firm reasoning—that such excellent and more divine virtues reside in all bodies without exception. It is most distant from all likelihood that all operations of things should be attributed to a hidden spirit; surely, since **Aristotle** and others have proven that all changes in sensible things <note>Things that can be perceived by the senses.</note> arise from sensible powers, the contrary opinion should be demonstrated, not merely assumed. Indeed, Aristotle and his old **Peripatetic** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the *peripatos* or covered walkways of the Lyceum in Athens where they taught.</note> school recognized such things only in "dissimilar bodies"—that is, in plants and animals—but never in "similar" <note>In Aristotelian terms, "similar" (homeomerous) bodies are uniform substances like stone or water, whereas "dissimilar" (anhomeomerous) bodies are complex organisms with distinct parts like organs or limbs.</note> ones.

<margin>Chapter 17, page 216.</margin>

Truly, there is nothing that proves the presence of any celestial body. For it would certainly have to be free from all corruption, and devoid of heat, cold, weight, and lightness. However, such a thing is nowhere to be found in the sublunary region <note>The earthly realm below the moon, which in ancient science was the only place where things could change, decay, or die.</note>. It has already been stated above that **Rupescissa** <note>Jean de Roquetaillade (c. 1310–1366), a French Franciscan and alchemist who famously sought a "quintessence" to prolong life.</note> himself acknowledged the corruptibility and lightness of his "heaven." It has likewise been shown above, by the confession of **Girolamo Rossi** <note>original: "Hieronymi Rubei"</note> and **Jean Beguin** <note>original: "Ioannis Beguini," a famous 17th-century chemist whose "Tyrocinium Chymicum" was a standard textbook.</note>, that this same "heaven" is rendered hotter and hotter by long-lasting circulation, and therefore it is nothing other than the thinnest and hottest parts of wine produced through **fermentation**. Those other things which are called **quintessences** <term>quintessence: From "quinta essentia" (fifth essence). ### CHAPTER XXII.

It is quite obvious to Chemists—indeed, one can almost touch it with their hands—that these substances are of an elementary nature, not a celestial one. For many things deserve this name: certain subtle oils of plants, "burning spirits" <note>This usually refers to distilled alcohol or "spirit of wine."</note>, purified juices, and the solid residues or spirits of metallic juices like vitriol <note>original: "chalcanthi," a term for copper or iron sulfates</note>, salt, niter, and sulfur. Frequently, various magisteries <note><term>Magistery</term>: From the Latin *magisterium*, this refers to a concentrated medicinal preparation where the "essence" of a substance like pearl or coral is extracted without changing its fundamental nature.</note> of gemstones, pearls, corals, and metals, as well as the more refined parts of animals, are also called by this name. Yet, there is not one of these that is not subject to the elementary changes arising from heat and cold, nor do they differ in any way from elementary bodies.

<margin>Paracelsus, Book 4, *Archidoxis*</margin>

And yet, **Paracelsus** himself defined the Quintessence as follows: *it is a matter that is physically extracted from all growing things, and from everything in which there is life, separated from all impurity and mortality, most purely refined, and separated from all elements.* Although, with his usual inconsistency, he immediately adds these words: *And it must also be understood in this way: that the quintessence is not a quintessence beyond the elements, because it is an element. And it might perhaps be thought that the Quintessence is a balanced temperament—not cold, not hot, not moist, and not dry. This is not the case. For it is not a thing consisting of a specific temperature <note>In this context, "temperature" refers to the "temperament" or the balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note>, or something by which it withdraws from the elements; rather, all quintessences derive their nature from the elements. Thus, the Quintessence of Gold comes from Fire; the Quintessence of the Moon <note>original: "Lunae," the alchemical name for silver</note> from Water; the Quintessence of lead from Earth; and the Quintessence of Mercury from Air.* 

All of these statements are just as consistent with one another and with a sound mind as the examples of quintessences produced in that same book. These substances cannot even be prepared in the way he prescribes, and even if they could, they would be nothing more than purely elementary bodies. <meta>catchword: unless</meta>

...encompass all the power and nature of bodies, such that some [parts of the body] clearly have nothing or very little of it. For neither those things produced by the intervention of fermentation—such as **fiery spirits** <note>original: "spiritus ardentes"; likely referring to distilled alcohol or flammable extracts.</note>—nor much less those produced by the violence of a bright fire, or dry metallic spirits, or those produced by very sharp **solvents** <term>menstrua: In alchemy and early chemistry, a "menstruum" was a solvent used to dissolve or extract metals and minerals.</term>, reflect the nature of those whole things from which they were made. Instead, they possess another nature that has newly arisen, as we have already shown. 

Some of these extracts do, to a certain extent, exhibit that original nature, but by no means in its entirety. Indeed, neither the juices, nor the oils, nor the so-called "spirits"—whether of plants, animals, stones, or metals—are worthy of the name **essences**, even if they contain some of their medicinal powers. For where the essence of a thing is, there the thing itself is present. Yet none of those extracts are the plant itself, nor the animal, nor the stone, nor the metal. 

Not even the **souls** themselves are the essences of plants or animals. This is true if you take the word "soul" not according to the usage of **Aristotle**, but according to the common and widely accepted view. For to Aristotle, the soul signifies the complete principle of all vital functions, and thus it encompasses the nature of the body at the same time. In common speech, however, "soul" refers only to that by which life chiefly consists, which is nonetheless an incomplete principle of the being. This distinction has been ignored by many interpreters, which has rendered the entire doctrine of the soul very obscure and difficult. 

Specifically, the essence of an organic thing (such as a plant or animal), whether it is natural or made by art, requires a certain quantity, a specific shape, and a particular arrangement of the body's parts. Other **homogeneous parts** <term>similaria: A term from Aristotelian biology referring to uniform substances like bone, flesh, or sap, as opposed to complex "organic" parts like a hand or a leaf.</term> likewise cannot be of just any size or be made of just any combination of tangible qualities. For if they are changed too much, they cannot perform the duty for which nature destined each individual thing—a fact that is clearer than the sun in the case of organic bodies.

Suppose indeed that they are the principles of all bodies; surely the <term>Paracelsians</term> should have added to those three a <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; often called the "quintessence" or ether, believed to be the pure substance of the heavenly bodies.</note> or their own <term>divine spirit</term>, if they wished to keep their doctrine sound. Furthermore, it is false that they are fit for doing nothing at all: the <term>Paracelsians</term> themselves are certainly accustomed to attribute the power of moistening to phlegm, and the power of drying to the <term>dead head</term>.

<meta>This page continues the critique of Paracelsian principles, specifically addressing the residue left after burning (the "dead head") and questioning whether the three-principle system (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) can truly be applied to all matter, including the heavens and non-combustible elements.</meta>

[[page number: 308]]

### ->ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...for **Paracelsus**, the residue is a **dead and damned head** <note>original: "caput mortuum & damnatum"; a term used by early chemists to describe the useless, inert remains left in a flask after a substance has been heated or distilled to exhaustion.</note>. Perhaps, therefore, Paracelsus intended that name only for that which remains flavorful within the ash.

But let us imagine that these definitions are correct: how will **Paracelsus** prove that all bodies—and indeed even the very things called **elements**, and even the **heavens** themselves—are composed of three principles of this kind? For first, suppose that these three are actually found in all bodies; is it likely that the constitution of all bodies is fulfilled by three things, through whose intervention bodies are fit either to burn, or to go up in smoke, or to be turned into ashes? Certainly, such a trio performs nothing extraordinary for the constitution of any body: it is far from the case that all **similar** and **dissimilar** <note>In classical philosophy, "similar" parts (homoeomerous) are things like bone or flesh where any piece is the same as the whole; "dissimilar" parts (anhomoeomerous) are complex organs like a hand or eye.</note> things clearly take their constitution from this.

But in truth, there is no sign or argument to show that three things of this kind are found in all bodies. The **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the medical and chemical system of Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> argue indeed that all bodies are reduced to these three, and thus consist of those three. However, regarding the **heavens**, it is certainly not established by any experiments that they can be reduced into those three; therefore, this at least is said without reason. 

But how would you reduce all **sublunary things** <note>Refers to the region of the universe below the Moon, which in ancient science was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> into these three? Is it by **combustion** <note>burning</note>, as Paracelsus did with wood? But not all things can be burned. Surely you cannot burn water, nor air, nor earth, nor fire, nor **gold**, nor **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyrum"</note>, nor **talc**, nor certain other things. Furthermore, combustion is not a **resolution** <note>The chemical process of breaking a substance down into its original components.</note> properly so called, but a violent transformation; and therefore combustion does not prove that whole bodies were actually composed of those substances into which they change through burning. I would not say, for my part, that nothing of those things which are separated through combustion was actually present, even if altered...

## CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>Book *On Consensus*, Chapter 11, page 153.</margin>
...then. I only deny that all things which arise in this way <note>That is, through chemical separation or burning.</note> were present in **actuality** <note>The author is using the Aristotelian distinction between "actuality" (being fully formed) and "potentiality" (having the capacity to become something). He argues that smoke and flame aren't "hiding" inside wood, but are created during the process of burning.</note>. For the statement of our friend **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a famous physician and chemist who tried to reconcile Aristotle’s philosophy with the new chemical theories of the time.</note> is quite absurd: *Fire generates nothing but fire, and produces no mixture.* It is better put in what follows immediately: *since, therefore, in the violent breaking down by fire certain things emerge from mixtures which could not have come from the action of fire—whether through itself or by accident, whether by univocal or equivocal generation—it is necessary that those things were already in the mixture.* I say the latter part is correct; but it is most false that nothing but fire can be produced by the action of fire, whether through itself or by accident. Certainly this is resisted by all the senses; to believe Sennert’s bare assertion that they are deceived in this matter is a **very great demand** <note>original Greek: λίαν μέγα αίτημα (*lian mega aitema*); a logical term for an outrageous assumption or "begging the question."</note>. It is clear from what was said above that the Chemists themselves recognize the power of fire in transforming things.

Indeed, that neither the **smoke** nor the **flame** which arise through combustion were hidden in actuality within the whole bodies is proven by their weight and coldness. For all smoke, as well as flame, is light; yet in combustion such a quantity of both is produced that the weight of the heavy ash which remains is far exceeded, especially since sometimes no ash remains at all. If truly such a great quantity of light things were present in actuality within the whole bodies, they would surely not have been heavy, but light, since the movement of any body follows that which predominates within it. The same reasoning applies to heat and even to light. For every flame of things being burned shines and is hot, yet the whole bodies do not shine, nor are they of a fiery heat. **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who championed atomism.</note> cleverly says of combustible wood:

> *But if such a great flame were hidden in the woods,*
> *The fires could not be concealed for any length of time;*
> *They would consume the woods everywhere and burn the thickets.*
> <note>original Latin: *Quod si tanta foret silvis abscondita flamma / Non possent ullum tempus celarier ignes / Conficerent vulgò silvas, arbusta cremarent.* From Lucretius' "On the Nature of Things," Book I.</note>

### ### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

Not even that salt—which either evaporates or remains behind in the ashes when things are burned—is shown by the sense of taste to have been present in the whole, unburned bodies, for nothing salty is detected in them. It could not remain hidden, however, since ashes usually yield a fairly large quantity of it. Nor is it right to blame the judgment of the taste on the grounds that the tongue does not detect salt when it is only lightly sprinkled on food; for indeed, by mixing it with many tasteless things, that saltiness is changed into another flavor. Just as if you mix black and white pigment, they no longer remain what they were, but are converted into a third thing.

<margin>Discussion on Salt, nos. 21 and 22.</margin>
Therefore, the salt—whether fixed or volatile—which remains in the ashes, is not present **actually** in the whole bodies, but only **potentially** <note>original: *actu* and *potentiâ*. These are Aristotelian terms: "actually" means the salt exists as a distinct substance already; "potentially" means the substance has the ingredients or capacity to *become* salt when transformed</note>. It is born, in fact, through a certain separation of a moisture, whether tasteless or sweet, which previously displayed a different flavor. Combustion brings about that separation; however, it is not the only thing that does so (as many believe), but sometimes also a certain putrefaction <note>decay or fermentation</note>. To this belongs that method of preparing the salt of plants proposed by **Jean Beguin** <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620) was the author of *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, one of the most influential early chemistry textbooks</note>. But more on this matter elsewhere. It is enough for now to have proved that salt is not truly inside whole bodies. If these things are true—as they are most true—it is also clear at the same time that this salt is not a **Principle** <note>In this context, a "Principle" is a fundamental, irreducible building block of all matter</note> of whole bodies; indeed, both smoke and that which actually burns are to be excluded from that list of Principles.

<margin>Section 1, aphorism 40.</margin>
Furthermore, it is established that salt cannot be produced from all bodies by combustion or by any other artifice. For **Sala** <note>Angelo Sala (1576–1637), a pioneer in chemistry who was skeptical of the more mystical claims of alchemy</note> himself correctly asserted concerning corals, pearls, <term>crab's eyes</term> <note>original: *oculi cancrorum*. These are not actual eyes, but small stony concretions found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine to treat acidity</note>, mother of pearl, shells, and other things of a nature halfway between bones and stones: *The ash of these things is of the same form...*

<meta>catchword: ...of the same form</meta>

### CHAPTER XXII.

...is in the form of the lime of stones; from which no salt can be extracted that is similar to the salts of vegetables. Its substance is merely more earthy, appearing to the taste as lime <note>original: *calx*. In early chemistry, this referred to the powdery residue left after a substance was burned or "calcined"</note>: it is not easily dissolved, nor is it compressed into granules as other salty things usually are. And indeed, what is commonly called the salt of *Corals and Pearls* is not any salt belonging to those bodies themselves, but a "magistery" <note>original: *magisterium*. A term for a precipitate where the whole substance is supposedly converted into a new form, often using an acid</note> which, by the benefit of the spirit of vinegar clinging to it, fakes a certain form of salt. 

<margin>Section 1, aphorism 43.</margin>
**Angelus Sala** <note>Angelus Sala (1576–1637) was a physician and chemist who famously argued that many "alchemical" salts were actually just the acids used in the process reacting with the base material</note> likewise rightly denies that salt can be drawn from precious stones. Certainly, that which is circulated by Chemists under the name of "salt of gems" is of exactly the same nature as the salt of corals, as the same Sala has excellently warned. Just as it is with gems, so too does the lime of other stones behave.

Among the metals, since gold, silver, and mercury cannot be broken down into parts by any fire or any other method known thus far, it is quite clear that they also cannot yield any salt. Lead, tin, copper, and iron are indeed resolved into smoke by a most vehement fire, but the slag that remains is entirely tasteless. Similar is the nature of the ashes of all marcasites <note>A term then used for various shiny minerals and iron pyrites</note>, antimony, sulfur, vitriol, and in general all metallic things. 

<margin>Chrysologia, section 1, chapter 20.</margin>
Concerning these, Sala rightly says: *Even if those very ashes were soaked in water for a whole year, not even an atom of truly salty salt could be extracted from them.* He adds: *I am not unaware that there are those who boast they can extract such a salt by the benefit of distilled vinegar or some other acidic liquor. But I also know this: they are utterly mistaken themselves, and they equally deceive others. For what they put forward as Salt is not truly the salt of these bodies; rather, it is the Spirit of the Solvents, which have combined with part of the metallic ashes into that sort of salty mass;* as Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, used here as a metaphor for the heat of the chemist's furnace</note> bears witness, who [the spirits...]

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...can separate coagulated spirits <note>In early chemistry, "spirits" referred to volatile substances or vapors; "coagulated" means they have been fixed into a solid state</note> once more from metallic ashes, so that these ashes, deprived of their spirits, return to their solid and water-insoluble form and consistency. All of this was clearly demonstrated elsewhere by Angelo Sala <note>A 17th-century physician and chemist who championed experimental evidence over alchemical theory</note>, who showed that the substance called **salt of vitriol** <note>original: *sal vitrioli*; likely iron(II) sulfate or copper sulfate</note> is so named without good reason.

It is granted that salt can be extracted only from burnt plants and animals; yet not even all of their ashes become salty, but almost only those that are endowed with flavor. For this reason, all burnt bones and all burnt horns lack any fixed salt. Since this is well known to the craftsmen of the mint <note>original: *monetariae rei artificibus*; those involved in coin-making and metal assaying</note>, they use no other ashes for their **cupels** <note>original: *capellas*; shallow, porous bowls used in the "cupellation" process to separate precious metals from lead and other impurities</note> (as they call certain tools for testing metals) more successfully than those made from bones and horns. And yet, they find it most certain that all saltiness is absent from these cupels. Furthermore, those very ashes are certainly natural bodies; and yet, if their salt has been thoroughly drained away by **lye** <note>original: *lixivium*; a liquid used to leach soluble salts from ashes</note>, they never become salty again by any amount of fire.

All of these facts surely make it clear how empty the boast of the Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who taught that all matter is composed of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> is, as if it were obvious to the senses themselves that salt is **actually present** in all bodies. Certainly, it is so far from being manifest to any of the senses that, if we were to stand by their judgment, it would have to be said that not even a trace of salt can be produced from all bodies through transformation. Therefore, those words of Sennert <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a prominent physician who attempted to reconcile atomism with Aristotelian and alchemical theories</note> cannot be endured:
<margin>Book on the Consensus, ch. XI</margin>
*That salt is in all things and can be made from them is very well known to all who are practiced in chemical resolutions.* Likewise: *That salt is in lime is detected both by taste and by other operations.*

And indeed, that something flammable and smoky—or to speak in Paracelsian terms, **Mercury** and **Sulphur**—is present in compound bodies...

## CHAPTER XXII.

...in such bodies, it is much more correctly affirmed: yet we do not have this confirmed by experience, at least concerning gold and **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyro*; literally "water-silver"</note>. For **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), an influential German physician who attempted to bridge the gap between traditional Galenic medicine and the new chemical theories of Paracelsus</note> wrongly strives to prove that sulfur or **a flammable principle** <note>original: *φλογιστόν τι* (phlogiston ti); a Greek term meaning "something flammable." This predates the formal "Phlogiston Theory" of the 18th century but refers to the same concept of an internal fire-element</note> exists within gold by using the example of **fulminating gold** <note>original: *auri fulminantis*; an explosive gold compound. Sennert argued its explosiveness proved gold contained internal sulfur</note>. In truth, all that explosive power is added to the gold from the **Stygian waters** <note>original: *aquis stygiis*; a term for corrosive mineral acids, likely *aqua regia* (a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acid) used to dissolve gold</note> by which it was prepared. This happens to gold in the same way it happens to other metals dissolved by **aqua fortis** <note>Nitric acid</note> or distillates of vinegar. The followers of Paracelsus vainly boast that "flammable spirits" can be drawn out of metals in this way. The proof against them is that when these metals are freed from their **solvents** <note>original: *menstruis*; in early chemistry, a "menstruum" was a solvent used to extract the "essence" of a substance</note>, they are found to have lost none of their original nature. This would certainly be different if some "spirituous" part had actually been led out of them. It is not even certain—though commonly believed—that the smell of sulfur during the smelting of metals means that sulfur is a part of the metal itself. Many things cling to metals that are distinct from their actual substance, and these react in various ways when the metals are worked by fire.

Furthermore, it is clearer than the midday sun from what we have said that experience teaches us something very different about the existence of those "Three Principles" in natural bodies than what the Paracelsians claim. Even if we assume things are as they describe, it has not been demonstrated that bodies are composed of only these three, or that these three are anything different from the four primary elements <note>The traditional Aristotelian elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. Indeed, we have already warned (and it is very well known to the public) that **flammability**, **volatility** <note>original: *effumabilitatem*; literally "the ability to be smoked out" or evaporated</note>, and **saltiness** contribute very little to the actual essence of bodies. Moreover, it is very easy to show that these three qualities stay within the limits of elemental nature. For what else is "volatility" but the ability to be changed into something thin and light? What is "flammability" but the same ability combined with...

<header>ON HERMETIC MEDICINE</header>

...to be able to be acted upon, and at the same time to be able to be converted into a bright fire? Certainly, every **passive power** <note>original: *potentia passiva*; an Aristotelian concept referring to the capacity of a substance to be changed or acted upon by an external force</note> of this kind is not brought into action except by some elementary force. The actualizations of these powers—lightness, thinness, fiery heat—are tactile things, and therefore purely elementary. Thus, the passive powers corresponding to them cannot but be of the same character. There are also many tactile properties of **Salt**, and thus they are elementary as well. **Salty taste** <note>original: *salsus sapor*</note>, just like the light of a flame, is indeed of another kind, yet even these adhere to elementary matter; and just as that matter is transformed in various ways by the force of heat and cold, so also saltiness and light arise and pass away no less than other tastes and other visible things.

These things are indeed very manifest to the senses themselves if you wish to pay even slight attention; so that it truly becomes worthy of wonder that the **Paracelsian** <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus (1493–1541), who replaced the four elements of the Greeks with three chemical principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> doctrines could have been pleasing even to **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), an influential physician who attempted to reconcile traditional Aristotelian philosophy with the new chemical theories of the time</note>. For although he sometimes speaks ambiguously—namely, whether those "three" are either the first mixtures or just as simple and primary as earth, water, air, and fire (the commonly called **elements**); yet he asserts the latter everywhere and boasts of such a principle, from which this necessarily follows. However, **he cuts his own vines** <note>original: *Propria autem vineta cædit*; a Latin idiom meaning to damage one's own cause or contradict oneself</note>. For he admits that those tactile qualities—heat, cold, humidity, and dryness—are properties of the elements, and therefore adhere in elementary matter. Now, indeed, nothing is more certain than that all taste as well as all odor is found nowhere except in a body which is endowed with those elementary qualities; on the other hand, many elementary bodies lack all taste and smell. It is also well established that everything tasty and everything odorous are composite bodies. From which it is clear that that which has taste or smell is an entirely elementary thing, and indeed not a simple but a mixed body. Certainly, nothing is [more manifest] to sense and

# CHAPTER XXII.

...nothing is more contrary to experience than the idea that a thing in which taste and smell reside is not an **elementary body** <note>original: *corpus elementare*; a body composed of the four classical elements (earth, air, fire, water) rather than the three chemical principles</note>. For indeed, it is manifest to those witnesses [the senses] that tactile qualities <note>Properties perceived by touch, such as heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</note> reside in the very same point where taste or smell is found; and accordingly, these are the properties of one and the same body. Unless, of course, one were to admit that many bodies could exist in one and the same place; a notion which is both absurd in itself and is simultaneously rejected by **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a physician and chemist who tried to reconcile traditional philosophy with new chemical theories</note>. Furthermore, every smell is so connected with taste that there is no scent that does not also possess a taste, even if that which has taste is occasionally devoid of smell. This was certainly noticed by the ancient philosophers. Furthermore, the senses themselves teach us that light and color do not reside in bodies of their own, but plainly in those things which consist of tactile properties—indeed, things which sometimes possess taste and smell, or are able to emit sound. Nothing, therefore, is further from the truth than that **Paracelsian** <note>Referring to the followers of Paracelsus, who believed that qualities like color or "spirit" were distinct substances</note> dogma: as if those properties also had some specific body of their own in which they resided.

This evidence has forced some supporters of the Paracelsian cause to affirm that their **three principles** <note>The *Tria Prima*: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsians believed were the building blocks of all matter</note> are the first mixed bodies formed from the elements. However, this is also affirmed without any argument being brought forward, and for that reason, it cannot be deservedly admitted by Philosophy. To this, we have already proved that in many bodies not a trace of those three is found; moreover, those first mixtures ought not to be absent from bodies consisting of greater composition <note>The author argues that if these three were the "first" mixtures, they should be found in all complex substances, which they are not</note>. Furthermore, even if everything that is inflammable, or tasty, or odorous is some mixed body, nevertheless that which is colored or bright can be something most simple, as is clear regarding the heavens and other things. Therefore, if **Mercury** and **Salt** are mixed bodies, neither of them surely...

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

...[the subject] was the <term>primary recipient <note>original: "πρῶτον δεκτικὸν" (*proton dektikon*). A philosophical term for the underlying substance that receives qualities.</note></term> of colors; the former is commonly affirmed by the school of **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the founder of iatrochemistry who proposed that all things are made of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt.</note>, while the latter was affirmed by the master himself.

Truly, we have already shown that nothing is more absurd than that which is brought forward by **Sennert** as a fundamental ground for proving the **Paracelsian opinion**. It is this: that inflammability, taste, smell, and heat are properties <note>original: "affectiones"</note> entirely different from elementary qualities <note>The four primary qualities: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>, and therefore cannot reside in an elementary subject. To be sure, it becomes manifest to our senses at every moment that the most diverse things are born from one and the same matter, and so in one and the same subject, things that are not indeed contrary, but yet varied and greatly diverse, are present.

<margin>The book *On the Origin of Things from Nature* <note>Likely referring to a specific text in the Paracelsian corpus, *De ortu rerum ex natura*.</note></margin>
We too admit—and have most clearly proved elsewhere—that all things are not made from one and the same potential entity of matter; but in truth, there are many **potentialities** in one matter. Thus, many and most diverse things can be born from the same material principle and can subsist together in the same thing at once.

**Sennert** himself is forced to admit this if he wishes to defend his thesis regarding the **three principles** <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsian chemistry: Sulfur (the principle of inflammability), Mercury (the principle of volatility), and Salt (the principle of stability/solidity).</note>. For indeed, inflammability and odor are one thing; taste and the power of coagulating another; **effumability** <note>The quality of being able to be turned into smoke or vapor.</note> and color yet another; and yet he attributes all these things to those three principles. Indeed, he teaches that **volatility** is common to those same three.

Furthermore, it is false that all these are different from elementary properties: it has already been shown that inflammability and effumability belong to that category. What is **volatility** itself other than **lightness**? And yet Sennert himself reckons this among the elementary properties. ...acquires various [qualities] through the force of heat and cold. It is also true that tastes are very closely related to tactile qualities, so much so that taste is almost a kind of touch. It is clear in itself that not all coagulation comes from saltiness <note>A rebuttal to the Paracelsian idea that "Salt" is the principle of fixity and solidification.</note>, since very few solid bodies contain any of it. Equally far from probability is the inference of the same **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a physician who tried to blend Aristotelian physics with the newer chemical theories of Paracelsus.</note>, which he nevertheless uses most frequently in this and similar arguments: that those things we mentioned do not exist in elementary matter, or are not produced by elementary virtue, because they are not found in the simple elements themselves. For indeed, it is by no means necessary that an <term>efficient cause <note>The agent or force that brings something into being.</note></term> must formally be that thing, or actually possess the quality which it is suited to produce. Why then should an elementary power not produce that which it actually lacks, provided it has found suitable matter? Furthermore, most things cannot be made from a single simple matter, and for that reason the suitability of matter is very often derived from a certain composition and mixture of many things. This is most manifest regarding the various secondary tactile properties; it is common knowledge that these cannot arise unless matter is tempered in various ways through the composition of the moist and the dry, the hot and the cold. In truth, that through this same tempering, matter is made more or less suitable for other sensible qualities, is nothing...

Thus, they believe generation is nothing other than the bringing into the light of things that already exist in actuality, but lie hidden as if in darkness and the underworld <note>original Latin: *orco*; a reference to the Roman god of the dead, used here to mean a state of hiddenness or non-existence</note>. 

This matter, if it is common to many things, Paracelsus is accustomed to call *Cagastrum*, and if it is specific [to one thing], *Iliastrum*—words he coined in a barbaric fashion. Sometimes he also uses the name "mystery," and thus the primary chaos of the whole world is known to him as the **Great Mystery** <note>original Latin: *mysterium magnum*</note>. They ascribe all generative power to some more divine virtue, to which they also attribute the name of **Archæus** <note>In Paracelsian thought, a vital internal "architect" or force that directs the growth of organisms and the functioning of organs</note>, or more correctly "architect," lurking within some spirit-filled seed. For they claim all generations and changes happen not by the force of heat and cold (for they say these faculties are worth nothing, or, as they put it, "relollaceous" <note>original Latin: *relollaceas*; a nonsense term coined by Paracelsus to mock the traditional medical establishment</note>), but from seeds by the help of Spirits. *For in the seed (as they put it) are contained the mechanical Spirits and the tinctures of the entire anatomy of the species: and the seed administers each part, distributing the predestinations, duties, and laws of motion: while the spirits distribute the astral and invisible bodies,*

> *A body can be destroyed in various ways, but the spirit cannot: for the spirit always remains living, and it is also the subject of life; it preserves its own body as long as it is alive, but in the overthrow of the body, it is separated from it, leaves the dead body, and returns to the place from which it came—namely, into the chaos and the air of the upper and lower firmament.*

Thus speaks Paracelsus himself.

However, whether any of this is consistent with the ancient Hermetic philosophy of the Egyptians is not easy to say; for this doctrine cannot be read in those records that are currently in circulation. On the contrary, many things occur there that directly oppose it. Yet it is clear that many chemists of a later age were prone to similar opinions. Certainly, their common belief is that all generation occurs through <term>composition|original Greek: συγκρίσει (syngkrisei); the joining together of parts</term> or <term>separation|original Greek: διακρίσει (diakrisei); the dividing of parts</term>. Many of the Greek philosophers were also once of this opinion, until Aristotle explained the nature of matter more clearly. But as for that hidden "generating force," I do not know if anyone besides the Chemists ever asserted it, except for the fact that many have taught that the soul constructs its own dwelling place. For even if <term>Albert the Great|Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval philosopher and theologian</term>, <term>John of Baconthorpe|Iohannes de Baccone (c. 1290–1347), an influential English scholastic known as the 'Prince of Averroists'</term>, and other philosophers of the Latin Theological School thought that their "substantial forms" lay hidden in matter—in the same way that the Paracelsians believe their <term>seminal spirits|spiritus seminales; the internal blueprints or life-forces that direct growth</term> are hidden—they did not, however, ascribe the power of generating to them. What they have said regarding the procreative power likewise cannot be accepted. First, they offer no argument for such a great paradox, nor can one easily imagine one. Nor are the objections of any importance which have been raised so far—either by the Paracelsians or by others—against that famous Aristotelian doctrine concerning the properties of similar bodies, contained in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>The 4th book of Aristotle's *Meteorology* was considered the "chemistry" of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, explaining how heat and cold transform matter</note>, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere.

For indeed, those bodies certainly consist at the same time of sensible differences; these, however, are nothing but the effects of heat and cold. Therefore, the Paracelsians foolishly ascribe all power of generating plainly to their secret spirits and <term>archaei</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, an *archaeus* is a hidden "inner alchemist" or vital force that directs the functions of an organ or the growth of a plant</note>...

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### *That all remaining Paracelsian doctrine is partly impious and partly empty and absurd.*

It remains for us to briefly examine what is left of the Paracelsian doctrine.

We mentioned above that the ancient Hermeticists <note>original: *priscos Hermeticos*; those who followed the teachings attributed to the legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> spent much effort on all the mathematical disciplines—I mean Geometry, Arithmetic, Astronomy, and that which usually follows it, the divining art of Astrology. On the contrary, in the Paracelsian school, there is the deepest silence regarding Geometry and Arithmetic; so far are they from being cultivated there. They do indeed mention Astronomy sometimes, yet so far no one has come out of that school who has taught even the first rudiments of this science. They have Astrology on their tongues as much as possible, but who among them understands it, being most ignorant of the whole of Astronomy? And indeed, none of them has even graced this subject with any writing: they only boast of the obsolete and silly opinions of the common people, or the empty figments of their own brains, supported by no use and no argument. Therefore, in this regard at least, our Paracelsian school falls far short of the praise given to the ancient Hermetic school.

It also yields greatly to that same school in all **practical philosophy** <note>original: *Philosophia practica*; the branch of philosophy concerned with ethics, social conduct, and the laws of living</note>. For Paracelsus has not even touched upon this so far; whereas Hermes was once especially famous for his wisdom and for the laws he laid down, just as the Egyptian sages claimed this gift almost as their own.

Whether Paracelsus treated **THEOLOGY** [is something we] above...

In a German document—these are the words of *Erastus*—proceeding from his disciples, it is written that he asserted that absolutely no religion among all those which now flourish is true: that only the text of *scripture* should be read, and no *interpretation* should be admitted, for shortly thereafter a new and true religion would arise. All his followers, as many as there are, also differ greatly from the universally accepted formulas of religion, even when they present an appearance of a consenting mind. In this respect, therefore, *Paracelsus* was in some way similar to *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and alchemical works were attributed</note>.

The *Theology* which is discovered in the *Paracelsian* books is, however, closer to Christian truth than to *Hermetic* teachings. Nevertheless, it differs immensely from *Catholic Christian* doctrine. *Thomas Erastus* <note>a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his opposition to Paracelsianism</note> charged *Paracelsus* as guilty of seven blasphemies:
I. That, like *Arius* <note>a 4th-century priest whose "Arian" heresy denied that Christ was of the same substance as God the Father</note>, he imagines that the Word through which *God* created all things has an essence other than *God*, was created, and is subject to corruption and therefore to judgment.
II. That he posits several *gods* of a lower order, through whom the highest *God* designed this world.
III. That he openly denies *Christ* is the creator, but calls him only a "separator" from the "great mystery" <note>original: *mysterio magno*; in Paracelsian thought, the primordial matter from which all things were separated</note>, and indeed with several companions added to him.
Fourthly (*Erastus* writes), he denies that *Adam* was created perfect by *God* from the beginning, but asserts in his book *On Worms* that he was "perfected" by the eating of the apple—that is, by the devil. For he thinks that *Satan* poured all his wisdom, and thus himself, into that apple, and in that manner it then passed into *Adam*. <margin>Response to Aubertus, book 1, epistles 1 and 3.</margin>
These and many similar things are read everywhere in the writings of Paracelsus. I consider it a waste of effort to prove at length here that these things are not in agreement with Holy Scripture nor with right reason, but are impious fabrications—the kind of things the worst heretics of old devised. And indeed, they shrink so far from the truth that many of his own disciples do not dare to openly support the man's theology. *Concerning Paracelsus*, says Quercetanus <note>The Latinized name of Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent physician who adopted Paracelsian chemical medicine while trying to distance himself from Paracelsus’s more radical religious ideas.</note>, *I have by no means set out to take up the defense of his theology, nor have I ever thought to agree with him in everything.* Yet it is only too clear that not only were his first followers infected with Arianism <note>A significant early Christian heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ, a charge often leveled at Paracelsians due to their complex "celestial body" theories.</note>, as the most learned Conrad Gessner <note>A famous Swiss physician and naturalist (1516–1565) known for his "History of Animals."</note> wrote, but almost all his followers have drunk in various heresies from their master's writings. Indeed, the entire impious teaching of Valentin Weigel <note>A German mystic and theologian (1533–1588) whose ideas on inner spirituality were heavily influenced by Paracelsus.</note> and some others emerged primarily from the school of Paracelsus. However, as we said before, it is not our place to touch upon this Paracelsian heresy and impiety here, especially since to have recited these views is the same as having refuted them.

<margin>See chapter 18.</margin>
We have already related above how <term>Magic</term> <note>In the Paracelsian context, "Magic" (Magia) refers to the "Light of Nature"—the ability of a person to understand and manipulate the hidden forces of the natural world through spiritual attunement.</note> is held in great esteem by the same Paracelsus and his followers, as if it relies on the forces of nature and is performed with the help of certain spirits who are by no means of ill repute. At the same time, it was briefly shown how impious all those things truly are in reality. But I intend to approach this argument with proper effort at another time, and for that reason, we will refrain from more sharply attacking this disgrace for now.

<header>CHAPTER XXIII. 331</header>

<margin>
See the books of Nicolas Guibert <note>A physician and critic of alchemy.</note> and Thomas Moresin <note>Thomas Moresinus, a Scottish physician who wrote on the "deceptions" of alchemy.</note>; and from the notebooks of Janus Lacinius; Benedictus Pererius, *On the Origin and Destruction of Things*, book 1, chapter 12; Delrio, *Magical Investigations*, book 1, chapter 5.

Likewise, it is not our present purpose to argue at length here whether that **chemistry of gold-making** <note>original: *CHEMIA illa χρυσοποιητικὴ* (alchemy)</note> is entirely vain or not, or by what means it might be possible to effect that transmutation of metals. However, the reasons brought forward by others so far—suggesting that all such transmutation is impossible—are indeed trivial, and some are even fundamentally opposed to ancient philosophy. For you may see that the primary argument for those opponents is that things which differ in **species** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "species" refers to the essential nature of a substance; critics argued that because lead and gold were different species, one could not become the other.</note> cannot be transmuted among themselves. And yet, this claim overturns the entire doctrine regarding the **origin and passing away of things** <note>original: *de ortu atque interitu rerum*, a reference to Aristotle’s work *On Generation and Corruption*.</note>, which it is a constant tenet of—at least—the **Peripatetic** <note>The Peripatetic school refers to the followers of Aristotle.</note> philosophy that such things occur **through change** <note>original: *διὰ μεταβολῆς*</note>; one can demonstrate this at any moment with countless examples. It is of equal importance that the generations of nature cannot be perfected by art. For indeed, art can produce nothing unless a certain native potential resides within the matter; yet either art alone, or nothing as readily as art, can lead that potential to its proper perfection. Thus nature sometimes provides health without any help from art, yet often only when assisted by its aid. If it were certain, as many chemists hand down, that metals consist of a secret virtue which they receive partly from heaven and partly from subterranean places, then one would indeed have to doubt the possibility of the craft. But it seems more likely that their entire nature and essence is defined primarily by tactile and other sensible qualities, and is thus brought about only by the power of heat and cold. Furthermore, the artificial transmutation of metals—indeed, **gold-making** <note>original: *χρυσοποίησις* (chrysopoiesis)</note> itself—seems to be established by so many and such illustrious testimonies that it would perhaps border on impudence to deny them credit. It will suffice to read the books *On Gold* by **Giovanni Francesco Pico** <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), an Italian philosopher who defended the reality of alchemical transmutation.</note> and the histories of **Ewald von Hoghelande** <note>A Dutch physician and alchemist who provided anecdotal "proofs" of successful transmutations.</note> on this matter...

His follower **Severinus** <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), a Danish physician whose work systematized Paracelsian thought.</note> asserts that the <term>categories</term> <note>Original: *prædicamenta*. This refers to the Aristotelian categories of being, which were the foundation of traditional logic.</note> should be judged within diseases, rather than diseases being judged within the categories.
