On the other hand, **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), an influential professor of medicine and alchemist.</note> states: *“A Physician must be born from the Light of Nature and Grace, from the internal and invisible man, the internal angel, the light of nature.”* <margin>page 29.</margin> Regarding that **Light of Nature**, he speaks as follows: *“The firmament is the light of Nature, which naturally flows all things into man. For just as his body grows from the earth, so also for the spirit of the sidereal man—the invisible man who inhabits the outer house—his food grows from the fire of the firmament: all arts, crafts, languages, and faculties. For Heaven is the father and teacher of all arts except Theology (which is said to come from the Holy Spirit); and the sidereal spirit of man attracts all human wisdom, all arts, sciences, and faculties from the rays of the superior stars.”* 

The same author says elsewhere: *“Known are the two lights, within which are all things, and outside of which is nothing, and no perfect knowledge of things. The **Light of Grace** begets the true Theologian, yet not without philosophy; the **Light of Nature** produces the true philosopher, yet not without Theology, which is the foundation of true wisdom.”* 

However, neither Crollius nor Paracelsus teaches how one may actually receive that favor of the Heavens. Nor, indeed, will you easily read anything in their works concerning those superstitious machines of **Artephius** <note>A legendary Alchemist often said to have lived for a thousand years.</note> or the "Mirror of **Almuchephi**," both of which were praised by **Roger Bacon**. <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English philosopher and friar who emphasized empiricism but was often associated with "magical" optical devices in later legends.</note> Furthermore, those earlier authors declared that a singular observation of the stars was necessary for the construction of such items—a skill in which both Paracelsus and Crollius were unrefined. The light of grace, or divine revelations, or <term>enthusiasms</term> <note>original: *ἐνθουσιασμοὺς* (enthousiasmous) — divine inspirations or states of being "filled with the god."</note>, are promised by Crollius and the Paracelsians to anyone with a strong imagination who expects such a thing. Paracelsus mentions this elsewhere, as in his *Book on Images, chapter 11.*

# CHAPTER XXIII.

He [Paracelsus] maintains that knowledge is acquired partly through some fabricated image, and partly even without an image through what he calls **Ascendants** <note>original: *Ascendentes*; in Paracelsian thought, these are celestial or spiritual intermediaries that "ascend" to reveal hidden truths</note>; he claims that in this way one may receive a voice from the air that answers questions, and that this is not the work of **Necromancy** <note>original: *Necromantiæ*; the forbidden art of conjuring the dead</note>.

In a certain way, another point pertains to the principles of knowing: the Paracelsian school denies that the sciences and arts should be sought from their ancient practitioners, on the grounds that those men were pagans or **Muslims** <note>original: *Muhamedani*</note>; for they argue that such men could not have been endowed with that specific skill.

But indeed—to address this last point first—by what argument or what sign have they made it probable that nothing of true doctrine could be understood by pagans or Muslims? Certainly, in the Holy Scriptures, that which must be avoided and shunned by a Christian man is indeed accurately handed down; however, it is nowhere taught that all doctrine of the **gentiles** <note>Non-Christians, particularly the ancient Greeks and Romans</note> is impious and to be shunned. Even the very best of the fathers of the most holy Church highly valued that **external learning** <note>original: *την ἔξω* (tēn exō); a Greek term used by Church Fathers to distinguish secular Greek philosophy and "outside" literature from "holy" Christian scripture</note> and received it from the gentiles themselves. This is well known regarding, among others, **Clement of Alexandria**, **Origen**, **Eusebius**, **Didymus**, **Anatolius of Laodicea**, **Jerome**, **Augustine**, **Basil**, and **Gregory Nazianzen**. 

Augustine skillfully <margin>Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, Chapter 39</margin> *advises that we should reclaim that doctrine from the heathens, as if from unjust possessors, for our own use;* something which Gregory the Priest writes that Basil and Gregory did vigorously in the *Life of Nazianzen*. There exists a famous dissertation on this subject by **Saint Basil the Great**. In Basil's funeral oration, Nazianzen writes: *that it is established among all men of sound mind that even that external learning holds the first place among human goods, though by a perverse judgment it is rejected by many Christians as insidious and dangerous, and as turning one far away from God.*

...honest and learned men, who knew the man in Zurich <note>original: "Tiguri"</note> at that time. <margin>Erastus, part 1, page 239</margin> I conferred with him once and again on various matters, even on Theological or Religious topics. ### CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>Erastus, part 1, page 238.</margin>
Since these things are established by so many illustrious testimonies, they certainly cannot be called into doubt without the charge of impudence. He himself confesses in a certain preface, as Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who was one of the most vocal critics of Paracelsian medicine.</note> writes, that he was a brawler <note>original: "percussorem"; a term for someone prone to physical violence or striking others.</note>, and was cast into prison several times for that reason, or even for other matters. Regarding his commerce with demons, and with what great praises he did not hesitate to pursue Magic, everything is clearly confirmed by those things we brought forward in chapter 18. There are those who report that in Salzburg, a demon was seen in the form of a boy dictating certain things to Paracelsus for his pen <note>original: "ad calamum"; meaning he was writing down what the spirit dictated.</note>; however, the credibility of this story remains with the original authors.

Furthermore, if no piety could be detected in Paracelsus, if he did not pray to God, if he was entirely a drunkard, and if he was a cultivator of demonic Magic, then surely whatever learning and skill was in him is not to be attributed to a unique divine revelation. For the Holy Spirit does not dwell in such an impure vessel. Nor do good spirits <note>original: "genij"; refers to guiding or protective spirits.</note> inspire anything in such impious men. Therefore, it was not without impudence that Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus.</note> wished it to be said that God spoke through him. Those who indeed attribute this to him—such as Croll <note>Oswald Croll, an important Paracelsian alchemist.</note>, Scheunemann <note>Henning Scheunemann, a physician and follower of Paracelsus's mystical chemistry.</note>, the Brothers of the Rosy Cross <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret spiritual and cultural movement that often integrated Paracelsian ideas.</note>, and others—are surely triflers in an impious manner. Paracelsus’s life alone is truly sufficient to refute that lie. Although it is otherwise easy to refute it by the vanity and impiety of his doctrine itself, indeed by his monstrous slanders and insults, and finally by his innumerable contradictions. For such things do not have God as their master. Moreover, it is known that Paracelsus acted as a lying prophet <note>original: "mendaciloquum vatem"</note>, both from many other things and from the fact that in *Magical Figures 21* <note>Referring to one of Paracelsus's prophetic works.</note>, he did not hesitate to promise the world a golden age free of all vices in the sixtieth year of his age. Certainly, with no miracle having been shown

[[page number: 348]]

Paracelsus claimed to be a prophet; yet without proof, we cannot safely trust men who present themselves as prophets, as we have demonstrated elsewhere.

Moreover, if during that age and at the time when Paracelsus wrote most of his books, he was almost never sober, it is certainly clear that he was not far from madness when he strove to eliminate all the old teachings and replace them with his own. Indeed, that definition by Cato <note>Referring to Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman known for his moral strictness.</note> is well known: ***drunkenness is voluntary madness***. Even men outstanding in talent and learning eventually lose command of their own minds and become brutish through daily intoxication. It has even become a proverb that wisdom dwells in "dryness," as in that old saying of Heraclitus: *a dry light is the wisest soul* <note>original Greek: "αὐγὴ ξηρὴ ψυχὴ σοφωτάτη" (augē xērē psychē sophōtatē). Heraclitus believed fire and dryness were the elements of a healthy, wise soul.</note>. Therefore, though Paracelsus may have possessed excellent talent, that very drunkenness stands greatly in the way of his doctrine's authority. For it would not seem probable to anyone that this man was at his wisest when he was most raving, or that all the most sober men of all ages were forced into a circle of reasoning by a drunkard—that is, that all men of sound mind were surpassed in the study of wisdom by a madman. It is more likely, unless I am mistaken, that the unusual inconsistency and absurdity of the dogmas which shine forth in his writings should be attributed, at least for the most part, to his perpetual drunkenness.

In addition to this, it certainly could not have happened that at the age when Paracelsus was still temperate, he had already unrolled <note>A metaphor for reading or studying from scrolls or books.</note> all of ancient medicine and philosophy—especially if he spent that time on such long journeys.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

...to recite in its place: but his own writings show how well-versed he was in the reading of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon was the Roman-era physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over 1,000 years.</note>. Elsewhere he was not ashamed to tell the story that he read the true and uncorrupted volumes of Galen and Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook; he is often cited alongside Galen.</note> in a monastery at Brünn in Bohemia; <margin>Preface</margin> <margin>& The Treasury of Alchemy</margin> but no one with even a little intelligence fails to detect the lie. It is certainly more likely what he says elsewhere: *that he received letters from Galen from hell; that he had disputed with Avicenna in the vestibule of hell about his **potable gold** <note>A legendary alchemical medicine made of gold dissolved in liquid.</note>, the **tincture of the physicists**, the **quintessence** <note>The "fifth element," thought to be the pure essence of a substance.</note>, the **philosophers' stone**, **Mithridatium**, and **Theriac*** <note>Two famous ancient "universal" antidotes against poison.</note>: for the devil was doubtless mocking the magician. Whatever the case, he was certainly not well-versed in the reading of ancient writers. It is therefore intolerable that this man dared to condemn all the ancients, whom he perhaps never even looked upon, let alone read through with care. He therefore criticized and condemned things he had not read and did not understand, and he did so with the greatest impudence and intolerable arrogance. Truly, one might rightly question a supporter of Paracelsus in this way: "O good man, how did the vanity of the ancient doctrine become known to Paracelsus? How did Paracelsus know that Aristotle, Galen, Avicenna, and others had strayed so far from the truth? Why does he believe the leadership of wisdom is owed to him, why does he boast of being the monarch of all doctors, as if all the rest flit about like shadows? <note>A reference to Homer's *Odyssey*, where the dead in the underworld are described as flitting shadows compared to the living.</note>" when nevertheless he saw almost nothing of that ancient doctrine, and certainly read or understood nothing of it. None of us would fail to accuse of extreme madness a man boasting of having overthrown a Turkish army <note>The Ottoman Empire was a major contemporary military threat when this was written.</note> he never saw nor could see; likewise, no one would fail to immediately think of administering hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity as a harsh treatment for insanity.</note> to one who, in an empty theater, commands everyone to rise for him, or claims they did rise when he entered. Finally, no one would fail to say that a judge is worthy of lashes who not only pronounces a verdict without hearing either side, but also pronounces the verdict in his own favor.

### CONCERNING HERMETIC MEDICINE ###

<meta>catchword: gymnasium</meta>

All of this can indeed be perceived in **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who founded the "Hermetic" or "Iatrochemical" school of medicine, which emphasized minerals and chemicals over traditional herbal humorism.</note>. He boasts that ancient learning has been conquered and has bowed its neck to him, and yet he never caught sight of that learning even in a dream. He orders all the learned men of every age to yield the first place to him as if to a **monarch** <note>Paracelsus famously styled himself the *Monarcha Medicorum* (Monarch of Physicians), a title his critics found insufferably arrogant.</note>; indeed, he claims they do so of their own accord—yet none of them is actually present to do so. Finally, he accuses everyone of error and ignorance while attributing wisdom to himself alone, yet he has never truly heard or studied any of them.

Furthermore, it is well known that Paracelsus was not skilled in the art of investigating the truth, but rather condemned it. What sort of wisdom, then, should we expect from a man who lacked the very means by which truth is uniquely grasped? To whom will it seem likely that this one man, with a blind gaze, saw the sun of truth more clearly than all those who, through all ages, with the greatest zeal and by employing that **mirror of truth** <note>original: "catoptro." A reference to logic or dialectical reasoning as a reflective tool for the mind.</note> (so to speak), focused the eyes of their mind? 

Surely no one would rashly believe a man boasting of having crossed the Ocean—and indeed having crossed it more successfully than all others—if he were lacking a **magnetic compass** <note>original: "pyxis magnetica." The author uses the relatively new technology of the mariner’s compass as a metaphor for a systematic scientific method.</note>. Moreover, to the investigation of truth, one must bring a tempered character, a modest soul, and a mind solely desirous of the truth. It is indeed difficult to see what is true if the soul suffers from ambition, greed, partiality, love, or hatred. 

That Paracelsus was most boastful and of a most ambitious nature shines more clearly than the sun from all his writings. Certainly, even if he had surpassed everyone born before him, he still should not have boasted of himself with the title of "monarch," and indeed so insolently, so often, and with such an unheard-of pursuit of everyone else that the matter is without precedent. Therefore, although he may have been of sharp intellect, he did not possess that tempered character which the **gymnasium** <note>original: "palæstra." A Greek term for a wrestling school, used here metaphorically for the rigorous training ground of intellectual debate and truth-seeking.</note> of truth requires.

# CHAPTER XXIV. #

...gymnasium of the mind. <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the "gymnasium" or wrestling-school of intellectual training.</note> Certainly, those very manners, unless I am mistaken, create a great prejudice against the **Paracelsian doctrine**.

Furthermore, what solid and true doctrine can be expected from a man who is a **Magician**? I would not deny that a demon can inspire a person with some true knowledge. But surely it has not been found so far that anyone has become so wise through a demon's help without simultaneously being led into many errors: the "father of lies" compensating for one truth with a thousand falsehoods. Indeed, **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was an Italian polymath who claimed to have a "guardian spirit" or demon that aided his intellect.</note> himself despised the use of his **meddling** <note>original: "περιέργου" (periergou). Referring to a spirit that is overly curious or intrusive.</note> demon, despite the slight help he obtained from it, and he advises others to despise such spirits in his work **The Proxeneta** <note>A book by Cardano regarding social and personal wisdom.</note>. Whatever Paracelsus learned with that teacher, though it may have some good mixed in, is undoubtedly for the most part impious and full of errors. And truly, we should not doubt that he used the help of a **meddling** <note>original: "περιέργου"</note> demon when, in a drunken state, he gripped the hilt of his sword and dictated his books. <note>Critics of Paracelsus frequently claimed he was an alcoholic and that he kept a "familiar spirit" hidden in the hollow pommel of his longsword.</note> **Erastus** <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a physician and theologian who was one of Paracelsus's most vocal opponents.</note> rightly concludes this from those immense and monstrous slanders and insults, in which he surpassed all living men by a wide margin, as well as from that **glory-madness** <note>original: "δοξομανίᾳ" (doxomania). An obsessive craving for fame or reputation.</note>; the writings themselves clearly indicate that he was full of all these things.

<margin>Book on Occult Philosophy, near the end</margin>
We can believe that he attempted to learn the medical art from all kinds of people consulted during his travels, and indeed among others from **Necromancers** <note>Those who practice magic involving the summoning of the dead.</note> and **Chemists** <note>Here referring specifically to alchemists, who often operated in secret.</note> lurking in monasteries (as he writes in the preface to his **Great Surgery** <note>original: "Chirurgia magna." Published in 1536, it was Paracelsus's most successful work during his lifetime.</note>). Perhaps he learned many things from them. But it is certainly not likely that he attained the art through such masters. Indeed, with these words, he did not hesitate to commend that kind of teacher: *A physician cannot learn and know everything he ought to be able to do and know in the Academies,*

...but it is necessary that he sometimes approach old wives <note>original: "vetulas"; the author is referencing Paracelsus's claim that he learned more from common folk and "wise women" than from university doctors.</note>, Gypsies, necromantic quacks <note>original: "agyrtas"; wandering charlatans or street performers who often sold "miracle" cures.</note>, elderly peasants, and the like, and learn from them. For such people have more knowledge of such things than all the Academies. Indeed, since he speaks there of diseases brought on by incantations and their magical cure, perhaps he has spoken the truth thus far. Yet he himself, in that preface to the *Great Surgery* <note>original: *Chirurgia magna*; one of Paracelsus's most famous works on wound treatment.</note>, explicitly confesses that not even through those people was he able to arrive at a true skill in the Surgical Art.

<margin>See Erastus, part 4, page 300.</margin>
Indeed, he praises no one by name through whom he progressed in the medical Art; in fact, he mentions almost no one without attacking their reputation: as if, forsooth, he himself, as a prince of medicine, either discovered those things or was divinely taught. However, that this was done with a lack of candor is shown by the surviving books of many authors today. Johannes Crato <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), a highly influential physician to three Holy Roman Emperors and a staunch opponent of Paracelsianism.</note> wrote as follows in a certain letter to Erastus:

> *The remedies which he is said to have used at times are not his; I am certain of this because I saw a book written nearly two hundred years ago by a certain monk of Ulm, in which the same medicines that he has now scattered piece by piece into various papers are clearly written.*

The same man says elsewhere:
<margin>Preface to Scaliger’s Exercises</margin>
> *There was in the library of that excellent and most upright man Marcus Singmoser, first Private Secretary to the most Sacred Emperors, a book composed two hundred years ago by a certain Monk. I used it for many months, and I noticed that everything which those followers of Paracelsus mutter about as if they were Eleusinian mysteries <term>Eleusinian mysteries: the most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece; used here to denote "occult secrets."</term> were so clearly handed down that they could deceive no one.*

It is very clear—and was even then pointed out more than once by his own supporters—that Paracelsus transferred many things from the writings of Basilius Valentinus <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, though many works under his name are now believed to have been written later.</note> into his own works, while suppressing the name. Bernard Penotus <note>Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1522–1620), a French alchemist and physician who initially followed Paracelsus but later became critical of certain aspects of his work.</note>, by no means the least of the Paracelsian flock, did not hesitate to write these words at the end of his booklet on the Medical Denary:

> *If the works of Johannes Isaac Hollandus <note>A 15th-century Dutch alchemist whose works focused on the transmutation of metals and the "elixir of life."</note> were extant and brought to light, the works of Paracelsus would be buried.*

### CHAPTER XXIV.

...Isaac Holland is himself that person about whom Paracelsus prophesied, saying: *“And after me shall come Elijah the Artist <note>original: "Elias Artista"; a legendary figure in alchemy predicted by Paracelsus who would reveal all the secrets of nature and the Great Work.</note>, who shall reveal the hidden things of nature.”* Paracelsus foresaw that Isaac’s works would eventually become manifest and reach the hands of the most learned men. And later: *“When I came upon Isaac’s book on the vegetable work, I found, word for word, the doctrine of the three principles <note>The "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> and the separation of the four elements taken from him.”* From this it is clear that he [Paracelsus] stole his principal works and fished them out from here and there; such as the *gradations of medicines* from Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>; the *Archidoxa* <note>One of Paracelsus's most famous works on the "higher" medicines.</note> from Raymond Lull’s *Art of Operation*; the *Arcana* from [John of] Rupecissa; absolutely nothing from himself, except for insults and curses; and various things from Trithemius. If anyone reads Arnold and Raymond attentively in their *Art of Operation*, they will notice that Paracelsus truncated <note>cut short or mangled</note> and claimed for himself the writings of those men. Read Lanfranc <note>Lanfranc of Milan (c. 1250–1306), a pioneer of surgery.</note>, and you will notice Paracelsus took his *Surgery* from him. Why does he not cite Arnold in the chapter on paralysis, regarding his Galbanetum <note>A medicinal preparation made from galbanum resin.</note> described in the book on *Tartaric Diseases*? These are the words of Penotus <note>Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617), a physician and alchemist who was once a follower of Paracelsus but later became a vocal critic.</note>; though they may not be true in every detail, they are for the most part very true.

Knowledge of languages does not, strictly speaking, belong to medical doctrine; however, it is established that the writings of learned men in any art cannot be conveniently understood if the language they used remains unknown. Furthermore, it is a sign of no common <note>original: "proletariæ"; here meaning "low-class" or "mediocre."</note> erudition to be able to correctly express what one thinks. However, it is clearer than the midday sun from his writings that in Paracelsus there was almost no skill in the Greek and Latin languages—indeed, that these were held in contempt by him. What then? Even the method of writing in German he understood so little that no common writer <note>original: "scriptorum ex trivio"; literally "writers from the crossroads," meaning vulgar or unrefined street writers.</note> does not surpass him by a long interval.

Since these things are so, how greatly are the followers of Paracelsus deceived, while attributing to their master more than to all...

The author systematically dismantles Paracelsus’s authority by arguing that he lacked divine inspiration, formal training, and the necessary linguistic skills to even understand the ancient texts he claimed to reject.</meta>

-># ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

...attribute to the doctors of various ages, it is manifest. For one might rightly ask them: Why, O good sirs, does *Paracelsus* seem so great to you? Was he divinely instructed? No. He was a magician, he was impious, he was a drunkard. Was he taught by good spirits <term>genijs: from the Latin *genius*, meaning a guardian spirit or supernatural being</term>? No. Magicians, the impious, and drunkards have no commerce with good angels. Did he obtain from evil spirits a doctrine greater than common human knowledge? One can indeed obtain something from them, but not the power of true doctrine; furthermore, whatever good might remain from them is rightly rendered suspect.

Did *Paracelsus* surpass all others in his natural gifts of talent? This is evident by no sign; moreover, talent makes no one learned unless cultivation is added. Did *Paracelsus* therefore cultivate his mind to such an extent from his earliest youth? No. He spent his life as a wanderer in almost perpetual errors: from the twenty-fifth year of his age he was entirely devoted to drunkenness <term>temulentiæ: habitual intoxication or being "drunk on wine"</term>; he died an untimely death; finally, he had no skill in Logic, which is the only guiding star <term>cynosura: literally the constellation of the "Dog's Tail" or Little Bear, used here to mean a guiding principle or focal point</term> for reaching the truth. 

Was he well-versed in reading all the ancients, so that after a proper examination he could reject them? No. He read very few things, and those he did read he could not understand, at least because of his lack of skill in languages <note>Paracelsus was often criticized by his contemporaries for his poor command of Latin and Greek, writing many of his works in vernacular German instead.</note>. Therefore, *Paracelsus* is not the one whose bare assertions we must stand by: but arguments must be demanded from him no less than from anyone else; as these present themselves, *Paracelsian* opinions are either to be admitted or rejected. I need not add now that, having weighed what we have said, it cannot but seem that *Paracelsus* should be pursued with contempt rather than any praise.

## CHAPTER XXV.

*That the reputation of Paracelsus regarding his skill in gold-making and his success in healing, if not empty, is at least uncertain.*

However, although these matters are quite evident, two things seem to be affirmed in praise of Paracelsus with such constancy that they can scarcely seem to be denied. The first is his success in curing; the second is his skill in gold-making <note>original: "της χρυσοποιϊκῆς" (tēs chrysopoiikēs), the art of making gold</note>.

<margin>Oporinus in his letter.</margin>
Indeed (to speak of the latter point first), there are those who gather this from what Oporinus <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a famous Swiss printer who served as Paracelsus’s secretary and assistant for two years.</note> wrote: *He was a lavish, wasteful spender of money, and often so destitute of it that I knew not even a single small coin <term>obolum: an ancient Greek coin, used here as a metaphor for a penny</term> remained to him. Yet the very next morning he would show that he had a well-filled purse again. Thus I frequently wondered from where it had been supplied to him.* Truly, this has nothing to do with the matter. For it could not have been hidden from Oporinus, his servant and confidant in all that Paracelsus did, if any gold had been produced by art. From where (you might say) could that immediate abundance of minted gold come, if not from the exchange of unminted gold? But this itself would have been known to Oporinus. Yet nothing of this was known to him, and for that reason he was amazed.

A letter by a certain Franciscus argues more plausibly in favor of Paracelsus; this letter, which Michael Neander included in German in his *Geography*, was later translated into Latin and inserted by Andreas Libavius <note>Libavius (1555–1616) was a German physician and chemist who, while critical of Paracelsus’s mysticism, defended the possibility of alchemy.</note> into the second book of his *Defense of Transmutatory Alchemy* against Guibertus. <margin>Book 2, page 153.</margin> For in this letter he affirmed by his testimony that he saw, in Basel, nearly a whole pound of quicksilver <term>argenti vivi: literally "living silver," the archaic term for mercury</term> transmuted into gold by Paracelsus. But truly, how could even this have escaped the notice of Oporinus, who was then most intimate with Paracelsus, if what is told is true? Certainly

Upon departing Basel, *Paracelsus* left to *Oporinus*—whom he used as a sort of <gloss>butler and steward <note>original: "promo condo," a household manager who handles provisions.</note></gloss>—his chemical vessels, as *Melchior Adam* <note>Melchior Adam (died 1622) was a famous biographer of German scholars; his "Lives" are a primary source for the history of science and the Reformation.</note> records in his life of the man. How could it be that such a reputation [for making gold] did not spread among the common people of *Basel* at that time? That it reached the ears of neither *Oporinus* nor others of that city is proven by the fact that neither he nor any other resident of *Basel* mentioned it, even when they were busy singing *Paracelsus’s* praises. Did that *Francis* wish to deceive *Neander*? <note>Franciscus Neander was a physician and contemporary of Paracelsus.</note> Suppose he did not. Perhaps he himself was deceived. Or truly, *Paracelsus* possessed from some other source a <term>gold-making <note>original Greek: χρυσοποιὸς (chrysopoios), refers to a substance or "projection powder" capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note></term> powder; just as it is well known to have happened to several others who were completely ignorant of how to prepare such a powder—perhaps a <gloss>genius <note>original: "genio." In the 16th century, this often implied a familiar spirit or a guiding demon rather than innate talent.</note></gloss> supplied it to him from time to time. From such generosity, I fear *Paracelsus* also occasionally obtained those purses full of coins.

<margin>Adam, in the *Life of Paracelsus*.</margin>
But truly, at other times he was accustomed to making a profit only through the medical art, as is manifest both from the story of *Conrad von Lichtenfels* which *Adam* relates, and from that invective against *Philip, Margrave of Baden* <note>Philip I, Margrave of Baden-Sponheim (1479–1533). Paracelsus successfully treated him but was denied the promised fee, leading to a bitter legal dispute.</note> regarding the non-payment of the agreed-upon fee, which is found in volume 1 of the *Works of Paracelsus*, page 132 of the *Strasbourg edition*. He himself strives to prove his skill in the medical art in the preface to the *Hospital* <note>Likely referring to the "Grosse Wundarznei" (Great Surgery), which discusses hospital practice and charity.</note>, stating that even if he is a spendthrift, money does not usually fail him.

<margin>Libavius, in the work cited.</margin>
*Libavius* <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a chemist and physician who was a fierce critic of Paracelsian mysticism while supporting "rational" alchemy.</note> himself writes: 
> <note>original: "non habuisse tandem Paracelsum unde paupertati suæ succurreret, quæ enim bona dicitur pauperibus legasse ea negari tanti fuisse ut ad victum sufficerent."</note> *In the end, Paracelsus did not have the means to relieve his own poverty; for those goods he is said to have bequeathed to the poor were denied to be of such value that they would even suffice for food.*

<margin>Gesner, on surgical writers.</margin>
To this may be added the words of *Conrad Gessner* <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss polymath and "father of bibliography," who was deeply skeptical of Paracelsus's character.</note>: 
> <note>original: "Medicinam vagabundus exercuit dum pecuniâ careret, quâ modicâ acquisitâ, vino & ludis deditus ut constans fama est, nemini medebatur."</note> *He practiced medicine as a vagabond while he lacked money; once a small amount was acquired, he was devoted to wine and gambling—as the constant rumor goes—and would treat no one.*

*Ewald Vogel* <note>A pseudonym for Theobald van Hoghelande, an alchemist who wrote on the difficulties of the art.</note>, a man exceptionally knowledgeable in chemical matters, writes thus: 
> *Indeed, I would even dare to assert that the Philosophers' Stone was never known to Paracelsus, and that he [attained] neither the secrets of Ramon Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher to whom many later alchemical works were falsely attributed.</note> nor of other [teachers] of this art...*

# CHAPTER XXV.

The physicians were present, namely Lord Julius Alexandrinus, myself, and Nicolaus Biesius, when we were joined by the noble Baron, Lord Berthold of Lipá <note>Berthold of Lipá (Bertholdus à Leippa) was a prominent Moravian nobleman and high-ranking official in the Bohemian kingdom.</note>, Marshal of the Kingdom of Bohemia and Councilor and Chamberlain to his Imperial Majesty. When the conversation turned to the subject of physicians, he told us that when it was first widely rumored that Paracelsus could cure those suffering from gout <term>podagra: a painful form of inflammatory arthritis, often affecting the big toe</term>, his father, Lord Johannes of Lipá, the Marshal of the Kingdom of Bohemia, had summoned him from Switzerland at great expense. 

He said that Lord Johannes had suffered only intermittently and had never been confined to his bed for long. However, Paracelsus stayed at Krumlov <note>original: "Cromaviæ"; referring to Moravský Krumlov in the Czech Republic, where Paracelsus stayed in the 1530s.</note> for nearly two years and applied various medicines, but he rendered his father completely arthritic <note>meaning he became permanently crippled or lost the use of his joints</note>. Lord Berthold added that Paracelsus had also treated his own eye, which had been only slightly affected, in such a way that even now he cannot see out of that eye. 

At that time, Paracelsus was also summoned to a particularly noble woman, the wife of Lord Baron Johannes of Žerotín and daughter of the noble Lord of Pernštejn <note>original: "Bernstein"</note>. She was not seriously ill, though she suffered from abdominal pains <note>original: "ventris torminabaret"</note>, and she had never been epileptic. But when Paracelsus gave her certain medicines, she was seized by epilepsy <note>original: "epilepsia"</note> and, after suffering more than twenty paroxysms <note>sudden attacks or seizures</note>, she died that very same day. 

Paracelsus then returned to Krumlov, packed his things, and fled to Hungary. Not long afterward, the father <insert>Johannes of Lipá</insert>, worn out by the greatest pains, also departed this life. Paracelsus, however, had left a chest of books at Krumlov, some of which he had brought with him, and some of which he had dictated while drunk (for it was then that he wrote most frequently). Later, when Paracelsus had come to Vienna after his wanderings in Hungary, and his followers there had boasted of his "miraculous art" to Lord Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia and Hungary.</note>, these books were recovered by order of the Royal Majesty. 

He was always involved with the Jews and the most contemptible of men. Indeed, the Emperor—whom all good men know to have been most averse to slander and falsehood—called Paracelsus a most deceitful and impudent impostor, who never wished to associate with learned men. ### CHAPTER XXVI.

*How Chemistry was spread from Egypt through Asia and Africa after Emperor Constantine the Great.*

Those things which pertain not only to the medicine of the ancient Egyptians and the Paracelsians, but to their entire body of doctrine, we have perhaps pursued with such diligence and abundance that we may seem to have completed the task we undertook. to those who examine their writings, this cannot but be very well known. Yet this custom was never observed by any other nation of old. Furthermore, that enigmatic and <term>cryptic</term> <note>original Greek: "κρυπτική" (kryptikē), meaning hidden or secret</note> method of teaching was once most familiar to Egypt, and it did not pass randomly into the writings of anyone other than the Chemists. However, although the origin of that Chemistry began here, it is nonetheless clear from what has been stated above that it arose quite late. We have also shown that among the Egyptians, no medicines were prepared in the Chemical manner; and so, even if <term>metallurgy</term> <note>original Greek: "μεταλλουργική" (metallourgikē), the art of working metals</note> is owed to Egypt, the condition of Medical Chemistry was not yet the same.

It is likewise clear from the preceding sections that Metallic Chemistry reached those of the Greek language from the Egyptians. And indeed, those very men—Zosimus of Panopolis, Olympiodorus, Stephanus, and Synesius—who are today the most ancient of the writers on Chemistry, were both of Egyptian origin and used the Greek language in their writing. Moreover, historical records teach us that for several centuries there survived among the Greeks those who cultivated that art. For we have already proved that in the fifth Christian century, Olympiodorus of Thebes and Heliodorus inscribed books on this subject to Emperor Theodosius II. We have likewise heard what a certain member of the "chemical flock" <note>This likely refers to an alchemist or practitioner of the art</note> dared to do during the reign of Emperor Anastasius Dicorus in that same century, and what Aeneas of Gaza reports concerning the Chemists of that age. Perhaps Synesius also lived around this time. In the following century, under Emperor Justinian, Anastasius Sinaita numbered <term>chemists</term> <note>original Greek: "χημευτάς" (chēmeutas)</note> among the "corrupters of gems" <note>referring to the practice of creating imitation or "falsified" precious stones</note>. In the seventh century, to Emperor Heraclius himself, the <term>poets</term> <note>original Greek: "ποιηταί" (poiētai), here referring to "makers" or alchemical authors who wrote in verse</note> [offered] their <term>chemical</term> <note>original Greek: "χημευ-" (chēmeu-), an abbreviated form</note>...

### CHAPTER XXVI.

Stephanus of Alexandria inscribed his work. In the eighth century, it will be proved a little later that Geber—a Greek man—taught this art to the Arabs. In the ninth century, George Syncellus <note>A Byzantine chronicler and cleric</note> mentions those arts in his *Chronicles*. It appears more than once in the *Myriobiblon* <note>original Greek: "μυριοβίβλῳ" (Myriobiblō), also known as the *Library*, a massive 9th-century compilation of book summaries</note> of Photius that chemical books were seen. And indeed, since the magical arts were in great use in Constantinople under the Emperors Michael the Stammerer <note>original Latin: "Michaële Balbo"</note> and Theophilus, as Cedrenus and Zonaras teach us, why should Chemistry—which usually accompanies the magical arts—not have been in some esteem there at that time? Since records of the tenth century are very rare, they do not contain much memory of chemical matters; nevertheless, chemical studies undoubtedly did not cease to be cultivated. A certain ancient anonymous commentator on the *Ecclesiastical History* of Adam of Bremen, writing around the time of Emperor Otto III, and thus in the 10th century, noted that these things occurred:

> *Among them was a newcomer named Paul, a convert from Judaism to the Christian faith. Whether driven by greed or by wisdom, he traveled to Greece; upon his return, he attached himself to our bishop (of Bremen), boasting that he possessed talent in many arts—so much so that he could turn the illiterate into Philosophers within three years, and transform copper into pure gold <note>original: "aurum obrizum," referring to refined or pure gold</note>. He easily persuaded the Archbishop to believe everything he said, adding that at Hamburg <note>original: "Hammaburg"</note> he would suddenly produce public coinage from gold, and give <term>bezants</term> <note>Byzantine gold coins of high value</note> in exchange for common pennies.*

This is clear testimony that Alchemy was flourishing even then in Greece and was brought from there into other distant lands. The next century produced Michael Psellus, whose book on this art is addressed to the Emperor Constantine Doukas. At that time there also lived Suidas, Cedrenus, and Eustathius, in whose writings such a clear memory of Chemistry survives that it appears the art was then considered both established and very ancient...

...nothing prepared chemically is to be found. However, the most refined Johannes Langius <margin>J. Lang, book 1, epistle 53.</margin> seems to have thought somewhat differently. He suggests that Actuarius <note>Joannes Actuarius (c. 1275–1328), a prominent physician at the Byzantine court in Constantinople</note>—who was perhaps the first, yet also nearly the last, of the great Greek physicians—made mention of a distilled rose liquor. But this error of his was long ago exposed by Conrad Gesner <note>A Swiss polymath (1516–1565) known for his "Treasure of Euonymus," a foundational text on distillation and chemistry</note>, whose own words we shall cite here, so as not to claim the fruit of another's hard work as our own. 

<margin>Gesner, preface to *The Treasure of Euonymus*.</margin> *“Someone recently wrote that such distilled liquors were not unknown to us later Greeks—I will spare his name—using the argument that distilled liquors are named several times in the writings of Actuarius. And indeed, he does occasionally use the term* <term>rhodostagma</term> <note>original: "rhodostagma" — literally "rose-drop." While it sounds like a distillate, Gesner argues it refers to a simple syrup</note>*, as in a* <term>julep</term> <note>original: "Zulapio" — a sweet medicinal syrup</note> *against a cough; and a little later, in another julep, he mentions* <term>intybostagma</term> <note>original: "intybóstagma" — literally "endive-drop"</note>*. But by these words, nothing other than a simple syrup of roses or endive is meant. Paul of Aegina* <note>A famous 7th-century Greek medical writer</note> *describes* <term>rose-extract</term> <note>original: "Rhodostactum"</note> *in Book 7, Chapter 15, with these words: ‘Take two sextarii of the juice of roses with the white tips removed, one sextarius of honey; boil it down, skimming the foam, until a fourth part has been consumed.’ Furthermore, a little earlier he describes* <term>hydrorosatum</term> <note>original: "hydrorosatum" — rose-water</note>*, that is, rose water, which is also far different from a distilled liquor or distilled water. For it is composed of four pounds of roses with the white tips removed, five sextarii of water, and two sextarii of honey. The Arabs also, or their translators, when they speak of the ‘water’ of some plant, understand it as a decoction of it in water. The same applies to Nicolaus Myrepsus* <note>A 13th-century Byzantine physician who compiled a famous book on pharmacy</note> *who wrote on medical compositions in Greek; it is clear he is quite recent from the barbaric words he frequently uses. In his work, I marvel at this: that he makes no mention of waters or oils prepared by chemical instruments. He describes only* <term>capnistum oil</term> <note>An oil prepared by heating, literally "smoked oil"</note>*, which is distilled by descent* <note>A method of distillation where the heat is applied from above and the liquid drips into a vessel below</note>*, as Aetius* <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century royal physician</note> *also does.” These are Gesner’s words, and they are most true.*

Chemistry reached the Arabs only through the Greeks, as the very word **Alembic** signifies, being transformed from the Greek <term>ambix</term> <note>original: "ἄμβiξ" — a Greek word for a cup or the lid of a distilling vessel</note>. For by this Greek word, they did not mean just any

...cup, but clearly such as an alembic is, as even those words of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, c. 40–90 AD, a Greek physician and botanist whose work was the precursor to all modern pharmacopeias</note> in Book 5, Chapter 64, concerning the preparation of quicksilver <term>hydrargyrus: literally "water-silver," the ancient term for mercury</term>, may teach us:

Furthermore, that Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry," whose identity and works are a mix of historical fact and legendary attribution</note> lived a hundred years after Muhammad and was a Greek by nation will become clear shortly from the words of Leo Africanus <note>Joannes Leo Africanus, c. 1494–1554, a Moorish diplomat and traveler known for his descriptions of Africa and the Islamic world</note>. Beyond controversy, the Saracens or Arabs worked extensively in metallurgical <note>original: "metalleutikē", the Greek art of mining and refining metals</note> chemistry. Indeed, many of their small works, translated into Latin, are in our hands even today. <margin>See the *Life of Avicenna* written by Niccolò Massa <note>1485–1569, an Italian anatomist who wrote a biography of Avicenna</note>.</margin> That we may not doubt this, his disciple Sorsanus <note>Abu 'Ubayd al-Juzjani, the lifelong student and biographer of Avicenna</note> confirms it in his narrative of his teacher's life; he testified that in his book on *Alchemy*, Avicenna added two modes of *questioning and inquiry* which the ancient Sages had omitted. Albertus Magnus <note>c. 1200–1280, a Dominican friar and "Universal Doctor" of the Church who wrote extensively on the natural sciences</note> used that book, and speaks of it thus in Book 3 of *On Metals*, Chapter 9: *From all these things brought forward, we can consider whether it is true what some say Aristotle said, when according to the truth of the matter it was said by Avicenna: namely, "let the masters of alchemy know that the species [of metals] cannot be changed." Likewise: "This is the opinion of Avicenna, which he says is that of Hasen* <note>likely Alhazen or Ibn al-Haytham</note>*, a philosopher outstanding in natural and mathematical matters. However, Avicenna says in his own Alchemy that he found the contradiction of those who argued against the change of metals in alchemical matters; because of which he himself adds that the species are not changed, unless perhaps they are reduced into the first matter of metals, and thus by the help of art are led into the species of the metal they desire."*

### ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

Thus far Leo: to whom more credit is owed because he was more learned and more skilled in the history of his own people.

Furthermore, the Saracen <note>A historical term for Arabs or Muslims</note> princes used chemical arts for the benefit of medicine, beginning to establish remedies for diseases by this new method. Indeed, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, 980–1037, the Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note>—as in Book 4, Fen 6, treatise 1, summary 1, chapter 2—mentions sublimated mercury <note>original: "argenti vivi sublimati"</note>, and in Book 2, chapter 43, he mentions sublimated arsenic; he also makes mention of distilled rose water, though only of that one, which is an indication of its rarity. Moreover, he lived in Persia and died in the year 428 of the Hegira <note>The Islamic calendar; 428 AH corresponds to 1037 AD</note>, according to Massa <note>Nicolaus Massa, an Italian physician who wrote a biography of Avicenna in the 16th century</note> in his biography of him drawn from Sorfanus: a time which falls in the eleventh Christian century. Joannes Mesue of Damascus <note>Pseudo-Mesue, a 13th-century author whose works were attributed to an earlier physician and became standard medical textbooks</note> mentions both that rose water and another water of wormwood <note>original: "absynthij aquam"</note>: unless you prefer to think he is speaking of waters in which rose and wormwood have been soaked, which seems likely to someone reading what he has in Book 2 *On Purgatives*, chapter 10, and regarding rose julep <note>A sweet medicinal drink</note> in Book 3 of the *Antidotary*. Yet he recommends chemically prepared oils clearly enough when he is about to discuss the oil of eggs: *Oils are made,* he says, *through resolution in various ways, about which we shall begin a discussion and set down wonderful explanations; those who manifest and uncover what is hidden in things speak of these with broader discourse. Approach these also, you who are desirous of this thing, along with such famous men.* And when he had taught two ways of preparing the oil of eggs, he adds: *The third way is that it be distilled in a pan <note>original: "cazola"</note> and an alembic <term>alembic: a classic distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>, just as we shall describe regarding the "oil of the philosophers."* Concerning the oil of grain, he says the same: *Let the hulled barley be placed in a sublimation vessel, and let it be done as we shall describe.* Concerning the oil of amber <note>original: "succini"</note>: *The second way is with the work of sublimation, as we shall describe.* Finally, concerning the oil of bricks <note>original: "oleum laterum," literally oil of bricks, used for joint pain and as an alchemical solvent</note>: *The oil of the philosophers is the oil in which the ancients agreed, and they verified it to be the aid of all secrets. Some have called that the oil of wisdom: and others the blessed oil:*

### CHAPTER XXVII.

...and others called it divine; others indeed called it holy; and by many, it was called the **oil of the perfect mastery** <note>original: "oleum perfecti magisterij"; a term for a highly refined alchemical substance</note>. He describes its chemical preparation thus: *Place it in a crucible and seal the mouth of the crucible to the mouth of the alembic <note>A chemical distilling apparatus</note>, and seal it with the lutes of the alchemists <note>original: "luto alchymistarum"; a clay sealant used to make joints airtight</note>, and place it in the furnace, etc.* From these things it is certainly clear that the preparation of chemical oils was not only in some use at that time, but that the "oil of the philosophers" itself was considered among the ancient arts. 

Indeed, this Joannes Mesue <note>Refers to the author known as Pseudo-Mesue, whose identity was a subject of much historical debate</note> is more recent not only than Avicenna but also than Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr, 1094–1162, a prominent physician from Al-Andalus</note>, as is clear from Book 1, chapter 12 of the *Book on Purgatives*; in fact, he is more recent than Alkindus <note>Al-Kindi, c. 801–873, known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs"</note>, a contemporary of Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198</note>, as can be seen in Book 1, theory 2. He is clearly a different person from the Joannes Mesue who, according to the Jewish author Abraham Zacuthus in his *Chronicle* titled *Sepher Iuchasin* <note>original: "The Book of Lineage"; a history of the Jewish people written in the 15th century</note>, flourished under the Caliph al-Ma’mun <note>original: "Imino"</note>, the son of Harun al-Rashid, around the year 200 of the Hegira <note>The Islamic calendar; 200 AH corresponds to approximately 815 AD</note>. 

Furthermore, Andreas Bellunensis <note>Andrea Alpago, a 15th-century physician and translator who lived in Damascus</note> reports that he could not find the books of our Mesue among the Arabs, and that the writings of the other Mesue had not been translated into Latin. Those words of Avenzoar in Book 2 of the *Theizir* <note>Al-Taysir, or "The Simplification Concerning Therapeutics"</note>, treatise 6, chapter 1, also seem to pertain to the chemical preparation of medicines: *I also wished to know through experience the operations of medicines, and the skill required for the extraction of the virtue of medicines, and the composition of one with another.* 

Yet nowhere in his books can anything chemically prepared be found. It is also uncertain whether the oils that Averroes writes about in Book 5 of his *Colliget* <note>Kitab al-Kullyat, a major medical encyclopedia</note>, chapter 42, using the term *Al-zabit* <note>Likely referring to expressed oils or fats</note>—stating they are extracted from simple ingredients—are chemical in nature, since among their number are oil of sweet almonds, nuts, and sesame, which are usually extracted by the force of a press. Be that as it may, he writes: *Those oils are made in Babylon; but in our lands, they are not properly extracted from those things.* He soon adds that both the ancients and the moderns were accustomed to oils prepared with olive oil. Certainly, nothing specifically chemical is praised by name by Averroes.

# ON HERMETIC MEDICINE

This is evidence that in Africa and Spain in the twelfth century, chemical medicines were not used at all, even though *Avenzoar* <note>Ibn Zuhr, a famous physician of Al-Andalus</note> and *Averroes* <note>Ibn Rushd, the influential philosopher and physician from Córdoba</note> brought honor to those lands during that time. In Asia, however, we have just learned from *John Mesue of Damascus* <note>Referring to the author discussed on the previous page</note> that some were accepted. This is confirmed by the book of *Bulcasis Ben Abenazerim* <note>Albucasis, or Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, a pioneer of surgery</note> which is titled the *Servant* <term>Servitor: a famous medieval manual on how to prepare simple medicines and chemical distillations</term>. For although the author lived in Spain and taught one or two chemical techniques, when discussing **rose water** he writes that *its preparation is known among most nations*, yet he recommends the method which is in use among the **kings of Aharach** <note>Likely referring to Raqqa in Mesopotamia, a center of learning</note>, perhaps speaking of the princes living in Aracca in Mesopotamia. However, although so little memory of chemical medicines remains in the books of Physicians, the Alchemists undoubtedly used many more and kept them among their secrets. Indeed, it was not without reason that Mesue ordered people to consult them.

<margin>
See the letters of the Jesuits in China from the year 1607, Mainz edition.
</margin>
It is altogether likely that from the **Saracen** <note>A term used by Europeans in this period for Muslims</note> Chemists, both of those pursuits which the Chinese are still held by today reached them: namely, the pursuit of **making silver** <note>transmutation</note> and of preparing a certain **cup of immortality**. Perhaps this also began at the time when the **Tatars** <note>The Mongol Empire</note> ruled over the Chinese; for that the studies of the Arabs reached that place at the same time can be gathered from the mathematical machines which *Jacobus Pantogia* <note>Diego de Pantoja, a Spanish Jesuit missionary to China</note> mentions and highly commends on *page 110*. *Nicolas Trigault* <note>A Flemish Jesuit missionary to China</note> describes and attacks that madness of men at length in his work *On the Christian Expedition among the Chinese, Book 1, Chapter 9*. It is pleasing to insert what the same Pantogia wrote more briefly from China on the same subject at the beginning of this century: *There are two remarkable delusions of the leading men in China, and destructive beyond others. One is that they trust they can achieve a certain wonderful longevity of life by their own study. For this they devise a thousand arts and* **medicines**

# CHAPTER XXVI.

...they consume countless substances, which are better suited for shortening life than prolonging it. Moreover, the precepts of this madness have been recorded in many books and are explained by masters who are by no means insignificant or poor men. There are some who falsely claim to be extremely old; the common people flock to them as if they were celestial beings, desiring to learn from them the methods for living a long time—an art in which they believe their very destiny resides. When we <note>Referring to the Jesuit missionaries in China, such as Pantoja</note> profess our true age, they do not listen to us, suspecting that we are hiding the truth—that we have already lived for several centuries and hold the secret to living forever, and that for this reason, we abstain from marriage.

The other delusion is found in the struggle to create silver <note>transmutation</note>, an art about which many people have likewise written books. For this purpose, they use many herbs and **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: mercury, a primary ingredient in both Eastern and Western alchemy</term>. In this pursuit, they consume what little silver they actually possess, yet they never abandon their hope. Because the results have not yet matched their expectations, they boast that this is only because their "lucky break" has not yet occurred—a fortune which many attempt to summon through fasts lasting many years.

Thus far Pantoja <note>Diego de Pantoja (1571–1618), a Spanish Jesuit missionary who wrote extensively about Chinese culture and technology</note>. Since it is well established that the **Saracen** <note>A term used here for the Islamic world</note> Alchemists were once accustomed to laboring in both these areas <note>the search for long life and the transmutation of metals</note>, it seems quite probable that these follies were spread by them all the way to China. Certainly, the latest travel accounts of that kingdom report that even today, many in Persia suffer from both those "Chinese" maladies, a contagion that undoubtedly originated from the Saracens.

-># ON HERMETIC MEDICINE<-

However, this occurred in the thirteenth century; at which time books of all kinds were translated from Arabic into Latin, with the support of Emperor Frederick II <note>Frederick II (1194–1250) was a Holy Roman Emperor known as "Stupor Mundi" (the Wonder of the World) for his patronage of science and translation</note> himself. It is clear, especially from the highly learned work *On Metals*, that many books on metallurgy <note>original Greek: "τῆς μεταλλουργικῆς"</note> had already been diligently read by Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval philosophers, often cited as a pioneer of experimental science</note> at that time. Indeed, he indicates quite clearly that even then a huge number of alchemists existed everywhere, working on the making of gold <note>original Greek: "χρυσοποίησιν"</note>.

<margin>Albertus, Book 3, *On Metals*, Treatise 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
He writes of himself as follows: *“I was once made an exile, traveling far to mining regions so that I might experience the natures of metals.”* For this reason, I also sought out the transmutations of metals in alchemical works, so that from these their nature and their own properties might become known to some extent. Certainly, in the last three books of his work *On Metals*, he shows with great diligence and accurate judgment that he was well-versed in chemical matters. Especially worthy of mention are those words in *Book 3, Chapter 9*: *“Those who whiten through white substances and yellow through yellow substances <gloss>the process of 'tinging' or coloring a base metal to make it look like silver or gold</gloss>, while the appearance of the original metal remains in the matter, are undoubtedly deceivers, and they do not make true gold and silver. And almost all proceed in this way, either in whole or in part. Because of this, I had alchemical gold tested which was brought to me, and after it had withstood six or seven firings, it was eventually consumed and destroyed by further heating, and returned as if to dross.”* A book on that very art is also circulated under his name, though it is perhaps spurious, just as many other works falsely use that great man’s name. Nor indeed can you safely trust the herd of chemists in this matter, for it is far too common for them to deceive and be deceived in this way. Doubtless, a small book on this subject also circulates under the title of Thomas Aquinas; and yet in his commentary on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, *Book 2, distinction 7, question 3, article 1, in the fifth response*, he expressly denies that true gold can be produced by the alchemical art; however, in the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*</note>, *question 77, article 2, in the first response*, he speaks somewhat more mildly.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

writing: *“nothing prohibits art, by using natural causes, from producing natural and rare effects; however, he does not definitively state that it can be done.”* In the same century, Giles of Rome <note>Latin: Ægidius Romanus (c. 1243–1316), a prominent theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas</note>, a disciple of Thomas, in his *Disputed Questions* <note>Latin: "Quodlibeta" 3, question 8</note>, did not hesitate to deny every chemical transformation of metals. The same conclusion was reached then by Peter of Abano <note>Latin: Petrus Aponensis (c. 1257–1315), a famous Italian physician and astrologer</note>, a physician and philosopher of the highest learning, in section 209 of his work *The Conciliator*. From these indications, one can gather both that much labor was already being spent on these chemical matters in that age, and likewise that the truth of the art was not yet commonly recognized by any proven experiment.

<margin>Savonarola, in the preface to the book *On Water of Life*.</margin>
However, the *Consultations* of Thaddaeus of Florence <note>Thaddaeus Florentinus (1223–1303) was a foundational figure in academic medicine at the University of Bologna</note>—who at that very time taught and practiced medicine in Bologna with the highest reputation—show that not only metallurgical <note>original Greek: "μεταλλουργικὴν"</note> chemistry, but also our medical chemistry was already in use in some way. In these writings, besides "chemical water," "spirit of wine" <term>Spiritus vini: an early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol</term> is recommended against difficulty breathing <note>original Greek: "δύσπνοιαν"</note> and several other ailments; this spirit is something we certainly owe uniquely to the chemists. This very fact was also noted by Michele Savonarola <note>An influential physician and the grandfather of the friar Girolamo Savonarola</note>. Thaddaeus died in Bologna in the year 1270. Still in that same century (for he died in 1305, according to Bernardo Scardeone in *Book 2, Class 9 of the History of Padua*), Peter of Abano described other chemical remedies, and especially a certain excellent balsam, in his additions to the works of Mesue <note>Mesue the Younger, a likely pseudonymous author whose pharmaceutical texts were standard in medieval Europe</note> in the section *On Affections of the Heart, Discourse on Unctions*. William of Piacenza <note>Latin: Guilielmus Placentinus (c. 1210–1277), a surgeon also known as Guglielmo da Saliceto</note>, nearly a contemporary of Abano, includes similar findings in his volume of *Medical Practice*. At the beginning of the fourteenth century, around the year 1319, Guglielmo Varignana <note>A professor of medicine at Bologna</note>, in *Book 1, Chapter 3 of Sublime Secrets* and elsewhere, described waters to be prepared by an alembic <term>alembic: a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling volatile substances</term> for coloring the hair, including "honey water"; indeed, he even mentions a book written by himself titled *Experiments of Alchemy*.

...of future things and the coming of the Antichrist to the monks of the Ladder of God <note>original: *Scalae Dei*—likely referring to the Carthusian monastery of Scala Dei in Spain</note>, which predicted a term of one hundred years for these events. Arnold [of Villanova] valued this revelation highly because it had been produced in a Latin style by an illiterate man. It is also evident from his booklet *On the Operative Part* <note>original: *de parte operatrice*</note> that this same Arnold ascribed magical bindings <term>ligatures</term> <note>charms or physical knots believed to have supernatural effects</note> to the powers of nature; thus, he was not truly knowledgeable about the nature of things but was infected with much superstition.

In the fourteenth century, around the year 1375 as Bergomensis <note>Giacomo Filippo Foresti of Bergamo, a famous chronicler</note> records, lived John of Rupescissa <note>Jean de Roquetaillade, a French Franciscan friar and alchemist</note>, a man of a thoroughly Lullian character. Indeed, in imitation of Lull, he himself wrote a book *On the Quintessence*; in fact, he almost copied Lull word for word. He also wrote certain things concerning the art of making gold, but perhaps the title of the booklet lies about its author. For he clearly declares in *On the Quintessence*, part 1, chapter 22, that he will not teach the transmutations of metals, because it is not permitted for men of his religion (for he was of the Franciscan order) to deal with alchemical operations. 

He adds not long after: 
> I bear witness to all men of the Gospel, calling upon God as my witness, that if, by the devil’s instigation, they fall into alchemical operations, they will be given over to a depraved mind. And know this, that it is the way of perdition and evil: because none of the Philosophers wrote the truth in their books, except fictitiously and through parables, which are not able to be understood or grasped by human ingenuity. And note also, that no one is able to reach the heights of this art, unless his mind has first been deified through the highest contemplation and a most holy life, so that he not only knows all the inner secrets of nature, but also knows how to transmute <term>transmutable nature</term>; and this is granted to very few. Generally, those who seek this art are followers of fictions and sophistries, and they become forgers of mon— <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword indicates the full word is "moneta," meaning money or coinage.</note>

...thrust into prison, he wished to write many things about the future like a prophet: specifically concerning two antichrists, the treading down of the Church, the conversion of all nations to the Christian faith, and many other events which he asserted were "at the very gates." > *We read that John of Rupescissa, a theologian otherwise learned, was driven to such a point of madness that he refused to recant certain assertions he made about the future, despite threats or the prison in which he was held by the Minister of his Order; rather, he always asserted them even more vehemently. Finally, a lying spirit was found in his mouth, and now more than a hundred years have passed since he was revealed to be a liar.*

Besides these three, no one indeed acquired any significant fame for skill in both branches of chemistry. Nevertheless, it is beyond doubt that if not all, at least most of the devotees of <term>metallurgy</term> <note>original Greek: τῆς μεταλλουργικῆς (*tēs metallourgikēs*)—the art of working with metals and minerals</note> did not leave that other branch <note>The medicinal branch of chemistry, often called "chemiatria."</note> untouched either. And indeed, certain chemical works of a medical nature by Roger Bacon are circulated today, such as his treatise on the oil of antimony. Some <term>metallurgical</term> <note>original Greek: μεταλλουργικά (*metallourgika*)</note> as well as medical works of John Isaac Hollandus also remain. His writings, only recently published, tell us that Basil Valentine, a German monk of the Benedictine Order, was highly practiced in both works, especially the medical, toward the end of the fifteenth century—shortly after the outbreak of the <term>Venereal plague</term> <note>original: *Veneriam luem*—Syphilis, which began to spread rapidly through Europe in the 1490s.</note>. It is likely that many similar works still lie hidden in various places; for we have not forgotten those things we heard above from Crato <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim, a prominent 16th-century physician.</note> when he mentioned the writings of a certain Monk of Ulm.

Nor did Hieronymus of Brunswick <note>Hieronymus Brunschwig (c. 1450–1512), author of the first major printed book on distillation</note> emerge from the school of Paracelsus, for he was the first of all to publicly illustrate chemical matters in the German language; nor did Antonio Fumanelli, an Italian from Verona, who transferred not a few things from chemistry into his own works.

# CHAPTER 23.

Since both forms of chemistry <note>The author refers to "transmutational" alchemy (turning metals to gold) and "medical" chemistry (preparing drugs).</note> have been spread in this manner, it is clear to everyone how foolish those people are who attribute both, or even either one of them, to the leadership of **Paracelsus**. Furthermore, to those who examine the writings of those ancient authors, it is manifest that the use of **chemical medicines** began quite late, and indeed primarily within these last four hundred years among Europeans. The use of those preparations made from metals seems to be much more recent; you will not easily see them highly praised until the fifteenth century, by **Johannes Isaacus**, **Basilius Valentinus**, and a few similar men, although **Rupescissa** <note>Johannes de Rupescissa was a 14th-century Franciscan who pioneered the use of distilled "essences" for health.</note> also made mention of some of them.

Furthermore, in the writings of all the chemists of that entire era, one does not observe the followers of the generally accepted philosophy and medicine being torn apart by slanders and insults; rather, they labored so that chemical books might gain some authority by attaching those famous names to them through fiction <note>The author is referring to "pseudo-epigrapha," the common practice where alchemists wrote under the names of famous ancients like Aristotle or Galen to make their work seem more credible.</note>. We owe that entire slanderous and deceitful spirit to the character of Paracelsus.

Certainly, before him, one cannot find any singular "Hermetic" or "Chemical" Medicine in the writings of the chemists. Instead, the method of healing mostly observed was that path which **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and their followers—both Greeks and Arabs, and among them **Avicenna**—tread. This single fact cannot but appear clearer than the sun to anyone reading **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>. In those earlier writings, you see no sign—or certainly a very rare one—of Paracelsian Physiology, Pathology, or even Therapeutics. Nor does a new art of healing arise from any new preparation of remedies. For that preparation belongs to **Pharmaceutics** <note>The branch of medicine concerned with the preparation and dispensing of drugs.</note>, which...

Finally, their manner of writing is not much different from the **Paracelsian** method. It is, to be sure, rough, devoid of all demonstration, barbaric, enigmatic, and delighting in self-invented vocabulary: yet one might rightly approve of that older style more than the **Paracelsian** style, which clearly surpasses all the roughness and barbarism of its predecessors. There are, therefore, ways in which the earlier **Chemists** paved the way for **Paracelsus**; and there are ways in which **Paracelsus** followed the direction of his own natural talent. # A D D E N D A.

<note>Faded bleed-through text from the preceding page is visible in the upper margin.</note>

*Page 21. line 20. he carries.* Although a certain Julius Africanus was the author of the *Cesti* <note>original: "Cestorum"; the *Cesti* (meaning "The Embroideries" or "Girdles") was an encyclopedic work on various topics including magic and medicine</note>, it is nevertheless more likely that he is not that glory of the early Church <note>referring to Sextus Julius Africanus, the famous 3rd-century Christian chronographer</note>, but perhaps the same as that Julius Africanus whose *Book on Military Preparation*—divided into seventy-nine chapters—is held in the Bavarian Electoral Library. This work was stitched together in large part from the *Tactics* of Aeneas (who is perhaps the very same person as Aelian [Tacticus]), as noted by Isaac Casaubon <note>a renowned 16th-century classical scholar</note> in his *notes on Aeneas*. For it is not likely that that <term>military</term> <note>original: "στρατηγικὸν" (strategikon)</note> book is entirely the same as the work of the *Cesti*, as Angelo Poliziano <note>an Italian humanist</note> suggests in chapter 35 of his *Miscellanies*, especially since we have just heard that the subject matter of the *Cesti* was quite different.

*Page 21. line 23. mentioned.* For neither does that little verse of Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius, author of the astronomical poem *Astronomica*</note> in Book 4—*And the material is doubled by the hand with certain skill*—testify to the antiquity of Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiæ"</note>. For although I would not say, along with Joseph Scaliger <note>a dominant 16th-century scholar</note>, that the line is a forgery, it nevertheless does not seem to refer to the chemical art, but rather to gold-beating, by which any thicker leaf of metal is expanded by hand and drawn out to twice its size or much more. Much less should we dwell on the fables of some who claim that Moses, when he ground the golden calf into powder, acted as a chemist; or as if those bronze vessels of the Persian king, of "golden beauty," mentioned in Ezra <note>referring to Ezra 8:27</note> were truly gold but made from transmuted bronze. Indeed, Ezra clearly says they were made of "the finest shining bronze," and things which are bronze are not actually gold. Furthermore, in the treasury of King Darius, it was recorded that there were bronze cups of a completely golden color, which only the sense of taste could distinguish from true gold, as was long ago mentioned by the author of the book <term>On Marvelous Things Heard</term> <note>original: "περὶ θαυμασίων ἀκουσμάτων" (Peri thaumasion akousmaton)</note>, who is commonly believed to be Aristotle. These were surely <term>gold-bronze</term> <note>original: "χρυσοχάλκεα" (chrysochalcea); likely referring to a high-quality alloy like orichalcum</note> vessels, held in no less high honor then, because of the novelty and excellence of the craftsmanship, than that pottery work today called Porcelain.

Indeed, it seems that the Egyptians called many people by the name of Hermes, led by the opinion that those who bestowed great benefits upon the Egyptian region above all others deserved the title. Otherwise, it is clear from more reliable history that the stories they told about the public laws of the kingdom proceeding from Hermes are utterly false. Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note>, in Book 1, chapter 44, drawing from the accounts of the priests themselves, enumerates six kings who deserved the greatest credit for establishing laws in Egypt: Mnevis, Scesasyches, Sesostris, Bocchoris, Amasis, and Darius the Persian, son of Hystaspes.

**Regarding Mnevis, he says:** *“They say that Mnevis was the first—a man of great soul and best deserving of memory among those celebrated by this name—to lead the people to organize their lives according to written laws. He feigned that the laws had been handed down to him by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; the Roman name for Hermes/Thoth</note>, so that great blessings for life might flow from them.”* It seems, however, that Mnevis is the same person called Menas in chapter 45, who ruled Egypt after the time of the Gods, and therefore lived long after the era of Hermes. Moreover, in chapter 54, the same Diodorus attributed to Sesostris that beneficial division of Egypt into thirty-six *nomoi* <note>original: "νόμους" [nomoi]; administrative districts or prefectures</note>. Claudius Aelianus <note>a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> observed the same: *“The Egyptians say that their laws were polished by Hermes <note>original: "παρ’ Ἑρμοῦ τὰ νόμιμα ἐκμουσωθῆναι" [par' Hermou ta nomima ekmousothēnai]; literally 'brought to the Muses' or refined</note>, for in this way everyone chooses to honor their own traditions.”* This latter point is entirely true. Indeed, Petosiris and Nechepso <note>legendary founders of Egyptian astrology, often cited in Greco-Roman texts</note> also boasted that their astrology was handed down to them by the most powerful divinity of Mercury, as we learn from Firmicus Maternus <note>a 4th-century Latin writer and astrologer</note>—undoubtedly to secure a sense of majesty and authority for their work. It is in this same sense that Joseph Scaliger <note>a famous 16th-century Renaissance scholar</note> interprets those lines of the poet Manilius addressed to Mercury:
