The **Cynic year** <note>Also known as the Sothic cycle; a period of approximately 1,460 years based on the rising of the star Sirius, which the Greeks called the "Dog Star" or *Kyon*.</note> is completed in three hundred and sixty-five four-year periods. However, those one thousand four hundred and sixty years are to be understood not as common Egyptian years, but as Julian years. As for what Chalcidius says in that final passage regarding so many four-year periods constituting the **dog-star year**, his text either suffers from an overabundance of the little word *four times*, as I suspect, or from the lack of some other small word; namely, it ought to be written: *the great* or *greatest Cynic year*. Indeed, four times three hundred and sixty-five four-year periods make five thousand eight hundred and forty simple years.

Specifically, there was a triple system of letters among the Egyptians. It is best to understand this matter from Book 5 of Clement of Alexandria's *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromat." [Stromata]. Clement was a 2nd-century Christian theologian who provided one of the few surviving ancient descriptions of how Egyptian scripts worked.</note>. *Now then,* he says, *those who are taught by the Egyptians learn first of all that method of Egyptian letters which they call "epistolary"* <note>original Greek: "ἐπιστολογραφικήν" [epistolographikēn]; this refers to Demotic script used for everyday documents.</note>; *second, the "sacerdotal" or priestly,* <note>original Greek: "ἱερατικήν" [hieratikēn]; Hieratic script.</note> *which the "sacred scribes"* <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἱερογραμματεῖς" [hoi hierogrammateis]</note> *use; and finally, the "hieroglyphic." Of these, one speaks properly* <note>original Greek: "κυριολογεῖ" [kyriologei]</note> *through the primary elements; the other is symbolic. Of the symbolic, one method speaks properly through imitation; another is written, as it were, "tropically"* <note>In this context, "tropically" refers to the use of metaphors or rhetorical "tropes" rather than literal images.</note>; *and the third clearly uses allegories through certain enigmas. Thus, wishing to write "Sun," they make a circle; for the "Moon," a lunar shape, according to the literal* <note>original Greek: "κυριολογουμένων" [kyriologemenon]</note> *method. But in the tropical method, they form characters by transferring and diverting them according to a fit similarity, changing some, and transforming others in many ways. Thus, when they commit the praises of Kings to myths through which they are related to the Gods, they write them in those tropical or inscribed marks. ...that metals are made from true sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; also known as mercury</note>, an idea which pleased many of the ancient Chemists, cannot be easily proven. I confess our former teacher **Cornelius Martinus** <note>A 17th-century professor at Helmstedt known for his works on logic and metaphysics</note> once felt otherwise, not hesitating to write in his preface to **Georgius Agricola** <note>Known as the "father of mineralogy," author of *De re metallica* (1556)</note>: *The Chymists will challenge us, because that sulfur is found in all metals—excepting gold—is a truth more true than truth itself; I mean combustible sulfur, which both catches fire and exhales the odor of common sulfur.* He even nearly proved this: *that from every metal, with not even gold excepted—nay, especially from gold—running, white quicksilver is elicited, no different from that which is commonly sold.* So he indeed argued.

But regarding the fact that metals smell of sulfur during their smelting <note>original: *coctione*, or "cooking," a term used for refining ore</note>, whether that belongs intimately to their essence is certainly not free from doubt. I know indeed that many others boast that true quicksilver can be elicited from all metals, but the methods <note>original: *artificia*</note> for this matter praised in public thus far are full of errors, as our **Billichius** <note>Anton Günther Billich, a 17th-century physician and critic of Paracelsian alchemy</note> has rightly demonstrated, both in his booklet *On Reformed Spagyrics* <note>original: *Spagyrices emendatæ*; "Spagyric" is an early term for alchemy, specifically the separation and recombination of elements</note> and in *Chymical Delusions* <note>original: *Deliriis chymicis*</note> no. 4. In that place, he pursued the error of our Cornelius Martinus regarding Mercury elicited from gold with a specific and just critique. And indeed, if true Mercury could be so readily drawn out from all metals, it certainly would not have been handed down by most of the most learned Chemists that the matter of metals is not "common" Mercury, but another substance clearly known only to the philosophers—that is, to themselves alone. Whatever the case may be, those who recognize those **three principles** <note>The *Tria Prima* of Paracelsus: sulfur (soul/flammability), mercury (spirit/fluidity), and salt (body/solidity)</note> of all bodies understand the terms "Sulfur" and "Mercury" in a far different way.

I. *That the sect of **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who credited his chemical medical system to ancient "Hermetic" wisdom.</note> claims for itself the name of the **Hermetics**; an inquiry must be made into by what right they do so. 1.*

V. *Regarding the individual books which are commonly attributed to **Hermes Trismegistus** today, it is demonstrated that they are all either of no reliability or of uncertain reliability, and are not very ancient; therefore, Hermetic doctrine cannot safely be sought from them. 39.*

VI. *That the lost Hermetic writings, which the ancient authors mentioned, were likewise all forgeries <note>original: *supposititia*, meaning substitute or fraudulent works passed off as genuine.</note>. 52.*

VII. *That no ancient books by other authors survive from which the Hermetic doctrine can safely be sought; indeed, it seems that Hermes himself is merely a legendary fiction. 58.*

IIX. *If there ever was an ancient Hermetic medicine, it was entirely infected with magical vanity and impiety, no less than Hermes himself. 67.*

IX. *That in **Egypt**, from the most ancient times, a medicine was prized which can be called Hermetic; but beyond that, the medicine of the Greeks flourished there most greatly. 77.*

X. *That Egyptian **Physiology** and **Pathology** <note>Physiology refers to the study of how the body functions, while pathology is the study of disease.</note> regarding the human body were partly crude and partly foolish; certainly, they possessed very little true science. 88.*

XVIII. *Regarding the magical remedies for diseases used by both Hermetic schools, it is shown that more sins are committed today than in the past, and likewise that the **Weapon Salve** <note>original: *Unguentum Armarium*; a famous "sympathetic" medicine of the era believed to heal a wound by being applied to the weapon that caused it rather than the body.</note> is of a magical nature. 218.*

XIX. *That the **Paracelsian** school has indeed labored much in metallic medicines compared to the ancient Hermetic school; however, they commit dangerous errors in their use. 236.*

XX. *The same is demonstrated regarding medicines sought from stones, animals, and plants. 262.*

XXI. *That ancient **pharmacy** <note>original: *Pharmaceuticam veterem*; referring to traditional Galenic medicine based on herbs and humors.</note> is wrongly attacked by the Paracelsians, while the new chemical pharmacy has not yet been reduced to a proper art by them, but is infected with many errors, and therefore is not deservedly preferred to the ancient one; also, that public pharmacies are useful in themselves. 277.*
